b73df896b54311667fc70aaac32d082035ac6ae4.message:
cellSaveData: a save file another program holds is waited out, then written in place

A player's Demon's Souls (0.1.0, Avast in the process) failed every save on
its first file, ICON0.PNG, with ACCESS_ERROR ("failed, old file kept"), while
PARAM.SFO, written the same way just before, went through. The folder was left
with PARAM.SFO alone, which the game reads as a corrupted save; its "create
new SAVE DATA" then failed the same way, again and again. The same state on a
PC without that software saves normally in 0.1.0 and 0.1.1.

A virus scanner or a sync client opens a file the moment it is written; until
it lets go, Windows refuses a rename onto it or of it (sharing or lock
violation, or access denied). So, on Windows:

- file_replace tries the rename again while that is the reason: 1, 2, 4 ...
  512 ms apart, then 1 s, about 2 s in all, as RPCS3's vfs::host::rename
  waits its own out.
- When the hold outlasts that, or refuses the temp file's open, the file is
  written in place, as a title's partial write is. Only a crash during that
  one write can leave it short; a failure for any other reason (a full disk)
  still leaves the old file as it was.
- A save's picture, icon or sound (ICON0.PNG, ICON1.PAM, PIC1.PNG, SND0.AT3)
  that is refused both ways is left out and the save goes on. Demon's Souls
  loads its save without ICON0.PNG and PIC1.PNG.

PARAM.SFO goes through the same helper. POSIX renames never meet such a hold,
so Linux and macOS behave as before. test_savedata_held (Windows) holds files
the way a scanner does and checks each case.

b8263848271814189c2449aea7423829acefd598.message:
video: clip depth as the RSX does, from SET_ZMIN_MAX_CONTROL

The guest pipelines always clamped depth: their description is zeroed, so
DepthClipEnable was FALSE. The RSX clips by default (SET_ZMIN_MAX_CONTROL
resets to 1: clip on, clamp off), and Demon's Souls never writes the
register. A shadow map therefore kept casters outside the light's depth
range, squashed onto its near or far plane. Things on the floor above, or
behind the light, threw hard shadows where nothing stands: a dark slab on the
Boletarian Palace stairs, and shadows that jump when the player enters the
1-1 lever room (issue #286).

The RSX state now tracks the register (reset value 1, as RPCS3 has it), and
rsx_cull_key carries "depth is clamped" as bit 3: set when the clamp bits are
on or the clip bits are off, which is when RPCS3 turns on depth clamp. Both
today's renderer and the HAL path (pd->depth_clip) clip unless that bit is
set. Default draws keep their key values, so pipeline-index rows still match;
their pipeline descriptions change, and setup's pipeline pass rebuilds them
for a new build.

The field goes at the end of rsx_state, because captures hold the struct as
it is (section RSXS). A replay reads an older capture's shorter copy over the
reset state, instead of skipping it as "captured by another build", which
started those replays from the wrong state.

Checked: a capture in a Palace passage replays the same on d3d12 and
hal-d3d12 (0 differing pixels) and within 1/255 on Vulkan; the user saw the
stairs slab and the lever-room shadows gone in a live run; regress.sh ok.

bbfad9428f3e63718add611ddbf4ebfb343fe29f.message:
sys_event: a queue's lock is made once and kept; a queue goes live when set up

A tester's game crashed at start on Vulkan (DemonsSoulsRecomp #311):
access violation writing 0x24 in EnterCriticalSection, called from
cellAudio's mixing thread through sys_event_queue_push_by_id.

The mixer finds the game's notify queue by its key every audio period,
without the table lock. Demon's Souls sets that key before it creates the
queue. sys_event_queue_create marked the slot active, with the key, then
logged a line, and only then made the queue's lock. A mixer period in
that window entered a zeroed CRITICAL_SECTION (its null DebugInfo is the
0x24). sys_event_queue_destroy had the mirror race: it deleted the lock
before clearing active.

Now:
- Each slot's lock and condition variable are made the first time the
  slot is used, and never deleted or cleared (q_lock_make). Create clears
  only the fields before the lock.
- A queue goes live (active, a release store) only after it is set up,
  under its own lock. Destroy clears active under that lock.
- event_queue_push checks active again under the lock.
- The lock-free lookups (sys_event_find_queue_by_key and the check in
  sys_event_queue_push_by_id) read active with acquire.

test_event_queue_life makes and destroys 20,000 queues with one key while
two threads find it by key and push to it, then checks a live queue's
pushes and a destroyed one's refusal.

c0b1e46be37a709632c3ba751c037a0753349a37.message:
SPU: run lifted code with denormals flushed, as the SPU does

The SPU's single precision has no denormals: an input that would be one
reads as zero, and a result too small to be normal is zero. Lifted SPU code
ran with the host's float mode, so x86 did the full IEEE work instead, which
costs extra on many CPUs (Intel takes a microcode assist each time).

Demon's Souls' MultiStream synth (libsynth2, the "_synth2 Group" SPU thread)
raises the denormal and underflow flags in every 2-second window: its
decaying filters make denormals all the time. On a CPU that pays for them,
its replies to the game's mixer come late, the mixer falls behind, and the
last 85 ms of sound plays again and again (#403).

spu_run_with_halt, where every piece of lifted SPU code starts, now sets DAZ
and FTZ for the run and puts the caller's mode back afterwards (a PPU thread
can run a job inline). RPCS3 does the same for its SPU threads
(gv_set_zeroing_denormals). SPU_FTZ=0 keeps the host's mode.

test_spu_lifted_start checks the mode inside, a denormal product, and the
caller's mode after.

rsxcore: make the draw records when the backend starts, not in each backend's static data

s_d3d.draws, the frame's 16,384 draw records (17.75 MB), was an array in
s_d3d. rsxc_state.inc is in each backend's copy of the core (d3d12, vulkan,

  the rings it always did.

  as the array was by the memset of s_d3d. rc_abort_init frees them.

array let the compiler see it was not that field); they read it once now

cb767e37b5859b2ed715a6e3d57c95ce1b462484.message:
gpu: Vulkan's set 0 for t20 going back and forth (step V5v)

The clamp's vertex-shader form (RSX_CLAMP_FORM=vs, the pick on a device
without geometry shaders) binds t20 to the vertex ring and back to the fetch
ring around each of its non-fetch draws. On Vulkan a raw buffer's offset is
its set 0's, so each switch looked set 0 up again in the device's cache,
under its lock, twice a draw.

- The recorder keeps the last two sets 0 it found (key and set), newest
  first; binds_slow takes one from there before it asks the cache. Sets and
  buffer handles live as long as the device, so an entry never goes stale.
- The device counts the cache's lookups (n_set0_gets, a test hook).
- A raw range cut at maxStorageBufferRange says so once: the fetch's loads
  (E3) read 0 past the cut, so a corner table there would lose its corners.

The rest of what V5 listed for Vulkan was there already: every buffer is a
storage buffer too; a raw range runs from its address to the buffer's end
(the whole ring half the table sits in); E4 takes any one-uint member name
(uvc_tab); E1 puts UVBOUND0-7 at 13-20 and nointerpolation is Flat; the
format table maps R32G8X24_TYPELESS and D32_FLOAT_S8X24_UINT to
D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT, R32_FLOAT_X8X24 to its depth aspect and X32_G8X24 to its
stencil aspect. No pipeline of the core sets a depth bias, so nothing scales
on a float depth format.

d0a6149036515692ca27da18eb3d1f032efbda20.message:
gpu: the null backend, which records and checks for headless CI

gpu_null*.c/h: gpu.h's device functions and gpu_cmd_ops.h's commands with
no GPU under them, for CI on every system (plain C99, no system or GPU
headers). Buffers are CPU memory: maps, copies between buffers and host
imports move real bytes. Textures hold nothing, so their readbacks and
occlusion results are zeroes. The GPU is instant: fences complete at
submit and waits never block. Each command is static inline in
gpu_null_cmd.h, one call into the recorder, and so are the per-draw device
calls (GPU_FAST_FUNCS), so the core's frame file builds against it as
against D3D12.

Every command and the device calls around it are checked against the
contract, as they are recorded and as they run at submit, in submission
order: stale and freed handles; frees before the fence of the work using
them; barriers against each subresource's tracked state, with D3D12's
promotion from COMMON and decay; states a use does not allow; draws
missing a layout, pipeline, pass or bound slot; binds without their
GPU_USE bit or outside their buffer; cb_align and the copies' alignments;
boxes and footprints out of bounds; query reset, begin and end order;
table entries written while unfinished work reads them; fences never
reached, and slots or readbacks used before their fence was seen; recorders
used after their end; swap chain images used without an acquire. Failures
are counted by kind (gpu_null_errors), and the first of each kind is
printed with the command and its arguments.

gpu_null_stream_hash is FNV-1a 64 over the operation stream: every command
in submission order and the device calls that change what a GPU would see,
handles as creation numbers and pipelines by their contents, so a run
hashes the same on every system and compiler. GPU_NULL_DUMP=<file> writes
the stream as text. gpu_null.h has the encoding.

the guest pipelines' commands on two recorders and a swap chain with no
failure and th

d3a14d30d744844515fbc267f1e6b5e93f766f87.message:
Windows: guest memory on a 4 GB boundary

vm_reserve asked VirtualAlloc2 for the 4 GB guest space with no address, so
it went wherever Windows put it. The POSIX branch and vm_init (vm.h) put it on
a 4 GB boundary, and two things depend on that:

- GUEST_EA turns a host pointer back into a guest address by keeping its low
  32 bits.
- The HLE's string helpers (savedata_host_str and the like) take a value below
  4 GB for a guest address and leave anything above alone.

In a test here the reservation went at 0x2556BAD0000: above 4 GB, but off any
boundary. With bottom-up or high-entropy ASLR off for the process (for one
program or the whole PC, in Windows' exploit protection settings), it went at
0x7FFF0000. There guest memory's host addresses are below 4 GB. A player's
Demon's Souls then could never write a new save: cellSaveDataAutoSave2
translated the name, cellSaveDataAutoSave translated it again, and the second
translation pointed into the guest arena.

The placeholder is now 4 GB bigger than needed. The part on the boundary is
kept, and the head and the tail are given back; a placeholder splits and frees
in parts, so nothing else can take the address in between. Without
VirtualAlloc2, a 4 GB larger reservation shows where the boundary falls,
given back and taken again there, with retries, as vm_init does. Anywhere at
all stays the last resort.

d740ce6847f68e1ebca83d41cd2902ffe5c682b0.message:
rsx_d3d12: the FP constant memo copies nothing for a program without constants

fpk_extract_at's memo hit copied the program's constants with
memcpy(out, m->k, 16 * n), n = 0 for most programs. The CRT's copy for 64
bytes or less is an AVX-512 masked load and store over 64 bytes, even for
0 bytes, and a masked access that reaches a page nothing has touched
takes a microcode assist on every call (fault suppression; it never
really reads the page, so the page never gets mapped). An entry whose k
starts within 64 bytes of a page's end, with an unused neighbour, pays
that each draw.

Which entries end a page depends on where s_fpkm lands in the binary.
In today's build none of the hot ones do, so this costs nothing now. In
the portable renderer's copy of this code two did, and it cost the FIFO
thread about 6% at the Tutorial (-1.26% fps, 12 rounds; with this fix
+0.30%, no change). Any change that moves the array could bring that
here.

The hit skips the copy when n is 0, and a new entry clears its k array
once, so a short copy's tail always lands on a touched page. The bytes
written to the constant ring are the same.

d791b6ace351edc0697b9066e6d4ac62c7e38aa2.message:
rsxcore: no new sampler while a split part runs (RSX_SUBMIT_SPLIT)

With RSX_SUBMIT_SPLIT on, a batch's first parts are on the GPU while the rest
is recorded, and vp_sampler_table can make a new sampler in that time. That is
legal Vulkan, but lavapipe faults on it: llvmpipe_register_sampler (Mesa 25.2.8)
reallocs every texture's sample_functions array with no lock against the
rasterizer threads that read those arrays. The arrays are all one size, so a
freed one goes straight to the next texture, and a late read or write through
the old pointer gives a texture another texture's sample function. Those
functions have the texture's size compiled in, so the read runs off the end of
the memory: SIGSEGV in generated shader code, in 3 of 8 split runs and 0 without
the split. One core shows a sample function for a 256x1024 BC1 texture reading
from 60 KB of memory, on two threads at once.

Without the split the GPU is idle while a batch is recorded, so this never
overlaps. Now a sampler table new to the session waits for the parts first. It
is rare (128 tables at most) and only happens with the split on; the wait is the
same one this function already makes when it reuses a table.

Tested on Demon's Souls only. Not re-run: Virtua Fighter 5, The Simpsons Game, Tornado Outbreak, Tokyo Jungle, Midway Arcade Origins.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

de2096dee4bef7c8714100be7f416e333f1e79b0.message:
spu: the striped lock-line lock and its lock-free reads off Windows too

Off MSVC the lock-line lock was one global spinlock, with no pause and no
yield, and the lock-free reads always answered "take the lock". So every SPU
atomic on Linux queued on one cache line, a polling SPU wrote that line on
each read, and spu_llar_noop_commit gave up after its eight tries on every
fetch. Windows has had 64 stripes as sequence locks for a long time.

The Windows lock now builds everywhere. Only what differs by compiler goes
through macros: taking and giving a stripe, reading its odd bit, pause, yield
and the bit scan. Off MSVC the take and give are seq_cst, as the interlocked
calls are: spu_coh_notify_write and spu_lockline_read_ok rely on a full fence
between taking a stripe and reading a reservation. The read side already used
portable atomics. SPU_LOCKLINE_STATS stays a Windows tool.

Windows doesn't change: spu_coherency.c compiles to a byte-identical object
before and after, with the runtime's own flags and /Brepro.

The peer and coherency tests pass on Linux with clang and gcc, unoptimized
and at -O2, 36 runs at -O2 on 16, 8 and 2 threads. ThreadSanitizer finds no
new kind of problem: its new reports are the sequence lock's copy overlapping
a writer, which the second read of the stripe word throws away, and the
reservation fields the same lock-free path writes on Windows.

gpu: the Vulkan backend's gaps the core's replays found (step VC1)

The core's first replays on Vulkan, with the validation layer and its
synchronization validation, reported three kinds of message; the backend
now does what D3D12 does in each case, and two contract points are
written down in gpu.h.

- Table slots: set layouts of up to 16 entries are one layout
  (GPU_VK_TABLE_MIN), so a slot of up to 16 binds any table of up to 16.
  The core's blit binds the blit pool's 2-entry tables through a
  1-texture slot, which D3D12 allows and Vulkan's set layouts did not
  (VUID-vkCmdBindDescriptorSets-pDescriptorSets-00358).
- Vertex attributes: shader_create reads a SPIR-V module's Input and
  Output Locations, and a pipeline gets only the attributes its vertex
  shader reads (WARNING-Shader-OutputNotConsumed).
- Pixel shader outputs with no target (a depth-only pass's colour, slots
  past nrt): the pipeline is made with a copy of the module in which those
  outputs are Private variables, as D3D12 drops them
  (Undefined-Value-ShaderOutputNotConsumed-DynamicRendering). The copy is
  made from the words kept for pixel shaders with outputs and destroyed
  once the pipeline exists.
- Swap chains: GPU_SUBMIT_PRESENT_SIGNAL signalled the image's done
  semaphore in the first such submit only, so a present waited for none of
  the frame's later submits (the core says PRESENT_SIGNAL on every
  submit). The present's own empty submit now signals it, after them all.
- Textures with memory of their own start zeroed, as D3D12's committed
  resources: cleared in the init command buffer before their first layout
  (not BC formats; placed textures are what their heap held, on both).

spu, lift: the SSE paths build on arm64 through sse2neon

The SIMD paths are written with SSE intrinsics behind x86 guards, each
with a scalar loop beside it, so an arm64 build compiled but took every
loop: spu_shufb as a byte loop (about 11% of an FMOD mixer task), the
quadword byte shifts at ~70 instructions each, the scan and diff blocks
on lane loops, and the PPU lift's vperm/vsldoi/vmaxfp/vminfp/vrsqrtefp/
lvlx/lvrx as loops.

third_party/sse2neon is sse2neon v1.9.1 (MIT, pinned by commit, blobs in
its README), unmodified. include/ps3emu/ps3_sse.h includes it on arm64
under GCC or Clang and defines PS3_SSE2NEON; on x86 it defines nothing.
These guards now also take PS3_SSE2NEON, and keep including their own
x86 header on x86:

- spu_helpers.h: shufb, the quadword byte shifts/rotates, cbd/chd/cwd/cdd;
- spu_scan_hook.c: scan_run_sse;
- spu_diff_hook.c: diff_pass_sse;
- the PPU lifter's preamble: the VMX helpers.

Kept on the loop on arm64, with a note why: spu_coh_hint_match (its
loads are atomic in C; a movemask is several NEON instructions for a few
groups of four) and mfc_copy (the 8-byte copies are one ldp/stp pair).
rsx_d3d12_backend.c's vf_strip_native_w is not touched: it is frozen and
not built on Apple.

sse2neon's precision options stay at 0: on AArch64 div and sqrt are
then the exact vdivq_f32/vsqrtq_f32, and vmaxfp/vminfp handle NaNs and
equal operands themselves.

ed411b5e5da6d39b033c30985861dd6e53f9e4fc.message:
rsx: the GPU vertex fetch ring grows when a frame needs more

The GPU fetch path copies a strip's guest vertex bytes into vf_buf, a
ring of VP_FETCH_RING_MB (64 MB) per frame half. A strip that does not
fit takes the CPU path instead, which converts every vertex to 256
bytes. The ring never grew.

On Demon's Souls' dragon bridge in 1-2 a frame asks for up to ~120 MB
of ring. There, 41 million strip uploads fell to the CPU path for lack
of room against 29 million that fit, the CPU path wrote ~2 million
vertices a frame (vp_vb grew to its 1 GB cap), and the FIFO thread held
the frame rate at ~77 fps: 87% busy in upload_strip_vp_indexed,
rsx_fetch_vertex_arrays and memcpy (issue #288).

The ring now grows at the frame's end like vp_vb and vp_ib: a frame
counts the bytes it found no room for (s_vf_short), and vf_grow doubles
the ring until it holds that frame with an eighth to spare, up to
1024 MB a half. The old ring goes with the deferred releases (today's
renderer) or with its frame's fence (rc_ring_retire, the core). On the
bridge the ring grows once, to 128 MB a half, and the frame rate is
144, the display's cap.

The portable core gets the same change (rsxc_state, rsxc_vertex,
rsxc_writeback, rsxc_frame, rsxc_init), and its kind-4 corner table,
which also writes the ring, counts its shortfall too.

f0ec8cbb2b45ac512d2847d88fc09f3e617bd725.message:
gpu_vk: fewer driver calls a frame on the Vulkan route

The Vulkan route was 18% slower than D3D12 in the Tutorial and 8% at the
Palace (the night of 10-31), with the render thread busy on both. Most of
the extra CPU time was calls the D3D12 drivers would have dropped or merged:

- Barriers are held and sent as one vkCmdPipelineBarrier2 just before the
  next command that does work (a draw's pass, a copy, a query, the end).
  One that touches what a held one does sends those first, so the order is
  the same. 73 calls a frame become 31.5.
- The attachment-order barrier between passes is sent only when one of
  the pass's targets was an attachment since the last barrier that orders
  it, not before every pass.
- Descriptor sets are bound only when they change, in runs.
- Repeated state is not sent again: the pipeline, viewport, scissor,
  topology, depth writes, vertex and index buffers and push constants.
  Replay CPU against D3D12 went from +14.3% to +8.3%.
- A whole-target clear made before its pass opens becomes the pass's load
  op, the drivers' fast clear (the better path on AMD and tile-based
  GPUs); a read-only depth's clear stays inside the rendering.
- A typeless colour image names the formats its views may take (its D3D12
  family), so a driver need not drop its compression.

Images are unchanged: the capture gates pass with the validation layer
(synchronization validation on) quiet.

Tested on Demon's Souls only. Not re-run: Virtua Fighter 5, The Simpsons Game, Tornado Outbreak, Tokyo Jungle, Midway Arcade Origins.

f3c1c274f4c9ff7d5ce636c0ea3526b99996117f.message:
ppu: a guest longjmp lands in the frame of its setjmp

The lifted longjmp restored the guest registers from the buffer, then
returned to its own C caller. The function that called setjmp is a host
frame further up the stack, so execution went on after the throw with
the stack pointer and registers of the setjmp, in the wrong function.

Demon's Souls hits this when a script errors. Lua 5.0 raises an error
with longjmp (luaD_throw) back to the protected call that catches it
(luaD_rawrunprotected). In the Penetrator fight in 1-3, the boss
script 502000_battle errors at line 86 ("attempt to compare nil with
number"). That is the game's own bug: a PS3 catches it and the fight
goes on. Here the throw came back into luaV_execute, which then read a
NULL savedpc. The game's abort path then ended the process with
sys_process_exit(1), so the window closed with no crash report.

The lifter now finds the SDK's setjmp and longjmp by their first five
instructions (find_guest_setjmp). Each call of setjmp becomes
PS3_GUEST_SETJMP: a host setjmp in the caller's frame, beside the guest
call, recorded in a slot on a per-thread list (g_ps3_sjlj_top). The
function's scope object drops its slots when it returns. The guest
longjmp, after its own register restore, ends in ps3_guest_longjmp. That
takes the newest slot with the same buffer and stack pointer and host-
longjmps to it. With no such slot it returns as before, and says so once
on stderr. The thread proc empties the list before each run of a guest
thread's entry (ps3_sjlj_thread_reset). sys_ppu_thread_exit's own longjmp
out of the lifted frames can leave their slots behind, and an interrupt
handler runs its entry again on the same host thread.

The host setjmp and longjmp are the C library's. The Windows one unwinds
through the lifted frames by their unwind tables, as the runtime's thread
exit already does. __builtin_setjmp fails fast under clang-cl on Windows
x64. A freestanding game module gets _setjmp and longjmp from the host
as jump thunks (PS3_GAME_HOST_CRT_FUNCS, PS3_GAME

fb753cf3d581815c239705d5889ab006faba0df9.message:
RSX_CORE: the RSX thread alone on a core (Linux)

On a Steam Deck the RSX thread holds the frame, and two guest threads spin in
sys_timer_usleep beside it. With that thread alone on one CPU of a core and
every other thread off the core, its second hardware thread included, the
Deck ran 4.1% and 7.8% faster (kit 3, two rounds, taskset from outside).

plat_core_reserve (plat.h, Linux) picks the core by the system's own figures
(cpufreq's max, then ACPI CPPC's highest_perf), not the first core when others
tie, since CPU 0 takes most interrupts. It moves every other thread off the
core. A thread starts on its starter's CPUs, so the ones the RSX thread starts
later (vertex workers, the driver's) would share its CPU: plat_core_keep moves
them, every 64 flips, reading the thread list only when the count of threads
changed or every 16th call.

RSX_CORE=1 turns it on, auto only with SMT and at least 4 cores, 0 or unset
leaves things as they are (the default). Elsewhere than Linux it does nothing.
test_plat_core checks it on the machine it runs on.

fd32dbb8d4c61cc90a65a3ef69cac0085e0254d4.message:
SPU: libsynth2's synth thread two steps up

libsynth2 runs its synth on one SPU thread in a group the SDK names
"_synth2 Group". It mixes every voice of the title's sound engine, and the
engine's mixer waits on it every round with the next block due (Demon's
Souls: about 47 rounds a second, four jobs each). At normal priority its
replies queued behind the title's busy threads; the mixer fell behind and
the sound looped (#403).

Its thread now goes two steps up when it starts, as libmixer's threads do
(#257): highest on Windows, nice -10 on Linux through the same helper
(RealtimeKit when setpriority is refused). SPU_SYNTH_RAISE=1 is one step,
0 leaves it at normal.

fe930bb8705eebebcfe48987993b2827f5359053.message:
rsxcore: a frame waits for its slot's use before it, as today's does

With RSX_PRESENT=0 nothing is presented, so the swap chain's buffer index
never moves and every frame uses one slot. Today's move_to_next_frame then
signals the slot's fence value again, which render_frame's opening
wait_for_gpu has already reached, so it doesn't wait: the GPU runs the frame
while the next batch records. The new path signalled a fresh value and
waited for it, a full drain every frame. That was about 0.2 ms a frame of
extra waiting on capset0 (+5% to +9% in halgate --time at RSX_PRESENT=0,
the only mode a locked PC can time). With presenting, the slots alternate
and both behaved alike.

move_to_next_frame now waits for the new slot's point from before this
frame, then stores this frame's. frame_cmd_begin waits for the slot's point
before its recorder is reset. After the opening drain that is a fence read,
and it keeps a repaint, which opens a slot right after a present, from
resetting a recorder still in flight. The slot points are cleared before
init's first frame_cmd_begin, so a device made again starts from zero.

rsxcore: frames in flight: what still assumed the drain at a batch's start

Review of #253 (the drain at each batch's start is gone; these assumed it).

Write-backs lost: a copy of the last batch is stored once the GPU is done
with it, perhaps after the next batch's pre-pass, and a target the
pre-pass dropped in between (off_rt_get's size or format change, an
eviction) had its copy skipped, on exactly the drops where the store used

    copy keeps its guest range, WbCopy.dst/len).
The texture checksum workers stop first (tcj_stop: they read guest memory),
and their sums of that batch are not used. A copy still dropped un-stored
says so in a "[wb] not stored" line, and test_rsx_synth fails on it: the

cleared at each batch's start, where the drain had seen the last batch
through. A sampler table new to the session now waits for the GPU while a

# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

**[Join the sp00nznet recomp Discord](https://discord.gg/CRpzGWZFcu)** — the
community hub for sp00nznet's recomp projects, where ps3recomp development
happens in the open. Good place to ask questions, show a port you are working
on, or find out what people are stuck on before you duplicate the effort.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [ReXGlue](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [AnyPS5](https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5) (PS5 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — the output is C/C++, so it can target any platform a compiler does (see [platform support](#platform-support) for where the runtime actually stands today)

## Platform support

CI builds and tests every row on every pull request: Windows (clang-cl), macOS
arm64, Linux (GCC and Clang), and Linux with the Vulkan backend on lavapipe
under the validation layer. A green check means the runtime built and the tests
passed. It does not mean a game ran; the last row is the only one that claims
that.

| | Windows | macOS (arm64) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime library builds | yes | yes | yes |
| Lifter test suites + C unit tests | yes | yes | yes |
| Render backend | D3D12 | Metal | Vulkan (opt-in); null (headless, CI) |
| Runs a recompiled game, in this tree | **yes** | **no** | **no** |

**What stops macOS and Linux running a title is the PPU boot scaffold.**
`ppu_loader.cpp`, `boot_main.cpp` and the HLE dispatch are compiled per game,
not into the library. They compile on POSIX with zero errors (a CI ratchet
keeps it that way) and the frame clock runs there, but no title has yet been
booted to gameplay from this tree on either OS.

**The renderers are further along than that.** `ps3recomp_host` drives cellGcm
→ RSX → backend end to end with no game. With guest programs on, Metal and
Vulkan both run the title's own shaders on the shared register-file draw
engine. Every `ps3recomp_host` scene passes on both, including render-to-texture,
MRT, depth textures, cube maps and stencil. Linux's default stays the headless
null backend, a CPU triangle filler that CI draws with.

**Downstream, people are already past this.** Twisted Metal's menus run on
Linux/Vulkan, inFamous on macOS, and Killzone 3 under Proton (see
[In the community](#in-the-community)). Those ports carry patches that are
still on their way upstream, which is why the table still says "no".

## The Challenge

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

| Component | What It Is | Why It's Hard |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| **PPU** | PowerPC 64-bit main CPU | Custom ISA extensions, VMX/AltiVec SIMD |
| **6x SPU** | 128-bit SIMD vector processors | Proprietary ISA, 256KB local store, explicit DMA |
| **Memory** | 256MB XDR RAM | 128-byte alignment requirements, split bus |
| **LV2 Kernel** | Proprietary OS layer | ~300+ system calls, complex threading model |
| **PRX Modules** | Dynamic libraries | 100+ system libraries with intricate interdependencies |

We don't shy away from hard problems. We just break them into smaller ones.

## Architecture

```
ps3recomp/
├── tools/                    # Binary analysis & recompilation pipeline
│   ├── elf_parser.py         # Parse PS3 ELF/SELF/PRX binaries
│   ├── ppu_disasm.py         # PowerPC disassembler with PS3 extensions
│   ├── ppu_lifter.py         # PPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── spu_disasm.py         # SPU instruction set disassembler
│   ├── spu_lifter.py         # SPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── extract_spu_images.py # Extract embedded SPU images from PRX/ELF
│   ├── find_spu_functions.py # SPU function boundary detection
│   ├── wrap_spu_elf.py       # Wrap a raw SPU blob as a loadable ELF
│   ├── prx_analyzer.py       # Analyze PRX imports/exports and NIDs
│   ├── nid_database.py       # Function Name ID (NID) resolver
│   ├── find_functions.py     # Function boundary detection
│   └── generate_stubs.py     # Generate HLE stub skeletons from a NID list
│
├── runtime/                  # Core runtime for recompiled executables
│   ├── ppu/                  # PPU execution context
│   │   ├── ppu_context.h     # Register file, CR, LR, CTR, FPSCR
│   │   ├── ppu_memory.h      # Memory access macros (loads, stores, byte-swap)
```

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

10036dbff1459d1a3d5c4913a3047eff28f3aef7.message:
Setup: the first Python without curl or tar (Wine, CrossOver)

Setup's first step downloads Python with Windows' own curl.exe and unpacks it with its tar.exe, from System32. Wine
and CrossOver ship neither, so a Mac player on CrossOver stopped at "Setup could not start its first download", and the
log did not say why.

When curl or tar does not start, the host now does it itself. Machines that have curl and tar work as before.
- setup_http.cpp downloads with WinHTTP, which Windows and Wine both have. It does what the curl line does:
  - https only, TLS 1.2 or later;
  - redirects followed, but never from https to http;
  - a minute's timeouts;
  - a Range request carrying on from the .part file. A 200 answer starts the file over; a 206 for another range
    deletes it.
  Cancel closes its handles, which ends the call it is in.
- setup_unzip.cpp unpacks the zip:
  - stored and deflated entries, inflated by stb_image's zlib, which the UI already builds;
  - each file's CRC-32 checked;
  - zip64, encryption and several disks refused.
  The names go through the same check as tar's, and the archive's size and SHA-256 are checked first, as before.
- FIX lines (the reason under Details) now also go to the log, so a report has them.
- DES_SETUP_NO_SYSTEM_TOOLS=1 hides curl and tar, for tests.
- crc32.hpp is report.cpp's CRC-32, now shared with the zip reader, and its table is built once in a thread-safe way.
- docs/88 section 5 describes the fallback.

Off Windows nothing changes: setup_http.cpp has no download there, so a missing curl fails as before.

1089988defbd3135cbb475fa8285981ff979f772.message:
Setup: read a disc RPCS3 keeps on its hard disk, and let no leftover entry hide a copy

RPCS3 can hold a disc game three ways. A disc copy's folder in games.yml was
always read, for every disc. Two others failed, for every disc:

- A disc game kept in dev_hdd0/game/<TITLE_ID>: PS3_GAME's files in that
  folder, with no PS3_GAME folder inside it (RPCS3's "Disc game located in
  dev_hdd0/game"; games.yml has it with "/./" only after its first boot).
  The check stopped at "no PS3_GAME folder", or RPCS3's library looked empty.
- An entry stays in games.yml after its game has gone. The first listed disc
  won even with no game in its folder, so a leftover entry for another disc
  hid the copy the player has.

Setup now takes a library entry whose copy is there first. A disc kept in
dev_hdd0/game is read through a link in setup's own folder
(<data>/setup/disc-view/<TITLE_ID>/PS3_GAME: a junction on Windows, a
symbolic link elsewhere), so nothing is written in RPCS3's folders. A library
folder with no game in it now names that folder and what was looked for. The
command-line check names the disc it matched, not always the US one.

Issue #453.

17c28aac99235d025c5c8ac77573dd75f4a4815c.message:
Run defaults: Havok's threads at normal priority (PPU_RAISE_BELOW=0)

ps3recomp raises a title's threads below guest priority 1000 to above
normal, for audio and I/O pollers that sleep between blocks. In this game
those are Havok's: hkSpuUtil Helper (80), Havok PPU Thread (100) and
SPURuntimeService (200). The Havok PPU Thread polls the job queue's lock
with usleep(1), which waits in place (docs/77). Raised, on 2-4 CPUs it
likely keeps the SPU tasks of its own step off the cores: in a console
trace the long frames are the main thread waiting 34-42 ms for the step
while that thread makes no call for about 40 ms.

Held to 2 CPUs at 60 fps (PS3_AFFINITY=5, with ps3recomp #261), two
rounds, 9 roll-breaks each:
- raised (the runtime's 1000): 3.1% and 2.9% of frames over 25 ms away
  from breaks, jitter 2.8 ms, 68 and 88 frames over 25 ms after breaks;
- none raised (0): 0.5% and 0.6%, jitter 1.1 ms, 8 and 11;
- Havok PPU + helper raised (150): 2.1%, 84; helper only (90): as 0.
Audio gaps (AUDIO_GAPS=1) were fewer with 0: 1 and 4 against 5 and 12.
libmixer's threads still go up by name (PPU_MIXER_RAISE), and the
runtime's line stays at 1000 for other titles.

1de3a23e3fb3df7c2ac173f6b7d8f0ab5bbe7a11.message:
Freestanding game module: no C++ exceptions (setup's link, #304)

Setup's link of des_game.dll stops with "undefined symbol:
__CxxFrameHandler3", referenced from the .xdata of ppu_recomp_005, _010
and more (issue #304).

The freestanding module is C++ compiled with /EHsc and linked with
/NODEFAULTLIB: no C runtime, so no C++ unwind handler. That held while no
module function had a local with a destructor. ps3recomp #212 (pinned by
#297) gave every lifted function that calls the guest setjmp a scope
object, ps3_sjlj_scope, whose destructor drops its slots. Under /EHsc
clang has to run that destructor when a call throws, so the 7 chunks with
a setjmp call get __CxxFrameHandler3 as an unwind handler. Every setup
since #297 lifts again and then fails at the link. The single-exe build
links the C runtime and was not affected.

The module never throws or catches, so it is now compiled with C++
exceptions off: /EHs-c- on Windows and -fno-exceptions on Linux, beside
/GR- and -fno-rtti and for the same reason. On Linux the missing names
are __gxx_personality_v0 and _Unwind_Resume, and -z defs fails that link
too. A host longjmp still unwinds through the module's frames by their
unwind tables. The guest-setjmp code does not need the destructor on that
path: the guest longjmp sets the slot list itself, and the thread proc
empties it after a thread exit.

Both game build descriptions gain the flag for the four C++ objects
(ppu, libsre, spu_workloads, des_game_module). The Windows one matches
CMake's commands again (game_build_desc.py --check --commands-only, as
CI's job does). With setup's commands and the pinned clang, the 8 chunks
with the guest setjmp or longjmp no longer need __CxxFrameHandler3
(llvm-nm), and a link of them with game_module and game_libc leaves only
the other chunks' functions and the port's own names undefined. With
master's flags the same link lacks __CxxFrameHandler3, as in the issue.
The Linux objects no longer need __gxx_personality_v0 or _Unwind_Resume.
In chunk 005 only the cleanup paths change: .

27d85b1d73fe516de055145649639c3558825baf.message:
Problem reports: put the player's save in the zip

So that a reported problem can be loaded where it happened, instead of
played up to again, both kinds of report now hold the save: Report an
issue (the menu) and the crash, hang and lost-graphics dialog's Report on
GitHub.

report::save_files takes each save folder in the game's save root, found
as cellSaveData.c finds it (PS3_SAVEDATA_ROOT, else
gamedata/dev_hdd0/home/00000001/savedata in the working folder; the
crash dialog's process has the game's environment and working folder).
Each goes in as save/<folder>/<file>. Two kinds of file stay out:

- the folder's two pictures (ICON0.PNG, PIC1.PNG), which are the game's
  art;
- a file the runtime is still writing (.<name>.tmp).

If a file changed or was being written while the folder was read, the
folder is read again, at most twice and half a second apart. The limits
are 8 MB a file and 32 MB in all; a Demon's Souls save is ten 256 KB
files. game.txt (and the crash issue's System block) gets one line: the
folder, how many files and KB, how many minutes before the report it was
saved, and whether the game was saving meanwhile.

The save holds the characters and their names, and the issue is public.
So the texts that said a report has no save data now say it holds the
save, with the characters' names: the menu's box, the crash dialog's
three, the README and docs/74. The port writes its own PARAM.SFO, so no
PSN account is in it.

3dfb4ee2d121c86a58f93ffe972471477843b0bf.message:
The Linux download gets the Vulkan renderer and setup's shader step

Issue #351, the first Steam Deck report: long freezes when a new scene loads. The Linux download was still the legacy
renderer on vkd3d alone, which compiles each shader as the game first draws it. A level load needs 18 vertex and 27 pixel
programs: 8.2 s through the shipped vkd3d on the development PC, about 19 s scaled to the Deck, and the tester's notices read
16-23 s. docs/120 said Vulkan was Linux's default, which is true of the option but not of what shipped: host.yml built that
version only as a check, on a second build, and never uploaded it.

host.yml now builds the runtime with PS3RECOMP_RSX_HAL from the start, as on Windows, and the second build goes. So Linux
starts on Vulkan, and setup's shader step has its spv target (it was Pass::Off before). A Vulkan start that fails falls back
to the legacy renderer in the same process, and the next start after one that crashed uses it too.

The licences of what the renderer compiles in (glslang, SPIRV-Tools, SPIRV-Headers, volk, the Vulkan headers) go along, as
in the Windows job. README and docs/76 and 120 say what ships.

renderer (Linux: vulkan then legacy; Windows: d3d12 then vulkan;

from a copy of the tester's save, muted, offline, at the original 30 fps,
with the tester's input left out, and ends itself (DES_KIT_MAX stops it).

summary.json; results.txt (one line a run); system.txt (OS, CPU, RAM, session,
vulkaninfo where installed, each run's route and GPU lines). The shader caches
are deleted first. The home folder, user name and computer name are replaced
in every text file, and if any are left (in any case) nothing is packed.

bash 3.2 and later; no Python, jq or timeout. README.md is for testers.

590e464143824024bce1f7276e726e4f17f11b3f.message:
port: the game ending itself with an error shows the crash dialog

The game's fatal paths end in sys_process_exit with a non-zero code: abort()
and Lua's exit(1) on an error with no protected call. Neither is a fault, so
the crash report's filter and abort handler never ran and the window just
closed, with nothing for the player to report.

des_guest_exit.cpp takes the runtime's new hook. Several threads can get there
within a millisecond of each other, since exit() frees objects under threads
still playing. Each records what it knows, the first waits a moment and writes
the one report, and the others stay until the process ends.

The report says when it was Lua running out of memory and carries each
thread's HOST-bt line. There is no Settings row.

674155d64ca01e566600e8447f6097b531e24f3b.message:
port: enemies no longer T-pose for a frame above 30 fps

Havok's sample-and-combine fills a bone whose animation weight is under
the skeleton's reference-pose threshold (0.05) with the reference pose, a
T-pose. When an enemy starts a new move, the new clip can fade in from 0
with nothing under it, growing about as t^2. At 30 fps one frame of the
fade is under the threshold; above 30 fps several are, near weight 0, so
the enemy is drawn in the T-pose for 20-30 ms.

des_refpose_rate runs after each load of the threshold: the SPU sample
job's copy (0x01005978) and the four PPU sample paths. It scales the
threshold by (30 dt)^2, so a fade stays under it for about one frame at
any frame rate. Nothing changes at 30 fps or below. DES_TPOSEFIX=0 turns
it off live. Region rows for the European, Japanese and Asian discs.

Tutorial route, unlocked: with the fix off, a fade-in in view drew 5-6
frames at 72-100% reference pose; with it on, one frame at 26%.

69197fa8fc690237c990fe4e6082ba737a29502c.message:
Pantheon: take real characters' records, and send our own even when one fails

Players reached the Pantheon but saw no statues. The live server had 0
records on all five boards. Each player's own game refused its record
before sending it, and it did so without an error.

The record checks came from two records of one new character. Records
dumped from 20 saved characters (the game's own record builder, run on
each save) failed them 18 times, and 138 of 147 records rebuilt from save
slots failed too.

Widened, here and in the server's table (DemonsSoulsServer desrecord.go)
with the same rows:
- +0xAC: 0 to 100 (0 after the first area)
- +0xAE: 0 to 9999, and +0xB0..+0xCC eight counts, 0 to 999,999,999
  (it was "padding")
- +0xD4..+0xDC: signed, from -65536 (0xFFFF0000 unset; +0xD8 can be set)
- colours: 0 to 4 (up to 1.875 seen)
- list entries: kind 1 to 3, and any last word (list B's holds a stack
  leftover)
- list B: its order and count aren't checked (two entries, a count of 1)

All 20 dumped and 147 rebuilt records now pass both tables.

Going up, a record that fails is logged and sent all the same. The server
checks it with the same rows and logs the field it refuses, so a limit
still too tight shows in the server's log. This needs ps3recomp's
fix/score-refused-game-data (#286): without it, the game takes the
refusal for a lost connection and skips its later boards. A received
record that fails is still refused.

6927ea3b096b2f11f363722791c5f4fbffebbe4e.message:
Setup: when Python can't check a server's certificate, Windows' own curl downloads (#493)

#493: setup stopped at the compiler's download with "CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED:
unable to get local issuer certificate", and the update check said there was no
connection to GitHub. On the same PC Windows' curl had just downloaded Python.

On Windows, Python checks a server's certificate against the roots it copies from
Windows' store. Windows adds a root there only when its own check first needs one
(from Windows Update), so a PC where nothing Windows runs has needed that root yet
fails Python's check and passes Windows'. A TLS-scanning antivirus or proxy that
Windows trusts can look the same.

Now, when Python's check refuses the certificate, on Windows only:
- a tool's download (fetch.py) goes through Windows' own curl.exe, from the System
  folder, with the host's own options (setup_python.cpp): https only, -C - to carry
  on from the .part file, and a start over once when the server ignores the range.
  The size and SHA-256 checks are unchanged. Setup's log gets a note saying so.
- the update check (update.read_feed, with its ETag) and the release's small files
  (update._small) get the same: a GET through curl.
Any other failure, and any failure off Windows, is reported as before.

7c90c40e243e4a553e959d2a3774906f2ca0afaf.message:
port: the sun flare takes the probe's latest count above 30 fps (#290)

The flare's three readers (0x003E2D38, and in 0x003E5750 and 0x003E6368)
read report 1024 only once label 0x52 has reached the probe query's
counter, and otherwise keep the count they have. At 30 fps the RSX has
walked the last probe by the next frame's first check. Above 30 fps the
main thread runs 2-3 probes ahead of it, so the check fails every frame
and the count stays at whatever a rare pass took: the sun through walls,
or gone in the open. A trace at the reported Stonefang spot, uncapped
(about 315 fps), passed the check about once per camera sweep in 130 s.

des_sun_gate runs after each reader's load of the label (insn hooks at
0x003E2DF0, 0x003E6330, 0x003E6518) and raises it to at least the
counter, so the reader takes the latest stored count. With the fix the
held count followed the stored one within one check, at the same frame
rate. Only with DES_FPS; DES_SUNFIX=0 turns it off live. docs/28, "Sun
flare stuck above 30 fps".

81cb29d1690c7f23f73eef635c8ce6bc018e86da.message:
port: Lua takes room in the port's heap when its own heap is full

Each of the game's Lua states gets its memory through a small-block pool,
and the pool gets pages and every block over 128 bytes from a heap object.
Two heap classes stand behind the game's Lua states, and each hands
everything to one fixed arena of its own:
- 0x01852D20 serves the two script systems' states, in 2.375 MB;
- 0x01852EC0 serves a third, small state, in 9 MB.

When an arena can't give a block, luaM_realloc throws LUA_ERRMEM. Nothing
catches it on a character's script, so Lua calls exit(1) and the window
closes. The early collection (des_luagc.cpp) keeps the scripts well below
the limit above 30 fps. This change is the safety net under it.

Every method of the two classes that hands out or takes back a block is
wrapped (all calls to them go through their vtables). The classes are one
template over a different arena: the same methods at the same vtable
offsets, forwarding to the same functions.
- When an arena can't give an allocation, it comes from the port's own
  guest heap instead.
- Free, realloc, a block's size and "is this block yours" send those blocks
  back there. Every other block goes to the game's own method unchanged.
- Until an arena can't give a block, nothing changes.
- The pool finds a block's page by its address range, not by alignment, so
  pages from the port's heap work the same way.
- Lua 5.0 can't safely collect inside the allocator, so the net doesn't
  collect: it only gives room.

Which heaps a Lua state can get: the game's lua_open takes the heap, and a
state's threads share its pool. Only the state's constructor calls lua_open,
and the constructor is called from six places.
- Four are the script systems, and they read one global heap pointer.
- Two are "new state on this heap" methods, each reached only through its
  class's vtable. One is in the code with the second TOC and reaches the
  constructor through a TOC stub.
- Both methods are wrapped as well. Each writes a line to the log if a state
  ever lands

8fb4175e5f8f6062c0d63ae3dd90706b0a91c36d.message:
tools: DES_MEMSTAT, how full the game's own heaps get (docs/59 T1)

The game makes 13 heaps of fixed sizes at boot and never asks for more;
a full one ends in its error report. Mods with bigger files need more of
some of them. DES_MEMSTAT=1 shows which, and how close each comes:

- A thread reads each heap's arena every millisecond. It only reads (no
  lock taken, nothing in the game called), so the game runs as without
  it. Each class keeps its arena in a global of its own; the ten
  DLStaticHeap-like arenas keep their free bytes at +0x3C and their block
  list's ends at +0x04/+0x18, HAVOK's, MO's and TEMP's the same fields
  8 bytes lower (+0x34, +0x28/+0x2C).
- The log gets each heap's size, a line as its peak use passes another
  tenth from half full up, and a table (size, in use now, at most, share)
  every DES_MEMSTAT_EVERY seconds and on every game error.
  DES_MEMSTAT=2 adds each arena's first words.
- With DES_MEMSTAT off, a game error still prints one table: each heap's
  use at that moment (no peaks: no thread ran). A full heap ends in the
  game's error report, so a player's report zip then shows which one.
- A 14th row, LOCAL, is the game's heap over the RSX's local (video)
  memory, 248 MB. Its arena is in a static object: the base its heap
  object points at (0x01AD6358) + 0x18, as the class's methods take it.
- The addresses are in the region tables: European +0x280, Japanese and
  Asian +0x30, read from the game's own address table that the heap
  methods use (r30 = [r2 + slot], then [r30 + offset]).
- des_heap.cpp: ds_heap_usage, the port's own guest heap now and at most.

Off by default (apart from that one table). First numbers (1-2 bridge, 240 s): the file-loading heap
CORERES peaks at 92% of its 12.25 MB without mods and at 12.24 MB with a
large set of texture and model mods.

927ea39a8c365776ca4fd372fa5bd05edaee829d.message:
Mods: a mods folder, Settings > Mods, and offline play with gameplay mods

Each folder in <data folder>/mods is a mod. Settings > Mods lists them,
one row each, off until turned on (DES_MODS in settings.ini). At start
the mods that are on become PS3_VFS_MODS, which the runtime reads in
place of the game's files (ps3recomp: vfs mod folders). Nothing in the
game's own files changes.

- A mod's files are found flat, in wrapper folders, or in
  (PS3_GAME/)USRDIR, up to five folders deep. Folders named Original,
  Backup, Vanilla, Uninstall or Unmodded (the game's own files, shipped
  to undo a mod) are passed over. Notes and pictures beside the files
  are left out. A mod with an EBOOT.BIN, two versions of itself or no
  game files can't be used, and its row says why.
- Order: folder names A to Z; the first mod with a file gives it. A
  "Same files" row lists files that mods that are on share.
- Look or gameplay: textures, models, text, sound, effects, menus and
  lighting are look-only; parameters, map layouts and collision,
  characters, objects, scripts and unknown files are gameplay.
- A gameplay mod keeps the session offline: apply_network sets no
  network knobs, the runtime's network is locked off, and when Online is
  on a notice says why ("Playing offline: gameplay mods are on"). The
  Network and Mods tabs say so too.
- Problem reports get a "Mods:" line.
- settings.ini lines can be up to 8 KB (was 512 bytes), for long mod
  lists.
- mods_check (CI, Windows and Linux): the rules, finding a mod's files,
  the unusable cases, order, shared files and PS3_VFS_MODS.
- docs/143: how it works and what is planned.

Tested live with test mods and with published mods of each layout
(flat, a wrapper folder, a version folder with a backup copy beside
it): the runtime gave the mods' files and the level loaded; a gameplay
mod kept the session offline with the notice; a look-only mod left
online alone; toggling a row saved DES_MODS.

9c41cbadc4c000e6e1132849d5d2767928232295.message:
tools/des: halimg compares an HDR snapshot in 8-bit codes when its paper white is known

Under the vk rule an HDRP pair was held to 1e-3, with at most 0.01% of
the pixels allowed up to 8/255 (relative to the larger of 1 and the
value). That bound is in the snapshot's linear units, while the pixels
it is for, ones that sampled the next texel of an 8-bit texture, differ
by a step that grows with the paper white. At the settings a player
uses (RSX_HDR_WHITE=400, scale 300, AA 2, aniso 16) Vulkan's snapshots
of capsetu's courtyard and fog wall failed it with 19 and 119 pixels,
where the frames' own 8-bit shots pass: in codes those pixels are 1 to
5 apart, scattered one by one, nothing above 8.

- halimg.py --hdr-white <paper white, nits / 80> [--hdr-curve
  gamma|srgb]: under vk an HDRP pair is turned back into the codes the
  blit decoded (gamma 2.2, or the sRGB curve for RSX_HDR_GAMMA=1) and
  held to the 8-bit rule, heat map included. A NaN fails. Without it,
  and in the hdr mode, the rule is as it was.
- halgate.sh reads the paper white from A's "HDR snap" line and the
  curve from its "HDR: on" line.
- docs/120's G3 line says so.

The self-test gains the round trips (both curves), 120 pixels 4 codes
off (fails without the white, passes with it), 0.06% of pixels 2 codes
off and 0.02% 12 codes off (fail), the hdr mode and a NaN (fail).

af3fb1da919858470cb1ca109eebda71388404e6.message:
tools/region: data through the code's own address tables, and no guesses on the 1.04 discs

region_table.py find gave a confident wrong answer for data on the
Japanese and Asian 1.04 discs: +0x80 for the heap globals at 0x01AD6498..
0x01AD6AF0 ("data, 26 references"), where the game has them at +0x30. It
counted TOC slots holding a base below the address, read at the same slot
offset on the other disc. Two things break that on the 1.04 discs:
- their TOC starts 0x18 higher and many slots moved, so the same offset
  is another slot (kContextAspect's one exact vote pointed 0x60 off);
- their data moved in pieces (the 0x50 bytes below 0x01AD62C8 shrank, and
  some objects were reordered), so a base below can have moved by another
  amount than the address.

Changes:
- New way, find_table: code that loads the address from a TOC slot, or
  loads an address table's base and then the table's word at a fixed
  offset (lwz rX,d(r2); lwz rY,k(rX)), is matched on the other disc, and
  that disc's own slot gives the answer. This is how the heap classes
  reach their arenas.
- SlotMap: whether TOC slots keep their offsets is found from a sample of
  matched loads (yes on the European disc, no on the 1.04 discs); where
  they don't, find_data maps each slot through code that loads it, and
  the anchors (find_between) are not used.
- The ways that read the other disc (find_table, find_content) win; the
  ones that assume (find_data, find_between) only answer when those two
  don't, and a disagreement is noted. On a disc whose data moved in
  pieces, a base below is only a hint ("perhaps ..."), never an answer.

verify against each table (the tables as on master plus the DES_MEMSTAT
rows):
- European: 270 agree, 0 differ, 25 unchecked -> 285 / 0 / 10.
- Japanese and Asian (1.04 EBOOTs, the tables checked with the same code):
  before, the arena rows came out +0x80 (wrong) and kContextAspect's
  agreeing row would have been reported as differing; after, 280 agree,
  0 differ, 15 unchecked.
The 13 unit tests pass; check passes.

T

aspect: markers on a tall picture keep WorldToScreen's y (#472)

At 16:10 the lock-on reticle and the floating health bars sat 11% too far
from the middle, up and down.

WorldToScreen (0x0079EE00) builds its projection from the camera's own
FOV and shape (0x003DFF40 reads camera +0x50..+0x5C). On a tall picture
those stay 16:9, since only the recorded projection is taller
(cam_record_projection), so its y is 16:9's. In the taller picture a point
is (16/9) / A nearer the middle, and the taller canvas is (16/9) / A
taller: the two cancel. des_hud_w2s stretched y by the canvas's height on
top of that, as x is stretched at a wide shape.

- On the taller canvas (the default HUD), y is left as it is.
- With DES_HUD=stretch the canvas stays 720 high, so y comes nearer the
  middle by A / (16/9). Before, it was left 11% out there too.
- docs/39 section 9 says the same.

b82f2ba878889ea7919cbd87dca8cd6eb7c1c75f.message:
Pin: ps3recomp 079f5aad (#254 an empty SpursQueue poll takes no lock)

#254: with LIBSRE_OWN (the default since #390), a non-blocking
cellSpursQueuePopBody of an empty queue now reads the counts without
the lock-line stripe and returns AGAIN, as libsre's lwarx loop does.

HighGraphics' queue and its command ring share one of the 64 stripes.
Every poll took that stripe, so the ring's SPU reader fell off its
lock-free read and collided with HighGraphics' ring stores. On 2 CPUs
the game drew about a third fewer frames than on libsre (Linux) and
about 12% fewer draws (Windows). On all CPUs the two were even.

Counters, Windows on 2 CPUs, one boot a side: HighGraphics' contended
stripe takes per million, libsre 133, master 66,894, #254 205. One
Linux boot of #254 on 2 CPUs drew 2,207 frames in the window (master
averaged 1,479, libsre 2,272; one run on a PC in use, not a timing).

bfe7b859ab551ac790675ea6efbccdae65973cee.message:
European disc: Japanese, Chinese (Traditional) and Korean in Settings > Game > Language

The European disc carries the text and fonts for these three (Japanese
in the root of msg/ and font/, Chinese and Korean in their own folders),
but its program never picks them: on a PS3 set to one of them it shows
English.

The program keeps its language as one index (0 Japanese, 1 Asian
English, 2 Korean, 3 Chinese, 4 US English, 5-9 the European five) and
fills it at first use, only ever with 5-9. The text, the fonts and the
menus' language folder all follow it. For these three the port sets it
(0, 3 or 2) before the game runs.

Two other switches on the index are pointed at a Western case for 0-3,
so only the text changes:
- the balance file stays GameParamNA (0-3 would load the Japanese and
  Asian discs' GameParam), so weapons, enemies, saves and online stay
  the European disc's;
- the server info's tags stay UK English's (the Asian ones were the
  Japanese world on the original servers).

These are writes to guest memory before the game runs: no hook and no
new lift. Three new lines in regions/BLES00932.inc; region_table.py
verify matches the index word, and the two jump tables were checked by
hand.

The PC's language picks Japanese or Korean on such a PC, and Chinese
only on a Traditional Chinese one (Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau).
PS3_SYS_LANG given at start still wins, with the original behaviour.
Trophy names stay English for all three: the European trophy set has
no names in them.

cedeb063a02402a1fd11b6fbfd3d07bc18507ebd.message:
European disc: hook handlers read the instruction at the disc's own address

Six instruction-hook handlers decode the instruction their hook runs after,
to find the register to rescale: the camera eases and the bow zoom
(des_cam_rate, des_cam_step, des_cam_keep), the foot IK (des_ik_rate), the
locked-on twist (des_twist_rate), and the sound and fade rates (keep_rate,
des_fade_rate). They read it at the hook's key, which stays the US address,
so on the European disc they read an unrelated instruction. The camera,
noise and fade fixes did nothing there, and the IK and twist fixes could
rescale an unrelated register.

des_region_addr() gives the running disc's address for a key, and
hook_insn() reads the instruction there. Every hook's instruction is the
same on both discs, so nothing else changes.

e4cc08a9a6ac2614ac9c0dd2e46d0ac466ee474c.message:
A processor without SSE4.1 gets a clear message, not a crash

Issues #349 and #350: a player's Pentium E5400 crashed with c000001d as the window opened. The runtime and the game module
are built with SSE4.1, and that CPU doesn't have it, so the first such instruction ended the program (pmovsxdq in
create_window, rsxc_d3d12.c). The crash dialog then asked them to report it, with nothing saying what was wrong.

des_cpu_check.cpp now asks the processor first, and says so if SSE4.1 is missing. It runs ahead of the C++ static
initializers, and is the one source here built without SSE4.1, so it can run on such a processor. The check comes
before setup too, so nobody spends time on a build that can't run.

AVX, LZCNT, AES and the like in the exe are in Microsoft's runtime and mbedTLS, which ask the CPU before using them. SSE4.1
is the only one the program assumes, so it is the only one checked.

The README now names the requirement. CI runs the check both ways (DES_TEST_OLD_CPU=1, and plainly) on both systems.

There is no processor without SSE4.1 here: the message was checked with DES_TEST_OLD_CPU=1, on the path it takes.

ec1b9e91020e42ece19b1ee2f4fc576991c6c9c1.message:
des_prework: free the last shader pass's texts once it is done

run_passes resets the precompile module before each target's pass, but
not after the last one. So whenever the start's shader pass runs (after a
session that drew new fragment-program variants, or after an update), the
last target's work stays allocated for the rest of the session: every
decompiled HLSL text (3,654 on the US disc, 44 MB), the programs and the
pipeline index's rows.

It now resets after the last pass too. Nothing reads that state after it:
the rows were handed to the renderer during the pass
(rsx_out_pso_index_add, _ready), and run_pass leaves s_state at 3, so
des_prework_status no longer asks for the counts. reset() waits for the
compile threads first.

Found with a scratch walk of the process heap 30 s into the Tutorial
(d3d12, the regression save, DES_PRECOMPILE=force): busy blocks 113.5 MB ->
69.1 MB; text blocks 10,711 (44.0 MB) -> 2,481 (0.3 MB); the heap's
committed regions 81.9 -> 53.8 MB. A start whose passes are all up to date
queued nothing, so it changes nothing there.

f586581cba40c3ac525015aab8e7d754cb432b59.message:
Physics cap: stuck arrows follow the pose, ragdolls blend by the leftover

Above 30 fps, arrows stuck in the player still hopped back at every physics
step (up to 3-4 cm at a run), and ragdolls and debris moved on unevenly at
each step. Both treated the frames since a step as one step's time, but at
144 fps a step of 1/30 s comes every 4 or 5 frames (28 or 35 ms).

- Stuck arrows (DES_PARTINTERP): a keyframed part is drawn from the pose the
  game drives it to every frame. des_kf_target, a new hook after 0x00011768
  in the stub to Havok's hard keyframe, keeps each body's last two poses,
  with the frame time of the pass that set them (from des_phys_kf: the
  passes run before des_phys_rate, so the game clock is a frame late).
  des_body_sample carries the last pose on by the game's own look-ahead, and
  des_body_sampled, a new hook after 0x011B1D6C past the sampler's call,
  writes it over the sampled transform. That is where the world would have
  the part if it stepped every frame. Without fresh poses it carries the
  last step on as before.
- Ragdolls, debris and a dead character's parts (DES_RAGINTERP): the blend
  is the cap's leftover (the game time the world has not stepped yet) over
  the step length, for a body that got the world's last step, instead of
  the game time since the body's step changed.
- The two hooks' European addresses are in BLES00932.inc. They need a
  re-lift, which setup does.

Measured with a scratch trace on the deep Palace save under the 1-1
archers, old and new from the same frames: how far an arrow's part moves
against the player from one frame to the next, 95th percentile.
- 144 fps: 32.7 mm before, 7.5 mm after (no cap: 6.2-7.1 mm).
- 60 fps: 54.6 mm before, 19.5 mm after (no cap: 17.8 mm).
- Ragdolls at 144 fps (26 bodies): the 95th percentile of the unevenness
  went from 1.26 mm to 0.75 mm.
See docs/71, "Steps of 4 or 5 frames".

fd0a6cb56aff00de1ea6c82edea55797ee267c7a.message:
port: collect Lua early above 30 fps, the game ran out of script memory

The game's Lua has its automatic collector off and collects from two
countdowns in game time, every 1.0 s and 0.5 s. Scripts make garbage per
frame, so at high frame rates there is several times more of it between two
collections. The two Lua states share a small heap. When an allocation fails,
luaD_throw(LUA_ERRMEM) finds no protected call on a character's script and
Lua calls exit(1): the window closes, in the middle of play.

Once a frame, above 30 fps, expire a countdown early when its state has made
64 KB since its last collection. The game then collects at its usual place
in the frame. It counts the guest's own bytes, so it doesn't depend on the PC.

DES_LUAGC=0 keeps the game's countdowns only. DES_LUAGC_LOG=1 prints each
state's memory once a second. DES_LUAGC_HOLD=1 is a test knob: the countdowns
never reach zero, which with DES_LUAGC=0 is the crash on demand.
