# Soulbrandt **Demon's Souls, running natively on PC.** [![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt?filter=v%2A&sort=semver&display_name=tag&label=release&color=orange)](https://github.com/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt/releases/latest) [![downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt/latest/total?label=downloads&color=brightgreen)](https://github.com/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt/releases/latest) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1565536292324769832?label=Discord&logo=discord&logoColor=white&color=5865F2)](https://discord.gg/BzmwDeca8s)
Soulbrandt is a PC port of *Demon's Souls* (PS3, 2009). The game's original code has been converted to run directly on Windows and Linux, with no emulator. You need your own copy of the game: the US version, **BLUS30443**, or the European version, **BLES00932** (both version 1.00, on disc or from the PlayStation Store), or the Japanese or Asian disc, **BCJS30022** or **BCAS20071**, with its 1.04 update. This project includes no game files. ## Status **0.1.2, the current release, is an alpha.** Download it from the [Releases](https://github.com/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt/releases) page. The game plays from start to finish (a tester has beaten it), but not every part has been tried on every setting, so expect bugs. What [isn't supported yet](#not-supported-yet) is below; please [report](#problems) anything you find. Questions and help: [Discord](https://discord.gg/BzmwDeca8s). ## Highlights - Up to 240 fps or unlocked, with the game's timing fixed. Up to 4K, ultrawide, 16:10 and HDR. - The US, European, Japanese and Asian versions, each with its languages, plus Japanese on the US disc and Japanese, Chinese and Korean on the European disc. - Online play on this project's own server: messages, bloodstains, ghosts, co-op, invasions and the Pantheon. - Roll in any direction while locked on, not only forward, back, left or right. - A stat respec in the Nexus (optional): get back the souls your levels cost and spend them again. - Keyboard and mouse, Xbox controllers, DualSense and DualShock 4. ## Features Press **F1** (or **L3 + R3** on a controller) at any time to open the menu. Most settings apply right away. Each setting has a short help text in the menu. **Picture** - Frame rates of 30 (the original), 60, 120, 144, 165 or 240 fps, a number of your own, or unlocked. The game's timing is fixed so it still plays the way it should. Above 60 fps is less tested. - Cutscenes play at 30 fps by default, as they judder above it. You can play them at your frame rate instead. - V-sync on or off, "Even frames" for smooth motion, and G-Sync / FreeSync. - Render resolution up to 300% (4K), ultrawide aspect ratios (21:9 and 32:9), and 16:10 for the Steam Deck's screen. - Anti-aliasing (FXAA or SMAA), anisotropic filtering up to 16x, texture filtering and a sharp scaling filter. - HDR on HDR displays (Windows), with settings for brightness, peak and shadows. - Turn off the game's depth of field and motion blur. - Window, borderless fullscreen, or exclusive fullscreen on Windows (Settings > Display > Display mode). Alt+Enter switches. - Two renderers (Settings > Display > Renderer): DirectX 12 and Vulkan. Windows starts on DirectX 12, except with a GeForce GTX 10 series card or older, which starts on Vulkan. Linux starts on Vulkan. **Controls** - Xbox controllers, DualSense and DualShock 4, over USB or Bluetooth, with vibration. Pick which controller the game uses when several are connected. - Keyboard and mouse, laid out like the Souls games on PC. To turn the camera with the mouse, turn on **Mouse look** in Settings > Controls. - Change which buttons and keys do what. - The game's button prompts show the buttons of the controller you're using, or your keys (Settings > Game > Button icons). - A deadzone for each stick, set as how far you tilt it, with a live picture of the stick (Settings > Controls). - Mouse sensitivity, inverted axes, and switching lock-on targets with a flick of the mouse. - **Roll in any direction while locked on**: the roll goes where the stick points. It's on by default; turn off **Roll toward the stick** in Settings > Controls for the original's four directions. - The mouse in the game's own menus: point and click. Experimental, and off by default. **HUD** - Move, resize, hide or show each part of the HUD. - Change its size, and choose where it goes on wide screens. **Game** - Skip the logos and the opening movie, and go straight into your last save. - **Stat respec**: the Maiden in Black, or the statue in front of where you wake in the Nexus, puts your stats back to your class's and gives back the souls your levels cost, to spend again. Off by default: turn on **Stat respec in the Nexus** in Settings > Game. - Use several soul items at once, as Drop does. On by default: turn off **Use several souls at once** in Settings > Game for the original's one at a time. - **Change Appearance** at the statue in front of where you wake in the Nexus: the game's own Edit Appearance, with your character. Off by default: turn on **Change appearance in the Nexus** in Settings > Game. - Choose the language in Settings > Game > Language. The European disc has English, French, German, Spanish and Italian, plus Japanese, Chinese (Traditional) and Korean; the US disc has English and Japanese; the Asian disc has English, Chinese (Traditional) and Korean. It starts in your PC's language when it can. A change needs a restart. **Online** - On by default, on this project's own server: messages, bloodstains, ghosts, co-op and invasions. - Players of every supported version play together. - The Pantheon in the Nexus: its statues show the characters of the players at the top of each board. - Setup asks for your online name. You can change it, or turn online play off, in Settings > Network. - A matchmaking password, so you meet only your friends. - Show or hide other players' messages, bloodstains and ghosts. **Mods** - Put mods in the mods folder (Mods in the menu or on the start screen, then Open the mods folder) and turn each one on or off there. Mods for the PS3 game or RPCS3 that replace the game's files work, and the game's own files are never changed. - A mod that changes how the game plays keeps you offline, so you never meet players without it. Mods that only change the look or sound keep online play. - When two mods change the same thing, the one higher in the list wins; the arrows on each mod move it. The list is kept in `mods\load_order.txt`, which mod managers can use too (docs/143). **The program** - A setup that builds the game from your copy, with an Original and an Enhanced preset (see [How to play](#how-to-play)). - Updates: the game checks for a new version at start and asks before changing anything. Your saves and settings are kept, and you can go back one version. - In the menu, the Large Sword of Moonlight is the cursor and a crystal lizard dances in the corner. Both can be turned off. - Trophies, with pop-ups and a tune from the game. Setup can bring your trophies and save across from RPCS3. - A Discord status: your profile shows that you're playing, the area you're in and whether you're online (Settings > Network). - **Report an issue** in the menu opens a GitHub issue with your PC's details filled in, and a zip to attach that includes your save, so the problem can be seen where it happened. It has no game files. If the game crashes or stops responding, a window offers to do the same. ## What you need - Your own copy of Demon's Souls for the PS3, as a folder with `PS3_GAME` in it: the US (BLUS30443) or European (BLES00932) disc, version 1.00, or the Japanese (BCJS30022) or Asian (BCAS20071) disc with its 1.04 update, as a folder or a `.pkg` file that setup has RPCS3 install. The US and European PlayStation Store versions (NPUB30910, NPEB01202) work once installed in RPCS3. Setup cannot use ISO files yet. - RPCS3, the free PS3 emulator. Setup has it unlock the game's encrypted files. You don't need the PS3 system software. (Or decrypt the files yourself: see below.) - Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit) with a graphics card that supports DirectX 12, or Linux (see [Linux](#linux)). - A processor with SSE4.1, which most have since about 2011. - An internet connection during setup. Setup downloads a compiler and Python (about 60 MB on Windows, about 130 MB on Linux). ## How to play These steps are for the release download. 1. Download the zip for Windows (`DemonsSoulsRecomp-X.Y.Z-windows.zip`) or the tarball for Linux (`DemonsSoulsRecomp-X.Y.Z-linux.tar.xz`), and unpack it into a folder of its own. 2. Start `Soulbrandt.exe` (on Linux, `Soulbrandt`). Setup opens. 3. Pick how setup gets your game's files: - **Import from RPCS3**: setup finds the game in RPCS3's list and has your RPCS3 unlock its files. It can bring your save, trophies and some settings across too. If RPCS3 has several copies, setup lets you pick one. - **I have decrypted files**: your disc copy, plus the 27 files you decrypted yourself (`EBOOT.elf` and the `.sdat` files). - **Show me how**: step by step, with free tools only. 4. Start the build. It runs on your PC and can take a while; setup shows an estimate first. You can stop it and carry on later. Setup builds in AppData on Windows (`~/.local/share` on Linux) and needs about 4 GB free there; to build on another drive, press **Change** next to **Build folder** first. 5. Pick a preset: **Original** plays as on the PS3; **Enhanced** sets 60 fps, a resolution that fits your display, SMAA, 16x anisotropic filtering, fullscreen, and HDR when Windows has HDR on for your display. Then a few choices (HDR among them, on Windows) and your online name. You can change anything later in Settings. Then press **Play**. **A portable install:** put an empty file named `portable.txt` next to `Soulbrandt.exe` before its first start. Your settings, logs and setup's build then stay inside the program's folder, as your saves already do, and you can move or rename that folder. Windows may warn you the first time you start `Soulbrandt.exe` ("Windows protected your PC"), because the program isn't signed yet. Click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. If RPCS3 is set to run as administrator, setup cannot start it: untick that in `rpcs3.exe`'s Properties. ### Linux CI builds the Linux program on every change, and each release includes a Linux download. It needs x86-64 Linux with glibc 2.35 or newer, a Vulkan driver, and `curl` and `tar`. Nothing else needs installing. The game renders on Vulkan, and setup prepares its shaders. If Vulkan can't start, the game falls back to its older renderer on vkd3d (DirectX 12 on Vulkan), which compiles shaders as it goes, with long pauses when a new area loads. Linux is newer and less tested than Windows. Players run it on desktop Linux and on the Steam Deck, on Vulkan ([docs/106](docs/106-setup-on-linux.md)). macOS is not supported. On a Steam Deck, keys and the mouse stay out of the game while its controls are on, because Steam's desktop layout presses them too. To use a keyboard on a docked Deck, set `PAD_KEYBOARD_WITH_PAD=1`. On a Steam Deck the game runs best with **Manual GPU Clock Control** at **800 MHz** and the **Thermal Power (TDP) Limit** at **15 W** (Quick Access menu > Performance). ### Online play Online play is on by default and uses this project's own server. Setup asks for your online name; you can change it, or turn online play off, in Settings > Network. Players of every supported version meet on the same server. RPCS3 players use other servers, so you won't meet them. What the server keeps about you is in the [privacy note](PRIVACY.md). ### Not supported yet - The Japanese and Asian discs without their 1.04 update, the Japanese PlayStation Store version (NPJA00102) and the US demo don't work. - Setup can't read ISO files, and it needs RPCS3 to unlock the game's files (or files you decrypted yourself). - macOS isn't supported, and running the Windows download through CrossOver hasn't been tested all the way through. Linux and the Steam Deck are less tested than Windows. ### Problems Use **Report an issue** in the menu (F1), or open an [issue](https://github.com/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt/issues). For questions and help, join the [Discord](https://discord.gg/BzmwDeca8s). Report security problems privately, as [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) says. ## Building from source This is the technical part. The full notes are in [`docs/`](docs/). **Tools** | Windows | Linux | |---|---| | Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools, LLVM (clang), CMake, Ninja, Python 3, Git Bash | clang or GCC, CMake, Ninja, Python 3, SDL2, Vulkan and FFmpeg development files, vkd3d ([details](docs/76-native-linux.md#building)) | On Windows, step 4 downloads FFmpeg's MPEG-2 video decoder for the game's movies (about 1 MB) and puts it beside `des_boot.exe`. If that download fails, the build says so and goes on, and the movies then need Microsoft's free [MPEG-2 Video Extension](https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9n95q1zzpmh4) from the Microsoft Store; without either, they play their sound with no picture. (A paid app called "MPEG-2 Video Extensions", from another publisher, is a different thing; you don't need it.) **From your copy of the game** - The game disc's files (`PS3_GAME`) - RPCS3, to decrypt the game's `EBOOT.BIN` - Optional: `libsre.prx` from your PS3 firmware, decrypted. The game doesn't need it; it is only for the `LIBSRE_OWN=0` fallback ([docs/88](docs/88-setup-screens.md)). **Steps** 1. Get this repository, and its runtime inside it: ```sh git clone https://github.com/JonathanDC64/Soulbrandt.git cd Soulbrandt git clone https://github.com/JonathanDC64/ps3recomp.git ``` `ps3recomp.pin` names the ps3recomp commit this version of the port needs. `python tools/release/pin_ps3recomp.py local` checks your checkout against it. 2. In RPCS3, decrypt `PS3_GAME/USRDIR/EBOOT.BIN` (*Utilities > Decrypt PS3 Binaries*) to `work/game/EBOOT.ELF`. Copy `PS3_GAME/ICON0.PNG` next to it, for the program's icon. 3. Convert the game's main code: ```sh python ps3recomp/tools/ppu_loader.py work/game/EBOOT.ELF -o work/loader python ps3recomp/tools/ppu_lifter.py work/game/EBOOT.ELF \ --functions work/loader/EBOOT.functions.json --hle-stubs work/loader/EBOOT.imports.json \ --override-funcs "0x167AC88=ds_malloc,0x167AC58=ds_free,0x273D38=des_move_post,0x724E40=des_menu_tick" \ --insn-hooks @port/insn_hooks.txt --shadow-stack --chunk-lines 150000 --output work/recomp -j 16 python ps3recomp/tools/gen_hle_nids.py --all --out work/recomp/hle_nid_table.cpp python scripts/apply_boot_patches.py work/recomp ``` Then the SPU code with `python scripts/build_spu.py --eboot work/game/EBOOT.ELF` ([docs/09](docs/09-spu-spurs.md)), which first cuts the SPU programs out of the EBOOT, and, if you have `libsre.prx`, libsre with `python scripts/build_libsre.py `. The lifter's flags above are also in `scripts/lift_ppu.json`, which setup reads; change both together. 4. Compile the runtime, then the game. On Windows: ```sh cmake -S ps3recomp -B ps3recomp/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DPS3RECOMP_RSX_HAL=ON cmake -S port -B port/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE= -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG= -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS_DEBUG= cmake --build ps3recomp/build --target ps3recomp_runtime rsx_shader_precompile cmake --build port/build --target des_boot --parallel 4 ``` `PS3RECOMP_RSX_HAL=ON` builds the portable renderer: DirectX 12 through it, the default, and Vulkan beside it (Settings > Display > Renderer). Without it the game runs on the legacy renderer only. Its first configure downloads glslang and SPIRV-Tools at their pinned commits. On Linux, see [docs/76](docs/76-native-linux.md#building). 5. Copy `tools/des/local.env.example` to `tools/des/local.env`, set `PS3_VFS_ROOT` in it to the folder that holds `PS3_GAME`, and start the game with `tools/des/play.sh`. A direct start of `des_boot.exe` goes through setup instead, and keeps its saves in `port/build/gamedata`. Everything made from your copy of the game stays in `work/` and `gamedata/`, which git

# 🎮 Featured Native Port — Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception (BCES01175)

> **Project Status:** 🚧 Active Development

## About the Project

**Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception** is the flagship project built using the **ps3recomp** framework.

The goal is to transform the original PlayStation 3 executable into a fully native desktop application without relying on runtime emulation. Instead of interpreting the Cell processor instructions at runtime, the game's PPU and SPU code is statically recompiled into native C/C++ and linked against the ps3recomp runtime.

This project demonstrates the capabilities of static recompilation on one of the most technically demanding PlayStation 3 games ever released.

## Current Progress

The project has already reached several important milestones:

- ✅ Native PPU recompilation
- ✅ SPU recompilation and runtime integration
- ✅ Runtime, threading and virtual memory operational
- ✅ File system, archives and asset loading
- ✅ Audio subsystem initialization
- ✅ SPURS initialization
- ✅ RSX command processing
- ✅ Native Direct3D 12 rendering backend
- 🔄 Graphics pipeline completion
- 🔄 SPU task scheduling and rendering synchronization

### Status Summary (current focus)

Boot, runtime, filesystem/asset loading, SPURS initialization and the native
Direct3D 12 render pipeline are operational (the loading screen renders
correctly). The active frontier is **Phase 11 — SPU Handling** of the porting
guide: the SPU/SPURS asset-decode **completion** path.

Concretely, the front-end **main menu is not yet reached**. It is gated on the
render state-machine marking each resource *decode-ready* once its SPU-decoded
geometry lands, and on the menu-scene transition trigger. The deterministic SPU
executor and the lifted geometry decode are validated live end-to-end; the
remaining work is wiring the decode/residence **completion** back into the
render-readiness chain and the menu-scene construction. This is the documented
"hard part" for a complex AAA title.

**Next milestone:** a functional, rendered main menu (Phase 12).

## Future Goals

After the game reaches a fully playable state, future work will include:

- Native keyboard and mouse support
- Controller improvements
- High and unlocked frame rate support
- Performance optimization
- Modern multiplayer support using contemporary networking technologies
- Modding tools and debugging utilities

## Vision

The long-term objective is to preserve **Uncharted 3** as a native PC application while showcasing the capabilities of the **ps3recomp** framework.

The knowledge and improvements gained during this project will benefit future PlayStation 3 recompilation efforts.

## Legal Notice

This repository does **not** include any copyrighted Sony Interactive Entertainment or Naughty Dog assets.

Users must provide their own legally obtained PlayStation 3 game files.
Only clean-room tooling, runtime libraries and original source code are distributed.

# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [360tools](https://github.com/sp00nznet/360tools) (Xbox 360 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — compile for Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM, whatever

## The Challenge

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

| Component | What It Is | Why It's Hard |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| **PPU** | PowerPC 64-bit main CPU | Custom ISA extensions, VMX/AltiVec SIMD |
| **6x SPU** | 128-bit SIMD vector processors | Proprietary ISA, 256KB local store, explicit DMA |
| **Memory** | 256MB XDR RAM | 128-byte alignment requirements, split bus |
| **LV2 Kernel** | Proprietary OS layer | ~300+ system calls, complex threading model |
| **PRX Modules** | Dynamic libraries | 100+ system libraries with intricate interdependencies |

We don't shy away from hard problems. We just break them into smaller ones.

## Architecture

```
ps3recomp/
├── tools/                    # Binary analysis & recompilation pipeline
│   ├── elf_parser.py         # Parse PS3 ELF/SELF/PRX binaries
│   ├── ppu_disasm.py         # PowerPC disassembler with PS3 extensions
│   ├── ppu_lifter.py         # PPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── spu_disasm.py         # SPU instruction set disassembler
│   ├── spu_lifter.py         # SPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── extract_spu_images.py # Extract embedded SPU images from PRX/ELF
│   ├── find_spu_functions.py # SPU function boundary detection
│   ├── wrap_spu_elf.py       # Wrap a raw SPU blob as a loadable ELF
│   ├── prx_analyzer.py       # Analyze PRX imports/exports and NIDs
│   ├── nid_database.py       # Function Name ID (NID) resolver
│   ├── find_functions.py     # Function boundary detection
│   └── generate_stubs.py     # Auto-generate HLE stubs from RPCS3 modules
│
├── runtime/                  # Core runtime for recompiled executables
│   ├── ppu/                  # PPU execution context
│   │   ├── ppu_context.h     # Register file, CR, LR, CTR, FPSCR
│   │   ├── ppu_memory.h      # Memory access macros (loads, stores, byte-swap)
│   │   └── ppu_ops.h         # Instruction operation macros
│   ├── spu/                  # SPU execution context
│   │   ├── spu_context.h     # 128×128-bit register file, 256KB local store, image_id
│   │   ├── spu_channels.c    # Channel ops + per-image function-table dispatch
│   │   ├── spu_helpers.h     # SPU intrinsics (incl. float conversions)
│   │   ├── spu_dma.h         # DMA (MFC) transfer engine
│   │   └── tests/            # Self-contained SPU runtime tests
│   ├── memory/               # Memory subsystem
│   │   ├── vm.h              # Virtual memory manager (256MB address space)
│   │   └── atomic.h          # PS3 atomic operations (lwarx/stwcx)
│   └── syscalls/             # LV2 kernel system call implementations
│       ├── sys_ppu_thread.h  # Thread creation/management
│       ├── sys_mutex.h       # Mutex/cond synchronization
│       ├── sys_memory.h      # Memory allocation/mapping
│       ├── sys_fs.h          # Filesystem operations
│       ├── sys_prx.h         # PRX module loading
│       └── lv2_syscall_table.h # Full syscall dispatch table
│
├── libs/                     # HLE library implementations (from RPCS3's module system)
│   ├── audio/                # cellAudio, cellAdec, libmixer, libsnd3, libsynth2
│   ├── video/                # cellGcmSys, cellResc, cellVideoOut, cellVpost, cellVdec
│   ├── input/                # cellPad, cellKb, cellMouse, cellGem
│   ├── network/              # cellNetCtl, cellHttp, cellHttps, cellSsl, sceNp*
│   ├── filesystem/           # cellFs, cellGame, cellSaveData, cellStorage
│   ├── system/               # cellSysutil, cellSysmodule, cellRtc, sysPrxForUser
│   ├── spurs/                # cellSpurs, cellFiber, cellSpursJq, cellDaisy (SPU task management)
│   ├── sync/                 # cellSync, cellSync2 (cross-PPU/SPU synchronization)
│   ├── codec/                # cellJpgDec, cellPngDec, cellGifDec, cellPamf, cellDmux, cellAdecAtrac3p, cellAdecCelp8, cellVdecDivx
│   ├── font/                 # cellFont, cellFontFT, cellFreeType, cellL10n
│   └── misc/                 # cellScreenshot, cellSubdisplay, cellImeJp, cellVideoExport, cellMusicExport, cellGameRecording, etc.
│
├── include/ps3emu/           # Public API headers
│   ├── ps3types.h            # Fundamental PS3 types (u8-u128, s8-s64, be_t<>)
│   ├── endian.h              # Big-endian <-> little-endian conversion
│   ├── nid.h                 # NID hashing and lookup
│   ├── module.h              # Module registration framework
│   └── error_codes.h         # PS3 system error codes (CELL_OK, CELL_E*)
│
├── templates/project/        # Starter template for new game ports
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # Build system
│   ├── main.cpp              # Application entry point
│   ├── stubs.cpp             # Game-specific function overrides
│   └── config.toml           # Recompiler configuration
│
├── config/                   # Reference configurations
│   └── example.toml          # Example recompilation config
│
├── patches/                  # Patches for upstream tools
│   └── xenonrecomp-ppu.patch # XenonRecomp adaptations for PPU (Cell != Xenon)
│
└── docs/                     # Documentation (incl. ARCHITECTURE, RUNTIME, SPU_LIFTER, RSX_GRAPHICS, ...)
    ├── ARCHITECTURE.md        # Cell processor and recomp pipeline deep-dive
    ├── GETTING_STARTED.md     # How to recompile your first PS3 game
    ├── MODULE_STATUS.md       # Implementation status of all HLE modules
    ├── MODULES_REFERENCE.md   # Detailed per-module documentation (all 77+)
    ├── RUNTIME.md             # Runtime reference: VM, PPU/SPU contexts, types
    ├── SYSCALLS.md            # All LV2 kernel syscall implementations
    ├── NID_SYSTEM.md          # PS3 NID linking system explained
    ├── TOOLS.md               # Recompiler pipeline tools reference
    ├── BUILDING.md            # Build system, compilers, platform notes
    ├── GAME_PORTING_GUIDE.md  # Step-by-step game porting walkthrough
    └── PLATFORM_ABSTRACTION.md # Win32/POSIX cross-platform details
```

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [360tools](https://github.com/sp00nznet/360tools) and [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) projects, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

# God of War II HD — native macOS port by static recompilation

**God of War II HD** (PS3, `NPUA80491`) running **natively on Apple Silicon**:
no emulator, no JIT. The PowerPC (PPU) and Cell SPU code is translated ahead
of time into C/C++, compiled with clang for arm64, and runs on a
reimplementation of the PS3 OS and libraries with **Metal** for graphics,
**VideoToolbox** for cutscenes and **CoreAudio** for sound.

> This repository contains **no game code and no game assets**. Like
> [Dusk](https://duskport.com/dusk/), you bring your own legally dumped copy,
> and the setup kit decrypts, translates and builds it **on your machine**.

| | |
|---|---|
| ![Combat in the palace of Rhodes](docs/img/palace-combat.jpg) | ![The Colossus of Rhodes through the palace windows](docs/img/colossus-window.jpg) |
| ![Blades of Chaos effects](docs/img/blades-of-chaos.jpg) | ![Volumetric light in the palace](docs/img/palace-lighting.jpg) |

*Captured from the native Metal renderer on an M-series Mac (1280×720 internal,
MetalFX upscaled).*

---

## Status

| Area | State |
|---|---|
| Boot, intro videos, logos | ✅ natural path, videos decoded by VideoToolbox |
| Main menu, New Game, saves | ✅ memory-card saves on disk |
| Rhodes gameplay (combat, HUD, particles, lighting) | ✅ 45–60 fps on Apple Silicon (Mac, Metal; measured numbers in [Estado por plataforma e desempenho](#estado-por-plataforma-e-desempenho-2026-10-02)) |
| Colossus of Rhodes fight | 🟡 playable; the bronze drape on its shoulder is skinned with a sheared bone matrix (under investigation) |
| After the Colossus cutscene | ✅ fixed 2026-09-22: a lifted SPU program (spu1) was writing into the PPU code segment, which produced `ICALL-BAD 0x80029F47`; validated with 305 s of New Game → gameplay, 0 ICALL-BAD ([log](https://github.com/andrebrumdev/ps3recomp/blob/spurs-bringup/docs/re_sessions/2026-09-22-spu1-6074-texto-corrompido.md)) |
| iOS (iPhone) and Android (tablet) | 🟡 experimental; see [Estado por plataforma e desempenho](#estado-por-plataforma-e-desempenho-2026-10-02) (pt-BR) |
| Audio | 🟡 music/SFX through the SCREAM mixer SPU program; clock still partly host-driven |
| Controllers | ✅ DualShock 4 / DualSense / Xbox / MFi via GameController, keyboard + mouse |

The engineering log (every wall, the hypotheses refuted by measurement and the
fixes) lives in [`docs/`](docs/) and in the engine repository.

## How it works

```
EBOOT.ELF (your copy, decrypted)
   │
   ├── PPU  ── ppu_lifter.py ──► ~650 C++ chunks, 69k functions ──┐
   │          (functions.json: curated function bounds,           │
   │           jump tables, mid-function entry points)            │
   │                                                               ├─► clang -O1/-O2 arm64 ─► g2play
   └── SPU  ── spu_lifter.py ──► SPU jobs / SPURS policy modules ─┘            │
                                                                                ▼
                               ps3recomp runtime (MIT): LV2 syscalls, PPU threads,
                               lwmutex/lwcond, SPURS, FIOS, cellGcm → RSX FIFO walker
                               → Metal backend (MSL from RSX VP/FP), cellVdec → VideoToolbox,
                               cellAudio → CoreAudio, cellPad → GameController
```

What makes a PS3 title hard to recompile, and what this port had to solve:

- **Cell B.E.**: one PPU plus up to six SPUs with their own ISA and 256 KB local
  store; SPU programs (SPURS workloads, job chains, policy modules) are lifted
  separately and scheduled on host threads.
- **Indirect control flow**: 64-bit PowerPC function descriptors (`.opd`/TOC),
  vtables, computed `bctr` jump tables and mid-function entries, all of which
  the lifter must resolve statically.
- **RSX**: the command FIFO (with CALL/JUMP, wait points and ring wraps) is
  walked on the host, and the NV40-class vertex/fragment programs are
  decompiled to Metal Shading Language.
- **Faithfulness over shortcuts**: fixes follow console behaviour (RPCS3 is
  used as a measurement oracle via its GDB stub); diagnostics are gated off by
  default.

## Launcher (macOS)

![GoW2 Recomp launcher](docs/img/launcher-play.jpg)

`GoW2 Recomp.app` is a native SwiftUI launcher in the spirit of Dusk:
point it at your own `EBOOT.ELF` and `USRDIR`, pick graphics/audio/control
options, manage mods and play. Build it with:

```
launcher/macos/build_app.sh     # -> ./GoW2 Recomp.app
```

- **No Python, no interpreter**: validation, config, autosave checks (SHA-256
  per file) and mod import run in Swift inside the app.
- **RPCS3-style patches**: the launcher computes your executable's RPCS3 PPU
  hash by streaming the ELF (for NPUA80491 01.00 it is
  `PPU-31e32090ea333902dbf322c24487bab7e8c8d0d1`), reads RPCS3's
  `patch.yml` (anchors, aliases, configurable values) or any `.yml` you
  import, and passes the enabled ones to the runtime (`PS3_PATCH_FILE`). Data
  patches (e.g. aspect ratio) take effect; code patches are flagged, because
  the code was already recompiled and would need a re-lift.
- Design system in [`launcher/macos/MASTER.md`](launcher/macos/MASTER.md).

## Bring your own game (macOS kit)

A [Dusk](https://duskport.com/dusk/)-style kit: point it at your own game
folder (`PS3_GAME`, from RPCS3's `dev_hdd0/game/NPUA80491` or your PS3) and
your license (`UP9000-NPUA80491_00-GODOFWARIIHDUS00.rap`), and it builds the
native binary on your Mac:

```bash
./kit/setup.sh /path/to/PS3_GAME        # finds the .rap in RPCS3's exdata or ~/Downloads
./jogar_g2.sh
```

`setup.sh` does the following:

1. It decrypts `EBOOT.BIN` itself, the same way RPCS3 does (engine
   `tools/unself`).
2. It recompiles the PPU code with the pinned lifter, the patch scripts and a
   small delta.
3. It recompiles the seven SPU programs.
4. It extracts the movies from your `gow2.psarc`.
5. It links `./g2play`.

Every generated file is checked against the hashes in `kit/`. The result is
byte-identical to the build the project tests. Details are in
[`kit/README.md`](kit/README.md).

Controls: WASD move, mouse camera, Space/E/J/K = ✕/○/□/△, Enter = Start,
F11 or Cmd+Enter = fullscreen, Esc releases the mouse.

## State of the art in game recompilation

| Project | Platform | Approach | Notable result |
|---|---|---|---|
| [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) | Nintendo 64 (MIPS) | Static recompilation to C | *Zelda 64: Recompiled* and many more; modding framework |
| [XenonRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/XenonRecomp) | Xbox 360 (PowerPC) | Static recompilation to C++ | *Unleashed Recompiled*, the first 360 recomp playable start to finish |
| ReXGlue | Xbox 360 | Static recompilation | Tooling for 360 ports |
| PS2Recomp | PlayStation 2 (MIPS R5900) | Static recompilation | Early stage |
| [psprecomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/psprecomp) | PSP (Allegrex MIPS) | Static recompilation to C | Toolkit |
| [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) | PlayStation 3 (PPU) | Static recompilation runtime | The base of this port's engine |
| **This port** | **PlayStation 3 (PPU + SPU)** | **Static recompilation, PPU and SPU, native Metal** | **A commercial PS3 title in gameplay on macOS/arm64** |
| [Dusk / Dusklight](https://duskport.com/) | GameCube | Decompilation (source rebuilt by hand) | *Twilight Princess* native port; you supply the ISO |
| [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net/) | PlayStation 3 | Emulation (LLVM JIT/AOT) | The reference used here as an oracle |

Catalogs: [Recompendium](https://nio03.github.io/unricopie/en/),
[decompilation & recompilation list](https://readonlymemo.com/decompilation-projects-and-n64-recompiled-list/).

Static recompilation sits between emulation and decompilation: like a
decompilation it produces native code with no interpreter or JIT (so it can
use native APIs such as Metal directly), but like an emulator it needs no
hand-written game source. It only needs the original binary, which is why the
user has to supply it.

## Project Structure

The root holds only entry points; everything else lives in a folder with one
purpose. The full map (with the old root path of every moved script) is
[`scripts/README.md`](scripts/README.md), and `scripts/check_layout.sh` keeps
the root clean.

```
gow2-recomp/
├── jogar_g2.sh rodar_gow2*.sh testar_fix.sh gow2_launcher.py  # launchers
├── env_gow2.sh                 # environment recipe (sourced by launchers, smokes, iOS/Android builds)
```

1301326557.description: Native PC port of Sony's Bigduck (Rubber Ducky) PS3 tech demo via ps3recomp static recompilation
1301326557.readme_excerpt:
# Rubber Ducky Tech Demo — Static Recompilation

> A native PC port of Sony's *Bigduck* E3 2006 tech demo, rebuilt from the PS3 binary through static recompilation.

![The demo running natively on Windows](docs/images/ducky.png)

The **Rubber Ducky** (internally *Bigduck*) demo was one of the first pieces of PS3 tech Sony showed publicly — a bathtub full of rubber ducks and toy boats bobbing on simulated water, shown at E3 2006 to sell the PlayStation 3's RSX + Cell horsepower. It later shipped as a downloadable SDK sample (`NPEA00003`). It never received a standalone PC release.

This project takes the demo's PS3 `EBOOT` binary, disassembles every PowerPC function, lifts them to C++, and links against [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) — HLE runtime libraries that replace the PS3 operating system with native host implementations. The result is a standalone Windows executable, no emulator required.

The demo ships as a **debug build with a full symbol table and DWARF** — a rare luxury for a PS3 port. All 8,530 recompiled functions carry their real names (`_jsGcmAllocateMemory`, `gmmAllocFixed`, `spu_memcpy_elf`, …), which makes the lifted code and every crash backtrace directly readable.

## Status

The demo boots, runs its own code, and **renders its own scene**: tiled walls, the blue mosaic tub, the checkered towel, the chrome faucet, and the rubber duck. The bathroom above is the port's own output, captured from the running executable.

| | |
|---|---|
| Title | Rubber Ducky / *Bigduck* Sample (`NPEA00003`) |
| Engine | Sony Cell graphics sample (jsGcm / PSGL "debugrsx", Gmm allocator) |
| ELF | ET_EXEC, PowerPC64 big-endian, self-contained — **debug build**, 8,582-symbol `.symtab` |
| Functions lifted | 13,484 emitted from 8,530 detected (99.0% recall vs. `.symtab`) |
| Target | Windows x86-64 (clang-cl + Ninja) |
| Renders | Scene geometry, textures, cube maps, the duck |
| Not yet | The simulated water surface — see [Known Issues](docs/STATUS.md#known-issues) |

Roughly 4–5 fps with the SPU simulation running (about 16 M interpreted SPU instructions per frame on one thread), or ~12 fps without it.

Full per-phase detail lives in **[docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md)**.

## Quick start

You must supply your own legally obtained copy of the demo — this repo contains no game binary or assets.

```bash
# ps3recomp checked out alongside this repo, on the research/proto-builds branch
cmake -S ../ps3recomp -B ../ps3recomp/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl
cmake --build ../ps3recomp/build

# generate the lifted C++ from your own EBOOT, then build the harness
#   (full sequence: docs/PIPELINE.md)
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl
cmake --build build

PS3_VFS_ROOT=input RD_SPU_INTERP=1 RT_DISPLAY_BY_SIZE=1 TEX_OFF_BIAS=3 RSX_ACCUM_FRAME=1 \
  ./build/rubberducky input/EBOOT.elf
```

The full reproducible pipeline — SELF carve, analysis, symbol extraction, NID table, lifting, post-lift patches — is in **[docs/PIPELINE.md](docs/PIPELINE.md)**.

### Prerequisites

- Python 3.9+
- CMake 3.20+, Ninja
- LLVM/clang-cl 14+ (the loader uses `__builtin_bswap` and weak symbols MSVC lacks)
- A Visual Studio 2022 dev environment (MSVC headers + Windows SDK for clang-cl)
- [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) on the `research/proto-builds` branch, at `../ps3recomp`

## Project structure

```
rubberducky/
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── CMakeLists.txt          # links the runtime + the generic boot harness
├── config.toml             # analysis-driven pipeline config
├── docs/                   # status, pipeline, changelog
├── input/                  # your own EBOOT.elf + USRDIR assets (gitignored)
├── meta/                   # analysis outputs, regenerated from your ELF (gitignored)
├── tools/
│   ├── post_lift.py        # idempotent post-lift patches (allocator override)
│   └── symrva.py
└── src/
    ├── boot_main.cpp       # ps3recomp boot harness, rebranded for this title
    ├── rd_malloc.cpp       # guest heap override (bump allocator)
    ├── rd_spu.cpp          # raw-SPU MMIO / MFC proxy DMA
    ├── compat/             # <dirent.h>/<unistd.h> Win32 shims
    ├── gen/                # generated HLE NID table (committed)
    └── recomp/             # lifted C++, ~105 MB (gitignored; regenerate)
```

## Documentation

- **[docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md)** — per-phase progress, what works, known issues
- **[docs/PIPELINE.md](docs/PIPELINE.md)** — the reproducible build pipeline and how it fits together
- **[docs/CHANGELOG.md](docs/CHANGELOG.md)** — release history

## Related projects

- **[ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp)** — the PS3 HLE runtime this builds against
- **[N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp)** — the project that proved static recompilation works at scale

## Legal

This project contains no proprietary Sony code, game binaries, encryption keys, or copyrighted assets. It is a clean-room reimplementation of PS3 system libraries paired with automated binary-translation tools. Everything derived from the demo's own binary — the lifted C++ under `src/recomp/`, the analysis JSON under `meta/`, and the extracted SPU images — is generated locally from a copy you supply and is not committed here.

Licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

1304063097.description: Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
1304063097.readme_excerpt:
# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [360tools](https://github.com/sp00nznet/360tools) (Xbox 360 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — compile for Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM, whatever

## The Challenge

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

| Component | What It Is | Why It's Hard |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| **PPU** | PowerPC 64-bit main CPU | Custom ISA extensions, VMX/AltiVec SIMD |
| **6x SPU** | 128-bit SIMD vector processors | Proprietary ISA, 256KB local store, explicit DMA |
| **Memory** | 256MB XDR RAM | 128-byte alignment requirements, split bus |
| **LV2 Kernel** | Proprietary OS layer | ~300+ system calls, complex threading model |
| **PRX Modules** | Dynamic libraries | 100+ system libraries with intricate interdependencies |

We don't shy away from hard problems. We just break them into smaller ones.

## Architecture

```
ps3recomp/
├── tools/                    # Binary analysis & recompilation pipeline
│   ├── elf_parser.py         # Parse PS3 ELF/SELF/PRX binaries
│   ├── ppu_disasm.py         # PowerPC disassembler with PS3 extensions
│   ├── ppu_lifter.py         # PPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── spu_disasm.py         # SPU instruction set disassembler
│   ├── spu_lifter.py         # SPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── extract_spu_images.py # Extract embedded SPU images from PRX/ELF
│   ├── find_spu_functions.py # SPU function boundary detection
│   ├── wrap_spu_elf.py       # Wrap a raw SPU blob as a loadable ELF
│   ├── prx_analyzer.py       # Analyze PRX imports/exports and NIDs
│   ├── nid_database.py       # Function Name ID (NID) resolver
│   ├── find_functions.py     # Function boundary detection
│   └── generate_stubs.py     # Auto-generate HLE stubs from RPCS3 modules
│
├── runtime/                  # Core runtime for recompiled executables
│   ├── ppu/                  # PPU execution context
│   │   ├── ppu_context.h     # Register file, CR, LR, CTR, FPSCR
│   │   ├── ppu_memory.h      # Memory access macros (loads, stores, byte-swap)
│   │   └── ppu_ops.h         # Instruction operation macros
│   ├── spu/                  # SPU execution context
│   │   ├── spu_context.h     # 128×128-bit register file, 256KB local store, image_id
│   │   ├── spu_channels.c    # Channel ops + per-image function-table dispatch
│   │   ├── spu_helpers.h     # SPU intrinsics (incl. float conversions)
│   │   ├── spu_dma.h         # DMA (MFC) transfer engine
│   │   └── tests/            # Self-contained SPU runtime tests
│   ├── memory/               # Memory subsystem
│   │   ├── vm.h              # Virtual memory manager (256MB address space)
│   │   └── atomic.h          # PS3 atomic operations (lwarx/stwcx)
│   └── syscalls/             # LV2 kernel system call implementations
│       ├── sys_ppu_thread.h  # Thread creation/management
│       ├── sys_mutex.h       # Mutex/cond synchronization
│       ├── sys_memory.h      # Memory allocation/mapping
│       ├── sys_fs.h          # Filesystem operations
│       ├── sys_prx.h         # PRX module loading
│       └── lv2_syscall_table.h # Full syscall dispatch table
│
├── libs/                     # HLE library implementations (from RPCS3's module system)
│   ├── audio/                # cellAudio, cellAdec, libmixer, libsnd3, libsynth2
│   ├── video/                # cellGcmSys, cellResc, cellVideoOut, cellVpost, cellVdec
│   ├── input/                # cellPad, cellKb, cellMouse, cellGem
│   ├── network/              # cellNetCtl, cellHttp, cellHttps, cellSsl, sceNp*
│   ├── filesystem/           # cellFs, cellGame, cellSaveData, cellStorage
│   ├── system/               # cellSysutil, cellSysmodule, cellRtc, sysPrxForUser
│   ├── spurs/                # cellSpurs, cellFiber, cellSpursJq, cellDaisy (SPU task management)
│   ├── sync/                 # cellSync, cellSync2 (cross-PPU/SPU synchronization)
│   ├── codec/                # cellJpgDec, cellPngDec, cellGifDec, cellPamf, cellDmux, cellAdecAtrac3p, cellAdecCelp8, cellVdecDivx
│   ├── font/                 # cellFont, cellFontFT, cellFreeType, cellL10n
│   └── misc/                 # cellScreenshot, cellSubdisplay, cellImeJp, cellVideoExport, cellMusicExport, cellGameRecording, etc.
│
├── include/ps3emu/           # Public API headers
│   ├── ps3types.h            # Fundamental PS3 types (u8-u128, s8-s64, be_t<>)
│   ├── endian.h              # Big-endian <-> little-endian conversion
│   ├── nid.h                 # NID hashing and lookup
│   ├── module.h              # Module registration framework
│   └── error_codes.h         # PS3 system error codes (CELL_OK, CELL_E*)
│
├── templates/project/        # Starter template for new game ports
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # Build system
│   ├── main.cpp              # Application entry point
│   ├── stubs.cpp             # Game-specific function overrides
│   └── config.toml           # Recompiler configuration
│
├── config/                   # Reference configurations
│   └── example.toml          # Example recompilation config
│
├── patches/                  # Patches for upstream tools
│   └── xenonrecomp-ppu.patch # XenonRecomp adaptations for PPU (Cell != Xenon)
│
└── docs/                     # Documentation (incl. ARCHITECTURE, RUNTIME, SPU_LIFTER, RSX_GRAPHICS, ...)
    ├── ARCHITECTURE.md        # Cell processor and recomp pipeline deep-dive
    ├── GETTING_STARTED.md     # How to recompile your first PS3 game
    ├── MODULE_STATUS.md       # Implementation status of all HLE modules
    ├── MODULES_REFERENCE.md   # Detailed per-module documentation (all 77+)
    ├── RUNTIME.md             # Runtime reference: VM, PPU/SPU contexts, types
    ├── SYSCALLS.md            # All LV2 kernel syscall implementations
    ├── NID_SYSTEM.md          # PS3 NID linking system explained
    ├── TOOLS.md               # Recompiler pipeline tools reference
    ├── BUILDING.md            # Build system, compilers, platform notes
    ├── GAME_PORTING_GUIDE.md  # Step-by-step game porting walkthrough
    └── PLATFORM_ABSTRACTION.md # Win32/POSIX cross-platform details
```

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [360tools](https://github.com/sp00nznet/360tools) and [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) projects, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

## Module Status

We're building HLE implementations based on RPCS3's module system. **97 modules complete, 1 partial (media decode), 283 files, ~74,000 lines of code.**

| Category | Modules | Status |
|----------|---------|--------|
| **Kernel Threading** | sys_ppu_thread, sys_mutex, sys_cond, sys_semaphore, sys_rwlock | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Events** | sys_event (queues, ports, flags), sys_timer | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Memory** | sys_memory, sys_mmapper (containers, shared mem) | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Filesystem** | sys_fs (path mapping, real I/O) | ✅ Complete |
| **Filesystem** | cellFs (real file I/O, dir ops, stat, path translation) | ✅ Complete |
| **Save System** | cellSaveData (callback-driven, PARAM.SFO), cellGame | ✅ Complete |
| **Input** | cellPad (XInput/SDL2), cellKb, cellMouse | ✅ Complete |
| **Audio** | cellAudio (WASAPI/SDL2, mixing thread, multi-port) | ✅ Complete |
| **Video Output** | cellVideoOut (resolution config, 720p default) | ✅ Complete |
| **Codecs** | cellPngDec, cellJpgDec, cellGifDec (stb_image) | ✅ Complete |
| **Font** | cellFont (stb_truetype backend + fallback metrics) | ✅ Complete |
| **Network** | sys_net (BSD sockets), cellNet, cellNetCtl, cellHttpUtil, cellSsl, sceNp*, sceNpTrophy | ✅ Complete |
| **Hardware** | cellUsbd (USB), cellCamera (PS Eye), cellGem (PS Move) — stub, no devices | ✅ Complete |
| **Sync** | cellSync (atomic spinlocks, LF queue), cellSync2 (OS-backed) | ✅ Complete |
| **System** | cellRtc, cellMsgDialog, cellOskDialog, cellUserInfo, cellGameExec | ✅ Complete |
| **Localization** | cellL10n (UTF-8/16/32/UCS-2, ISO-8859-1, generic converter) | ✅ Complete |
| **Resolution** | cellResc (display modes, scaling, interlace, aspect ratio) | ✅ Complete |
| **Fibers** | cellFiber (PPU fibers via Windows Fibers/ucontext) | ✅ Complete |
| **AV Config** | cellAvconfExt (audio output info, gamma, sound availability) | ✅ Complete |
| **Input Util** | cellKey2char (HID scancode → Unicode, US-101 layout) | ✅ Complete |
| **Graphics** | cellGcmSys (cmd buffer, IO mapping, tile/zcull, flip handlers, timestamps, FIFO walker + ring recycle), RSX command processor (NV47xx parsing, state tracking, backend callbacks), **live D3D12 backend** (executes the title's real NV4097 vertex/fragment programs — indexed draws, per-draw VP constants + textures, render-to-texture, MRT, FP predication), null backend (Win32 window) | ✅ Complete |
| **SPURS** | cellSpurs (management APIs, event flags, task/workload tracking), cellSpursJq (job queues with wait/signal), cellDaisy (real ring buffer FIFO) | ✅ Complete |
| **Core Runtime** | cellSysutil (BGM, cache, disc), cellSysmodule, sysPrxForUser (real lwmutex/lwcond/threads) | ✅ Complete |
| **Media Pipeline** | cellPamf (real PAMF header + stream descriptor parsing), cellDmux (callback sequencing), cellVdec/cellAdec (PICOUT/PCMOUT callbacks, no actual decode — needs FFmpeg), cellSail (state machine) | 🔨 Partial |
| **HTTP/HTTPS** | cellHttp (real HTTP/1.1 via native sockets), cellHttps (TLS stub with cert management) | ✅ Complete |
| **Misc/Export** | cellSubdisplay, cellImeJp, cellVideoExport, cellMusicExport, cellPhotoExport/Import, cellGameRecording, cellPrint, cellRemotePlay | ✅ Complete |

Full status tracking: [docs/MODULE_STATUS.md](docs/MODULE_STATUS.md)

## Documentation

We've written extensive docs covering every aspect of the project. Whether you're contributing, porting a game, or just trying to understand how PS3 static recompilation works, there's a doc for you.

| Document | What It Covers |
|----------|---------------|
| **[Getting Started](docs/GETTING_STARTED.md)** | Prerequisites, installation, first recompilation walkthrough |
| **[Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)** | Cell processor overview, recomp pipeline stages, memory model, comparison with RPCS3 |

| **[Custom Modules](docs/CUSTOM_MODULES.md)** | Step-by-step tutorial for writing new HLE modules — NID system, calling convention bridge, patterns |
| **[FAQ & Troubleshooting](docs/FAQ.md)** | Common questions, build errors, runtime crashes, lifter issues, performance tips |
| **[Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)** | Development setup, code style, PR guidelines, ways to contribute |
| **[Runtime Reference](docs/RUNTIME.md)** | Virtual memory manager, PPU/SPU execution contexts, type system, endianness, syscall dispatch, DMA engine |
| **[Syscall Reference](docs/SYSCALLS.md)** | All LV2 kernel syscalls: threading, sync, events, timers, memory, filesystem |
| **[NID System](docs/NID_SYSTEM.md)** | How PS3 function linking works, NID computation, module registration framework |
| **[Module Reference](docs/MODULES_REFERENCE.md)** | Detailed documentation for all 93+ HLE modules — what they do and how they're implemented |
| **[Module Status](docs/MODULE_STATUS.md)** | Quick-reference status table for all modules |
| **[RSX Graphics](docs/RSX_GRAPHICS.md)** | RSX GPU translation architecture: command processor, D3D12/Vulkan backends, shader strategy |
| **[Tools Reference](docs/TOOLS.md)** | Every recompiler pipeline tool documented: ELF parser, disassembler, lifter, NID database |
| **[SPU Lifter](docs/SPU_LIFTER.md)** | SPU ISA decoding/lifting, the runtime model (local store, channels, DMA, per-image dispatch), and the SPU tests |
| **[Platform Abstraction](docs/PLATFORM_ABSTRACTION.md)** | How we handle Win32 vs POSIX: threading, sockets, timers, audio, memory, fibers |

## Getting Started

> **Prerequisites**: Python 3.10+, CMake 3.20+, a C17/C++20 compiler (MSVC 19.x, GCC 12+, or Clang 15+)

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp.git
cd ps3recomp

# Install Python tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Analyze a decrypted PS3 ELF
python tools/elf_parser.py /path/to/EBOOT.ELF --output analysis/

# Disassemble PPU code
python tools/ppu_disasm.py analysis/EBOOT.ELF --output disasm/

# Lift to C
python tools/ppu_lifter.py disasm/ --output recomp/

# Build with the runtime
cd templates/project
cmake -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
```

See [docs/GETTING_STARTED.md](docs/GETTING_STARTED.md) for the full walkthrou

0a697c278024c1c24b1873aa0a6044ca2f06b6c7.message:
threadman: a park hands the CPU over, it does not race for it

Releasing the baton and taking it straight back makes "give the CPU away" a
race with the host's own scheduler, which is free to run the parking thread
first. Measured on this branch: a thread started immediately before a
DelayThread had not been scheduled yet when the delay ended (a park waits
REAL_TICK_US of *host* time for a wakeup a delay never gets), so the delay
returned before the thread it was supposed to let through had run. The suite's
own test failed on it in about one run in ten.

So a park does not take the CPU back while someone wants it: while a started
thread has never run (cpu_pending, set by StartThread before the host thread
exists and cleared by the thread itself on its first acquisition -- cleared
while it holds the baton, which is what makes the ordering a guarantee rather
than a hope), or while a host thread is already sitting in baton_acquire
(g_baton_waiters). Neither is waiting for anything else, so the wait cannot be
a deadlock, and it is capped anyway: a park that gives up says so once and
counts it, because a wait that was never needed has to stay distinguishable
from one that timed out.

The delay's real duration is unchanged. What changes is that after the handover
the two threads are equal peers, which is what hardware does -- so the test
asserts that the thread *ran* (stage >= 1) rather than where it stopped. The
old assertion encoded a race between two equal threads and flaked on exactly
that once the handover was in place; the failing run now reports its own
numbers (stage, started, handovers, expiries) instead of needing a second one.

Measured: 190 consecutive runs of the suite with the handover, 0 failures
(150 + 40, two samples), against 5 failures in 74 runs without it -- and 2 in
150 in a later, quieter sample, which is why the argument above is structural
and the numbers are named as samples rather than as a rate.

4c61dcdb35b1d66ae1049b73bf186296981efaa7.message:
hle: rate-limit the unimplemented-call message, and widen the counter behind it

Bringing a game up produces runs that spin on a call nobody implemented. Two
things in this file break exactly there -- in the instruments that exist to be
read in exactly that situation.

The message naming the call printed once per call. A single 30-second run of
LocoRoco (UCES00304) waiting on one stubbed call wrote 26 926 971 lines -- 1.37
GB, measured -- for one NID worth naming. It is now printed a bounded number of
times, followed by one line that says so and gives the running total. That
second line is the point: a message that went quiet because it was silenced must
not read as a message that stopped happening, since "bringing a game up is
largely the process of watching those messages stop appearing" is how progress
is measured here. The total stays available as psp_hle_unimplemented_calls().

The same run made psp_hle_dump_recent print `last -1396532617 firmware calls`.
The counter behind it was an `int` fed by every zero-returning call, so it
wrapped -- and the wrap travelled into the dump, which printed a negative count
and computed its ring index as (g_zero_n - i) % ZERO_HISTORY, going negative
with it: an out-of-bounds read on top of a nonsense number. The counter is a
uint64_t, the header reports the true total next to the ring, and the index is
now computed unsigned.

Neither is visible on a short run, which is why both survived: a game that makes
a handful of unimplemented calls, or returns zero a few thousand times, shows
nothing wrong.

test_hle.c covers the ceiling, the exact total and the dump's header: 100 000
calls at an unregistered NID, every one counted, at most nine lines printed.
ctest 10/10.

6340c7af23f20cfa0d0a6b00cbfe6ce26cf3eed7.message:
emit: keep a terminal transfer terminal, so it stays a sibling jump

A body that ends by transferring into another body -- falling out into a gap
owned by another function, `j` to a function entry, the taken path of a likely
branch -- is emitted as a call followed by `return`. Only a call in tail
position lets the compiler reuse the caller's frame instead of growing one, and
the stack observation these three sites wrap around that call is a statement
after it, so clang has to grow a frame for a transfer that pushes nothing on the
hardware.

Measured on one machine (clang -O2, arm64), on the two shapes alone:

    { ...; callee(); PSP_SP_CALL(...); }   stp x20,x19,[sp,#-32]! ... bl callee
    callee(); return;                      b callee

32 bytes of host stack per guest transfer against none. The consequence is that
a loop the hardware runs forever without touching its stack consumes the host
stack: on LocoRoco a worker thread reached 16385 KB of its 16396 KB in a guest
loop whose back-edge crosses a body boundary, and the run died in
___chkstk_darwin with the backtrace repeating two recompiled bodies. With these
three sites left terminal, the same loop ran 371 million iterations to the
30-second watchdog and the high-water mark was 9 KB.

Nothing is given up here. What PSP_SP_CALL compares -- the caller's $sp at the
call against the callee's on return -- is the same pair the callee's own
PSP_SP_CHECK compares, where it names the exit that failed instead of the call
site. The fall-out site keeps its own check on the body being left, moved in
front of the transfer so it cannot cost a frame.

The ordinary-branch path and the end-of-body fall-through already emitted bare
calls; this makes the remaining three consistent with them.

Emission on LocoRoco changes 5502 sites, 174 of them the fall-out family where
the check also moves.

6388dfdaa96fa2cae82f1bc5bc5b274e2213e9b6.message:
emit: run a branch's delay slot on the taken path

The previous commit stops the walk from stepping past a delay slot this
body did not emit, and hands the not-taken path to the body that owns
it. That covers one path only. A branch delays BOTH: the slot executes
whether or not the branch is taken, so the taken path was transferring
with a register the slot was supposed to set still holding its old
value.

The taken path now runs the slot before it transfers, in all three
shapes: an ordinary branch, an ordinary branch that leaves the body, and
a likely branch (which nullifies its slot when not taken, so the slot
belongs there and nowhere else).

Measured on LocoRoco (UCES00304): 0x1571C is `beq $v0,$zero,0x15774`
whose slot at 0x15720 is `lui $v0,0x1C`, and 0x15774 loads eight
kilobytes through $v0. With the taken path leaving it zero, the game read
the module's own code as a table and reported the word `lw $ra,12($sp)`
-- 0x8FBF000C -- as an address, twice. 30 branch sites in this module
have a slot another body owns. With this change those two accesses are
gone, three more guest threads start (6 of 11 before, 9 of 11 after, 0
dispatch misses, the initialiser table still reaching entry [99]), and
the run still ends on the watchdog with no fault.

Only a plain instruction is repeated: an instruction that transfers
control in a delay slot is architecturally unpredictable, so those are
left alone.

Two things this does not cover, both measured: a call (`jal`) whose slot
is another body's still runs its slot after the call rather than before
it, on 2 sites plus 1 `bltzal`; and a likely branch whose slot another
body owns still reaches the slot on the NOT-taken path through the
fall-out, on 4 sites, all of them in a region that is data read as code.

The tests build the three shapes by hand -- what matters is where a body
ends and who owns the slot, and discovery decides that by an order-
dependent walk -- and each assertion is scoped to the body under test,
because the slot is also the neighbour's first statement. A

688bfd3f3b8d06bc49cf95966ceb2e4f335b4590.message:
threadman: real threads, one CPU handed over explicitly

sceKernelStartThread ran the thread body inline and never returned, so a game
that starts a worker and then posts work to it never got past its own
StartThread call. Measured on LocoRoco: the worker sat in
`while (!flag) sleep();` waiting for work the still-unreturned caller was
going to post, and the flag was never armed.

Now one host thread per guest thread, and one CPU handed over explicitly: the
holder of the baton owns `psp_cpu`, a thread that blocks saves its registers
into its own record and reloads them when it gets the CPU back. StartThread
creates the host thread and returns; SleepThread parks until WakeupThread;
WaitSema/WaitEventFlag/WaitThreadEnd park until signalled; DelayThread parks
for its duration in virtual time; the vblank wait hands the CPU over.

An unbounded wait is capped at a tick and reports what it was waiting for,
because a poll loop that nothing wakes has to keep the run moving: the
faithful alternative is a thread that never returns, which produces no
evidence at all. Interrupt masking moved into the scheduler and became
per-thread, since a critical section belongs to the thread that opened it.

Also here, because LocoRoco asked for them on the same path: the variable-pool
family (CreateVpl, AllocateVpl[CB], TryAllocateVpl, FreeVpl, ReferVplStatus,
CancelVpl, DeleteVpl) and sceKernelMaxFreeMemSize. A stubbed create returning
zero is indistinguishable from a successful create of pool 0 -- a zero that is
also a valid answer -- and both of these are what a game reads to decide
whether it can allocate at all.

The function-entry ring went from 32 to 4096 entries: a module that walks a
table of 100 initialisers runs deeper than 32, and the entry it is stuck in
falls out of the window exactly when it is needed.

888e3949862774727672004d4b56858f1df10f47.message:
hle: a callback runs on the thread that created it, where that thread waits

Callbacks were registered and never delivered: sceKernelCreateCallback
built the object, and nothing ever ran it. That is cheap to miss, because
most callbacks never fire in a run anyway -- but it is not invisible, and
LocoRoco is where it showed: `sceKernelCheckCallback` is reached from a
failed sceIoOpen, six times over, in a load loop that checks callbacks
between attempts. It came back unimplemented, so the loop had nothing to
check, and the notification it was polling for had nowhere to be
delivered.

The shape of the mechanism is ownership. A callback belongs to the thread
that created it and runs *on that thread* -- an interrupt goes to every
enabled handler whoever is running, while a callback waits for its own.
So the delivery points are the points where that thread can be disturbed:
every wait (the same four places a sub-interrupt is delivered, which is
why the delivery now goes through one function instead of two lists), and
sceKernelCheckCallback, which reports 1 if a callback ran and 0 if none
was pending -- the two answers a guest uses to decide whether to keep
polling.

And a notification queues rather than running in place, because the
notifier is often another thread entirely: it is delivered when the
owner next reaches a check point, carrying the argument the notification
carried (the callback's first argument is what create time gave it, which
is a different thing).

Guarded like the interrupt path, for the same reason: no re-entrance (a
callback that notifies itself must not eat the host stack), nothing
delivered inside a critical section, and a per-pass ceiling with a
counter, so a callback that keeps re-arming itself is visible instead of
silently dropped. A callback whose address discovery never found is
counted and named rather than quietly skipped -- that failure is
indistinguishable from the bug this fixes.

scePower comes with it, because its slots are the same mechanism one
level out: scePowerRegisterCallback(

8e9b5ca0bbc0738b28b5a5d9f5a4aa02267ff626.message:
emit: consume a delay slot only when this body emitted it

A delay slot is the branch's, but discovery does not always hand it over: on a
real module the slot address is routinely promoted to a function entry of its
own. `have_slot` is false then, so the slot is correctly not emitted inline --
its own body has it -- and the walk stepped over it anyway. That left the
body's `end` one instruction past the address control actually reaches, and the
continuation was looked for there. With the slot's own address being a function
entry and the address after it neither a function nor a label, nothing was
emitted at all: the body ended in a silent `return`.

A body that stops early usually still holds a frame that only the continuation
pops, so this is not cosmetic. Measured on LocoRoco (UCES00304): 0x1003C is a
`beq` whose delay slot at 0x10040 begins the body of the next function, so the
body of 0x10038 ended in that silent return. Ten negative stack-imbalance sites,
-192 down to -16, in the 0xF4xx..0x16Axx region all traced back to it -- 0x10150
never had its 16 bytes popped, 0x1001C and 0x100D4 each kept theirs as the chain
went deeper -- and the caller reloaded $s5 656 bytes low. The same run now
reports zero negative imbalances.

The rule is the hardware's: a slot counts as consumed only when this body
emitted it. When it did not, the walk visits it, and the existing fall-out path
continues there, through the slot's own body, which runs the instruction exactly
once (the test asserts a single occurrence, so folding it in here as well cannot
pass).

Scope, by diffing the emission before and after: one shape, nothing else moved.

  on main                    3 hunks, +12/-0
  the working tree          29 hunks, +114/-36

The 29-site figure and the run above come from a working tree that also carries
the thread-entry discovery from an open PR and this game's bring-up patches; on
main alone 0x10040 is not a function entry, so the shape does not arise there and
the end-to-end run cannot be reproduced from main. Said plain

9036e28bf86c1883953b99957b63054ee603a266.message:
emit: spell non-finite VFPU immediates as NAN/INFINITY, not nanf/inff

A half-precision immediate can encode an infinity or a NaN, and neither
survives the float conversion: `%.9gf` renders a NaN as `nan` and an infinity
as `inf`, and the format's literal `f` suffix then glues itself on. The
generated C contained the invalid tokens `nanf` and `inff`, and the file did
not compile at all. LocoRoco (UCES00304) hits it on two real words.

The C99 macros are used rather than a division literal because they need no
assumption about the compiler's constant folding. They require <math.h>,
which every generated unit already pulls in through
<psprecomp/recomp_rt.h>, so that is where the include goes.

The tests cover all three branches -- NaN, +Inf, -Inf -- plus a finite value
to show the ordinary path is unchanged, since a fix that quietly reformats
every immediate would be worse than the bug.

Verified end to end: 40 MB of C emitted from a retail EBOOT (14,245
functions, 361,473 instructions) now compiles with `clang -c` where it
previously failed on two lines.

90aeff7c9ff95875988c2639e64096648c653800.message:
runtime: define the two calls the emitter emits and nothing implemented

The emitter declares `psp_syscall()` and `psp_unimplemented()` in the generated
header and calls them from every site it cannot translate, but no source in the
runtime defined them. The generated C therefore compiled and then failed to
link for any module that contained one: LocoRoco (UCES00304) emits 11 `syscall`
sites and 15 646 `psp_unimplemented` sites, and the link fails on both symbols
unless the host supplies them itself. That is a bigger failure than a compile
error -- the file looks finished, and the toolchain reports nothing wrong until
someone tries to build a program out of it.

They now live in `src/traps.c`, declared once in `<psprecomp/recomp_rt.h>`, the
same rule that header states for the rest of the runtime's semantics ("so they
exist in exactly one place"). The emitter's duplicate declarations are dropped:
every generated unit already includes that header.

The behaviour is the one `docs/BRINGUP.md` relies on -- count, say the first
few, keep going. The log ceiling is not cosmetic: a game stuck in a loop
reaches millions of these per second and would bury the rest of the journal.
The totals stay readable through `psp_syscall_total()` and
`psp_unimplemented_total()`, and `psp_trap_reset()` lets a host measure before
and after a fix instead of comparing totals accumulated since start-up.

Verified end to end on a real module rather than by inspection: with these
definitions in the runtime and no host shim at all, the emitted C for LocoRoco
links, and the resulting run is identical to the shim's -- same allocations,
same five unimplemented firmware calls, same bad memory accesses. `ctest`:
10/10.

b3edace7fa47dbe76d608c728b7d4dc22f5441f4.message:
decode: viim/vfim destination is bits 16..22, not the generic vd

The immediate loads spell their single destination in the field the other
VFPU forms call `vt` (bits 16..22); this family has no `vd`. The case did
assign that field -- but to `out`, and a_decode closes with `*out = in`, so
the assignment was undone before any caller saw it. Callers were handed the
generic `vd = word & 0x7F` instead, and the emitter therefore wrote a
different VFPU register than the hardware would.

Measured on LocoRoco (UCES00304): 0xDF967E81 is a vfim to register 22, and
the emitted C read `psp_vimm(1, ...)`. Cross-checked against an independent
implementation, the ghidra-allegrex sleigh, where the destination operand of
`:vfim.s vt_s, immed` is `vt`, defined as bits 16..22.

`vsize` is set to 1 as well, since an immediate load writes a single lane.
`imm` needs no assignment here: the epilogue's default is SIMM16, which is
exactly this field's signed low halfword.

The change covers A_VIIM and A_VFIM only. The prefixes sharing this opcode
(vpfxs/vpfxt/vpfxd) do not encode a destination register, so their fields are
left as they were.

c36526c13a62d373c74d3e08efeba548a2786184.message:
sp: judge a hand-over by its own sign, not by a return's

A transfer that ends a body hands over mid-frame: a fragment whose flow falls
out into another fragment has, in the case that matters, allocated the frame its
function's first fragment started, and the epilogue that returns it lives in the
function's last fragment. PSP_SP_CHECK at that site compares the fragment's own
entry with the mid-frame $sp and reports the difference as a leak, which it is
not -- the delta is exactly the frame the fragment allocated.

Measured on LocoRoco: 206 reports on one run, 12 sites, every one of them a
fall-out label, and every delta equal to the frame in the fragment's prologue.
Verified at the disassembly on three of them -- 0x1A294 allocates 2112 and
0x1A380 returns 2112 in its `jr $ra` delay slot, 0x3E4 allocates 64 and 0x4C4
returns 64, 0x1A3D4's frame is 1040 and 0x1A3E4 returns it -- so the chains are
balanced and the guest code is right.

The cost is not the noise, it is the sign it buries: at such a transfer the defect
is $sp *above* the entry, a fragment that released a frame it never took, and
those reports were indistinguishable from the 41 million expected violations of
the same counter on the same run.

PSP_SP_LEAVE and psp_trace_sp_leave carry the other invariant: silent when the
hand-over leaves $sp below the entry, reported when it hands over high. A
`jr $ra` exit keeps PSP_SP_CHECK, which is the rule it does have.

The emitter test scopes its assertion to the gap, because the fall-out names its
target and that target's own `jr $ra` names itself, so both labels read
0x08804008 and only the position separates them.

One emitter hunk and its runtime share the earlier commit in this series, which
is what made the second sign visible at all: before it, the run died before
reaching a fall-out that had a prologue of its own.

c3c6851d33c79b5f83c39c867c525d4c481f803e.message:
emit: read the jr/jalr target before the delay slot, and link jalr's rd

jr and jalr read their register before the delay slot runs, but the
emitter ran the slot first and then dispatched on the register, so a slot
that writes it sent control to the new value. Capture the target into `_t`
first, the way a branch captures its condition into `_c`.

jalr also linked $ra unconditionally. It now links the rd it encodes, and
links nothing for rd = $zero.

Measured on Killzone: Liberation (KZL.PRX, v1.20 US): discovery is
unchanged. All 16,530 indirect transfers now dispatch through `_t`; two of
them (`jr $t4` / `addiu $t4,$t4,8` at 0x0031D9AC and the $t5 twin at
0x0031D9BC) change behaviour. No jalr there links a register other than $ra.
