ce9ea45331fc6c88b8b77ff3d20fd837a02bea66.message:
cellPad: a port with no controller reports centred sticks, not zero

cellPadInit zeroed the host state, and with the SDL2 backend (every
non-Windows build) and no controller plugged in nothing ever set the
sticks again. Port 0 is served with no device behind it, so titles read
all four axes as 0: both sticks pushed to the top-left corner. Windows
was spared only because its keyboard fallback writes 128 on every poll.

In Twisted Metal the car drove itself in circles and the chase camera
pitched up at the sky, so the player's own vehicle left the screen within
seconds of a match starting. With the sticks held at 128 (PAD_STICK) the
car stays in front of the camera for the whole match.

pad_host_release() puts a port at rest (no buttons, sticks at 128) at
init and whenever a backend finds no device on it, which also stops an
unplugged pad from keeping its last report.

ps3recomp_host --audio-pad, which CI runs on Linux and macOS with no
controller, now reads port 0 and requires all four sticks at 128. With
master's cellPad.c it reads 0 on each and fails.

d5759c227b426baeb97eb3e4078f091db5500a11.message:
cellSysutil: ps3_host_quit, for the window's close button and Cmd+Q

Closing the game's window stopped the presents and left the game
running with no window until it was killed, and Cmd+Q did nothing: the
host turns a plain run loop with no app menu, so AppKit had no Quit to
send it to.

ps3_host_quit does what the console's Quit Game does. Every registered
sysutil callback gets CELL_SYSUTIL_REQUEST_EXITGAME on the title's next
poll, and a title that tidies up and calls sys_process_exit ends there.

ended for it with exit(0), so stdio is flushed and the atexit handlers
run, but never while a save is being written: cellSaveData counts the
saves in flight (ps3_savedata_busy), and the quit waits up to 10 s for
that to reach 0. It runs on its own thread, so the caller returns at
once, and a second request is ignored.

template on a closed window.

d682e9c49e2bfbbb7fb30f003acaa3a9e46d4f15.message:
rsx_d3d12: draw indexed triangle lists with their indices

The VP path expanded every indexed draw into a triangle list, copying the
256-byte converted vertex once per index reference. God of War HD gameplay
makes 6.4M references a second to 2.0M distinct vertices, about 2,300
indexed draws a frame, so the drain wrote ~1.6 GB/s into the upload heap
and the indexed uploads took ~20 ms of a 55 ms frame.

Indexed TRIANGLES now convert each distinct vertex once, straight into the
vertex buffer, and keep their indices in a new per-frame u32 index buffer
(vp_ib, double-buffered by frame parity like vp_vb). The record carries
the index range and is drawn with DrawIndexedInstanced, base vertex at
the run's first vertex. Batches that the list path merged (a BEGIN/END
stream cut into counts that are not multiples of 3) continue the same
run: they share its vertices and append indices. A run that would leave
the tables (index >= 2^20) or overflow the buffers falls back to the list
path, as do the other primitives. VTX_LIST=1 restores the expansion.

VTX_STATS=1 reports, every 5 s, draws by primitive, index references
against distinct vertices, conversions, attribute formats and the time
the indexed uploads take.

Gameplay: indexed uploads ~20 ms -> ~12 ms a frame, 18.2 -> 20.6 fps
(VTX_LIST=1 against the default, same build).

d7054ab6a820c28ec38c00393e9073d8f7402119.message:
spu: estimates, interpolate and float/int conversions four lanes at a time with AVX2

spu_fi, spu_frest, spu_frsqest, spu_cflts, spu_cfltu, spu_csflt and
spu_cuflt computed one lane at a time, while fa/fm/fma already have an
AVX2 path. frest followed by fi is how SPU code divides, so the scalar
loops sit in the middle of the hot loops of lifted jobs.

Each instruction's lane rule is integer work on the bit fields, so the
vector forms are exact by construction and no lane falls back:
- fi: the 33-bit fixed-point magnitude on 64-bit lanes, then one
  normalising shift picked per lane;
- frest/frsqest: the fraction tables read with a gather;
- cflts/cfltu: the significand shifted with per-lane variable shifts,
  saturated with compares;
- csflt/cuflt: the integer's exact double gives its top bit and the next
  23 bits, truncated.

The scalar versions stay as spu_*_ref and are still used without AVX2.
test_spu_float_est.c checks every one bit for bit against them (random
words, normal/extended-range boundaries, zeros, denormals, integers of
every magnitude, every scale immediate); linux.yml runs it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

daa17fbccb66d40e67197bdbf1e16f3bb9a9cc39.message:
ppu_loader: re-check the reservation once the lock-line lock is held

stwcx./stdcx. check the caller's reservation, then take the lock-line lock
for a line an SPU has reserved, then CAS. An SPU commit that lands
between the check and the lock breaks the reservation (via
ppu_resv_break_line, under that lock) too late to be seen, and the CAS
goes ahead on a line whose other words just changed. Re-check under the
lock.

dc37f00b2d8c883b3b1f3eb45445d40adfc779f4.message:
sysPrxForUser lwmutex: an atomic lock word; the semaphore only wakes

Every sys_lwmutex_lock and _unlock went through a Win32 semaphore, two
kernel calls a pair even when nobody else wanted the lock. On the PS3
an uncontended lwmutex is a few atomic operations in user space. God of
War HD makes about 320,000 pairs in one frame when the first fight's
next wave spawns, and that frame took 360 ms.

Each slot now has a state word: 0 free, 1 held, 2 held with a waiter.
Lock is a compare-and-swap 0 -> 1, unlock an exchange to 0; only a
contended lock sleeps on the semaphore (now a wake channel that starts
empty), and only an unlock that finds 2 posts it. A waiter that times
out leaves the word at 2, so a later unlock may post a wake nobody
takes; the next waiter consumes it and waits again. Recursion, timeouts
(ETIMEDOUT), trylock (EBUSY), unlock from another thread and unlock of
a free lock behave as before. sys_lwcond_wait releases and re-takes the
lock through the same two helpers; tools/test_lwcond_layout.py stubs
them.

God of War HD: HLE time in that frame 200 -> 66 ms (traced), the frame
354 -> 234 ms, and the boot-time stalls at 21.8 s and 27.5 s about a
fifth shorter. The rendering check passes.

ddf65a66d17efe396ec7594c9555e99b098eb895.message:
vulkan: VK_DRAW_BATCH=1 records engine draws, depth snapshots, texture uploads and clears into one submission

Every engine draw used to submit its own command buffer and wait on a fence,
because the vertex, index and uniform buffers and the descriptor set are
single objects rewritten per draw. With VK_DRAW_BATCH=1 a draw takes slices
of three host-visible ring buffers and a descriptor set from a pool, records
into the open command buffer behind a full memory barrier (render-to-texture
ordering without hazard tracking), and only a pending counter grows. Depth
snapshots copy through a persistent device-local buffer, texture uploads
stage through a ring and record a buffer-to-image copy, and colour and
depth/stencil clears record too. vk_begin, every object destroy, the present
and the engine's submit point flush first, so all other backend work still
sees everything before it complete. VK_DRAW_BATCH_MAX (default 512, max 1024)
caps the draws per submission. Off by default.

eb5c6832611192c72eb52130957e24d743bcbb2f.message:
spu: SPU_IRQWAIT_DIAG reports an SPU waiting for an interrupt that never comes

An SPU that enables interrupts and spins until its handler runs looks,
from outside, like any busy SPU. SPU_IRQWAIT_DIAG=1 reports it: every
2^22 dispatches with interrupts enabled and nothing pending to take (24
lines at most), the pc, the event status and mask and the MFC list-stall
mask and status. SPU_IRQWAIT_LS=<hex> adds 16 bytes of local store, for
the waiter's own state once its layout is known.

In Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) this showed the WWS job manager
waiting for an Sn interrupt whose event bit was already gone.

The dispatch loop calls it only when interrupts are enabled with nothing
pending, behind g_spu_irqwait_diag (an SPU_GATE like g_spu_smc_watch):
-1 until the first call reads the variable, then 0 or 1, so with it off
the loop pays one predictable load.

runtime/spu/tests/test_spu_irqwait_diag.c
(tools/test_spu_irqwait_diag.py): off by default, the gate settles at 0;
on, exactly one report per 2^22 waits, with the expected state.

ec5a7a6f257eb849585140ebd38c73a44b7a4a57.message:
rsx engine: release a depth target's stale snapshot

A depth clear invalidates the sampleable snapshot of a depth target and
the next DEPTH24_D8 read takes a new one, but the old one was never
released. A shadow map cleared and read every frame leaked one backend
texture per frame per depth target. On Metal the object table filled
during play, and every texture created after that came back as 0 and
sampled black. Release the old snapshot when a new one replaces it, and
when the depth target is recreated at a larger size. Metal keeps a
released object until no recorded draw can still name it, and Vulkan
hands back the same handle refilled, which is left alone.

cellVdecOpen wrote the slot index as the handle, so the first decoder a
title opened got handle 0. Some titles treat a 0 handle as "no decoder
open": Killzone 2's movie player
keeps the handle as its "decoder open" flag, its AU submit returns
without calling cellVdecDecodeAu while the handle is 0, and the intro
movie stalls with no AU ever decoded.

The handle is now the slot index plus one. Every entry point maps it
back, 0 and out-of-range handles are rejected with CELL_VDEC_ERROR_ARG,
and the callback receives the handle the title was given.

test_vdec_decode checks that Open never returns 0, that StartSeq(0) and
StartSeq(0xFFFFFFFF) are rejected, and that the callback's first
argument is the handle Open returned.

The runtime's explicit -O2 was tied to Release and RelWithDebInfo, and

with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE matched neither, so the whole runtime (FIFO
walker, draw engine, MFC) and every lifted PPU TU compiled at -O0. The

f825519199b20712213504374feedd4586008d9d.message:
cellGcmSys: a resync replays the label releases it skips; re-read a park before leaving it

A FIFO resync moves get straight to put. The fences in the skipped range were
already swept up, but a label release in it was simply lost, and a title
that waits on that label waits for the rest of the run. inFAMOUS 2's light
task kicker waits on a texture-read release (0x1D74) that sits in a
command block an SPU job writes; a jump-park resync that stepped over it
froze the title in its first open-world area.

- After the fence sweep, the skipped range is walked as a command stream:
  each header and its data, NOPs, flip markers and self-JUMP parks stepped
  over, forward JUMPs inside the range followed, stopping at a CALL, a
  RETURN or a word that is not a method header. NV406E SEMAPHORE_OFFSET /
  RELEASE (0x64/0x6C) are replayed into the label window as the walker
  does, and the NV4097 semaphore context, offset and back-end /
  texture-read releases (0x01A4, 0x1D6C, 0x1D70, 0x1D74) go through
  rsx_process_method, so they land where the walker would have written
  them (label window or main memory, byte swap included). Draws in the
  range are still dropped.
- The jump-park resync reads the park word again first. An SPU job that
  fills an Edge-style command-buffer hole (a self-JUMP until it is
  written) can land between the pass's read and the resync, which would
  then jump over the commands just written.

libs/video/tests/test_gcm_resync_labels.c (run by
tools/test_gcm_resync_labels.py) parks the walker in front of a NOP, an
NV406E release, a forward JUMP over non-command words and an NV4097
release, waits out GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS and checks that the resync wrote the
first label and handed the second to rsx_process_method.

#504 replaces two plain `plan->base_offset + fetch->desc.offset` additions
with rsx_dsp_resolve_vertex_offset(), which wraps at 28 bits as the hardware
does. One of its two hunks merged clean -- the prefix used to compute
stable_base. The other conflicted, because #458 (earlier in this wave)
restructured the fetch loop from per-vertex to attribute-major and #504's

longer reach. Verified afterwards that both base_offset uses in the file go
through rsx_dsp_resolve_vertex_offset(): a wrap applied on one of two paths
is worse than none, because the two would disagree about where a vertex is.

Merge PR #444: verified job-module regions and embedded SPU program coverage (@tekulvw)

The interesting conflict of the wave so far. #444 refactors the --jobmods
loop in tools/lift_jobmods.py into a lift_module() helper (so --engine-elf
can share it) and adds reachable()/module_code_end()/module_seeds(). #488
(@erikomis, wave 3) rewrote that same loop for a different reason: the LS
address a module is linked for comes out of its header at +0x28, and is
0x7000 rather than 0x4000 for some of Resistance: Fall of Man's modules.
Lifting those at 0x4000 puts every lifted address 0x3000 short of where
the job manager runs them.

#444 was written against master, so lift_module() and module_seeds()
hardcode BASE throughout -- the ELF wrap base, --base, the seed window,
base + 0x30, the manual-link and switch-table scans, and the manifest's
"base" field. Taking #444's side as written compiles, runs, and silently
reverts #488 on exactly the modules #488 exists for. Nothing in CI would
have caught it: no test ships a 0x7000 module.

Resolved by keeping #444's refactor and threading #488's base through it.
module_seeds(raw, base=BASE) and lift_module(..., base=BASE), and the
--jobmods loop passes base=module_base(raw). module_base() itself is #488's,
unchanged.

The --engine-elf path keeps BASE, and that is correct rather than an
oversight: find_engine_modules() only accepts an image whose header says
+0x28 == BASE, so every module it yields is linked at 0x4000 by
construction. The same goes for the code-slice and region-registration
arithmetic in lift_engine_elf()/emit_register_verified().

Dropped on the way through: #488's "sha = name.split('_')[1]", assigned and
never read.

tools/build_spu_workloads.py is a plain both-added conflict in the argparse
block -- #549's --merge-chunks and #444's --handled/--image-ids. All three
kept.

fb89154950c6ffb10e3d92e06da99258af5d363a.message:
rsx_d3d12: depth surfaces per zeta offset, readable as textures

The guest path had one depth buffer, cleared whenever a pass changed
targets. God of War HD keeps two depth surfaces: the scene's 2x-AA one
at 0x17F0000 and a resolved one at 0x2240000. Its resolve pass samples
the AA depth as an A8R8G8B8 texture to compute fog and the alpha the
shadow pass blends with. That surface never existed in guest memory,
so the read returned nothing: distant cliffs came out black and the
whole scene too dark.

- Each zeta offset gets its own D24S8 surface (R24G8_TYPELESS, so it
  can also be read). It keeps its contents across passes and is
  cleared only by the guest's own clears. Passes without a depth
  surface keep the shared buffer as before.
- A colour target of NONE with a depth surface binds no RTV (a
  depth-only pass). The register now defaults to target A, as libgcm
  sets it, so a title that never writes it still draws.
- A draw sampling a depth surface reads a colour copy refreshed just
  before it when the depth has changed since the last copy: the bytes
  a guest sees in memory for D24S8 read as A8R8G8B8 (A = depth[23:16],
  R = depth[15:8], G = depth[7:0], B = stencil).
- The pool grows a surface for a larger pass, never shrinks it, and
  evicts an entry no pass used this frame.

fe84fa460d078b41fdad94f702554ea41a01ebe8.message:
Merge PR #436: memoize indirect-dispatch registry lookups per thread (@tekulvw)

The largest semantic conflict in the release so far. #436 was written
against master, where spu_lifted_lookup() was a single spu_lookup() and
spu_indirect_branch() carried the identity-ownership order inline. Wave 4
changed both: #419/#420 moved the ownership order into
spu_lifted_lookup_full(), and #481 put a per-thread dispatch cache in
front of it in spu_lifted_lookup().

Taken as written, #436 replaces spu_lifted_lookup()'s whole body with
"return spu_lookup_memoized(lsa, ctx ? ctx->image_id : 0)" and replaces
spu_indirect_branch()'s call with its own inline identity walk. That
compiles, and it deletes #481's dispatch cache outright while forking the
ownership order into a second copy that would then drift from the
resolver's. Three PRs' worth of wave-4 work, silently undone.

So the structure stays wave 4's and #436 goes in underneath it, which is
where it belongs and what it was for: spu_lifted_lookup_full() now makes
every one of its registry probes through spu_lookup_memoized() instead of
spu_lookup(). The resolver issues up to three probes per resolution
(resident_task, then resident_ovl, then image_id) and the first two
usually miss, and a generation-keyed memo that caches misses is exactly
the thing that stops each of those walking the address's hash chain again
-- which is the cost #436's own commentary describes.

The two layers compose rather than overlap: #481's cache is keyed on the
resolved answer for a (context, residency) pair and only stores hits;
#436's is keyed on (address, image) at the registry and stores misses too.
Definition order checked -- memo at 1633, resolver at 1673, cache at 1747.

Tests: #436 adds test_registry_lookup_memo and wave 4 added
test_verified_resident_code_regions, test_resident_interpreter_rejoin and
test_dispatch_cache. git offered them as one conflict because they share a
trailer; all four are kept and all four now run from main(). Verified that
every test defined in the file is called

# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

**[Join the sp00nznet recomp Discord](https://discord.gg/CRpzGWZFcu)** — the
community hub for sp00nznet's recomp projects, where ps3recomp development
happens in the open. Good place to ask questions, show a port you are working
on, or find out what people are stuck on before you duplicate the effort.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [ReXGlue](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [AnyPS5](https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5) (PS5 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — the output is C/C++, so it can target any platform a compiler does (see [platform support](#platform-support) for where the runtime actually stands today)

## Platform support

CI builds and tests every row on every pull request: Windows (clang-cl), macOS
arm64, Linux (GCC and Clang), and Linux with the Vulkan backend on lavapipe
under the validation layer. A green check means the runtime built and the tests
passed. It does not mean a game ran; the last row is the only one that claims
that.

| | Windows | macOS (arm64) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime library builds | yes | yes | yes |
| Lifter test suites + C unit tests | yes | yes | yes |
| Render backend | D3D12 | Metal | Vulkan (opt-in); null (headless, CI) |
| Runs a recompiled game, in this tree | **yes** | **no** | **no** |

**What stops macOS and Linux running a title is the PPU boot scaffold.**
`ppu_loader.cpp`, `boot_main.cpp` and the HLE dispatch are compiled per game,
not into the library. They compile on POSIX with zero errors (a CI ratchet
keeps it that way) and the frame clock runs there, but no title has yet been
booted to gameplay from this tree on either OS.

**The renderers are further along than that.** `ps3recomp_host` drives cellGcm
→ RSX → backend end to end with no game. With guest programs on, Metal and
Vulkan both run the title's own shaders on the shared register-file draw
engine. Every `ps3recomp_host` scene passes on both, including render-to-texture,
MRT, depth textures, cube maps and stencil. Linux's default stays the headless
null backend, a CPU triangle filler that CI draws with.

**Downstream, people are already past this.** Twisted Metal's menus run on
Linux/Vulkan, inFamous on macOS, and Killzone 3 under Proton (see
[In the community](#in-the-community)). Those ports carry patches that are
still on their way upstream, which is why the table still says "no".

## The Challenge

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

| Component | What It Is | Why It's Hard |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| **PPU** | PowerPC 64-bit main CPU | Custom ISA extensions, VMX/AltiVec SIMD |
| **6x SPU** | 128-bit SIMD vector processors | Proprietary ISA, 256KB local store, explicit DMA |
| **Memory** | 256MB XDR RAM | 128-byte alignment requirements, split bus |
| **LV2 Kernel** | Proprietary OS layer | ~300+ system calls, complex threading model |
| **PRX Modules** | Dynamic libraries | 100+ system libraries with intricate interdependencies |

We don't shy away from hard problems. We just break them into smaller ones.

## Architecture

```
ps3recomp/
├── tools/                    # Binary analysis & recompilation pipeline
│   ├── elf_parser.py         # Parse PS3 ELF/SELF/PRX binaries
│   ├── ppu_disasm.py         # PowerPC disassembler with PS3 extensions
│   ├── ppu_lifter.py         # PPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── spu_disasm.py         # SPU instruction set disassembler
│   ├── spu_lifter.py         # SPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── extract_spu_images.py # Extract embedded SPU images from PRX/ELF
│   ├── find_spu_functions.py # SPU function boundary detection
│   ├── wrap_spu_elf.py       # Wrap a raw SPU blob as a loadable ELF
│   ├── prx_analyzer.py       # Analyze PRX imports/exports and NIDs
│   ├── nid_database.py       # Function Name ID (NID) resolver
│   ├── find_functions.py     # Function boundary detection
│   └── generate_stubs.py     # Generate HLE stub skeletons from a NID list
│
├── runtime/                  # Core runtime for recompiled executables
│   ├── ppu/                  # PPU execution context
│   │   ├── ppu_context.h     # Register file, CR, LR, CTR, FPSCR

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

## Module Status

HLE implementations of the PS3 system libraries, written for this project. RPCS3 is a behavioural reference, not a code source. Most modules are complete. The ones still marked Partial are the media decoders (cellVdec, cellAdec, cellDmux, cellAtrac, cellAdecAtrac3p) and cellSpurs. [docs/MODULE_STATUS.md](docs/MODULE_STATUS.md) has one row per module and is the source for the counts.

# Twisted Metal (2012) — PS3 Native PC Port

**Project initiated and coordinated by Franklin Wilster (FranklinCG) — Brazil 🇧🇷**

[Português brasileiro](README.pt-BR.md) · [Current status](docs/STATUS.md) · [Choose an area](docs/HOW_TO_HELP.md) · [Roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md) · [Credits](CREDITS.md)

> **Research / pre-menu stage. Not a playable release.** This independent initiative targets the **2012 PlayStation 3 game**, not the 1995 PlayStation title. Menu rendering and gameplay have not been verified for this initiative. No download here installs or runs the original game.

## What is being built?

A community research effort toward a faithful native Windows PC port, with a reproducible development pipeline and small, reviewable runtime improvements. Work starts from existing open-source research rather than claiming a first-ever port or rebuilding every subsystem.

This first public export contains the collaboration structure, a portable synthetic Taskset layout probe, selected historical host-model sources for review, publication safeguards, and concrete contribution tasks. **It is not yet the complete redistributable runtime or a self-contained game build.** Exporting the remaining source and its exact build inputs is tracked as work item PUB-001. The private development workspace and its Git history are not mirrored here.

## Where help is useful now

| Area | Current contribution | Can start independently? |
|---|---|---|
| SPURS / shared state | Review context lifetime, cleanup, lock order and launch identity | Yes, through host-only cases |
| Guest ABI | Byte-order, layout and ownership regression tests | Yes |
| PPU / SPU memory | Review actual writer coverage and reservation contracts | Yes, no game execution |
| Build / source export | Audit permissive source dependencies and reproduce a public host build | Yes; highest onboarding priority |
| Graphics, audio, input, storage | Design interfaces and synthetic fixtures; do not claim game integration | Yes, with an agreed scope |
| Scheduler | Define semantics from references, without forcing a progress bit | Research only; integration blocked by coherent state |
| Modding / editor / PT-BR / online / other platforms | Record requirements and interfaces | Future track, not a current runtime dependency |

Pick a task from [the work board](docs/WORK_ITEMS.md), comment with your proposed scope, then open a focused pull request. Major architecture changes need a short proposal first. Contributions in Portuguese or English are welcome. Text-based collaboration is sufficient; calls are not required.

## Run something without owning the game

Python checks (Python 3.10+):

```sh
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python tools/render_progress.py --check
python tools/audit_public.py
```

Synthetic C host probe (CMake 3.20+ and a C compiler):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release
ctest --test-dir build -C Release --output-on-failure
```

These commands **do not build, link, launch or emulate Twisted Metal**, access a game installation, download assets, or rerun the private port's historical experiments. See [BUILDING.md](BUILDING.md) for the exact scope.

## Honest progress

The current development milestone is guest Taskset state coherence, followed by integration evidence and then a decision on scheduler work. A passing component test is not a passing port. [The dashboard](docs/PROGRESS.md) distinguishes host models, integration, visual evidence and playable milestones. There is **no defensible overall port-completion percentage or release date yet**.

Franklin initiated and coordinates **this independent initiative**. No original game executables, disc images, extracted commercial assets, firmware, keys, saves, private memory dumps, personal files or unrelated projects. Do not upload such inputs to issues or pull requests.

1370143167.readme_excerpt:
# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

**[Join the sp00nznet recomp Discord](https://discord.gg/CRpzGWZFcu)** — the
community hub for sp00nznet's recomp projects, where ps3recomp development
happens in the open. Good place to ask questions, show a port you are working
on, or find out what people are stuck on before you duplicate the effort.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [ReXGlue](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk) (Xbox 360 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — the output is C/C++, so it can target any platform a compiler does (see [platform support](#platform-support) for where the runtime actually stands today)

## Platform support

Every row is exercised by CI on every push, and **all three are green on
`master`** — the PPU boot scaffold ratchet that had been red since before v0.11.0
([#139](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp/issues/139)) is at zero on all
four toolchains. The rows below describe what those jobs actually do, not what a
green tick would imply: building the runtime and passing the suites is not the
same as running a game, and only one row claims that.

| | Windows | macOS (arm64) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime library builds | yes | yes | yes |
| Lifter + 8 test suites | yes | yes | yes |
| Render backend | D3D12 | Metal | null (headless software) |
| Runs a recompiled game | **yes** | **no** | no |

The gap on macOS is the PPU boot scaffold — `ppu_loader.cpp`, `boot_main.cpp`
and the HLE dispatch are still Win32-only (thread creation, VirtualAlloc, SEH,
stack walking), and they are compiled per-game rather than into the library.
So macOS builds the runtime, renders through Metal and passes the full test
suite, but cannot yet load and run a title. `ps3recomp_host` drives
cellGcm → RSX → Metal end to end without a game, which is what makes further
graphics work possible there.

Linux builds and passes the same suites under both GCC and Clang, and runs
`ps3recomp_host` end to end, on every push. Its backend is the null backend's
headless software path: a host-memory framebuffer with a CPU triangle filler,
enough to prove the guest's command stream produced the pixels it asked for on
a runner with no display and no GPU. It is not a renderer — no depth, no
blending, no textures — so Linux is still one real backend, plus the same PPU
boot scaffold macOS needs, away from running a title.

### What each platform needs next

Both non-Windows platforms are blocked on the *same* two things, in this order.

**1. The PPU boot scaffold, on POSIX.** This is the shared blocker and the only
one that gates "runs a recompiled game" on both. `ppu_loader.cpp`,
`boot_main.cpp` and the HLE dispatch are compiled *per game* rather than into
the library, and were Win32-only — thread creation, `VirtualAlloc`, SEH, stack
walking. v0.10.0 took it to zero errors on POSIX and put it under CI so it
cannot rot again, and ported the guest-pointer trap, thread-locals and host
backtraces. What is left is running it: load a lifted image on POSIX and reach
the guest's first instruction, then `main`. Until that works, neither platform
can run a title no matter how good its renderer is.

**2. One real backend each.** The RSX abstraction landed in v0.10.0 (#101, #102,
#103) — texture conversion, the `TEXTURE_CONTROL1` crossbar, texture layout and
a neutral draw record all live outside the D3D12 file now, so a backend no
longer has to reimplement them to draw anything.

- **macOS** has the furthest to go that is *interesting* rather than
  mechanical: [@slushiimusic](https://github.com/slushiimusic)'s Metal backend
  (#96) does clear, flip, guest vertex fetch, a pipeline-state cache and blend
  translation. Reaching D3D12 parity means the guest's own fragment programs
  through the decompiler, then textures. `ps3recomp_host` already drives
  cellGcm → RSX → Metal with no lifted game, so each step is testable before a
  title exists to run.
- **Linux** has no renderer at all — the headless backend is a CPU triangle
  filler for CI, deliberately. Vulkan is the obvious target, and it starts from
  the same neutral draw record Metal reads.

**Deliberately not claimed:** the table above says "no" for running a game on
macOS and Linux, and it will keep saying "no" until a title actually boots to
gameplay on one of them. Building the runtime, passing the suites and rendering
through `ps3recomp_host` are all real, and none of them is that.

## The Challenge

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

| Component | What It Is | Why It's Hard |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| **PPU** | PowerPC 64-bit main CPU | Custom ISA extensions, VMX/AltiVec SIMD |
| **6x SPU** | 128-bit SIMD vector processors | Proprietary ISA, 256KB local store, explicit DMA |
| **Memory** | 256MB XDR RAM | 128-byte alignment requirements, split bus |
| **LV2 Kernel** | Proprietary OS layer | ~300+ system calls, complex threading model |
| **PRX Modules** | Dynamic libraries | 100+ system libraries with intricate interdependencies |

We don't shy away from hard problems. We just break them into smaller ones.

## Architecture

```
ps3recomp/
├── tools/                    # Binary analysis & recompilation pipeline
│   ├── elf_parser.py         # Parse PS3 ELF/SELF/PRX binaries
│   ├── ppu_disasm.py         # PowerPC disassembler with PS3 extensions
│   ├── ppu_lifter.py         # PPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── spu_disasm.py         # SPU instruction set disassembler
│   ├── spu_lifter.py         # SPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── extract_spu_images.py # Extract embedded SPU images from PRX/ELF
│   ├── find_spu_functions.py # SPU function boundary detection
│   ├── wrap_spu_elf.py       # Wrap a raw SPU blob as a loadable ELF
│   ├── prx_analyzer.py       # Analyze PRX imports/exports and NIDs
│   ├── nid_database.py       # Function Name ID (NID) resolver
│   ├── find_functions.py     # Function boundary detection
│   └── generate_stubs.py     # Auto-generate HLE stubs from RPCS3 modules
│
├── runtime/                  # Core runtime for recompiled executables
│   ├── ppu/                  # PPU execution context
│   │   ├── ppu_context.h     # Register file, CR, LR, CTR, FPSCR
│   │   ├── ppu_memory.h      # Memory access macros (loads, stores, byte-swap)
│   │   └── ppu_ops.h         # Instruction operation macros
│   ├── spu/                  # SPU execution context
│   │   ├── spu_context.h     # 128×128-bit register file, 256KB local store, image_id
│   │   ├── spu_channels.c    # Channel ops + per-image function-table dispatch
│   │   ├── spu_helpers.h     # SPU intrinsics (incl. float conversions)
│   │   ├── spu_dma.h         # DMA (MFC) transfer engine
│   │   └── tests/            # Self-contained SPU runtime tests
│   ├── memory/               # Memory subsystem
│   │   ├── vm.h              # Virtual memory manager (256MB address space)
│   │   └── atomic.h          # PS3 atomic operations (lwarx/stwcx)
│   └── syscalls/             # LV2 kernel system call implementations
│       ├── sys_ppu_thread.h  # Thread creation/management
│       ├── sys_mutex.h       # Mutex/cond synchronization
│       ├── sys_memory.h      # Memory allocation/mapping
│       ├── sys_fs.h          # Filesystem operations
│       ├── sys_prx.h         # PRX module loading
│       └── lv2_syscall_table.h # Full syscall dispatch table
│
├── libs/                     # HLE library implementations (from RPCS3's module system)
│   ├── audio/                # cellAudio, cellAdec, libmixer, libsnd3, libsynth2
│   ├── video/                # cellGcmSys, cellResc, cellVideoOut, cellVpost, cellVdec
│   ├── input/                # cellPad, cellKb, cellMouse, cellGem
│   ├── network/              # cellNetCtl, cellHttp, cellHttps, cellSsl, sceNp*
│   ├── filesystem/           # cellFs, cellGame, cellSaveData, cellStorage
│   ├── system/               # cellSysutil, cellSysmodule, cellRtc, sysPrxForUser
│   ├── spurs/                # cellSpurs, cellFiber, cellSpursJq, cellDaisy (SPU task management)
│   ├── sync/                 # cellSync, cellSync2 (cross-PPU/SPU synchronization)
│   ├── codec/                # cellJpgDec, cellPngDec, cellGifDec, cellPamf, cellDmux, cellAdecAtrac3p, cellAdecCelp8, cellVdecDivx
│   ├── font/                 # cellFont, cellFontFT, cellFreeType, cellL10n
│   └── misc/                 # cellScreenshot, cellSubdisplay, cellImeJp, cellVideoExport, cellMusicExport, cellGameRecording, etc.
│
├── include/ps3emu/           # Public API headers
│   ├── ps3types.h            # Fundamental PS3 types (u8-u128, s8-s64, be_t<>)
│   ├── endian.h              # Big-endian <-> little-endian conversion
│   ├── nid.h                 # NID hashing and lookup
│   ├── module.h              # Module registration framework
│   └── error_codes.h         # PS3 system error codes (CELL_OK, CELL_E*)
│
├── templates/project/        # Starter template for new game ports
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # Build system
│   ├── main.cpp              # Application entry point
│   ├── stubs.cpp             # Game-specific function overrides
│   └── config.toml           # Recompiler configuration
│
├── config/                   # Reference configurations
│   └── example.toml          # Example recompilation config
│
├── patches/                  # Patches for upstream tools
│   └── xenonrecomp-ppu.patch # XenonRecomp adaptations for PPU (Cell != Xenon)
│
└── docs/                     # Documentation (incl. ARCHITECTURE, RUNTIME, SPU_LIFTER, RSX_GRAPHICS, ...)
    ├── ARCHITECTURE.md        # Cell processor and recomp pipeline deep-dive
    ├── GETTING_STARTED.md     # How to recompile your first PS3 game
    ├── MODULE_STATUS.md       # Implementation status of all HLE modules
    ├── MODULES_REFERENCE.md   # Detailed per-module documentation
    ├── RUNTIME.md             # Runtime reference: VM, PPU/SPU contexts, types
    ├── SYSCALLS.md            # All LV2 kernel syscall implementations
    ├── NID_SYSTEM.md          # PS3 NID linking system explained
    ├── TOOLS.md               # Recompiler pipeline tools reference
    ├── BUILDING.md            # Build system, compilers, platform notes
    ├── GAME_PORTING_GUIDE.md  # Step-by-step game porting walkthrough
    └── PLATFORM_ABSTRACTION.md # Win32/POSIX cross-platform details
```

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

## Module Status

We're building HLE implementations based on RPCS3's module system. **97 modules complete, 1 partial (media decode)** — 219 files and ~76,000 lines under `libs/`.

| Category | Modules | Status |
|----------|---------|--------|
| **Kernel Threading** | sys_ppu_thread, sys_mutex, sys_cond, sys_semaphore, sys_rwlock | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Events** | sys_event (queues, ports, flags), sys_timer | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Memory** | sys_memory, sys_mmapper (containers, shared mem) | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Filesystem** | sys_fs (path mapping, real I/O) | ✅ Complete |
| **Filesystem** | cellFs (real file I/O, dir ops, stat, path translation) | ✅ Complete |
| **Save System** | cellSaveData (callback-driven, PARAM.SFO), cellGame | ✅ Complete |
| **Input** | cellPad (XInput/SDL2), cellKb, cellMouse | ✅ Complete |
| **Audio** | cellAudio (WASAPI/SDL2, mixing thread, multi-port) | ✅ Complete |
| **Video Output** | cellVideoOut (resolution config, 720p default) | ✅ Complete |
| **Codecs** | cellPngDec, cellJpgDec, cellGifDec (stb_image) | ✅ Complete |
| **Font** | cellFont (stb_truetype backend + fallback metrics) | ✅ Complete |
| **Network** | sys_net (BSD sockets), cellNet, cellNetCtl, cellHttpUtil, cellSsl, sceNp*, sceNpTrophy | ✅ Complete |
| **Hardware** | cellUsbd (USB), cellCamera (PS Eye), cellGem (PS Move) — stub, no devices | ✅ Complete |
| **Sync** | cellSync (atomic spinlocks, LF queue), cellSync2 (OS-backed) | ✅ Complete |
| **System** | cellRtc, cellMsgDialog, cellOskDialog, cellUserInfo, cellGameExec | ✅ Complete |
| **Localization** | cellL10n (UTF-8/16/32/UCS-2, ISO-8859-1, generic converter) | ✅ Complete |

## Platform support

| | Windows | macOS (arm64) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```

         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

│   └── error_codes.h         # PS3 system error codes (CELL_OK, CELL_E*)
│
├── templates/project/        # Starter template for new game ports
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # Build system
│   ├── main.cpp              # Application entry point
│   ├── stubs.cpp             # Game-specific function overrides
│   └── config.toml           # Recompiler configuration
│
├── config/                   # Reference configurations
│   └── example.toml          # Example recompilation config
│
├── patches/                  # Patches for upstream tools
│   └── xenonrecomp-ppu.patch # XenonRecomp adaptations for PPU (Cell != Xenon)
│
└── docs/                     # Documentation (incl. ARCHITECTURE, RUNTIME, SPU_LIFTER, RSX_GRAPHICS, ...)
    ├── ARCHITECTURE.md        # Cell processor and recomp pipeline deep-dive
    ├── GETTING_STARTED.md     # How to recompile your first PS3 game
    ├── MODULE_STATUS.md       # Implementation status of all HLE modules
    ├── MODULES_REFERENCE.md   # Detailed per-module documentation
    ├── RUNTIME.md             # Runtime reference: VM, PPU/SPU contexts, types
    ├── SYSCALLS.md            # All LV2 kernel syscall implementations
    ├── NID_SYSTEM.md          # PS3 NID linking system explained
    ├── TOOLS.md               # Recompiler pipeline tools reference
    ├── BUILDING.md            # Build system, compilers, platform notes
    ├── GAME_PORTING_GUIDE.md  # Step-by-step game porting walkthrough
    └── PLATFORM_ABSTRACTION.md # Win32/POSIX cross-platform details
```

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

## Module Status

We're building HLE implementations based on RPCS3's module system. **97 modules complete, 1 partial (media decode)** — 219 files and ~76,000 lines under `libs/`.

| Category | Modules | Status |
|----------|---------|--------|
| **Kernel Threading** | sys_ppu_thread, sys_mutex, sys_cond, sys_semaphore, sys_rwlock | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Events** | sys_event (queues, ports, flags), sys_timer | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Memory** | sys_memory, sys_mmapper (containers, shared mem) | ✅ Complete |
| **Kernel Filesystem** | sys_fs (path mapping, real I/O) | ✅ Complete |
| **Filesystem** | cellFs (real file I/O, dir ops, stat, path translation) | ✅ Complete |
| **Save System** | cellSaveData (callback-driven, PARAM.SFO), cellGame | ✅ Complete |
| **Input** | cellPad (XInput/SDL2), cellKb, cellMouse | ✅ Complete |
| **Audio** | cellAudio (WASAPI/SDL2, mixing thread, multi-port) | ✅ Complete |
| **Video Output** | cellVideoOut (resolution config, 720p default) | ✅ Complete |
| **Codecs** | cellPngDec, cellJpgDec, cellGifDec (stb_image) | ✅ Complete |
| **Font** | cellFont (stb_truetype backend + fallback metrics) | ✅ Complete |
| **Network** | sys_net (BSD sockets), cellNet, cellNetCtl, cellHttpUtil, cellSsl, sceNp*, sceNpTrophy | ✅ Complete |
| **Hardware** | cellUsbd (USB), cellCamera (PS Eye), cellGem (PS Move) — stub, no devices | ✅ Complete |
| **Sync** | cellSync (atomic spinlocks, LF queue), cellSync2 (OS-backed) | ✅ Complete |
| **System** | cellRtc, cellMsgDialog, cellOskDialog, cellUserInfo, cellGameExec | ✅ Complete |
| **Localization** | cellL10n (UTF-8/16/32/UCS-2, ISO-8859-1, generic converter) | ✅ Complete |
| **Resolution** | cellResc (display modes, scaling, interlace, aspect ratio) | ✅ Complete |
| **Fibers** | cellFiber (PPU fibers via Windows Fibers/ucontext) | ✅ Complete |
| **AV Config** | cellAvconfExt (audio output info, gamma, sound availability) | ✅ Complete |
| **Input Util** | cellKey2char (HID scancode → Unicode, US-101 layout) | ✅ Complete |
| **Graphics** | cellGcmSys (cmd buffer, IO mapping, tile/zcull, flip handlers, timestamps, FIFO walker + ring recycle), RSX command processor (NV47xx parsing, state tracking, backend callbacks), **live D3D12 backend** (executes the title's real NV4097 vertex/fragment p

1384054367.description: Uncharted: Drake's Fortune (PS3) statically recompiled to a native Apple Silicon macOS app, rendered with Metal. Fork of ps3recomp.
1384054367.readme_excerpt:
# ps3-uncharted **Uncharted: Drake's Fortune (PS3, 2007) running natively on Apple Silicon Macs** — not emulated, but *recompiled*: the game's code is translated into C++, compiled for ARM64 and drawn with Metal. 🇮🇹 [Leggi in italiano](README.it.md)
This port — native macOS app The same scene in RPCS3, the reference emulator
> **Status: work in progress.** The game boots, reaches the main menu, saves, > and loads the first level at around **28 frames per second** (the original > targets 30). It is not yet playable from start to finish. --- ## What is this, in plain words? Old console games normally run on a PC or Mac through an **emulator**: a program that pretends to be the console and interprets the game's instructions one by one, while it runs. That works, but it is heavy. **Static recompilation** takes a different route. The game's program is translated *once*, ahead of time, into ordinary source code, and that code is compiled into a normal Mac app. Nothing is interpreted while you play: the game's logic runs as native code on the Mac's processor. The catch is that the PS3 is a very unusual machine, so "just translating the code" is only the start. This project is about everything else: the PS3's six helper processors, its graphics chip, and the Sony system libraries the game expects to find. This repository is a fork of [**ps3recomp**](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) by sp00nznet, a general toolkit for recompiling PS3 games. ps3-uncharted takes that toolkit to **macOS** and pushes it on one specific, very demanding game. It is developed independently from the original project. ## What works | | | |---|---| | ✅ Boot | All 172 system-library imports the game needs are resolved | | ✅ Loading | Levels, audio banks, cutscene data, subtitles | | ✅ Menus | Main menu readable and usable, "New Game" creates a save | | ✅ First level | `dive-boat` on screen with HUD, lighting, shadows and post-processing | | ✅ Characters | Drake fully rendered and animated; death and restart from checkpoint | | ✅ Audio | In-game sound without crackling | | ✅ Speed | ~28 fps in the level (it started at 8) | | ⏳ Stability | An intermittent freeze in about 1 run out of 10–15 is being hunted | | ⏳ Beyond | The rest of the game has not been tested yet | Tested on a MacBook Pro with an **Apple M4 Pro** and 48 GB of memory. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Game disc
(your own copy)"] --> B["Decrypted
EBOOT.elf"] B --> C["PPU lifter
PowerPC → C++"] B --> D["SPU lifter
SPU programs → C++"] C --> E["clang
→ ARM64"] D --> E E --> F["Native macOS app"] G["Runtime
PS3 system libraries,
SPURS, audio, input"] --> F H["Graphics
RSX commands → Metal"] --> F ``` The PS3's processor is a **Cell**: one general-purpose core (the **PPU**) plus six small, very fast helper cores (the **SPUs**). Uncharted leans heavily on the SPUs for animation, geometry, physics and audio. The port handles each piece separately: 1. **Main program (PPU).** The game's executable is decrypted from the disc and translated into C++ by `tools/ppu_lifter.py`: about **18,600 functions, 2.2 million lines** of generated code, compiled to native ARM64. 2. **Helper processors (SPU).** The SPU programs are translated the same way and run on ordinary Mac threads, with our own implementation of **SPURS**, the Sony job scheduler that hands work out to the SPUs. 3. **System libraries.** Everything the game asks of the PS3 operating system — files, saves, controller, audio, video decoding, threads and locks — is re-implemented in `runtime/` and `libs/`. 4. **Graphics.** The commands the game sends to the PS3's GPU (the **RSX**) are read and translated to **Metal**, including the game's own shader programs, which are converted to Metal's shading language on the fly. When it is unclear what the original code was supposed to do, the answer is checked against [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net/), the PS3 emulator, rather than guessed. ## A few of the bugs along the way Getting here took 40+ working sessions, each one logged with measurements in [`docs/STATO.md`](../docs/STATO.md) (in Italian). Some highlights: - **The black screen that was not a graphics bug.** The game draws in an old "immediate mode" (every vertex written as a separate GPU register) that the toolkit had never needed. Zero draws were reaching Metal. - **Drake without arms and legs.** The SPU has no concept of "NaN": a value that is simply a big number on the PS3 is an invalid number on a Mac, and `0 × invalid` erased every limb. The SPU math now follows the Cell spec. - **The freeze when Drake dies.** A job meant for exactly one SPU was being run on six at once; they overwrote each other's "done" flag and the game waited forever. - **Crackling audio.** The game was told the playback position as an ever-growing counter instead of a slot in an 8-block ring, so it wrote over sound that had not been played yet. Clicks dropped from 22% of block boundaries to 0.1%. - **From 8 to 28 fps**, the biggest jump coming from letting each simulated SPU pick its own work like the real hardware does, instead of waiting for the slowest one every time. ## Building You need an Apple Silicon Mac, the Xcode Command Line Tools and [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) (`cmake`, `ninja`). ```bash export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH" cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release # configure cmake --build build # build the runtime and tools ``` This builds the runtime and the tools. **No game files are included** in this repository, and none ever will be: to build the actual game you need your own disc and its decrypted executable. The step-by-step recipe that turns your copy into the Mac app is in [`uncharted/`](../uncharted/README.md). ## Repository map | Path | What is inside | |---|---| | `runtime/ppu/` | Loading the executable, guest memory, system-library imports | | `runtime/spu/` | Simulated SPUs, DMA, SPURS and the job manager | | `runtime/syscalls/` | The PS3 kernel (lv2) system calls | | `libs/` | Sony system libraries: graphics, audio, input, saves, video… | | `libs/video/rsx_metal_backend.m` | The Metal renderer | | `runtime/host/`, `runtime/platform/` | Window, macOS and Windows compatibility | | `uncharted/` | Scripts that build and launch the game from your own copy | | `tools/` | PPU and SPU lifters, analysis tools | | `docs/` | Technical docs; `STATO.md` is the work diary | A complete map is in [`ATLANTE.md`](../ATLANTE.md). The original ps3recomp README is still in [`README.md`](../README.md). ## Credits and legal - Built on [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) by sp00nznet, MIT license. - [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net/) as the reference for how the hardware behaves. - Developed by Elia Venturi. *Uncharted: Drake's Fortune* is a trademark of Sony Interactive Entertainment, developed by Naughty Dog. This is a personal, non-commercial study project with no affiliation to either. It contains no game code or assets; you need a legally owned copy of the game to use it.

1385569785.description: Ben 10 Omniverse (PS3, BLUS31017) — native macOS port by static recompilation. No game code or assets.
1385569785.readme_excerpt:
# Ben 10 Omniverse — native macOS port by static recompilation

**Ben 10 Omniverse** (PS3, `BLUS31017`, version 01.00) running **natively on Apple Silicon**: no emulator, no JIT.
The PowerPC (PPU) and Cell SPU code is translated ahead of time into C/C++, compiled with clang for arm64 and linked
against a reimplementation of the PS3 OS and libraries. Graphics use **Metal**, cutscenes **VideoToolbox**, sound **CoreAudio**.

> This repository contains **no game code and no game assets**. You need your own legitimate copy of the game; the
> files below only describe how the build is made and how it is measured.

Sister project: [gow2-recomp](https://github.com/andrebrumdev/gow2-recomp) (God of War II HD), same engine.

## Status

| Area | State |
|---|---|
| Boot, logos, intro videos (H.264) | ✅ videos decoded by VideoToolbox |
| Title screen, front-end hub, New Game | ✅ |
| First level (Training Simulation 1): walking, dialogue, HUD | ✅ plays; later levels not verified |
| Frame rate | 🟡 the game is locked at 30 fps by its own limiter and has a 60 Hz mode of its own; on a fanless MacBook Air M5 the machine reaches 27–59 fps depending on heat and load |
| Audio | ✅ music, voices and effects; short dropouts only on some loading screens |
| Controllers | ✅ GameController (DualShock 4 / DualSense / Xbox / MFi) and keyboard |

Measured, not claimed: the per-job cost of the lifted SPU code follows the SoC clock, not the runtime; the notes in
[`notes/`](notes/) and the harness in [`bench/`](bench/) show how the numbers were taken.

## What is here

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `recomp.toml`, `functions.json`, `spu_jobs.toml` | lifter configuration: function bounds, mid-asm hooks, SPU jobs/tasks to lift |
| `host/` | host-side code linked into the binary (frame-step hooks, frame pacing policy) with unit tests |
| `bench/` | measurement harness: scripted pad input, event-window analysis, A/B scripts |
| `notes/` | engineering log: what was measured, what was refuted |
| `build_macos.sh`, `run_ben10.sh` | build and run recipes (environment variables are documented in the script header) |
| `boot_macos.cpp` | macOS entry point (guest on its own thread, window pumped on the main thread) |

## Building

The port is built by [`build_macos.sh`](build_macos.sh) against the engine's runtime library. The engine is a fork of
[sp00nznet/ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) with a macOS/Metal port and additional work on the SPU
runtime; **that fork is not public yet**, so a clean build from this repository alone is not possible today. Pieces that
apply to the upstream engine are being sent there as pull requests
([#206](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp/pull/206), [#207](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp/pull/207),
[#208](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp/pull/208)).

## Notes

- Everything that is an experiment is gated by an environment variable and off by default.
- Findings are written down with the evidence that supports them; refuted hypotheses are kept in the notes.

1385782942.description: Native PC port of PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale (BCUS98472) via ps3recomp static recompilation. Boots to FIOS init; was in active development but i have moved onto other projects, feel free to continue what i left off if you feel like it!
1385782942.readme_excerpt:
# allstars-ps3

Native PC port of **PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale (BCUS98472)** via
[ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) static recompilation.
PPU is lifted to C and linked against the ps3recomp runtime (D3D12 backend on
Windows). No emulator required.

> **Legal:** you must own the BCUS98472 disc and dump it plus its `.dkey`
> yourself. This repo contains no Sony code, keys, firmware, game binaries,
> or assets — only the port project, scripts, and runtime patches.

## Status

- Decrypted `EBOOT.BIN` -> `EBOOT.BIN.elf` (13.2 MB, PPC64) with own `.dkey`
- Analysis: 25 modules / 376 imports, 24,530 PPU functions, 3 SPU images
- Lift: 25,544 PPU functions (with `--hle-stubs`) + 1098 HLE handlers,
  2095 SPU functions across 3 images
- Builds: `MyGameRecomp.exe` (~170 MB) with clang-cl 23 + MSVC
- Boots: CRT -> SPURS "Main"+"SCREAM" -> `cellGame BootCheck (BCUS98472)` ->
  FIOS 1.3.5 -> D3D12 init -> stalls on `fios worker cond` (invalid lwcond)
- Zero `unresolved NID` at boot (8 fixed: 7x cellSpursJq + _sys_spu_printf)

See [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md) for the detailed boot log and blockers.

## Layout

```
allstars-ps3/
  CMakeLists.txt   # port build (based on ps3recomp templates/project)
  main.cpp         # runner + PARAM.SFO title-id init fix
  stubs.cpp        # game-specific overrides (currently empty)
  config.toml      # recompiler/module settings reference
  tools/
    decrypt_iso.py # Redump ISO -> decrypted ISO with own .dkey (AES-CBC, IV=LBA)
  patches/
    ps3recomp-runtime-allstars.patch  # 8 missing HLE handlers (JQ attrs, spu printf)
  docs/
    STATUS.md      # current boot status + next steps
```

## Build

Prerequisites: Python 3.10+, CMake 3.20+, Ninja, VS 2022, LLVM (clang-cl).

```bat
:: 1. ps3recomp checkout + our runtime patch
git clone https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp.git
cd ps3recomp
git checkout 39e4f49286447b3ae3dcc2358700c840860ee677
git apply ..\allstars-ps3\patches\ps3recomp-runtime-allstars.patch

:: 2. lift (needs decrypted EBOOT.BIN.elf from your own dump)
set PYTHONUTF8=1
python tools\ppu_loader.py EBOOT.BIN.elf -o loader_out
python tools\ppu_lifter.py EBOOT.BIN.elf ^
  --functions loader_out\EBOOT.BIN.functions.json ^
  --hle-stubs loader_out\EBOOT.BIN.imports.json ^
  -o ..\allstars-ps3-work\recompiled
python tools\gen_hle_nids.py --all ^
  --out ..\allstars-ps3-work\recompiled\ppu_hle_nids.cpp

:: 3. configure + build (VS prompt for headers, LLVM for compiler)
call "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\Community\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat"
set PATH=C:\Program Files\LLVM\bin;C:\Program Files\CMake\bin;%PATH%
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl ^
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl ^
  -DPS3RECOMP_DIR=<ps3recomp> -DRECOMP_DIR=<recompiled> <allstars-ps3>
cmake --build build
```

Run (needs decrypted game files for VFS):

```bat
set PS3_VFS_ROOT=C:\path\to\vfs
build\MyGameRecomp.exe C:\path\to\EBOOT.BIN.elf
```

`tools/decrypt_iso.py` decrypts a Redump ISO with the `.dkey` sitting next
to it (same basename). It parses the region table (even regions plain, odd
encrypted) and AES-CBC decrypts per sector with IV = 12 zero bytes + BE LBA.

## Upstreaming

`patches/ps3recomp-runtime-allstars.patch` should go upstream to sp00nznet/ps3recomp:
the 7 `cellSpursJobQueueAttribute*` setters and `_sys_spu_printf_initialize`
are generic, not title-specific. The `main.cpp` PARAM.SFO init is already
upstream behavior in newer templates.

1388035287.description: Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
1388035287.readme_excerpt:
# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

**[Join the sp00nznet recomp Discord](https://discord.gg/CRpzGWZFcu)** — the
community hub for sp00nznet's recomp projects, where ps3recomp development
happens in the open. Good place to ask questions, show a port you are working
on, or find out what people are stuck on before you duplicate the effort.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [ReXGlue](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk) (Xbox 360 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — the output is C/C++, so it can target any platform a compiler does (see [platform support](#platform-support) for where the runtime actually stands today)

## Platform support

Every row is exercised by CI on every push, and **all three are green on
`master`** — the PPU boot scaffold ratchet that had been red since before v0.11.0
([#139](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp/issues/139)) is at zero on all
four toolchains. The rows below describe what those jobs actually do, not what a
green tick would imply: building the runtime and passing the suites is not the
same as running a game, and only one row claims that.

| | Windows | macOS (arm64) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime library builds | yes | yes | yes |
| Lifter + 8 test suites | yes | yes | yes |
| Render backend | D3D12 | Metal | null (headless software) |
| Runs a recompiled game | **yes** | **no** | no |

The gap on macOS is the PPU boot scaffold — `ppu_loader.cpp`, `boot_main.cpp`
and the HLE dispatch are still Win32-only (thread creation, VirtualAlloc, SEH,
stack walking), and they are compiled per-game rather than into the library.
So macOS builds the runtime, renders through Metal and passes the full test
suite, but cannot yet load and run a title. `ps3recomp_host` drives
cellGcm → RSX → Metal end to end without a game, which is what makes further
graphics work possible there.

Linux builds and passes the same suites under both GCC and Clang, and runs
`ps3recomp_host` end to end, on every push. Its backend is the null backend's
headless software path: a host-memory framebuffer with a CPU triangle filler,
enough to prove the guest's command stream produced the pixels it asked for on
a runner with no display and no GPU. It is not a renderer — no depth, no
blending, no textures — so Linux is still one real backend, plus the same PPU
boot scaffold macOS needs, away from running a title.

### What each platform needs next

Both non-Windows platforms are blocked on the *same* two things, in this order.

**1. The PPU boot scaffold, on POSIX.** This is the shared blocker and the only
one that gates "runs a recompiled game" on both. `ppu_loader.cpp`,
`boot_main.cpp` and the HLE dispatch are compiled *per game* rather than into
the library, and were Win32-only — thread creation, `VirtualAlloc`, SEH, stack
walking. v0.10.0 took it to zero errors on POSIX and put it under CI so it
cannot rot again, and ported the guest-pointer trap, thread-locals and host
backtraces. What is left is running it: load a lifted image on POSIX and reach
the guest's first instruction, then `main`. Until that works, neither platform
can run a title no matter how good its renderer is.

**2. One real backend each.** The RSX abstraction landed in v0.10.0 (#101, #102,
#103) — texture conversion, the `TEXTURE_CONTROL1` crossbar, texture layout and
a neutral draw record all live outside the D3D12 file now, so a backend no
longer has to reimplement them to draw anything.

- **macOS** has the furthest to go that is *interesting* rather than
  mechanical: [@slushiimusic](https://github.com/slushiimusic)'s Metal backend
  (#96) does clear, flip, guest vertex fetch, a pipeline-state cache and blend
  translation. Reaching D3D12 parity means the guest's own fragment programs
  through the decompiler, then textures. `ps3recomp_host` already drives
  cellGcm → RSX → Metal with no lifted game, so each step is testable before a
  title exists to run.
- **Linux** has no renderer at all — the headless backend is a CPU triangle
  filler for CI, deliberately. Vulkan is the obvious target, and it starts from
  the same neutral draw record Metal reads.

**Deliberately not claimed:** the table above says "no" for running a game on
macOS and Linux, and it will keep saying "no" until a title actually boots to

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘

   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

| **Font** | cellFont (stb_truetype backend + fallback metrics) | ✅ Complete |
| **Network** | sys_net (BSD sockets), cellNet, cellNetCtl, cellHttpUtil, cellSsl, sceNp*, sceNpTrophy | ✅ Complete |
