1430407098.readme_excerpt:
# Battride War Recomp

An **experimental** native Linux port of Kamen Rider: Battride War (Japan), **BLJS10220**, built with PS3Recomp 0.17.0 and Vulkan. This project is not affiliated with the game's rights holders.

This repository contains the port's code, configuration, tests and instructions. **It does not include the game, ISO, EBOOT, firmware, keys, saves, a compiled game executable, or generated PPU/SPU sources.** You need your own copy of the Japan disc.

**Download:** the [latest release](https://github.com/robertoqimin/battride-war-recomp/releases/latest) (v0.5.2) is an AppImage that imports your ISO, translates your own EBOOT and compiles the game on your computer. See [System requirements](#system-requirements-appimage).

The project was called **Battride War Port** (repository `battride-war-port`) until v0.5.0. Old links redirect here, and the data folder keeps its old name, `~/.local/share/battride-war-port`, so existing installs and saves carry over.

## Current status (October 26, 2026)

**Playable through the opening mission.** The intro movie, title screen, menus, the opening cutscene and mission **STG02** work, and STG02 was completed by hand, returning to mission select. The rest of the game has not been played.

What works in the tested parts:

- **Graphics:** scenery, characters with animation, enemies, HUD, special-attack effects and character shadows, which fall from the characters' feet. Shadows, lighting and effects in the opening cutscene and STG02 were compared with footage of the original game and match.
- **Audio:** music, voices and effects, with the game's audio SPU task, the module it loads and its MP3 codec translated to native code.
- **Saves and data:** game data installation and saves; 21,107 installed files matched the disc byte for byte.
- **Movies:** PAMF playback through `cellSail`.
- **Input:** controllers through SDL2, and keyboard and mouse (see [Controls](#controls)); both can be used together.
- **Display:** windowed, borderless fullscreen or exclusive fullscreen at a chosen resolution, internal rendering at up to 4× the PS3's resolution, AMD FSR 1 upscaling, and 16:9 kept with black bars (see [Display options](#display-options)).
- **Launcher:** a GTK 4 / libadwaita window that imports the disc, builds the game, and sets the display, keyboard, controller and performance options, with a live log (see [Using the AppImage](#using-the-appimage)).

Known issues ([docs/ISSUES.md](docs/ISSUES.md) has the full list, in Portuguese):

- **Frame drops in the most crowded fights.** Ordinary fighting runs at about 55-58 fps, but the heaviest moments drop to about 45 fps: there the game's own command building on its main thread is the limit (see [Performance](#performance)).
- **Audio** was measured without gaps in the title music and scripted combat, but a manual session still reported breakups during heavy fights, coinciding with frame drops.
- **One graphics glitch:** a large untextured polygon was seen for a single frame at the start of a special attack and could not be reproduced.
- **Not validated:** the full game, sessions longer than about 30 minutes, a clean exit on every path, and the ATRAC audio codec.

### Performance

Measured on a Ryzen 5 4600H with a GTX 1650 with `scripts/bench_combat.py`: 60-second windows of STG02 fighting (the first fight, after the tutorial prompt), with the game built on this computer by the AppImage:

| Build | Average | p95 frame | Worst 5 seconds |
|---|---|---|---|
| AppImage v0.5.0 (bundled GCC 11, optimization profiles) | 55.6 fps (runs of 57.0, 51.9 and 57.9) | 21.2 ms | 46.1 fps |
| v0.4.x code on the same route | about 48 fps | 24 ms | about 45 fps |

These are guest frames per second: the game runs its logic in real time and caps itself at 60. The run at 51.9 fps met a heavier fight (up to 960 draws a frame against about 800). In the heaviest moments the game's own command building on its main thread is the limit ([docs/PERFORMANCE.md](docs/PERFORMANCE.md)); a manual session before v0.4.0 reported about 25 fps on this laptop in the heaviest fights, not re-measured since.

What got it there, from about 6 fps at the start (details in [docs/PERFORMANCE.md](docs/PERFORMANCE.md)):

- `-O2` for the translated code, batched Vulkan command buffers, non-blocking presentation (MAILBOX when available) and a frame clock driven by the game's own fences.
- Real blocking for the game's lightweight condition variables (`sys_lwcond`): the SDK's polling version made the render thread redraw each frame dozens of times and overflow its 4 MiB command buffers.
- The audio SPU task and its codec translated instead of interpreted.
- Inline guest memory access in the hottest translated chunks, SIMD vertex decoding, and reuse of Vulkan constant buffers, descriptors and pipeline binds.
- Guest mutex locks no longer read the system clock twice per call, which cut frames over 33 ms by about two thirds.
- The translated code runs from transparent huge pages where the kernel allows them.
- GCC profile-guided optimization, trained on the opening mission and shipped with the AppImage.
- In 0.5.0: the busiest threads on physical cores of their own, render targets kept instead of recreated every frame, faster vertex and index processing on the RSX walker, and the guarded fast store for every translated store.

## System requirements (AppImage)

The AppImage contains no game code or assets. It includes GCC optimization profiles: counts of how often each branch of the translated code ran while the developer played the opening mission, which make the build on your computer faster. They contain no game code, text, graphics or sound. On first launch it imports your disc, translates your EBOOT and compiles the game on your computer with its bundled toolchain (see [docs/APPIMAGE.md](docs/APPIMAGE.md)). Only one system has run the game end to end: Fedora on a laptop with a Ryzen 5 4600H and GTX 1650 (Radeon integrated graphics alongside; the backend picks the discrete GPU). The on-device build was also verified in an Arch Linux container, and the import helpers in Ubuntu 22.04. Everything below meets the checks in `packaging/launcher.py`, `packaging/graphics_probe.c` and the Vulkan backend, but has not been run.

**First launch:** an internet connection to download the official RPCS3 build (83 MB) that reads your disc, unless you already have that exact file; about 8 GB of RAM (the build runs one compiler job per 2 GB available, at least one), about 8 GB of free space in the data folder (game files, plus about 4 GB while building) and time: the compile took 12-14 minutes with 3-4 jobs on the 4600H; expect 15-60 minutes depending on the CPU. It happens once; the built game is reused until the AppImage version or the CPU changes.

**CPU:** x86_64 with SSSE3 and SSE4.1. The game is compiled with `-march=native`, so each CPU gets code for its own instruction set (AVX2 where available).

| Supported | Not supported |
|---|---|
| Intel Core 2 45 nm (Penryn/Wolfdale/Yorkfield) and newer | Intel Core 2 65 nm (Conroe/Merom): no SSE4.1 |
| Every Intel Core i3/i5/i7/i9 and Core Ultra generation, Xeon from Nehalem | Intel Atom Bonnell/Saltwell (Silvermont and newer are fine) |
| Intel Pentium/Celeron from Silvermont/Goldmont, N100/N200 | AMD Athlon 64, Phenom, Phenom II (K8/K10): SSE4a only |
| AMD FX (Bulldozer/Piledriver), A-series APUs, Jaguar | ARM and RISC-V |
| Every AMD Ryzen, Threadripper and EPYC generation | |

Per-core speed decides the frame rate in combat: each frame is the RSX command walker followed by the game's main thread, one after the other. CPUs slower per core than a Ryzen 5 4600H will drop further in crowded fights; old CPUs without AVX2 will be noticeably slower. With four or more physical cores the busiest threads get a core each (`PORT_THREAD_PIN=0` turns that off).

**GPU:** Vulkan 1.0 with a graphics queue that can present to the window, `VK_KHR_swapchain` and `textureCompressionBC` (PS3 DXT textures). The launcher's graphics check rejects devices without BC textures.

| Vendor | Supported | Driver |
|---|---|---|
| NVIDIA | GeForce 600 (Kepler) and newer: GTX 700/900/10/16, RTX 20/30/40/50 | Proprietary (470 legacy for Kepler); NVK (Mesa 24.1+) for Turing and newer |
| AMD | Radeon HD 7000 (GCN 1) and newer: R7/R9, RX 400/500, Vega, RX 5000-9000, Ryzen APUs, Steam Deck | Mesa RADV (`amdgpu` kernel driver for GCN 1/2) |
| Intel | Ivy Bridge/Haswell graphics and newer (HD 4000+, UHD, Iris Xe), Arc A/B | Mesa ANV (`hasvk` for Gen7/Gen8) |

Not supported: GPUs without Vulkan (NVIDIA Fermi and older, AMD TeraScale / HD 6000 and older, Intel Sandy Bridge and older). Software Vulkan (lavapipe) passes the check but is far too slow. The GTX 1650 is not the limit at the frame rates above; older integrated and entry-level GPUs may be.

**Distribution:** glibc 2.35 or newer, with the host Vulkan loader (`libvulkan.so.1`) and GPU driver installed. The AppImage does not bundle libc, the Vulkan/GL loaders, Mesa or the X11/Wayland libraries. FUSE 3 (`fusermount3`) is needed, or run with `--appimage-extract-and-run`.

| Supported | Not supported |
|---|---|
| Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04 and newer; Kubuntu, Xubuntu, Linux Mint 21+, Pop!_OS 22.04+, Zorin OS 17+, elementary OS 7+ | Ubuntu 20.04 and older, Linux Mint 20 |
| Debian 12 (Bookworm), 13 (Trixie) | Debian 11 and older |
| Fedora 36+; Nobara, Bazzite | RHEL / AlmaLinux / Rocky 9 (glibc 2.34) and older |
| RHEL / AlmaLinux / Rocky 10 | openSUSE Leap 15.x |
| openSUSE Tumbleweed, Leap 16 | musl distributions (Alpine, Void musl) |
| Arch, Manjaro, EndeavourOS, CachyOS, Garuda | NixOS without `steam-run` / `appimage-run` |
| Recent SteamOS 3 (Steam Deck): likely, unverified | |

On hosts whose libstdc++ is older than RPCS3 needs (below `GLIBCXX_3.4.32`, e.g. Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12) RPCS3's own `AppRun` uses its bundled `checkrt` libstdc++/libgcc_s. No compiler or development package is needed on the host: the bundled Ubuntu 22.04 toolchain builds against its own sysroot.

**For more frames:** set the CPU governor to performance (`powerprofilesctl set performance`), leave the launcher's **GameMode** switch on if GameMode is installed, and keep laptops plugged in.

## Using the AppImage

```sh
chmod +x BattrideWarRecomp-v0.5.2-x86_64.AppImage
./BattrideWarRecomp-v0.5.2-x86_64.AppImage
```

The launcher has five pages:

- **Game:** your ISO and the data folder (game files, saves, logs). **Install & Play** in the header imports the disc and builds the game the first time, and starts it afterwards; it becomes **Stop** while something runs.
- **Settings:** display mode, resolution, upscaling, internal resolution, MangoHud and GameMode.
- **Keyboard** and **Controller:** bindings, mouse sensitivity, stick dead zone and controller buttons (see [Controls](#controls)).
- **Log:** the import, the build and the game's output as they happen, with copy and save buttons and the logs folder.

Settings and bindings are saved as you change them and apply the next time the game starts. The status and the frame rate stay in a bar at the bottom of every page. For a report, send the `logs/` folder from the data folder (default `~/.local/share/battride-war-port`).

## Controls

A controller (anything SDL2 recognises: DualShock, DualSense, Xbox, Switch Pro...) works as the PS3 pad. Keyboard and mouse work at the same time, as pad 1:

| Keyboard / mouse | PS3 pad |
|---|---|
| W A S D | left stick (move) |
| mouse | right stick (camera) |
| left button, J | □ (normal attack) |
| right button, I | △ |
| middle button, L | ○ |
| Space, K | × (jump) |
| Q / E | L1 / R1 |
| Left Shift / R | L2 / R2 |
| V / C | L3 / R3 |
| arrow keys | d-pad |
| Enter / Backspace | ○ / × (confirm / back in menus, as on a Japanese PS3) |
| Esc | START (pause) |
| Tab | SELECT |

Click in the window to let the mouse move the camera (in fullscreen it is captured automatically); Alt or switching away releases it. Close the game with the window's close button.

**Remapping:** the launcher's **Keyboard** page lists every pad control: the pencil replaces its key (press the key or mouse button to use), **+** adds another, the clear button unbinds it; changes are saved at once. The same page sets the mouse camera sensitivity (0.1 to 5.0, default 1.0), inverts the camera's up/down, and can bind keys to the camera for playing without a mouse. Keys follow the keyboard layout (on AZERTY, the key labelled Z is Z). The launcher writes the choice to `controls.cfg` in the data folder; outside the launcher, point `PORT_CONTROLS` at such a file (one `control = key, key` per line, SDL key names such as `W`, `Space`, `Left Shift`, or `Mouse Left`/`Middle`/`Right`/`X1`/`X2`). `PORT_MOUSE_SENSITIVITY` overrides the file's sensitivity.

**Controller:** the first controller connected is player 1, and when it is unplugged the next one takes its place. Buttons follow their position, not their label: the bottom face button is × on Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo layouts alike. The launcher's **Controller** page sets the stick dead zone (default 0.15 of the stick's travel; raise it if the camera or character drifts with the sticks released) and which controller button each PS3 button reads (`pad_cross = A` and so on in `controls.cfg`; names `A`, `B`, `X`, `Y`, `LB`, `RB`, `LT`, `RT`, `L3`, `R3`, `Start`, `Back`, `Guide`, `Up`, `Down`, `Left`, `Right`, `Misc`, `Touchpad`, `Paddle1` to `Paddle4`). Rumble works. Besides the mappings inside SDL, the AppImage loads the community [SDL_GameControllerDB](https://github.com/mdqinc/SDL_GameControllerDB) (`PORT_CONTROLLER_DB`), so controllers newer than its SDL 2.0.20 are recognised. `game.log` names each controller as it connects (`[cellPad] controller on port 1: ...`), or names a device SDL does not know together with its GUID; a mapping for it can be given in `SDL_GAMECONTROLLERCONFIG`, which takes precedence over the database.

## Display options

The launcher's **Settings** page sets how the game is shown; Alt+Enter or F11 switches between the window and fullscreen while playing.

- **Windowed:** a resizable window, starting at the chosen size.
- **Borderless fullscreen:** a window covering the desktop at its own resolution.
- **Fullscreen:** exclusive fullscreen, switching the monitor to the chosen resolution (the closest it offers).
- **Rendering (internal resolution):** the PS3 renders the game at 1280 × 720. The port can render it 2×, 3× or 4× larger in each direction (2560 × 1440, 3840 × 2160, 5120 × 2880): every render target, shadow map included, is that much bigger, so geometry, shadows and effects are drawn at the higher resolution instead of being stretched. Measured in STG02 combat on a GTX 1650 with v0.4.x: about 45 fps at native resolution, 42 at 2×, 31 at 3× and 21 at 4×; above 2× that GPU becomes the limit.
- **Upscaling:** when the rendered frame is shown larger than it was rendered, it is upscaled with **AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution 1.0** (edge-adaptive upscaling and sharpening) or plain bilinear filtering; shown smaller (for example 2× on a 1080p screen), it is filtered down with a single bilinear sample per pixel, which at 4× on a 1080p screen skips part of the rendered detail (a proper area downscale is planned: [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md)). The picture always keeps 16:9, with black bars on other aspect ratios.

Outside the launcher, the same settings are environment variables of the game: `PORT_DISPLAY_MODE` (`windowed`, `borderless`, `fullscreen`), `PORT_DISPLAY_SIZE` (for example `2560x1440`), `PORT_RENDER_SCALE` (`1` to `4`), `PORT_DISPLAY_FILTER` (`fsr`, `linear`), `PORT_DISPLAY_STRETCH=1` to fill the window, and `PORT_FSR_SHARPNESS` (sharpening in stops, default 0.2; 0 is the strongest). `PORT_WINDOW_DUMP=<file>` writes one frame as the window receives it, for checking without a screenshot tool (after `PORT_WINDOW_DUMP_FRAME` frames, or when the file named by `PORT_WINDOW_DUMP_TRIGGER` appears). `PORT_FPS_LIMIT=<fps>` caps the frame rate.

## Building from source

Follow [docs/BUILD.md](docs/BUILD.md) for Fedora dependencies, the pinned SDK revision, data layout, the EBOOT hash and PPU/SPU generation.

After preparing the SDK and local data in a fresh checkout:

```bash
../ps3recomp/.venv/bin/python scripts/generate.py --jobs 4
cmake --preset linux-vulkan \
  -DPython3_EXECUTA

fix(build): avoid SIGPIPE false negative in the PS3_MAC_VULKAN=0 check

Under pipefail, grep -q exiting early SIGPIPEs nm and the pipeline reads as not found; capture nm's output and match it in-shell instead (Codex review).

89c95ad8c12d2dbde2650b45903b6106acd9df85.message:
fix(build): target macOS 14 by default and make Vulkan optional

TGT for GOW2_TARGET=macos was empty, so objects carried the host SDK minos.
Now -mmacosx-version-min=${GOW2_MACOS_MIN:-${MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET:-14.0}}
reaches every compile and the link. PS3_MAC_VULKAN=0 skips libvulkan/shaderc/

a7c1f64c825a04bce836059671d8deb2ec0db983.message:
fix(build): validate PS3_MAC_VULKAN before compiling and fail on nm errors

Grok review: the PS3_MAC_VULKAN=0 gate ran only after the whole lift build, and a failing nm (bad archive, missing tool) passed as 'no Vulkan'. The gate now runs right after the RUNTIME_LIB check and aborts if nm fails. The test asserts the abort message, that it happens before any compile, rejects invalid values and checks GOW2_MACOS_MIN precedence over MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET.

**English** · [Português (Brasil)](README.pt-BR.md)

# God of War II HD — native macOS port by static recompilation

**God of War II HD** (PS3, `NPUA80491`) running **natively on Apple Silicon**:
no emulator, no JIT. The PowerPC (PPU) and Cell SPU code is translated ahead
of time into C/C++, compiled with clang for arm64, and runs on a
reimplementation of the PS3 OS and libraries with **Metal** for graphics,
**VideoToolbox** for cutscenes and **CoreAudio** for sound.

> This repository contains **no game code and no game assets**. Like
> [Dusk](https://duskport.com/dusk/), you bring your own legally dumped copy,
> and the setup kit decrypts, translates and builds it **on your machine**.

| | |
|---|---|
| ![Combat in the palace of Rhodes](docs/img/palace-combat.jpg) | ![The Colossus of Rhodes through the palace windows](docs/img/colossus-window.jpg) |
| ![Blades of Chaos effects](docs/img/blades-of-chaos.jpg) | ![Volumetric light in the palace](docs/img/palace-lighting.jpg) |

*Captured from the native Metal renderer on an M-series Mac (1280×720 internal,
MetalFX upscaled).*

---

## Status

| Area | State |
|---|---|
| Boot, intro videos, logos | ✅ natural path, videos decoded by VideoToolbox |
| Main menu, New Game, saves | ✅ memory-card saves on disk |
| Rhodes gameplay (combat, HUD, particles, lighting) | ✅ 45–60 fps on Apple Silicon (Mac, Metal; measured numbers in [Estado por plataforma e desempenho](#estado-por-plataforma-e-desempenho-2026-10-02)) |
| Colossus of Rhodes fight | 🟡 playable; the bronze drape on its shoulder is skinned with a sheared bone matrix (under investigation) |
| After the Colossus cutscene | ✅ fixed 2026-09-22: a lifted SPU program (spu1) was writing into the PPU code segment, which produced `ICALL-BAD 0x80029F47`; validated with 305 s of New Game → gameplay, 0 ICALL-BAD ([log](https://github.com/andrebrumdev/ps3recomp/blob/spurs-bringup/docs/re_sessions/2026-09-22-spu1-6074-texto-corrompido.md)) |
| iOS (iPhone) and Android (tablet) | 🟡 experimental; see [Estado por plataforma e desempenho](#estado-por-plataforma-e-desempenho-2026-10-02) (pt-BR) |
| Audio | 🟡 music/SFX through the SCREAM mixer SPU program; clock still partly host-driven |
| Controllers | ✅ DualShock 4 / DualSense / Xbox / MFi via GameController, keyboard + mouse |

The engineering log (every wall, the hypotheses refuted by measurement and the
fixes) lives in [`docs/`](docs/) and in the engine repository.

## How it works

```
EBOOT.ELF (your copy, decrypted)
   │
   ├── PPU  ── ppu_lifter.py ──► ~650 C++ chunks, 69k functions ──┐
   │          (functions.json: curated function bounds,           │
   │           jump tables, mid-function entry points)            │
   │                                                               ├─► clang -O1/-O2 arm64 ─► g2play
   └── SPU  ── spu_lifter.py ──► SPU jobs / SPURS policy modules ─┘            │
                                                                                ▼
                               ps3recomp runtime (MIT): LV2 syscalls, PPU threads,
                               lwmutex/lwcond, SPURS, FIOS, cellGcm → RSX FIFO walker
                               → Metal backend (MSL from RSX VP/FP), cellVdec → VideoToolbox,
                               cellAudio → CoreAudio, cellPad → GameController
```

What makes a PS3 title hard to recompile, and what this port had to solve:

- **Cell B.E.**: one PPU plus up to six SPUs with their own ISA and 256 KB local
  store; SPU programs (SPURS workloads, job chains, policy modules) are lifted
  separately and scheduled on host threads.
- **Indirect control flow**: 64-bit PowerPC function descriptors (`.opd`/TOC),
  vtables, computed `bctr` jump tables and mid-function entries, all of which
  the lifter must resolve statically.
- **RSX**: the command FIFO (with CALL/JUMP, wait points and ring wraps) is
  walked on the host, and the NV40-class vertex/fragment programs are
  decompiled to Metal Shading Language.
- **Faithfulness over shortcuts**: fixes follow console behaviour (RPCS3 is
  used as a measurement oracle via its GDB stub); diagnostics are gated off by
  default.

## Launcher (macOS)

![GoW2 Recomp launcher](docs/img/launcher-play.jpg)

`GoW2 Recomp.app` is a native SwiftUI launcher in the spirit of Dusk:
point it at your own `EBOOT.ELF` and `USRDIR`, pick graphics/audio/control
options, manage mods and play. Build it with:

```
launcher/macos/build_app.sh     # -> ./GoW2 Recomp.app
```

- **No Python, no interpreter**: validation, config, autosave checks (SHA-256
  per file) and mod import run in Swift inside the app.
- **RPCS3-style patches**: the launcher computes your executable's RPCS3 PPU
  hash by streaming the ELF (for NPUA80491 01.00 it is
  `PPU-31e32090ea333902dbf322c24487bab7e8c8d0d1`), reads RPCS3's
  `patch.yml` (anchors, aliases, configurable values) or any `.yml` you
  import, and passes the enabled ones to the runtime (`PS3_PATCH_FILE`). Data
  patches (e.g. aspect ratio) take effect; code patches are flagged, because
  the code was already recompiled and would need a re-lift.
- Design system in [`launcher/macos/MASTER.md`](launcher/macos/MASTER.md).

## Bring your own game (macOS kit)

A [Dusk](https://duskport.com/dusk/)-style kit: point it at your own game
folder (`PS3_GAME`, from RPCS3's `dev_hdd0/game/NPUA80491` or your PS3) and
your license (`UP9000-NPUA80491_00-GODOFWARIIHDUS00.rap`), and it builds the
native binary on your Mac:

```bash
./kit/setup.sh /path/to/PS3_GAME        # finds the .rap in RPCS3's exdata or ~/Downloads
./jogar_g2.sh
```

`setup.sh` does the following:

1. It decrypts `EBOOT.BIN` itself, the same way RPCS3 does (engine
   `tools/unself`).
2. It recompiles the PPU code with the pinned lifter, the patch scripts and a
   small delta.
3. It recompiles the seven SPU programs.
4. It extracts the movies from your `gow2.psarc`.
5. It links `./g2play`.

Every generated file is checked against the hashes in `kit/`. The result is
byte-identical to the build the project tests. Details are in
[`kit/README.md`](kit/README.md).

Controls: WASD move, mouse camera, Space/E/J/K = ✕/○/□/△, Enter = Start,
F11 or Cmd+Enter = fullscreen, Esc releases the mouse.

## State of the art in game recompilation

| Project | Platform | Approach | Notable result |
|---|---|---|---|
| [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) | Nintendo 64 (MIPS) | Static recompilation to C | *Zelda 64: Recompiled* and many more; modding framework |
| [XenonRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/XenonRecomp) | Xbox 360 (PowerPC) | Static recompilation to C++ | *Unleashed Recompiled*, the first 360 recomp playable start to finish |
| ReXGlue | Xbox 360 | Static recompilation | Tooling for 360 ports |
| PS2Recomp | PlayStation 2 (MIPS R5900) | Static recompilation | Early stage |
| [psprecomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/psprecomp) | PSP (Allegrex MIPS) | Static recompilation to C | Toolkit |
| [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) | PlayStation 3 (PPU) | Static recompilation runtime | The base of this port's engine |
| **This port** | **PlayStation 3 (PPU + SPU)** | **Static recompilation, PPU and SPU, native Metal** | **A commercial PS3 title in gameplay on macOS/arm64** |
| [Dusk / Dusklight](https://duskport.com/) | GameCube | Decompilation (source rebuilt by hand) | *Twilight Princess* native port; you supply the ISO |
| [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net/) | PlayStation 3 | Emulation (LLVM JIT/AOT) | The reference used here as an oracle |

Catalogs: [Recompendium](https://nio03.github.io/unricopie/en/),
[decompilation & recompilation list](https://readonlymemo.com/decompilation-projects-and-n64-recompiled-list/).

Static recompilation sits between emulation and decompilation: like a
decompilation it produces native code with no interpreter or JIT (so it can
use native APIs such as Metal directly), but like an emulator it needs no
hand-written game source. It only needs the original binary, which is why the
user has to supply it.

## Project Structure

The root holds only entry points; everything else lives in a folder with one
purpose. The full map (with the old root path of every moved script) is
[`scripts/README.md`](scripts/README.md), and `scripts/check_layout.sh` keeps
the root clean.

```
gow2-recomp/
├── jogar_g2.sh rodar_gow2*.sh testar_fix.sh gow2_launcher.py  # launchers
├── env_gow2.sh                 # environment recipe (sourced by launchers, smokes, iOS/Android builds)
├── build_macos.sh              # Mac build; compiles boot_macos.cpp, gow2_boot.h, host_gow2_*, movie_eos_arm.*, gow2_overlay_provider.*
├── functions.json              # curated PPU function bounds (truncation repairs, mid-function targets)
├── apply_all_patches.sh verify_lift.sh accept_relift.sh  # lift pipeline entry points
├── <old paths>                 # deprecated wrappers to the moved scripts (until 2026-12-31)
├── recomp_mid_v2/              # hand-written glue: SPU registration, overrides, mid-asm hooks, patch_*.py (survive re-lifts)
├── config/gow2_recomp.toml     # lifter configuration (hooks)
├── hooks/                      # function overrides and mid-asm hook sources
├── kit/                        # bring-your-own-game installer (kit/setup.sh) and its release tooling
├── launcher/ ios/ android/     # macOS launcher app, iOS app, Android build
├── scripts/
│   ├── smoke/                  # boot/intro/Metal smoke runs
│   ├── lift/                   # relift gates, promotion, bisect, patch helpers
│   ├── diag/                   # Mac diagnostics on a running boot
│   └── archive/windows/        # the 2026 Windows bring-up scripts (machine-bound, not maintained)
├── tools/                      # PKG/SELF extraction, RPCS3 source search
├── claude_runs/                # agent measurement runs (run for N s / until a capture, then sample)
├── tests/ lift_baseline/       # offline tests and the lift baseline
├── notes/                      # dated investigation notes (+ artifacts/)
└── docs/img/                   # README images
```

Excluded on purpose (see `.gitignore`): `EBOOT.ELF`, `extracted/`, `*.psarc`,
SPU images, lifted PPU/SPU sources, texture dumps and build output. Those are
derived from the game and are regenerated from your own copy.

# inFamous PC (Europe + USA)

An unofficial native Windows port of **inFamous** (PlayStation 3, 2009). The game's PowerPC (PPU) and
SPU code is statically recompiled to x86-64 C/C++ with [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp),
so it runs as a normal Windows program rather than under an emulator.

This is a fork of [whompay/inFAMOUSreborn](https://github.com/whompay/inFAMOUSreborn) that adds the
**USA release (`BCUS98119`)** next to the European one (`BCES00220`). See [USA-PORT.md](USA-PORT.md)
for how the European port was carried over to the USA disc.

**This repository contains no game code or data.** You build the game yourself, on your own PC, from
your own copy of the game: a disc image (`.iso`) or a game folder.

## Supported discs

| Release | Title ID | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Europe | `BCES00220` | The upstream port |
| USA | `BCUS98119` (executable SHA-256 `4f2db3fb…f9befb4`) | Boots, title screen, new game into gameplay |

Other revisions of the USA executable need their own address map; the installer checks the hash and
stops rather than build something broken.

## Easy install

Download **inFamous Setup.exe** from the latest release, run it, choose your `.iso` (an encrypted 1:1
image works with its `.dkey` next to it) or your game folder (the one with `PS3_GAME` in it), pick an
install location and press **Install**.

Setup checks for Python and the C++ build tools and offers to install them, copies the game out of the
disc image, regenerates the recompiled code from your copy, builds it and adds an inFamous shortcut.
The first build takes roughly 20 to 60 minutes.

For the USA disc the installer never writes into your game folder: it decrypts a private copy of the
executable under `.installer/usa` and points the game at your files.

## Command-line install

The repository ships the command-line installer as `installer/bin/infamous-installer.exe`:

```bat
installer\bin\infamous-installer.exe install --game "D:\Dumps\inFamous [BCUS98119]" --rpcs3 "C:\RPCS3\rpcs3.exe"
installer\bin\infamous-installer.exe install --game "D:\Dumps\inFamous.iso"
```

`--game` takes a game folder or an `.iso`; `--dkey FILE` or `--key HEX` give the key of an encrypted
image. Run it without arguments (or drop a folder or image on it) to be asked for everything.
`infamous-installer doctor` checks the requirements only. Finished steps are skipped when you run it
again, so an interrupted install continues where it stopped.

When it finishes it writes `Play inFamous.cmd` and `inFamous.exe` (the launcher) in the checkout.

## Updating

**Update now** in Setup, the **Update inFamous** Start-menu shortcut, or `Update inFamous.cmd` in the
install folder compare the install with this repository (`aphixe/infamousRebornUsa`, branch `main`),
download only what changed and rebuild what that needs. Your saves and settings are kept.

## Requirements

- Your own inFamous disc or dump: European (`BCES00220`) or USA (`BCUS98119`).
- Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit) and a GPU with Direct3D 12 support.
- A CPU with SSE4.1 (2008 or newer). Without AVX2 the installer builds a slower compatibility version.
- [Python 3.10+](https://www.python.org/downloads/) with "Add python.exe to PATH" ticked.
- [Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools](https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/downloads/) with the
  **Desktop development with C++** workload and the **C++ Clang Compiler for Windows** component,
  plus CMake and Ninja (both come with that workload).
- [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net) (with the PS3 firmware installed), to decrypt `EBOOT.BIN`. Retail discs
  ship it encrypted; the installer runs RPCS3 only to decrypt it.
- About 20 GB of free disk space (more if you install from an `.iso`, which is copied out) and 16 GB of RAM.

## Building from source

```bat
cd installer
cargo build --release
target\release\infamous-installer install --game "D:\Dumps\inFamous"
```

Maintainers: `python tools/build_usa.py` runs the USA generation and build by hand (USA-PORT.md), and
`infamous-installer export --out DIR` / `package --out "inFamous Setup.exe"` produce the publishable tree
and the one-file setup. See [installer/README.md](installer/README.md) for every step.

## Playing

Run **inFamous** (the shortcut Setup made, or `inFamous.exe` in the install folder). It opens a small
options window first (vsync, frame cap, resolution, language and more, saved to `settings.ini`); **Play**
starts the game. Controllers work as on the console; keyboard and mouse are supported (WASD to move,
mouse to look, Space = Cross, Esc = Start / pause).

**F10** opens the in-game trainer (God Mode, Infinite Energy, Super Speed, Player Model and more).
`TRAINER=0` turns it off.

**= / +** or **numpad +** raises game volume; **-** or **numpad -** lowers it, in 5% steps.
A padded bottom-left indicator shows the percentage. Adjustments are saved to
`infamous-recomp/audio.ini` (`[audio]`, `volume=0` through `100`) and restored on launch.
Explicit debug launches still start at the requested debug volume.

Your saves live in the install folder (`infamous-recomp/gamedata`); they are never part of an update or
a published tree.

## Known limits of the USA build

- Tested from boot through the opening of a new game. Longer play, saving and loading, the trainer and
  the pause menu's added Settings / Quit Game rows have not been checked on the USA disc yet.
- The keyboard/mouse HUD prompt textures are built from European texture IDs and are skipped on the
  USA disc; controller prompts show instead.

## How it works

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `ps3recomp` | The recompiler toolkit and runtime: PPU and SPU lifters, HLE system libraries, RSX on Direct3D 12, audio and input |
| `infamous-recomp` | The inFamous-specific parts: program entry, game hooks and fixes (`infamous_region.h` holds the per-release addresses), asset tools |
| `installer` | Setup and the command-line installer: reads the disc, regenerates the code from your game, applies `installer/patches`, builds |
| `installer/infamous.toml` | Everything about the game and the port: pipeline steps, generated files, build and launch settings |
| `installer/generated.lock` | Hashes of each generated file before and after the port's patches |
| `tools/build_usa.py`, `tools/port_ppu_patches.py`, `tools/eu2usa.py` | The USA pipeline: relocates the European patches onto the USA executable |

0650a59088532c1a0a3469cdd8812fa457a80bf0.message:
cellGcm: _cellGcmSetFlipCommandWithWaitLabel queues the label wait and the flip

libgcm appends NV406E SEMAPHORE_OFFSET and SEMAPHORE_ACQUIRE for the
label, then the flip, so the RSX flips only once the label holds the
value. RPCS3's _cellGcmSetFlipCommandWithWaitLabel writes the same two
methods into the context before its flip command. The import here
ignored its context, wrote the label itself from the PPU, and flipped
at call time: whoever owns the label was overruled, and the flip
waited for nothing.

Write the two semaphore methods into the context and queue the flip
behind them with gcm_flip_into_fifo, as _cellGcmSetFlipCommand already
does. A context that is not a mapped command buffer, or has no room,
falls back to the immediate form as before.

0ba1229e2c0b4b6003604a06e80fb330dccc1083.message:
sys_ppu_thread: non-joinable threads free their slot when they end

sys_ppu_thread_create ignored its flags and made every thread joinable, so a
thread created without SYS_PPU_THREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE stayed FINISHED after
its exit and held its slot for good. Once 63 such threads had run, every
later create returned CELL_EAGAIN.

joinable is now flags & 1. A non-joinable (or detached) thread frees its
slot at the end of ppu_host_thread_proc, after closing its event and handle
(Windows) or destroying its mutex/cond (POSIX, where the host thread is
detached at creation), under the table lock. sys_ppu_thread_exit leaves the
freeing to that epilogue; the main thread is still marked FINISHED there.
The create log line shows the flags.

tests/test_ppu_thread_slots.c (tools/test_ppu_thread_slots.py): 192
non-joinable threads created and finished in turn all succeed and leave no
slot in use; 63 unjoined joinable threads still fill the table, and a join
frees a slot. Fails on master at the 64th create (0x80010001).

maps main memory before Init got its next map placed on top of Init's

table (never io page 0) and returns 0xFFFFFFFF when none is free.

cellGcmInit and when IO space is full, and logs the io it returns. The
cellGcmAddressToOffset auto-map runs only after Init.

is refused; after Init maps land at 0x800000, 0xE00000 and 0x1000000 and the
Init window is kept; freed holes are reused; IO-full refusal.

0e26194770079d251b113cbc28bb41e27199ac76.message:
sys_spu: an SPU's user event finds the port the PPU binds, and waits for it

An SPU's send_event (interrupt mailbox, code 0..63) was routed only through the ports the group binds with
sys_spu_thread_group_connect_event_all_threads, and answered ENOTCONN at once when there was none. Two things go
wrong with that:

- A port bound for one SPU thread with sys_spu_thread_connect_event was never found by the delivery, only by the
  plain out-mailbox path.
- The SPU thread starts running at sys_spu_thread_group_start while the PPU is still on its way to the connect
  calls that follow it (a real SPU needs far longer to boot than a lifted one). The first request of the program
  was answered ENOTCONN and the SPU program gave up. SoulCalibur II HD's audio engine (MultiStream) binds its ports
  with sys_spu_thread_connect_event, after group_start, and failed this way.

The delivery now looks at the thread's own bindings before the group's (spu_port_queue_locked) and, when the port
is not bound yet, waits for a binding for up to 200 ms on a condition variable that both connect calls signal
before it answers ENOTCONN. An SPU whose thread does not exist is answered at once, since nothing will bind its
port. The out-mailbox path reads the bindings through the same helper under the lock.

The test calls the real handlers and spu_deliver_user_event: bound for the thread, bound for the group, bound 40 ms
late either way, never bound (answers after about 200 ms) and an SPU with no thread (answers at once). On v0.15.0
it fails six checks; with the change it passes (five runs in a row).

video/tests: a flip queued in the command stream

test_gcm_flip_wrap.c, and checks on a title context:

1. _cellGcmSetFlipCommandWithWaitLabel puts SEMAPHORE_OFFSET and
   SEMAPHORE_ACQUIRE for the label, then the flip marker, into the
   context, moves current past them, and leaves the label alone.
2. A tick before the drain is a vblank, not a flip.
3. Once the drain has executed up to the marker, the next tick
   completes the flip.
4. A flip written but not flushed does not complete; an executed one
   does, even with a newer flip written behind it and not flushed.
5. A flip the walker abandons when it resyncs out of unmapped IO does
   not hold back the flip status.

122690f29d9d566a679fce9944c4718a674ed79b.message:
fp decompiler: biased unsigned remap and _bx2 fetches return signed values

Two ways a fetch comes back re-centred to -1..1 were ignored, so the
shader saw 0..1 encodings:

- SET_TEXTURE_ADDRESS bit 12, UNSIGNED_REMAP_BIASED, applies to every
  fetch from the unit: (round(x*255)-128)/127 on the lanes the crossbar
  fills from a source channel (16-bit X16/Y16_X16 channels: /32767),
  after gamma and not on gamma lanes, and not on lanes the filter flags
  signed. rsx_texture_expand_mask computes the lanes, for the formats
  RPCS3 gives RSX_FORMAT_FEATURE_BIASED_NORMALIZATION.
- EXP_TEX (OPDEST bit 21, the _bx2 modifier) belongs to the instruction,
  not the texture: x*2-1 on every lane of any unit, bypassing gamma
  (RPCS3 _process_texel). It applies from every entry point.

inFAMOUS 2 reads its normals G-buffer through a biased unit and its
tangent-space normal maps and occlusion-cone lookup tables with TEX_bx2
(about a quarter of its fragment programs). Read unexpanded, every
normal leaned towards (1,1,1), normal maps had no effect, and the
occlusion volumes round props drew as dark boxes.

The engine passes the expand masks of the units a program samples
through a new entry point, rsx_fp_decompile_buffered_shadow_color_expand_ex,
and hashes them into the pipeline key. A program with neither feature
is byte-identical.

d3d12: key the per-draw vertex program cache on the program, not on the store behind it

vp_get_vs hashed the microcode from SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM_START to the end of everything uploaded. A title that
keeps several programs resident and uploads another one behind the program it draws with changes that hash on
every upload, so nearly every draw missed the cache and ran D3DCompile on the FIFO thread. SoulCalibur II HD on
Windows stalled after its opening movie that way, and its audio, fed from the same frame loop, starved.

The hash now ends at the program's end bit (rsx_vp_program_size_instrs, which the Metal backend and the draw engine
already use), and the decompiler is given that length. The cache holds 128 programs instead of 16: a fight in that
title draws with more than 16, and an eviction shifts the slots the recorded draws point at.

Not built with MSVC and not run on a D3D12 device from this branch: checked with a mingw -fsyntax-only (no new
diagnostics). The stall went away on Windows with this change carried as a patch on v0.14.0 (the toolkit this port was

17bf55aa590b12b5e2c37c6885718526f8b59804.message:
cellGcm: NV3089 source origin is 12.4, the copy counted it 256 times too small

IMAGE_IN_POINT is 12.4 fixed point per axis, and DS_DX / DT_DY step the source with 20 fractional bits (1.0 =
0x100000). nv3089_blit's copy loops added the origin to that position as origin << 8, so a source offset counted
1/256 of what it is: for any origin under 256 texels the loops started at column 0 and row 0. The GPU paths in the
same function (rsx_live_draw_blit, rsx_live_draw_resolve_blit) already took origin >> 4, so the two disagreed, and
nv3089_engine_read, which writes the source rectangle back from the draw engine before the copy, took it as origin >> 4
for its start and << 8 for its end.

A title that resolves a supersampled scene in 512x512 tiles with a one texel origin (in_uv 0x00100010, SoulCalibur II HD,
six 2:1 blits) got the first row and column of every tile black: the loops read column 0 and row 0, which the engine
write-back (starting at 1) had not covered.

The origin now enters every computation as origin << 16 (nv3089_origin), in the engine write-back and in both copy
loops (linear and the NV309E swizzled one), so the loops read from the texel the origin names and the write-back covers
exactly what they read. Also reported by undecuple on the first version of this change, which made the write-back follow
the wrong loop.

The test plays the engine (guest_read stores, into the rectangle it is given, a pixel that names its own source position)
and checks that destination pixel (x, y) is the source pixel at (origin + x * scale, origin + y * scale), for origins of
0, 1, 3 and 20 texels at 1:1, 2:1 and 4:1; five of the six cases fail on v0.15.0.

18993f185aa89d35a2b7c7cb2d25483e00508434.message:
metal engine: PS3_AA=fxaa and PS3_SHARPEN in the present pass

Both off by default; off, the present is the same copy (and gamma) it
was.

PS3_AA=fxaa runs FXAA 3.11 (quality preset 29, luma from RGB, alpha
kept) over the display buffer at the guest's resolution, into a texture
of its own, before the present samples it. PS3_SHARPEN=0..1 adds AMD
FidelityFX CAS (the non-scaling form) to the present pass itself, with
its taps one source texel apart, ahead of the video out gamma. CAS
weighs its sharpening by the headroom in each 3x3 neighbourhood, so it
does not ring or clip where an edge is already at black or white.

test_metal_present_post.m drives eng_blit_to_display on synthetic
images: off is an exact copy, FXAA blends a staircase and leaves flat
areas and alpha alone, CAS steepens a soft edge, less at 0.2 than at 1.

rsx engine: 3D textures

A unit whose SET_TEXTURE_FORMAT dimension is 3 with a depth in CONTROL3
was uploaded as its first slice and sampled as a 2D texture. inFAMOUS 2's
occlusion volumes look up an 8x8x8 cone table that way, and every prop

  depth as well. A backend without them keeps the old first-slice
  behaviour.

  The new rsx_fp_decompile_buffered_shadow_color_expand_vol_ex carries the

1e6f4c8e744a66f6f5163f6f8def38470742e50b.message:
vulkan: colour feedback snapshots for draws that sample their own target

A draw that samples the colour target it is writing gets, on Metal, a
copy of that target taken just before it (rsx_draw_backend.color_snapshot).
In-place deferred lighting works this way: read the albedo, write the lit
colour over it. The Vulkan backend had no such hook, so the engine fell
back to the guest-memory bytes at the target's address, which hold
whatever was last stored there.

On Twisted Metal (BCES01010) the G-buffer's first target (0x00AB0000) is
also the UI target. Its lighting passes therefore read the previous
frame's menu instead of the albedo just drawn, lit it, and composited it
into the next frame. That is the red frame, the red and green splatter
and the white logo on its main menu.

vk_eng_color_snapshot copies the target into a new image of the same
format and size, and ends with a barrier so the copy is visible to the
next draw. Every operation here is already one synchronous submission,
so the copy is in command order. The copy is a COLOR object marked
`snapshot`, so the engine can take a crossbar view of it; it is never an
attachment, so releasing it drops no framebuffer. A lit frame asks for
one copy per light, so released copies return their images to a pool of
eight, drained at engine shutdown.

32a85600293ba2cf2a21bcb1150bcc0dbd6fb63a.message:
vulkan: present on its own command buffer, in two halves a host can split

The FIFO walker and the present shared one command buffer and one
fence, and a present waited for two GPU round trips: the engine's blit
of the flipped surface into the offscreen target, then the copy of that
target into the readback buffer. A host that presents on the walker's
thread holds the walker for all of that, about 1.3 ms per frame headless.
One that moves the present to a thread of its own still had to hold its
walker lock for the whole present, since both recorded into s_vk.cmd.

On Twisted Metal (BCES01010) that is the window in which the title
moves put to its other ring segment and starts writing its next frame
over the one it left, JUMP out of it included. The walker resumes 2.4 ms
later and executes the new frame's data as commands.

The present now has its own command pool, command buffer and fences,
and comes in two halves:

- rsx_vulkan_backend_present_begin() records the blit and the copy out
  and submits them without waiting. It reads the flipped surface, so it
  runs under the host's walker lock, but only for the recording.
- rsx_vulkan_backend_present_finish() waits for that copy, reads the
  centre pixel and the dump back, and blits into the window. It may run
  while the walker drains the next frame.

rsx_vulkan_backend_present() is both, so existing hosts see no
difference. The fixed-function path, which draws into the offscreen
target itself, still finishes inside present_begin.

What keeps the two halves apart:
- vkQueueSubmit, vkQueuePresentKHR and vkDeviceWaitIdle go through
  queue_mu, since the queue is now used from two threads.
- The walker's next command buffer starts with a full barrier after a
  present's copy. Its per-image barriers already order most work after
  earlier submissions; this one covers the rest.
- No image is destroyed while a present's copy may still read it.
- present_mu keeps a flip in the command stream (presented on the
  walker's thread) from overlapping a host thread's finish.

spu_dma: the identical-transfer halt also needs wall time

mfc_submit halts an SPU after SPU_DMA_REPEAT_LIMIT (256) identical
transfers in a row, on the reasoning that a job doing nothing but the same
DMA is wedged. A job that polls a value another agent writes does the same:
God of War: Ascension's EDGE geometry jobs wait for ring space by re-reading
an RSX label until the GPU catches up. 256 reads take well under a
millisecond, so the guard halted healthy jobs and the frame never completed.

Halt only when the repeats have also lasted SPU_DMA_REPEAT_SECS (default
30 s) of wall time. A truly wedged job is still caught, 30 s later.

3ca13f66211402f8d9b2e62a1ad9d6a92334f04e.message:
fix(template): mmap the guest arena on POSIX so vm_commit can mprotect it

The POSIX branch of alloc_guest_vm() allocated the 0xE0000000-byte flat
arena with calloc. glibc serves an allocation that size from its own mmap
chunk and returns a pointer 16 bytes past the page start, so vm_base was
never page-aligned. vm_commit() hands vm_base + addr to mprotect, which
rejects unaligned addresses with EINVAL; every commit failed, and
sys_memory_allocate answered CELL_ENOMEM to every call. A title that
retries the allocation spins forever (Warhawk: 19.7 M calls in 60 s).

Map the arena with mmap(MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS|MAP_NORESERVE) instead,
as runtime/memory/vm.h already does: page-aligned, zero-filled, lazily
backed. ppu_vm_size and the Windows VirtualAlloc path are unchanged.
macOS was unaffected only because libmalloc page-aligns large blocks.

Verified: Warhawk NPEA00017 boots headless on Linux to its intro movie;
check_ppu_scaffold.py reports no regression.

3d5d03bdc7f627a424fb53ce42175984d596a377.message:
runtime: classify syscall 14 by guest address segment

sys_process_is_spu_lock_line_reservation_address answered EINVAL for
every address above the 256 MB VM_MAIN window (0x00010000..0x1000FFFF),
including the rest of segment 0x1 that the same guest allocator hands
out. SPURS validates its management areas through this syscall during
cellSpursInitialize and aborts init on failure, so a legitimate
management area produced a spurious CELL_SPURS_CORE_ERROR_PERM and every
SPU job the instance would have run stayed unstarted.

The contract is RPCS3's process_is_spu_lock_line_reservation_address
(Emu/Cell/lv2/sys_process.cpp): classify by the address segment
(0x0/0x1/0x2/0xC/0xE reservation-capable; 0xF refuses RawSPU; 0xD
refuses; sys_vm mappings refuse, holes in the mapped region EINVAL; rest
EINVAL) with the flags masked to the two SPU bits. The old sys_vm EPERM
check is kept, now through the tracked mappings (g_sys_vm_maps): a
covered address answers EPERM, a hole in the mapped region EINVAL,
matching RPCS3's default branch.

The classification moves to runtime/syscalls/lv2_lock_line.c so
tests/syscalls can unit-test it without linking the syscall layer.

Test: tests/syscalls/test_lock_line (27 checks: segments 0x0/0x1/0x2/
0xC/0xE OK, 0xF EPERM with RawSPU, 0xD EPERM, sys_vm covered/hole/empty,
flag validation).

45baa4791a794597cfaa0d0d4879347cb637b581.message:
rsx engine: 2D transfers read FP16 colour targets

A transfer out of a render target first writes the GPU's pixels back to
guest memory (rsx_draw_engine_guest_read), but only A8R8G8B8 surfaces were
looked up. Twisted Metal renders its bloom and Sweet Tooth's flaming hair
into an FP16 RGBA target and copies that out with NV3089 for its SPU
post-FX; the copy found no surface, the SPUs got stale memory, and neither
the bloom nor the flames reached the image.

The lookup now takes FP16 RGBA targets too. A transfer counts 32-bit
pixels, so the readback covers every surface pixel the transfer's bytes
touch and stores exactly those bytes, as big-endian R,G,B,A halves: the
layout rsx_texture_decode reads W16_Z16_Y16_X16_FLOAT from. A transfer
INTO an FP16 target is still not pushed: color_target_write takes
A8R8G8B8 rows.

4f223b376f890582608dcd00a3ae2b3ab9e7b483.message:
cellAudio: let WASAPI shared mode convert the 48 kHz stereo float stream

The Windows backend opens the default render endpoint in shared mode with
a fixed 48 kHz, 2-channel IEEE-float format. Shared mode only accepts the
device's own mix format unless the stream asks the audio engine to
convert, so on any output not running exactly that format (44.1 kHz, 5.1,
24-bit PCM mix) IAudioClient::Initialize fails with
AUDCLNT_E_UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT (0x88890008), the backend gives up and every
title runs silent.

Pass AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_AUTOCONVERTPCM | AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_SRC_DEFAULT_QUALITY
on both Initialize attempts (event-driven and polled). The flags are
defined locally when the SDK headers predate them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

517fc717f73030d62dbaa9a991c118c6bd3cd6a2.message:
spu: the single-precision fast path four lanes at a time with AVX2

On x86, spu_fa/fs/fm/fma/fms/fnms took the per-lane path: each lane
widened to double on its own, and a call per instruction. arm64 has had
a NEON path doing the four lanes at once. This is the same path for
x86 with AVX2: the lanes widened to one f64x4 (exact), the operation,
the 29 low significand bits cleared, narrowed (exact). The lane rules are
the NEON ones: an ordinary single or a true +-0 keeps the vector result,
a zero result loses its sign, fa/fs also needs the exponents within 29,
and fma keeps a lane only when TwoSum says the add did not round onto a
24-bit boundary. Other lanes are redone one by one by the exact path.

test_spu_float_neon compares the vector path with the exact references
bit for bit; it now runs on x86 with AVX2 too, and in the Linux CI.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

53efeaf1eb44ce9c40b96f46418b22818a3dba8d.message:
fp decompiler: the NV40 pack and unpack opcodes

PK4UB, UP4UB, PKG, UPG, PK4B, UP4B, PK2US, UP2US, PK2H and UP2H had no case:
each was skipped with a TODO comment and its destination kept whatever it
held. inFAMOUS 2's character materials convert sRGB<->linear with PK4UB->UPG
and PKG->UP4UB right before their outputs, so Cole's scalp rendered saturated
green and every skin tone was off.

The packed word travels on in a float's bits, so the packs bitcast (asfloat)
and the unpacks bitcast back (asuint); the sRGB forms follow RPCS3's

57570462551fcc9c6f2391276953b1a5c91c48f1.message:
cellFiber: the SDK's scheduler API in place of the made-up one

libs/spurs/cellFiber.{c,h} exposed cellFiberPpuInitialize/Finalize, a CellFiber handle, a
four-argument cellFiberPpuCreateFiber(fiber, entry, arg, attr), SwitchFiber, Sleep/Wakeup and
error codes from 0x80410801. None of that is the SDK's. The HLE binds by name, so a title
importing the real cellFiberPpuCreateFiber landed in the four-argument function and read its
eight arguments from the wrong registers.

The SDK's PPU fibers are scheduler based, and this implements them:

- _cellFiberPpuInitialize, _cellFiberPpuSchedulerAttributeInitialize and
  _cellFiberPpuAttributeInitialize (attributes are zeroed, 256 bytes each);
- cellFiberPpuInitializeScheduler / FinalizeScheduler, and
  cellFiberPpuCreateFiber(scheduler, fiber, entry, arg, priority, eaStack, sizeStack, attr);
- cellFiberPpuRunFibers: runs the fibers on the calling thread until every one has ended, lowest
  priority number first, creation order among equals. A scheduler whose fibers wait for a signal
  from another thread waits for it instead of returning;
- WaitSignal / SendSignal (a signal sent early is kept), JoinFiber (from a fiber, which hands
  control back to the scheduler meanwhile, or from any thread, with the exit status), Yield,
  Exit and Self.

Each fiber runs the guest entry through the PPU thread trampoline on its own host stack (ucontext,
Windows fibers on Windows) with its own ppu_context; r1 is inside the guest stack the caller
passed, r3 the argument, and the entry's return value the exit status. The error codes are the
SDK's 0x8076xxxx, and the structures have the SDK's sizes and 128-byte alignment (scheduler 512,
fiber 896, both attributes 256).

Not implemented: the contents of the attributes, and the cellFiberPpuUtil* worker control. Yield,
Exit and Self follow the documented behaviour and are covered by the unit test only; the port that
this was written for does not call them.

tests/fiber_switch is rewritten for the new API: run order and arguments, guest stack point

584181aba7a5fe736123213cefc269ea9a630e5c.message:
metal engine: each MRT target takes its own colour mask and blend enable

Every attachment of an MRT set took target A's COLOR_MASK and
BLEND_ENABLE. On the RSX, targets B..D have their own: a nibble each of
COLOR_MASK_MRT (0x0370, A,R,G,B at bits 0..3 of the nibble) and a bit
each of BLEND_ENABLE_MRT (0x036C), as RPCS3 reads them
(color_mask_*(index), blend_enabled_surface_*).

Giving every target A's state was wrong both ways. inFAMOUS 2's light
volumes add into target A with B and C masked off, and the shared state
added every light into the G-buffer: lit props blew out to white, with a
bright rectangle round each light. Its material passes write B and C's
alpha with A's alpha masked, which left them stale.

The engine decodes both registers into the render state (and the
pipeline key), and the Metal backend applies them per attachment.
PS3RECOMP_METAL_MRT_MASK=0 restores the old behaviour for bisecting.

627bba25c912461ed2afed98e6abaf60df5f2d02.message:
spurs_job: keep the job's first frame below its cache buffers

spu_run_spurs_job lays a job out as binary, I/O, output, scratch + stack,
then the cache-hinted inputs, so cacheBuffer[0] starts at the stack top.
$sp was set to stack_top - 16. A SPU function saves its link register in
its caller's frame at 16($sp), so the entry's first store wrote 16 bytes
over the start of cacheBuffer[0].

Twisted Metal's Edge geometry jobs keep their viewport there. They read
x = 0x3FF00 (the return address in $lr) and width = height = 0, so the
screen-space scale was zero, every triangle of a skinned mesh had zero
area, and the main view culled them all: Sweet Tooth was missing from the
main menu, while the shadow passes (which skip that culling) drew him.

Start $sp at stack_top - 32 so the caller's 32-byte frame is part of the
stack.

rsx engine: fragment-program debug knobs keyed by structural hash

changes from run to run with the order programs are first drawn in. A

name programs by it.

  offset basis). The pipeline cache keeps it, so a draw has it for free.

  programs.

  registers at the first draw through each, to diff a broken pass's state
  against a working one.
- RSX_FP_DEBUG=<hex>:<n>:<reg[.swz]> makes that program export register

spu/tests: the signalled bit against an SPU commit to the same word

Two cases, built with the lock-line lock as in test_spu_lockline_peer.c
rather than raced for. A peer SPU has the bitset line reserved, the main
thread holds the lock, a second thread starts the host operation and is
held at the lock, an SPU commit sets another task's bit under the lock,
and only then is the host operation let through.

- spu_taskset_signal_task(task 4) against a commit of task 3's bit:
  both bits must be set.
- spu_taskset_wait_signal(task 3) consuming its signal against a commit
  of task 4's bit: task 4's bit must survive.

On master both fail (0x08000000 for 0x18000000, 0 for 0x08000000),
the same lost bits as Twisted Metal's post-FX barrier. Run in the Linux
and macOS workflows next to the SPURS task wake test.

cellPad: the small motor rumbles at full strength, and a rumble lasts until it changes

A DualShock 3's small motor is on/off: motor[0] is 0 or 1. Forwarded as
motor * 257 it reached the host at 257/65535, 1/255 of full, which a pad
does not feel. And each SDL request ran for 100 ms, while a PS3 title
sets the motors once and they stay on until it sets them again, so a long
rumble stopped almost at once (inFAMOUS 2 only calls when the value
changes).

The small motor is now on at full, the large one keeps 0-255. The last
request per port is kept, sent with a 1 s duration and renewed from the
pad poll every 400 ms while it is non-zero, so it lasts as long as the
title wants and still stops within a second if the title stops polling.
Zero stops the motors at once. XInput holds its motors itself and only
gets the level fix.

6752b12939e5c6a34be15c85b9d1e813e19360ab.message:
cellGcm: bounded semaphore acquire; the stuck-get watchdog leaves waits alone

GCM_SEMA_ACQUIRE=1 makes NV406E ACQUIRE block the drain, as the hardware
does, but the stuck-get watchdog counts drain passes, not time: a drain
that stops on an acquire, or on a self-JUMP park, stops every pass at the
same get, so after eight passes (a few milliseconds) it resynced to put
and dropped everything in between. For a park that happens before the
title has patched it into a JUMP to the commands it just wrote at the
ring start, i.e. before GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS has had a chance to run out.
inFAMOUS 2 stopped presenting for good that way in about one run in five
("stuck-get" at a self-jump with no "jump-park" before it).

A pass that stops on an acquire or a park now resets the watchdog; each
of those waits has its own bound. The acquire gets one:
GCM_SEMA_ACQUIRE_MS=<ms> consumes an acquire that has waited that long on
the same label and value, and says so, so a label nobody ever writes
cannot wedge the drain. inFAMOUS 2 acquires a label its SPU lighting job
writes every frame; with GCM_SEMA_ACQUIRE=1 GCM_SEMA_ACQUIRE_MS=200 its
lit props stop flashing white and its characters stop rendering black.

rsx engine: convert a transfer's rows a pixel at a time, not a byte at a time

rsx_draw_engine_guest_read and _guest_wrote move a 2D transfer's pixels
between the backend's R,G,B,A and the guest's A8R8G8B8. Both copied a
byte at a time, testing TEX_RGBA for every pixel, and at the -O2 the
runtime builds with GCC vectorises neither.

On Twisted Metal (BCES01010), once #334 removed the NV3089 per-pixel
copy, the two loops were about a quarter of the FIFO thread's CPU time
during boot (in-process sampling of that thread: 19.5% guest_read,
9.0% guest_wrote).

Each pixel is now one 32-bit load, one rotate and one store
(eng_row_convert), and the TEX_RGBA case is a memcpy per row. A
1280x720 frame converts in 0.55 ms instead of 0.98 ms with the
runtime's flags (GCC 16, -O2 -msse4.1), with identical output. In the
same Twisted Metal window the two functions drop to 14.2% and 6.9%.

comment says AIO reads are absolute and leave the fd's position alone; they
moved it, so the next cellFsRead continued from wherever the AIO stopped.

the seek and the read.

The request id counter is atomic for the same reason.

7c1d6f128d3d5af2b0e992cb4e2fa88271931fa4.message:
cellGcmSys: don't let a wrapped ring overwrite commands the RSX hasn't read

God of War HD fills its 3 MB command ring at boot and wraps it through the
runtime's buffer-full callback. Three things then let it write over
commands the walker had not reached, after which the walker decoded vertex
floats as JUMPs (0x3F800000 -> JUMP 0x1F800000) and resynced away frames:

- The recycle waited for g_gcm_fifo_drained_ea == begin, which is also true
  before the walker has moved at all, so it often didn't wait. It now waits
  for the walker to take a backward JUMP, i.e. the JUMP-to-begin it wrote.
- The wait gave up after 2 s in total. A ring of hundreds of tiny frames
  takes the draw engine far longer than that, and it was making progress.
  The bound is now 2 s without progress (60 s overall).
- While that callback waits, the title's context still reads
  current == end, which the drain's own overrun recycle took as an overrun
  and teleported get to begin, dropping the tail. It stands down while the
  callback is waiting.

The drain also stops at every flip unless backlogged, and measured the
backlog as put - get, so a wrapped ring (put behind get, the most backlogged
case) looked like no backlog at all. It is now measured around the ring when
both pointers are inside the title's context; other layouts are unchanged.

GCM_RECDBG reports the walker during the recycle wait, and
GCM_DRAINDBG_EVERY=<n> sets how often GCM_DRAINDBG logs a pass. Not run
against the other ports' regression gate (their games aren't here).

spirv-cross writes GLSL.std.450 FMax, FMin, FClamp and Normalize as
fast::max/min/clamp/normalize. Their result for a NaN operand is
undefined, and MTLMathModeSafe on the library does not change that. D3D's
max/min return the other operand when one is NaN and saturate(NaN) is 0,
and the guest programs were written for hardware that behaves that way.
inFAMOUS 2 has a sky/bloom pass that produced NaN on Metal only.
The generated MSL now uses the precise:: overloads, which follow IEEE
fmax/fmin; PS3RECOMP_MSL_FAST=1 keeps the fast:: spelling.

88187d115b6f3904501b1ef8e1b2707b7aed56c6.message:
Log caps: stop the counter at its limit (PS3_LOG_FIRST)

About 300 diagnostics were capped with `static int _n; if (_n++ < N)`. On a hot path
(MFC channel accesses, DMA, the SPU drain and workload loops) the signed counter passes
2^31, wraps negative, `_n < N` is true again and the line prints on every call: millions
of "[spu] drain-resume" lines in a long fight.

include/ps3emu/log_first.h has PS3_LOG_FIRST(ctr, limit), `((ctr) < (limit) && ++(ctr))`:
true for the first `limit` evaluations, then false, and the counter stops at the limit.
Every `x++ < N` cap in libs/ and runtime/ now uses it, and so do the `if (x++ >= N)
return;` forms (as `if (!PS3_LOG_FIRST(x, N)) return;`).

Left alone on purpose:
- the four periodic lines (`n < N || n % P == 0`: cellGcmGetReport, EventFlagSet, the
  WAIT_SIGNAL line, the usercmd line) need a counter that keeps going; three are now
  unsigned (wrapping is defined) and the fourth was already unsigned long;
- unit tests under runtime/*/tests, where the counter is a mismatch count;
- `s_exit_seen++ == 0`, a one-shot flag.

tests/test_log_first.c (registered as the ctest `log_first`) covers the stop at the limit,
INT_MAX, array-element counters, a variable limit and an OR-ed condition.

93cccd1d3c5332fff9bd13de773666c816b76198.message:
fp decompiler: honour perspective_corr on texcoord reads

SRC2 bit 31 (perspective_corr) on an instruction's texcoord read
multiplies the input by 1/w, as RPCS3's decompiler does ("Perspective
correct flag multiplies the result by 1/w"). The bit was ignored. A
vertex program that writes uv*w relies on it: inFAMOUS 2's water does,
for the screen copy it samples, and read raw the coordinates land far
outside the copy and the river renders black.

1/w comes from the fragment position. FXC (D3D12) gives SV_POSITION.w as
clip w, but glslang lowers it to SPIR-V FragCoord, whose w is already 1/w
(and Metal's [[position]] is (x, y, z, 1/w)), so the glslang paths define
RSX_FRAGCOORD_W_IS_RCP and the helper picks the right form. The helper is
emitted only when a program uses it, so every other program is
byte-identical.

a4b4a21d8d089e79d28e751c52f433bccc5674ac.message:
sys_spu: an SPU thread starts in the lifted image its own bytes identify

spu_lifted_thread_setup chose the thread's image by asking the registry which image owns the thread's entry point.
SPU programs all start near the same LS addresses (0xD0..0xF0), so two registered images can have code at one entry,
and the entry resolves to whichever registered first: the thread ran the other program's lifted code. SoulCalibur II
HD has two such images, and its audio engine (MultiStream) ran the wrong one.

sys_spu_thread_group_start now fingerprints the thread's sys_spu_image (the lookup the registry fallback right
below it already did) and gives spu_lifted_thread_setup the id of the image registered for those bytes,
spu_lifted_thread_desc.image_id. 0 keeps the lookup by entry point, so a thread whose image is not registered
behaves as before. The fingerprint lookup is one helper now, shared with the fallback.

The test replaces the registry with two images that both have code at 0xD0, A registered first, and follows what group
start does: B's bytes give B (the entry-based lookup, shown by the third check, gives A), A's give A, bytes nothing
registered and a thread without an image give 0. The new interface does not exist on v0.15.0, so the test only
builds with this change.

a594fa06fe400bd0ae86c525bf9b82bad468d526.message:
rsx engine: re-hash cached textures sparsely, in full every eighth frame

Every cached texture was hashed in full at its first use in a frame, to
notice the guest rewriting it. In inFAMOUS 2's New Marais that is about
950 textures and 88 MB a frame, 2.5 ms of the RSX thread, for the four
or so that actually change.

Now each use checks 64 bytes out of every 2 KB plus the last 64, and the
full hash runs when that check differs, when 8 frames have passed since
the entry's last full hash (new entries start staggered by slot, so the
full hashes spread out), always for a texture of 16 KB or less, and on
the next use after a surface store the engine itself made into the
texture. A whole rewrite (video, UI, streaming) is still seen at once; a
small write between the sampled blocks of a large texture can take up
to 7 frames. PS3RECOMP_ENG_TEXHASH_FULL=1 restores the full hash every
frame.

a6cfb0f07fd4226fe6daac59f931e31f3d47e538.message:
cellGcm: the NV3089 row copy takes its source origin as 12.4

IMAGE_IN_POINT is 12.4 fixed point and DS_DX / DT_DY step the source in
20 fractional bits, so the origin enters the copy as origin << 16. The
row copy used << 8, the same mistake as the per-pixel loop it was
written to match, and started at column 0 and row 0 for any origin
under 256 texels. It now uses nv3089_origin(), the helper #358
introduces for the per-pixel loops, defined the same way so the two
changes merge without a conflict.

a8572e9962344fe5cb49b78f7b647888fcce15c1.message:
cellGcmSys: publish get past a semaphore RELEASE before its label

The FIFO walker wrote a RELEASE's label at once but published the control
register's get only at a JUMP and at the end of the pass. On the RSX the
semaphore write lands after the command has been fetched, so a title that
sees the label may read get once and take it as the RSX's position.
Ratchet & Clank: Tools of Destruction waits for a label, reads get, then
spins until its own put equals it; the snapshot from before the RELEASE
never did, and boot stalled there.

The RELEASE now publishes get past the whole command (unless
GCM_GET_EQ_PUT is set), then a release fence, then the label.
test_gcm_get_on_release drives OFFSET/RELEASE and a two-method
ACQUIRE+RELEASE through the walker and reads both from a user-command
probe mid-pass, with and without GCM_GET_EQ_PUT.

a98af7c9075a6911d4ec5021a512941cb9f9d11f.message:
cellGcm: get follows the walker across a JUMP

On the RSX, get is the fetch pointer, so a title polling it sees the
GPU leave a command segment as soon as the JUMP out of it is taken.
The walker published get only at the end of a drain pass. On a slow
host that comes tens of milliseconds after the JUMP: Twisted Metal
(BCES01010) has boot-time passes of 50 to 165 ms, mostly NV3089 blits
and surface readbacks.

Twisted Metal flushes put into its other ring segment, then writes the
next frame over the segment it left. When the walker reaches the JUMP
at the old put late, the JUMP has already been overwritten. The title
port works around this by waiting, after its flush, for get to leave
the old put. With get published only at the end of the pass, that wait
ran into its 100 ms bound 4 times per boot even though the JUMP had
been taken at once. With this change it does so 2 times in 12 runs.

A taken JUMP now publishes its target as get. A park (a JUMP to itself)
publishes nothing, and GCM_GET_EQ_PUT keeps its own value.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

b1f14fff9e8174b3575212691ebdaef7aae069b7.message:
rsx: cache HLSL -> SPIR-V translations, in memory and optionally on disk

glslang takes 20-150 ms per shader, on the thread that walks the FIFO,
and the engine asks for the same HLSL again for every pipeline that
shares a program. Twisted Metal (BCES01010) translates 236 shaders in
its first minute, 74 of them distinct: 4.4 s of glslang per 90 s run,
95 stalls over 20 ms.

rsx_hlsl_to_spirv now keeps each translation, keyed by the stage and the
whole HLSL text, so a hit returns exactly the words that text translated
to. PS3RECOMP_SPIRV_CACHE=<existing directory> also keeps them on disk,
one file per shader; the file stores the key, the glslang version and
the translator's build stamp, and any mismatch is a miss that rewrites
the file. Failed translations are not cached.

Twisted Metal, 90 s runs: glslang time 4.4 s -> 1.1-2.0 s with the
memory cache alone, 5 ms with a warm disk cache, and no translation
over 20 ms.

b883922940d53efafac47dcc0b63dac7535294c5.message:
rsx_draw_engine, vulkan: honour the depth bounds test

NV4097 SET_DEPTH_BOUNDS_TEST_ENABLE (0x0380) with SET_DEPTH_BOUNDS_MIN and
_MAX (0x0384, 0x0388, floats) rejects a fragment whose stored depth lies
outside the bounds, whatever the depth test says. The draw engine never
read those registers, so a bounded draw covered the whole target.

Twisted Metal's deferred renderer relies on it: its sun pass is bounded to
[0, 0.999984] (the geometry) and the sky drawn right after it to
[0.999984, 1] (the far plane), both with the depth test off. Unbounded, the
sky overwrote the sun light everywhere and the HDR buffer came out almost
black.

The enable is pipeline state (rsx_be_render_state.depth_bounds_test, part
of the pipeline key); the bounds reach the backend before every draw through
a new optional hook, set_depth_bounds, like the stencil reference, so moving
them does not build pipelines. Vulkan enables the depthBounds feature when
the device has it and sets the bounds dynamically, clamped to [0, 1];
without the feature the test stays off, as before, with one log line.
Metal and the fixed-function path leave the hook unset and draw as before.

Tests: test_rsx_draw_engine checks the key, the bounds and that moving them
builds no pipeline (4 new checks, failing without the engine change).
ps3recomp_host --depthbounds draws red at z = 0.25, then blue bounded to
[0, 0.5] and green bounded to [0.5, 1] with the depth test off, and expects
blue; it runs in the Vulkan workflow's engine pass under the validation
layer.

b8a7c5b30057bd863df592edb02e1d4875ca2551.message:
fp decompiler: read FACING, TC8 and TC9

Fragment program inputs 0xC/0xD (TC8/TC9) and 0xE (FACING) read as zero.
Two-sided materials multiply the interpolated normal by FACING; read as
zero, inFAMOUS 2's foliage and character heads normalised a null vector
into the G-buffer and lit black.

FACING is +1 on a front face and -1 on a back face (SV_IsFrontFace,
[[front_facing]] in MSL). TC8/TC9 come from vertex outputs o15 and o6, as
in RPCS3's register table (TEX9 shares the point-size register); the
vertex program and the engine's fixed VS write them after TEXCOORD7, so the
earlier interpolants keep their locations. The fragment side declares

program is byte-identical and keeps its cached pipeline.

c1cdab11912f442698f32c04fd7a2a64b7a1226b.message:
cellGcm: a flip queued in the command stream completes when the drain reaches it

The 60 Hz tick (cellGcm_request_tick, and cellGcmTickFlip) completed a
pending flip on every beat, wherever the walker was. For a flip queued
into the stream (gcm_flip_into_fifo) that is too early: the RSX flips
when it executes the flip, after everything queued before it.

Twisted Metal (BCES01010) paces itself on the flip status and rebuilds
a command segment once the flip after it is done. Completed early, the
title rewrote segments the walker had not executed yet; the walker then
read half-written segments as commands (JUMPs to float data, unmapped
CALLs, and junk register writes such as the vertex data base offset,
which shattered every later draw's geometry).

Count the flips queued into the stream and the markers the drain
reaches. A beat completes a flip only if the drain has executed a
marker since the last completion, or if no flip is waiting in the
stream (a flip that never went through it). A flip written but not yet
flushed does not hold back one already executed.

A flip must never wait on a marker that will not be executed. A resync
that skips over a marker counts it. When the walker is lost in unmapped
IO and jumps straight to put, every flip still outstanding is written
off: Twisted Metal's boot resyncs that way about one run in three
(get=0x0FD00000) and the flip it abandoned in the other ring segment
otherwise held the status at WAITING for good. reached never passes
queued, so a written-off marker that is executed later is not counted
twice. GCM_FLIP_NEEDS_FIFO keeps its meaning.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

e25898001640a13ef2863ec42b22c278740e9b3b.message:
spurs: update taskset bitsets atomically on task create and exit (#340 follow-up)

The ready/pending/enabled bitsets (+0x10/+0x20/+0x30) share the taskset's
first 128-byte line with the SPU task library (GETLLAR/PUTLLC). Three host
writers updated them without the lock-line lock around the whole change:

- cellSpursCreateTask searched the enabled bitset for a free id with
  vm_read8 and set the bit later in spurs_taskset_add_task;
- spurs_taskset_add_task set enabled and ready with spurs_bitset_set (a
  vm_read32 outside the lock, a vm_write32 inside it);
- spu_taskset_task_exited cleared the exiting task's bits under ts_lock,
  which no other writer of the line takes.

A task exit landing between CreateTask's read and its write was undone: the
exited task's enabled bit came back with no task behind it, and
cellSpursJoinTask2 on that id never returned. Killzone 3 hit it at quit to
menu: Havok's thread-pool destructor joined task 0 forever.

- spurs_taskset_take_slot(): the free-id search and the enabled bit as one
  step under the lock-line lock, so two callers never get the same id either.
- spurs_taskset_bitset_update(): a single bit set or clear on the raw guest
  bytes under the lock-line lock, then spu_coh_notify_write; add_task uses it.
- spu_taskset_task_exited: the bitset updates and the start scan under the
  lock-line lock, the dispatches after it is released.

Follows the signalled-bit fix (#340), which named these writers as left out.
New test runtime/spu/tests/test_spurs_taskset_bits_atomic.c, built like that
PR's: on the old code the exited task's bit comes back (0xE0000000 for
0x60000000); with the fix 6/6 pass.

e2ff37f3b699c5514c51f510d52ec1134c08b3e2.message:
rsx textures: present X16 like B8 (value in R, G and B)

X16 decodes to a one-channel R16 resource, but rsx_texture_component_remap
read it through the ARGB lanes, where G and B are the resource's empty
components. A crossbar that sources G or B therefore sampled zero.

God of War: Ascension's menu and HUD font atlas is X16 sampled through
crossbar 0xAAEE (every output from G or B): every glyph came out with zero
colour and zero alpha, so all text was invisible while the button icons
(DXT) drew fine. Present X16 the way B8 already is: the value in R, G and B,
A opaque.

Test: test_remap_x16_lanes.
