a97617bd6eef7845d393ee3e7f0f6541e389e68e.message:
EDGE lighting loops: a fast pass with one range test a call

The two lighting loops (0x7BB4, 0x7ED8) tested every op's result for the
native range (and, compare, movemask, branch, then +0), which made the
native loops barely faster than the lifted ones. Now a call runs fast
first with no test per op: under round-toward-zero an exact result beyond
FLT_MAX sets MXCSR's overflow flag, and operands with the SPU's exponent
255 are looked for in what the ops read (the constants and carried values
once, the loaded quadwords each iteration). Either one redoes the call
with the exact forms from the same start; the stores of the fast pass go
only to output arrays apart from everything read. A zero's sign never
changes a non-zero result of these ops, so +0 is applied where values
leave (stores, registers).

GOWA_EDGE_EXACT=1 forces the redo (to test the exact pass). Strict replay
0 differ both ways. Replay, the lit jobs: 100.3 -> 88.0 us (-12%).

aa60d2e2d2c0c5c7a190030a4b1290cef3ad6bd6.message:
EDGE's vertex unpacking (piece 0x75BD10) as native code

The lit jobs' vertex stream is 18-byte records: x y z, then a 48-bit code. The code holds two
unit vectors (attributes 3 and 4), each as two 10-bit components and a 4-bit pattern index.
The third component is a square root by frsqest and fi. The pattern, one of 12 the piece
writes to its frame, gives that component's place and sign and a handedness w. An index
past 11 reads the caller's stack; those pairs are done with the piece's own operations.

The format was mapped with a bit-exact model of the probed calls. The routine also leaves what
the piece leaves: the list and table entries, the frame's patterns, two zero quadwords past
two arrays, r1 and r3.

Checked identical in 188,416 calls in the game and by strict replay. The lit jobs: -6% in
replay. Gate, ABBA: 17.95 -> 17.91 flips/s, within the spread.

(e8f44fbc6dbf): matrix-palette skinning, two vertices an iteration, now in

float ops are native under the SPU code's MXCSR with the +0 rule, checked

range, and the last one, run in the lifted loop from the registers as it

Notes: design for a C implementation of the whole EDGE job

Analysis first, nothing implemented:

  with their arguments.
- Where the time goes, measured in the game at the gate. A position-only job is 35.8 us
  (natives 8, the job manager 10.5, glue ~17); a lit job is 113 us (natives 57, the job
  manager 12, glue ~42).

  hole's NOP data, which are stale local store.
- The state a job reads that is not its input.
- What the strict replay compares.

natives. It is used in the SPU job, in the replay (a new compare mode), and later as step 3's
oracle. It is built bottom-up, glue function by function, with the rare kinds and ring wraps
declined.

palette changes. So its key leaves the palette and the matrix out, and a hit skips

with its record, and the pass works out position, normal and tangent before it
lights them. A position job gets a record too.

goes on to 0xF538 stays on the SPU: no skinned job at the gate or in the fight does.

GOWA_EDGE_SKIN=2 compares every job with spu_edge_gpuskin.c's CPU version. In the
fight, 565 million vertexes: positions bit for bit, tangents at most a unit off,
98.4% of the normals within 2 units of 32767.

e7312e3b7ac6b13b11b598da328c11e14ce7499d.message:
Re-kick a stranded EDGE job list: the menu-start freeze

About one run in fifteen froze right after the opening movie, the RSX
standing at the first hole of one EDGE job list for good. The main thread
kicks an EDGE list when the MeshProc batch counter (0xA0B724) reaches 0,
and re-arms that counter for the next frame's list right after. When the
re-arm came before the kicked list's policy module had read its first
wait, the module saw the new count and went idle; the next zero kicked
the next list, and nothing kicked the first again.

wws_rekick, the park stall hook (GCM_PARK_STALL_MS=100 by default),
signals an EDGE list whose next entry is a wait already met, on a
workload nothing runs or has asked for. Interleaved A/B on one binary:

unchanged (19.65 -> 20.27 flips/s, two runs each, within the spread).

Keep EDGE's velocity jobs, their transforms in the vertex pass

A velocity job (output piece 0x75F580) is a lit job that also makes the
previous frame's position from slot 19's matrix, into 36-byte vertexes the
title's velocity draws read. They were never kept: the job reader did not
know the piece, and both matrices change every frame for a moving object.

GOWA_EDGE_VEL (1 on, 0 off, 2 the check): an unskinned one goes
GOWA_EDGE_RIGID's way. Its key leaves out slots 18, 19 and 4, its result
keeps what 0xF538 reads, and the vertex pass does the four transforms and
the packing, with a fourth set of constants (ER_PREV, ER_VEL). With a result
the output piece is left out and the ring gets the block's tag.

The check: 393 million vertexes the same as the SPU's; the GPU's positions
bit for bit against the CPU's. A velocity job 63.5 -> 46.2 us, 95-96% kept;
the fight about +10%. Notes in docs/notes/2026-11-11-edge-velocity.md.

ea6e9bbc981f58ae16494885c0dc26e50c22ad2d.message:
EDGE job: the skinning driver's loops and the context builder's table loops as native code

- native/spu_edge_skinmat.c (GOWA_EDGE_NATIVE bit 1048576, on by default):
  0xE550's matrix layout loop 0xE804 (word moves), and the skinned lit
  jobs' normal and tangent transform 0xF104. 0xF104 keeps its pipeline in
  eight 256-bit registers and makes one range test a pass, redoing a pass
  in the exact float forms when it fails. A first version with the
  pipeline in arrays saved nothing.

  over the descriptor's tables, as byte moves. A pass sets only its own
  path's scratch registers, so the natives work out the passes left and
  leave the last pass that copies, and those after it, to the lifted loop.

  registers and the whole local store: 378 calls of 0xE550 and 1719 of
  0x88B0 in replay, 90,114 and 413,696 in the game, 0 differences; 1720
  replayed jobs, 0 differences.

f9259bac0437b9b8879b3fb9aeb1fb21bbb2b7f1.message:
EDGE natives: order the MXCSR flag reads against the fast ops

The compiler takes the float ops for pure and moved some of them across a
plain _mm_getcsr: in the game the vertex pass (0xD250) stored FLT_MAX
where the SPU saturates to 0x7FFFFFFF in 6923 calls, its overflow flag
read before the op ran. The flags now go through volatile asm (ldmxcsr,
stmxcsr with a memory clobber), ordered by the values they carry: the
pass's register inputs come out of an empty asm after the clear, its
results go into one before the read.

The transform and the vertex pass read the flags once a call when their
output is apart from their input, and redo the whole call exact when they
show; in place, once a pass as before.

GOWA_EDGE_VERIFY=1 also checks each fast call of the two lighting loops
against the exact pass from the same start.

Checked in the game: the transform 1.13M calls, culling 414K, point lights
352K, the lighting loops' self-check, all identical; strict replay 0
differences both ways. Gate, ABBA: 15.34 -> 15.94 flips/s (+3.9%) over
main.

fef5ac98bd8fcf77b8dccb95efebd527f3ba0a55.message:
EDGE's index decompression (0xE4D0 -> 0xDCC0) as native code

Every EDGE job decompresses its triangle indices in place. The format, mapped stage by stage
from snapshots at each loop head and checked with a model of the whole local store:
- an 8-byte header (reuse count, delta bias, bitmask bytes, bits a reuse);
- a bitmask, 2-bit triangle codes, then k-bit reuse values.

The stages:
- the reuses are eight interleaved running sums of the k-bit deltas;
- the bitmask picks a reuse or the next new vertex for each slot of the vertex sequence;
- each triangle code is a fresh triangle of three sequence values, or a turn on one edge of
  the triangle before, reversed, with the next value.

The scratch past the indices goes out by DMA, so the routine makes it byte for byte, along
with c + 0x50/0x58, the frame and r3.

Bit reader, a pshufb expand a mask byte at a time, and one pshufb a triangle:
9,154 -> 4,737 cycles a call. Checked identical in 561,152 calls in the game and by strict
replay. Gate, ABBA: 18.14 -> 18.71 flips/s.

1434613489.readme_excerpt: # Ascension-R: a God of War: Ascension PC port [![CI](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) ![Platform: Windows x64](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows%20x64-lightgrey.svg) ![Status: alpha](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-alpha-orange.svg) An unofficial, native PC port of **God of War: Ascension** (PS3) for Windows, made by static recompilation with [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp). The game's PPU and SPU code is translated to x86-64 ahead of time and the RSX is drawn with Direct3D 12, so no emulator runs while you play. Website: [rigaz29.github.io/Ascension-R](https://rigaz29.github.io/Ascension-R/) > [!IMPORTANT] > This repository holds no game files. You build the port from your own copy of the game. See [Legal](#legal). ## Contents - [Status](#status) - [Features](#features) - [Download](#download) - [What you need](#what-you-need) - [Building from source](#building-from-source) - [Playing](#playing) - [Reporting a problem](#reporting-a-problem) - [How it works](#how-it-works) - [Project layout](#project-layout) - [Contributing](#contributing) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Legal](#legal) - [Credits](#credits) - [License](#license) ## Status It boots, plays the cinematics and goes through the menus into the levels. It has not been played from start to finish, so expect problems further in. - **Game:** God of War: Ascension, digital US release, NPUA80918, version 1.12: the game and its updates 1.04 to 1.12. - **Platform:** Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. Tested on Windows 11. - **Speed:** above 30 frames a second in the two scenes measured, a fight of the first level and the gate, on a Ryzen 5 4600H with a GTX 1650 Ti and the Smooth preset. - **Online:** not supported. The port is single player. - **Downloads:** the Kit, on the [releases page](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/releases). It holds none of the game's code and builds it on your PC from your copy. ## Features - **Launcher:** a ready check, three presets (Smooth, Balanced, Faithful) and every setting below. It finds the game's folder by itself, and says when a newer release is out, with a link to it. - **Picture:** internal resolution from 1x to 4x or native, AMD FSR 1 and FSR 3.1 scaling, FSR 3.1 frame generation, SMAA 1x and anisotropic filtering. - **Display:** windowed or borderless, ultrawide, VSync, a frame rate cap, and frame rate and load on screen. - **Shaders:** a compressed cache, pipelines built before the title, and every vertex shader built before the first start of each version, on an 8-bit screen with music of its own. - **Game patches:** switch off MLAA, depth of field, motion blur, mesh trimming or dynamic shadows. - **Cheats:** damage to and from Kratos, max red orbs, infinite magic and items, infinite rage and double jumps. - **Controls:** a controller or keyboard and mouse. Xbox and other XInput pads, and through SDL3 the DualShock 4, the DualSense, Switch controllers and many others; stick dead zone, confirm button, vibration and controller API settings. - **Saves:** backups kept before the game writes over a save. - **Problem reports:** one button makes a zip of the logs, with your paths hidden. [docs/FEATURES.md](docs/FEATURES.md) describes each one and its setting. ## Download The [releases page](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/releases) has the Kit: a zip of the program without the game's code. Its launcher finds your copy of the game, decrypts it with RPCS3 and builds the game's code on your PC, once, in about ten minutes. There is nothing else to install: the Kit brings its own Python and LLVM. Each release's notes have the steps. Your copy needs all nine of the game's updates, 1.04 to 1.12, installed in RPCS3 in that order. Each brings its own files: 1.12's is the EBOOT alone, and the archives come with the ones before it. With 1.12 alone the game stops on its first loading screen. ## What you need To build it from source: - Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. - A CPU with AVX2 and FMA, and a GPU with Direct3D 12. - The game, installed in RPCS3 with its license, and its updates 1.04 to 1.12, installed in that order. - Python 3.10 or later, Git, CMake, Ninja, Visual Studio with "C++ Clang Compiler for Windows", a Windows SDK, and about 20 GB free. - For the game's movies: an LGPL shared build of FFmpeg with its headers, unpacked under `..\ffmpeg`, for example `win64-lgpl-shared` from [BtbN/FFmpeg-Builds](https://github.com/BtbN/FFmpeg-Builds/releases). - Optional, for AMD FSR 3.1: [FSR SDK 2.4.0](https://github.com/GPUOpen-LibrariesAndSDKs/FidelityFX-SDK), unpacked under `..\fsr-sdk`. ## Building from source ``` git clone --recursive https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R cd Ascension-R python -m venv ..\.venv ..\.venv\Scripts\pip install -r ps3recomp\requirements.txt # 1. Decrypt USRDIR\GOWA.SELF to GOWA.elf with RPCS3 (Utilities > Decrypt PS3 Binaries). # 2. Point the project at the installed game. It is only read. ..\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\gowa.py setup --game-dir \dev_hdd0\game\NPUA80918 ..\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\gowa.py doctor ..\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\gowa.py analyze ..\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\gowa.py lift ..\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\gowa.py build ..\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\gowa.py run ``` `doctor` lists anything that is missing. The lift and the first build take about 13 minutes on a Ryzen 5 4600H. `run` starts the game straight away, with its log in `logs\`. ## Playing Open `build\Ascension-R.exe`. The launcher checks the game's folder and your setup, and **Play** starts the game. The first start of each version builds the game's vertex shaders before the game begins, on a screen of its own: a minute or two the first time, seconds after an update. Fragment shaders are built the first time they are needed, so expect some stutter at first. **Clear shaders**, in the launcher's sidebar, makes the next start build them again. A build from source keeps its settings, logs and shader caches in `build\`, and its saves in `gamedata\`. ## Reporting a problem **Report a problem**, in the launcher's sidebar, makes a zip in `logs\` beside the settings file, for you to attach to an [issue](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/issues/new?template=problem.yml). The launcher offers it by itself after a session that crashed, lost the graphics device, froze or stopped with no reason in its log. `Ascension-R --report [--with-saves]` makes one without the window. The zip holds the logs and pad recordings of the last three sessions the game ran in, your settings, the build, your hardware and driver versions, and Windows' records of crashes and hangs of this exe in the last two weeks. Folder paths and your Windows account and PC names are hidden. The game sends nothing by itself and no game file goes in. Saves go in only if you tick the box, without the game's images and sounds. If no new frame comes for 15 seconds, the log gets what each thread was doing, and again at 60 (`GOWA_FREEZE_WATCH=`, `0` = off). ## How it works 1. `gowa.py lift` translates the PPU code of `GOWA.elf` to C++, and `build` does the same to C for the SPU programs and job modules. Both are compiled for x86-64 with clang-cl. 2. The [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) runtime stands in for the PS3: its system calls and libraries, SPURS, the file system, audio, pads and save data. 3. The game's RSX commands are drawn with Direct3D 12. Its shaders are translated to HLSL and compiled with DXC. 4. Movies are decoded with FFmpeg. 5. SPU code that was not translated ahead of time runs in an interpreter. The session records it, and the next `lift` adds it. More detail: [what the game is made of](docs/ANALYSIS.md), [what has been measured](docs/PERF.md), and the [development notes](docs/notes), one per session. ## Project layout ``` port/ the port: entry point, launcher, game-specific code native/ hand-written routines for the SPU code that costs the most scripts/ gowa.py, the pipeline (doctor, setup, analyze, lift, build, run, symbolize), and the bench tools/ which of the game's imports the runtime answers, shader cache checks, RenderDoc helpers tests/ tests for the launcher's game search, shader compile guards and native routines docs/ analysis, measurements, features and development notes packaging/ text files that go beside the program in a package site/ the website, rigaz29.github.io/Ascension-R, published by .github/workflows/pages.yml third_party/ zlib ps3recomp/ the toolkit and runtime, as a submodule (fork rigaz29/ps3recomp, branch gowa) ``` ## Contributing Anyone can help: by playing and reporting, or with changes to the port or to the runtime under it. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) says where help is most useful, where a change goes, and what must never be committed. ## FAQ ### Is there an official PC version of God of War: Ascension? No. It came out on PlayStation 3 only. Ascension-R is an unofficial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony. ### How is this different from playing on RPCS3? RPCS3 emulates the PS3 and runs the game's code as it goes. Ascension-R translates that code to native x86-64 code ahead of time, on your PC, and draws with Direct3D 12, so no emulator runs while you play. RPCS3 is used only to decrypt your copy. ### Do I need to own the game? Yes. The download holds no code or assets of the game: its launcher builds the game's code from your own copy, with its license. ### Which copies of the game work? Only the digital US release NPUA80918 at version 1.12, with every update from 1.04 installed. European and disc releases are not supported yet ([#4](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/issues/4)). ### Does it run on Linux or the Steam Deck? One player plays it on Linux through Proton, in a Wine prefix made by Lutris ([#12](https://github.com/rigaz29/Ascension-R/issues/12)). The Steam Deck has not been tried. ### Is it safe to run? The code is open source and built in the open. Each release lists the SHA-256 of its download and what the package was checked for, and the game's code is built on your own PC. The program is not signed, so Windows SmartScreen may warn the first time. ## Legal No game files are in this repository, and none will be. You need your own copy of the game and its license, and you decrypt it yourself. What you build from your copy contains code translated from the game. Keep it on your machine: do not commit it or share it. God of War is a trademark of Sony Interactive Entertainment. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by it. ## Credits Built on [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) by sp00nznet. The other code and libraries the port uses, among them FFmpeg, AMD FSR, SMAA, zlib and Zstandard, are listed in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). ## License The code in this repository is under the MIT License, see [LICENSE](LICENSE). port/ui: on Linux, start again from the path the program started from

file: the swap has moved it into .previous/<version>, so the start ran
the old version from there, and program_dir() (the install folder, where

GetModuleFileNameW keeps the path the exe was loaded from on Windows, and
start_again spawns that path, falling back to /proc/self/exe only if it
cannot be started.

1eae80c49893cbe0e834e846d3d31078539ca73a.message:
CI: libxml2 for ld.lld in the Linux compiler download

LLVM builds its Linux lld with libxml2 (for lld-link's Windows manifests;
ld.lld never calls it) and links it as libxml2.so.2, which newer distros
no longer have (libxml2 2.14 is libxml2.so.16). The first run of the Linux
job stopped there: "ld.lld needs libraries a desktop Linux may not have:
libxml2.so.2" (run 40157860894; clang itself passed).

The job now builds libxml2 2.9.14 from GNOME's pinned source with every
option off, so it needs glibc alone, and packs it as lib/libxml2.so.2,
where lld's RUNPATH ($ORIGIN/../lib) finds it (llvm_pack.py pack --extra).

port: the foot IK smooths at the 30 fps rate at any frame rate

The foot placement (driver 0x002F5B08, Havok's foot placement solver
0x00FF4DC0) moves the pelvis offset, the solver's weight and each foot's
height by a fixed share an update, tuned for 30 fps. Above 30 fps they
settle faster (three times at 95 fps), so the hips and feet follow every
bump of the ground (issue #140). des_ik_rate turns each ease k into
1 - (1 - k)^(30 dt) and the pelvis keep r into r^(30 dt), with the
driver's own dt, so a second goes as at 30 fps. DES_IKFIX=0 turns it off
live; DES_IKLOG=<file> writes the player's pelvis offset each update.

2f391c1e6df082d8a7ee31a6968d8fafde385a43.message:
Updates: only releases signed with the project's release key

An update trusted whatever the GitHub release held: the zip was checked
against SHA256SUMS from the same release. Now SHA256SUMS must carry the
maintainer's signature, made offline with OpenSSH (ssh-keygen -Y sign,
namespace demons-souls-recomp-release) and uploaded as SHA256SUMS.sig.
The engine checks it against the keys in
tools/setup/des_setup/release-keys.txt, the installed version's list,
before it reads the checksums or downloads the zip. The check offers
only a signed release (an unsigned one is passed over, its notes
unread); update-apply refuses one with the new error code "signature".
With no key in the list, no update is installed.

signing.py checks Ed25519 (RFC 8032) and OpenSSH's SSHSIG format in
plain Python, as setup's Python has no Ed25519: about 10 ms. Its tests
check RFC 8032's vectors, a signature made by Windows' own ssh-keygen,
and signatures ssh-keygen -Y verify accepts. docs/105 section 7.1 has
the maintainer's steps for the key.

port: HDR settings, and the menus on an HDR back buffer

Settings, Display gets four rows for the runtime's HDR output: HDR
(RSX_HDR, off by default), HDR brightness (RSX_HDR_WHITE: Windows'
setting or 100 to 400 nits), HDR peak (RSX_HDR_PEAK: the display's or
400 to 1500 nits) and HDR shadows (RSX_HDR_GAMMA: gamma 2.2 or the
sRGB curve). All apply live.

On an FP16 scRGB back buffer the D3D12 menu renderer draws its finished
layer through a program of its own: decoded as the game's picture is
and scaled to the same paper white (rsx_d3d12_hdr), so the menus match
the game. Read-backs (UI screenshots, the problem report's picture)
convert the buffer back to 8-bit SDR.

The run defaults name Demon's Souls' composite as the scene program
(RSX_HDR_SCENE_FP=B42C01:2): it doubles the half-brightness scene and
clamps it to white before bloom; with HDR on it clamps at the scene
target's own limit, twice white, and the highlights above white reach
the display (docs/104).

hits, picked fresh every update. A ray that grazes a step riser or a curb
bevel returns a nearly horizontal normal, and the foot turns almost onto

the main thread's stack is in the stack area, 0xD0000000 up. guest_ptr_ok
took only addresses below 0x50000000. So des_body_xform skipped every
transform-to-matrix copy into a local of the main thread (r1 + 0x110,
0xB0, 0x130 at the copy's callers), and breakables and debris were drawn
at the 30 Hz physics rate again. Ragdolls were not affected: their pose
slots are on the heap. The check now takes the stack area too, in both
copies; every other hook that uses it (DES_NET_TENDENCY=own, the dev
cheats) gets the same.

setup: build the game with no Visual Studio (milestone 2's commands)

game_build.json held milestone 1's commands: the Visual C++ headers, the
Windows SDK, and ten Windows import libraries at the link, so setup could
build the game only on a PC with Visual Studio's build tools. It is now
written from a DES_SPLIT_FREESTANDING=ON build (docs/84): clang's own
headers and ps3recomp's shims (/X), no default libraries (/Zl), no stack
cookies (/GS-), a link with /NODEFAULTLIB /NOENTRY /MANIFEST:NO, and one
more object, ps3recomp's game_libc.c.

The link's one library is kernel32's import library for GetCurrentThreadId
(Windows sets up a DLL's thread-locals only when it has an import table).
CMake makes it with lld-link /lib from ps3recomp's .def file.
game_build_desc.py now reads that command too ("libs"), and compile.py runs
it as a journal step, lib:<name>, before the link, so the link needs no SDK
either. A changed .def makes the library and the DLL again and compiles
nothing; a missing .def stops with the file's name.

game_build_desc.py refuses a build that is not freestanding, and maps a link
input named relative to the build directory (the import library) to {gen}.
The description was written from a CMake build of a lift setup made, so its
headers include ps3emu/ppu_lift.h, which a new lift's ppu_recomp.h includes
(16 headers; endian.h is no longer read).

tools/des: test runs play from their own save copy; play.sh holds the save lock

regress.sh and levelcap.sh swapped the player's save folder for the pinned
one and put it back at the end. A play session started in that window, or a
game still ending when the save went back, could load or write the wrong
save.

- A build that reads PS3_SAVEDATA_ROOT (ps3recomp #80 and later) now plays
  from a copy of the save in the run's scratch folder (des_run_save). The
  player's save folder is never swapped, so a game left running can only
  write the copy. Older builds swap the save as before.
- des_kill_own waits until the games it ended have gone (taskkill only
  starts a process's end), looks once more for a game one of them had just
  started, and fails if one survives. The swap path then leaves the save and
  the lock for the next run, instead of putting the save back under it.
- play.sh holds the save lock for its session: it waits while a run has
  another save swapped in, and such a run waits for the session.

Checked with a stand-in exe (own copy, the old swap, a game that starts
another, play.sh waiting and holding the lock, an old-path run refusing to
start during play) and one regress run of the split build: exit 0, four
shots ok, the player's save unchanged.

7f80510c64b78118b92bd33b984449fdc89f00e9.message:
setup: the compile follows the memory as it goes

The job count was fixed at the start, from the memory free then: on a PC
with about 5 GB of 31 GB free that was one job, for 1,533 of the run's
1,602 s. Now each job starts only while the memory holds it: up to one a
processor, and a job starts while the memory free now, less 2 GB for the
rest of the PC and less what the running jobs are still expected to grow
by, holds its expected peak. When nothing runs the next job starts anyway.
The biggest start first, and a smaller one that fits starts beside them.

A job's expected peak is the one measured the last time (the journal keeps
it: the compiler's peak commit on Windows, VmHWM on Linux), else its kind's
figure, raised to the largest measured so far in this run among its kind.
One that took less never lowers it (chunk 012 peaks at 0.9 GB, chunk 009 at
2.4). Free memory counts the commit the system can still give too. A job
that runs out of memory runs once more with nothing beside it; -j N still
runs N at a time.

When memory has held jobs back for 5 s the engine says so (@memory short),
and the note under the bar reads "Closing other programs makes this
faster." The start screen's estimate counts the chunks that fit in the free
memory now, with the compile's figures, not in all of it.

The compile's progress counts source bytes, as docs/52 4.3 has it, not
objects: the small objects finish first and are nearly half of them, so the
bar read 78% and "About a minute left" with nine minutes to go. The screen
shows the count in MB.

9707d68e2eda82231094e081623ff4ac4818f8ad.message:
port: V-sync's Even frames and G-Sync / FreeSync choices

60 fps on a 144 Hz display judders: frames show for 2, 3, 2, 2, 3 refreshes
however evenly the game makes them. The V-sync setting (DES_VSYNC) gets two
choices beside On and Off, read live at each flip request:

- even: the rate goes to the nearest the display divides (the refresh over
  n: 60 becomes 72 at 144 Hz), the vblank clock ticks on the display's
  vblanks every n refreshes (ps3_vblank_lock_display), each frame is held n
  refreshes (RSX_VSYNC=n) and the game's step is whole frames. The game's own
  30 fps mode and the cutscenes keep the PS3's vblank and lock to the display
  only where it runs at a multiple of 59.94 Hz.
- vrr: presents at once and caps the rate at refresh x (1 - refresh / 3600),
  138 fps at 144 Hz, for a G-Sync or FreeSync display.

The port sets RSX_VSYNC from DES_VSYNC now (not the settings window), unless
RSX_VSYNC was given at start. ps3recomp.pin moves to afa453e (the display
timing, the vblank lock and RSX_VSYNC=2..4).

a1aa289998c1e6966f2cfe71e8805a43cd4b1810.message:
des_options: a roll while locked on goes where the stick points (DES_ROLLDIR)

Locked on, the game rolls only forward, back, left or right of the
target. The player's script asks function 110 (0x002EB3E8) once a roll
for the move set's roll k (0 forward, 1 back, 2 left, 3 right, 4 the
backstep), and the roll animation moves the character along its facing.

des_roll_dir, on three new instruction hooks, turns the player's facing
at that call to the target's bearing plus the stick's angle from k's
direction, at most 90 degrees. The locked facing update (0x0030F3C0)
would turn the character back to the target before the roll moves, so
for the roll's first 0.3 s of game time the hook adds the same angle to
the yaw that update aims at (0x0030F734). The roll keeps its facing to
its end, and the lock turns the character back after it as usual.

On by default (the user's choice), with a Settings row (Controls, Roll
toward the stick); DES_ROLLDIR=0 gives the original rolls, live.
DES_ROLLLOG=1 prints each roll's k, stick and turn. A stick along a
roll's direction, the backstep, rolls not locked on and other characters
are unchanged.

Needs a re-lift: three lines in port/insn_hooks.txt, and only
ppu_recomp_006.cpp changes.

a9fa24819a83fb1e567a61bb9c3b8a25acb659d3.message:
host: FFmpeg's DLLs beside des_host.exe, for the movies

Windows' own MPEG-2 decoder works only with the Microsoft Store's MPEG-2
Video Extension, and without it every movie has no picture and ends after
a moment (issue #202's "cutscenes skipped"). The Windows host now ships
FFmpeg's decoder beside it, as the Linux host does:

- host.yml's new ffmpeg-windows job builds FFmpeg 8.1.3 from the same
  pinned release as host-linux's, with the same options (the MPEG-2 video
  decoder and its parser only, LGPL 2.1 or later, nothing from the
  system), cross-compiled on Linux with mingw-w64: the win32 thread model
  and GCC's runtime linked in. A check fails on any import but Windows'
  own DLLs. Cached by the archive's SHA-256.
- The FFmpeg version and SHA-256 move to the workflow's env, so both jobs
  build the same archive (third_party_sources.py still reads them there).
- The host job builds the runtime with PS3RECOMP_FFMPEG_RUNTIME and those
  headers, stages avcodec-62.dll, avutil-60.dll and licenses/ffmpeg beside
  the exe, and checks the DLLs' imports for the Visual C++ runtime.
- package.py takes FFmpeg's DLLs and licenses/ from beside the exe into
  the player's zip (and its release-files.txt, so an update swaps them);
  release-check.yml packages stand-ins for them and looks for them.
- host-files-allow.txt lets the two DLL names through the game-file check.

The runtime uses FFmpeg's decoder on Windows from JonathanDC64/ps3recomp
(the sail_movie change); with an older pin the DLLs are shipped but unused.

Checked here: host.yml and release-check.yml parse; third_party_sources.py
reads the moved env; package.py with stand-ins puts the DLLs and the

b2b6c77bb8d32138bf15b5e419d4f881eac7de82.message:
setup: prepare the shaders after the compile

The engine's last phase, shaders, runs the host again as
`des_host --shaders <game folder>` (the host passes its own path with
--host). ps3_title_launch sees --shaders before anything else and runs the
game's own precompile pass (des_prework.cpp) with no window, into the game's
own cache and stamp, then exits. The first start then finds the cache up to
date. The pass prints its progress once the total is known, and its result;
the engine shows them as the phase's progress and keeps the output in
setup/logs/shaders.log. The des.log hook skips --shaders.

The phase never fails a setup: a pass that fails or does not start is a
note, and the game prepares the rest at its start. ready.txt is now written
once the compile is done, before this phase, so a pass that is stopped
leaves a game that plays. On Linux the precompile is D3DCompile's, so the
host answers "nothing to prepare".

# Demon's Souls Recomp **Demon's Souls, running natively on PC.**
This is a PC port of *Demon's Souls* (PS3, 2009). The game's original code has been converted to run directly on Windows and Linux, with no emulator. You need your own copy of the game: the US version, **BLUS30443**. This project includes no game files. ## Features - Higher frame rates, with the game's timing fixed so it still plays the way it should - Higher resolutions and ultrawide screens - Keyboard and mouse controls, laid out like the Souls games on PC - Controller support, including Xbox and PlayStation controllers - Change which buttons and keys do what - An in-game menu for settings, most of which apply right away - Windows, and Linux (newer and less tested) - Online play (experimental) ## Status Early. The game is playable from the start through the first level, Boletarian Palace 1-1. ## What you need to play - Your own copy of Demon's Souls for the PS3, US version (BLUS30443) - A PC running Windows 10 or 11, or Linux - A graphics card that supports DirectX 12 ## How to play An easy setup tool is on the way. It will turn your copy of the game into the PC version for you. Until then, the game has to be built from source: see [Building from source](#building-from-source). Once the game is running, press **F1** (or **L3 + R3** on a controller) to open the menu and its settings. ## Building from source This is the technical part. The full notes are in [`docs/`](docs/). **Tools** | Windows | Linux | |---|---| | Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools, LLVM (clang), CMake, Ninja, Python 3, Git Bash | clang or GCC, CMake, Ninja, Python 3, SDL2, Vulkan and FFmpeg development files, vkd3d ([details](docs/76-native-linux.md#building)) | **From your copy of the game** - The game disc's files (`PS3_GAME`) - [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net), to decrypt the game's `EBOOT.BIN` - `libsre.prx` from your PS3 firmware, decrypted **Steps** 1. Get this repository, and its runtime inside it: ```sh git clone https://github.com/JonathanDC64/DemonsSoulsRecomp.git cd DemonsSoulsRecomp git clone https://github.com/JonathanDC64/ps3recomp.git ``` 2. In RPCS3, decrypt `PS3_GAME/USRDIR/EBOOT.BIN` (*Utilities > Decrypt PS3 Binaries*) to `work/game/EBOOT.ELF`. Copy `PS3_GAME/ICON0.PNG` next to it, for the program's icon. 3. Convert the game's main code: ```sh python ps3recomp/tools/ppu_loader.py work/game/EBOOT.ELF -o work/loader python ps3recomp/tools/ppu_lifter.py work/game/EBOOT.ELF \ --functions work/loader/EBOOT.functions.json --hle-stubs work/loader/EBOOT.imports.json \ --override-funcs "0x167AC88=ds_malloc,0x167AC58=ds_free,0x273D38=des_move_post,0x724E40=des_menu_tick" \ --insn-hooks @port/insn_hooks.txt --shadow-stack --chunk-lines 150000 --output work/recomp -j 16 python ps3recomp/tools/gen_hle_nids.py --all --out work/recomp/hle_nid_table.cpp python scripts/apply_boot_patches.py work/recomp ``` Then the SPU code with `python scripts/build_spu.py --eboot work/game/EBOOT.ELF` ([docs/09](docs/09-spu-spurs.md)), which first cuts the SPU programs out of the EBOOT, and libsre with `python scripts/build_libsre.py `. The lifter's flags above are also in `scripts/lift_ppu.json`, which setup reads; change both together. 4. Compile the runtime, then the game. On Windows: ```sh cmake -S ps3recomp -B ps3recomp/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake -S port -B port/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-cl -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang-cl \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE= -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG= -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS_DEBUG= cmake --build ps3recomp/build --target ps3recomp_runtime rsx_shader_precompile cmake --build port/build --target des_boot --parallel 4 ``` On Linux, see [docs/76](docs/76-native-linux.md#building). 5. Copy `tools/des/local.env.example` to `tools/des/local.env`, set `PS3_VFS_ROOT` in it to the folder that holds `PS3_GAME`, and start the game with `tools/des/play.sh`. Everything made from your copy of the game stays in `work/` and `gamedata/`, which git ignores. **Never share your build:** it contains code converted from your game. ## Legal This project contains only its own code, scripts and documentation. It has no game code, no game files, no Sony firmware and no keys; you make those from your own copy ([docs/05](docs/05-legal.md)). *Demon's Souls* is a trademark of Sony Interactive Entertainment. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony Interactive Entertainment, FromSoftware or Atlus. ## Credits - [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) by sp00nznet and its contributors: the recompiler and runtime this port is built on - [RPCS3](https://github.com/RPCS3/rpcs3): a reference for how the PS3 behaves (no RPCS3 code is copied) - [RmlUi](https://github.com/mikke89/RmlUi) for the menus, and [vkd3d](https://gitlab.winehq.org/wine/vkd3d) for Linux ## License MIT, for this repository's own code, scripts and documentation ([`LICENSE`](LICENSE)). ps3recomp is MIT-licensed by its authors.

cdb581579fd7ba76d429fab741828ce9e04161d6.message:
Low-CPU update: fewer threads on weaker PCs, support for CPUs without AVX2

- SPURS: on PCs with 16 or fewer CPU threads the lanes/kernels spin less, wake the
  main thread sooner and run on fewer threads (4-thread PCs: ~10 fps -> ~29 fps,
  8 threads: ~38 -> ~50 fps). Big PCs keep the old behaviour.
- Vertex workers spin far less after each job, fewer workers on small CPUs.
- The once-per-second thread scan only walks the game's own threads.
- No exclusive core reservations on PCs with fewer than 20 CPU threads;
  P-core pinning only on hybrid CPUs with at least 8 P-core threads.
- CPUs without AVX2/FMA/BMI2 (pre-2013 Intel, AVX-less Pentium/Celeron, AMD before
  2015): Setup/the updater detect this and build an SSE4.1 compatibility version
  automatically (same results, slower). The game also checks the CPU at startup and
  shows a clear message instead of crashing.

# inFamous PC

> **Official repo: [github.com/whompay/inFAMOUSreborn](https://github.com/whompay/inFAMOUSreborn).**
> Only download the Setup from the [Releases page](https://github.com/whompay/inFAMOUSreborn/releases) here.
> Forks are not supported, and bugs from forks won't be fixed.

An unofficial native Windows port of **inFamous** (PlayStation 3, 2009, European
release `BCES00220`). The game's PowerPC (PPU) and SPU code is statically
recompiled to x86-64 C/C++ with [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp),
so it runs as a normal Windows program rather than under an emulator.

**This repository contains no game code or data.** You build the game yourself,
on your own PC, from your own copy of the game.

## Easy install

Adds linux/ (inFamous-Linux-Setup.run): an unprivileged setup that works

  file and the Windows build commands; CMake's CPU probe is skipped

  build itself on CPUs without AVX2/FMA/BMI2.

  hosts: CRLF for text writes without newline= and NTFS directory order,
  so generated files match generated.lock (ppu_recomp.h is CRLF there).

  recorded hash.

  inFamous.exe under Wine never sees a Linux absolute path.

Microsoft's d3dcompiler_47.dll (SHA-256 pinned, from the Windows SDK cab

Low-CPU update: fewer threads on weaker PCs, support for CPUs without AVX2

- SPURS: on PCs with 16 or fewer CPU threads the lanes/kernels spin less, wake the
  main thread sooner and run on fewer threads (4-thread PCs: ~10 fps -> ~29 fps,
  8 threads: ~38 -> ~50 fps). Big PCs keep the old behaviour.

- The once-per-second thread scan only walks the game's own threads.

  P-core pinning only on hybrid CPUs with at least 8 P-core threads.
- CPUs without AVX2/FMA/BMI2 (pre-2013 Intel, AVX-less Pentium/Celeron, AMD before
  2015): Setup/the updater detect this and build an SSE4.1 compatibility version
  automatically (same results, slower). The game also checks the CPU at startup and
  shows a clear message instead of crashing.

1434806111.readme_excerpt:
# inFAMOUS 2 Reborn

A native Windows PC port of **inFamous 2** (PS3) made by static recompilation. The game's PPU
and SPU code is translated to C/C++ and compiled for x86-64, with a D3D12 renderer standing in
for the RSX.

**This repository contains no game code or game data.** The installer regenerates everything
from your own legally dumped copy of the game, then compiles it on your PC.

## Requirements

- Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), a D3D12-capable GPU
- Your own dump of **inFamous 2, European/Australian release `BCES01143`**: a disc image
  (`.iso`, Redump images with their `.dkey` next to them) or a decrypted game folder
- About 25 GB of free space for the install; 16 GB of RAM recommended
- Python 3.10+ and Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools with the C++ and Clang tools. The setup
  program installs both through winget if they are missing.

## Install

1. Download **`inFamous 2 Setup.exe`** from the
   [Releases](https://github.com/whompay/inFAMOUS2reborn/releases) page.
2. Run it and pick your disc image or game folder.
3. Choose an install folder and let it work. The first install takes a while: the game code is
   lifted and compiled on your machine.
4. Start the game with **`inFamous 2.exe`** in the install folder. Its options window has
   V-Sync, shadows, mipmaps and button prompts.

To update, use **Update now** in the setup program or `Update inFamous 2.cmd` in your install
folder. Only changed files are downloaded and only the affected steps are redone.

## Controls

Xbox/XInput controllers work out of the box. Keyboard and mouse are supported too: bindings and
mouse sensitivity live in `infamous2-recomp\kbm.ini` (changes apply while the game runs). On-screen
prompts switch between keycaps and controller buttons depending on what you last used.

## Status

The game boots, plays its cutscenes and runs in the open world. Performance depends mostly on
CPU single-thread speed; busy scenes currently run around 20–27 FPS on the development PC.
Lighting is rendered exactly (no stale-frame halos). Expect bugs. Please report them with
`infamous2-recomp\play.err.log` attached.

## Repository layout

| Folder | What |
|---|---|
| `infamous2-recomp/` | The port: build files, entry point, input bindings, pipeline tools and the hand-written SPU registrations |
| `ps3recomp/` | The recompilation toolkit and the PS3 runtime (PPU/SPU lifters, HLE firmware libraries, D3D12 RSX backend) |
| `installer/` | The installer, setup program and launcher (Rust), the pipeline manifest `infamous2.toml`, and the patch set that turns the regenerated code into the port's maintained version |

See `installer/README.md` for how the setup is built and `infamous2-recomp/README.md` for the
port's technical notes and runtime switches.

## Credits and license

Built on the [ps3recomp](ps3recomp/README.md) toolkit (MIT; see `ps3recomp/LICENSE` and
`ps3recomp/CONTRIBUTORS.md`). Third-party components keep their own licenses under
`ps3recomp/third_party/`.

inFamous 2 is © Sony Interactive Entertainment, developed by Sucker Punch Productions. This is
an unofficial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony or Sucker Punch. You need to
own the game to use it.

sceNp: tickets, account region and network time answer OFFLINE

sceNpManagerRequestTicket2, GetTicket, GetTicketParam,
GetAccountRegion and GetNetworkTime were not implemented, so their
imports answered CELL_OK with nothing written. A title that asked for a
ticket waited for a GOT_TICKET manager event that never came, and one
that read the region or the time used whatever was in its buffer.

Implement them with RPCS3's argument checks and offline answers: without
a psnr server the NP manager is OFFLINE and so are these
(SCE_NP_ERROR_OFFLINE), and there is never a ticket, so GetTicket
reports a size of 0 and GetTicketParam INVALID_STATE. Signed in to a
psnr server, which issues no tickets, a request is answered at once with
a GOT_TICKET event carrying an error instead of a ticket size; the
region is the fake account's (US, English) and the network time is the
host clock as a CellRtcTick.

06b2292def31186d507aa8cfd38ed487ec220a9c.message:
.github/workflows: pin the five third-party actions to commit SHAs

release.yml fires on `push: tags: ['v*']` with `permissions: contents:
write`, so every action it invokes runs holding a token that can write to
this repo and attach release assets. Referenced by floating major tag, any
of those five actions could be retargeted upstream -- a tag is mutable, and
whoever controls it controls what executes inside that job. Pinning to a
commit SHA makes the referenced code immutable.

Each SHA is the commit the action's current major tag points at, so this
changes no behaviour: the same code runs, it just can no longer be swapped
out from under us. The readable version stays in a trailing comment because
a bare SHA tells a later reader nothing about how stale the pin is.

Only `uses:` lines and their comments change -- 13 references across all
five workflows, no other workflow edits.

(cherry picked from commit 903d023f4a88ace083b0d9843fd3cf71a40f6572)

window at DRAW_SRV_BASE. Since VP_TEX_SLOTS went to 96 they cover heap

or animated one) replaced a descriptor an earlier draw had already

0e8b9ef2ca28fae79e8e24d2dede074581350fb7.message:
rsx engine: a depth snapshot is the region the texture names

The engine's host depth target is at least canvas-sized
(eng_zdepth_get), but a depth texture covers only the top-left
width x height of it. eng_zdepth_snapshot resolved the whole target and
the Metal resolve sampled it with normalized coordinates, so a 128x160
shadow map in the corner of a 1280x720 target was stretched over the
whole canvas and the lookups landed outside the map.

eng_zdepth_snapshot takes the texture's size and asks the backend for
that region (clamped to the target); a cached snapshot is reused only at
the same size. The Metal resolve reads the depth 1:1 (src.read at the
fragment's pixel) instead of sampling it, so a smaller snapshot is the
top-left region. The Vulkan backend's copy already works this way.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) samples small shadow maps from
canvas-sized zetas. In the port, this together with #424 and the port's
other depth-texture changes removes the dark rectangles on the ground
under shadows; the effect was not isolated per change.

Tests: test_color_feedback_engine (a 128x160 texture over a 256x256 zeta
asks for a 128x160 snapshot), test_metal_depth_readback (a 2x2 snapshot
holds the top-left texels 1:1).

11690a51b493e28537e6b0601ce9bf3cc5016233.message:
spu: fi on 32-bit lanes, frest/frsqest tables without a gather

fi's fixed-point magnitude is 2^32 + d with d = base * 2^19 - step * y,
so one unsigned compare gives the normalisation and 32-bit lanes hold
the rest: no widening to 64-bit lanes and back.

The fraction tables are read with one cross-lane permute per eight
entries and a select on the row, not a gather: on Zen 2 the gather made
frest slower than the scalar loop. Throughput of frest + fi (the
reciprocal pair): GCC 8.5 ns scalar, 9.5 before, 6.4 now; clang 12.1
scalar, 6.1 before, 5.4 now. test_spu_float_est still finds no
mismatch under either compiler.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

118b6281a756697391f178e523a409e0b1f60ce1.message:
cellGcmSys: GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS sets how long a FIFO park may stand

When the drain stops on a self-jump park and `put` has moved, it waits
GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS (50 ms) for the title to patch the park and then follows
`put`. That suits a title that leaves a park standing when it switches
segments. It does not suit one that appends commands right after the
park, moves `put` there and patches the park last: if the patch comes
after the grace, the drain skips the commands in between.

God of War HD does the latter, and while it loads its menu the two stores
have been more than 50 ms apart: the drain jumped from 0x57C40 to put
0x5AA2C, dropped ~11 KB of commands with a fence among them, and the boot
stopped (once in about 45 runs). The RSX itself would wait.

GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS=<ms> now sets the grace; the default is unchanged.

13a7676ba2139314035649dd94cc7bc075de2868.message:
perf(spu): copy only the reserved lines of a PUT under the lock-line lock

A PUT whose span touches a reserved line held the global lock-line lock for
the whole copy, keeping every other SPU's GETLLAR/PUTLLC waiting behind a
multi-line memcpy. Only the reserved lines can be inside a peer's
compare-and-commit window. In a multi-line span the other lines are now
copied first, without the lock, as the unreserved path already copies a
whole span; the locked pass then copies the lines it skipped and notifies
every reserved line, including one reserved after its unlocked copy.

That late line is notified but not copied again: between the two passes a
peer can reserve it, read our bytes and commit, and a second copy would
write that commit back over. Single-line spans keep the single locked copy.

test_spu_lockline_peer: an unaligned PUT over a reserved middle line raises
once, lands exactly, and leaves the bytes either side alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

147e59a79e63cefcf0c2f53fc7314d83f54167e2.message:
rsx_d3d12: pass the FP depth-export bits of SHADER_CONTROL

Draws recorded only the 32-bit-exports bit of SET_SHADER_CONTROL, so a
fragment program that replaces the fragment depth (bits 1-3) was
translated without SV_Depth. God of War HD's resolve pass writes the
scene depth it reads from the 2x-AA depth surface into the resolved
one this way; without it the pass wrote the quad's own depth (0), and
every depth-tested pass after it failed everywhere: the stencil
shadows, the fog, rain, the waterfall mist and the glows.

The draw now records the export bits (32-bit exports and depth export)
as fp_ctrl, part of the pipeline key, and hands them to the
decompiler, which already emits SV_Depth from r1.z.

15265cf84c72fa3def867b7732f498108cd8f863.message:
feat(tools): --handled and --image-ids for SPU program discovery

build_spu_workloads --input discovers every embedded SPU ELF in a carrier,
lifts it and registers it by fingerprint, and reports coverage as complete
only when every program is registered. A title that already registers some
programs another way (a hand-reviewed lift, an interpreter route) could not
use it without registering those twice, and its content-derived image ids
(0x10000000 | sha prefix) cannot be reviewed or kept stable against ids the
title already uses.

--handled JSON {sha256: reason}: such programs are not lifted, count as
covered and carry the reason in inventory.json. --image-ids JSON
{sha256: id}: every registered program takes its pinned id; a discovered
program missing from the map is reported unsupported, so coverage fails
instead of silently assigning one. Entries naming programs that were not
discovered are errors. With both, inventory.json's `complete` is a usable
build gate: a newly discovered SPU program cannot go unregistered silently.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

1530be7cfd1295f9db57e380a3dc2314770a82c1.message:
ppu_lifter: per-function copy of the memory model; PPU_FAST_FP

A guest store goes through vm_base + ea, a byte pointer the compiler
cannot tell apart from the memory-model globals, so the inline load and
store paths reloaded vm_base, ppu_vm_size, ppu_hle_inject_base and the
two enable flags after every store. Each lifted function now copies them
into a local at entry (PPU_MM_SNAP) and its accesses use the copy. They
are all set before guest code runs. The SPU reservation bitmap and the
store watches can change while a function runs, so those are still read
from the globals. Code outside lifted functions keeps vm_read*_inl and
vm_write*_inl, which now take a fresh copy per access.

PPU_FAST_FP, off unless the build defines it, drops the NaN checks in
ppu_fp_bin and ppu_fmadd_core. The host's NaN differs from the PPC one
only in its sign and in which of two NaN operands propagates.

God of War HD, func_001BEFA4, built with FMA3: 6,195 instructions before,
5,855 with the copy, 4,553 with PPU_FAST_FP as well (branches 1,342,
1,063, 583).

test_ppu_lift.py: the conformance driver defines PPU_NO_INLINE_LOADS. Its
vm_read*/vm_write* are its own functions, and its statements do not run
inside a lifted function.

170be32ac21c17795a97d244d8fa559ed47e21f0.message:
ftrace: a span for each HLE import call

PS3_FTRACE recorded syscalls and timer sleeps but not HLE imports, so a
guest thread blocked or busy inside an import (a file read, a SPURS
wait, a lock taken hundreds of thousands of times) showed up nowhere.
ps3_hle_call's exit guard now closes a PS3_FT_HLE span (who = thread,
a = NID, b = guest lr) for calls at least PS3_FTRACE_MIN_US long. With
the trace off it costs one load per call.

This is what found God of War HD's 360 ms frame: 320,355 lwmutex
lock/unlock pairs in it (PS3_FTRACE_MIN_US=0), against 71 in a normal
frame.

1891b8fe718534bef9d143c7b665beb762adbc07.message:
gcm: count the drain's own ring recycle as the JUMP to begin

Once a title has been seen to overrun its ring, the drain recycles the
ring itself when current nears end. A title whose callback also
recycles (cellGcm_fifo_recycle) can be in that callback at the same
moment: it writes its JUMP and put, and only then marks itself waiting,
so a pass that read the mark clear still teleports get to begin. The
callback then waits for a backward JUMP that never comes, because get
is already at begin == put, and gives up after 2 s of no progress.

God of War HD stopped for 2-4 s this way at random points in about
half of the gameplay runs. Counting the teleport as the backward JUMP
ends the callback's wait at once.

1be9e80d533ae0ff253fa169f5d2f5f783a1364d.message:
rsx_shader_msl: compile a vertex program's position invariant

Titles draw the same geometry twice with two different vertex programs,
the second pass testing EQUAL against the depth the first one wrote. The
RSX runs the position arithmetic instruction by instruction, so both
programs land on the same depth. The Metal compiler optimises each
program on its own (it may fuse a multiply and an add into one FMA in one
of them and not in the other), the two depths can then differ in the last
bit, and the EQUAL pass leaves holes.

Resistance: Fall of Man's foliage writes depth through an alpha-tested
program, then colour through one that also lights it, with
SET_DEPTH_FUNC EQUAL.

The translator now marks a vertex program's position [[position,
invariant]], and the Metal backend compiles guest programs with
MTLCompileOptions.preserveInvariance (macOS 11 and later), so programs
that compute the position the same way get the same bits.
PS3RECOMP_MSL_INVARIANT=0 leaves the position as it was.

test_shader_msl checks the vertex program's MSL for
"[[position, invariant]]" (and for "[[position" under
PS3RECOMP_MSL_INVARIANT=0).

1c7c1d914374d59451f5b73421119af501606cfb.message:
rsx engine: a scissored CLEAR_SURFACE clears only the scissor

RSX clears what the surface clip and the scissor let through. The engine
cleared every colour and depth target whole, whatever the scissor said.

Resistance: Fall of Man's co-op split screen renders both views into one
2x1 antialiased 1280x720 scene target: the scissor on the left half, a
colour and depth clear and player 1's view, then the scissor on the right
half, a clear and player 2's view. The second clear wiped player 1's view,
and the left half of the screen was black under the HUD.

sink_clear now asks eng_clear_rect what the clear may write: the clip
from the origin, then the scissor (eng_scissor_rect, the draw path's
scissor code moved into a function). Only a scissor narrower than the
clip makes a clear partial; a clip smaller than the target alone stays a
whole clear, as before. A partial clear goes to two new optional backend
hooks, clear_color_rect and clear_depth_stencil_rect. A backend without
them, or PS3RECOMP_ENG_RECT_CLEAR=0, clears whole as before. A depth clear
that covers everything the zeta was ever bound with (ext_w/ext_h) stays
whole, and a partial depth clear keeps had_write.

The Metal backend records a rectangle clear as a clear record with the
rectangle in its scissor and encodes it as a pass of its own: the
attachment is loaded and a full-target triangle under that scissor writes
the colour, or the depth and stencil with the test always passing. Such a
record is never folded into a pass's load action.

New test_clear_rect in test_rsx_draw_engine (the co-op frame, whole and
empty scissors, a zeta only bound at a small clip, a backend without the
hooks), and test_metal_rect_clears.m (tools/test_metal_rect_clears.py) on
the GPU: a rectangle clear of the right half keeps the left half, for
colour, depth and stencil, and a whole clear after one covers the target.

211cdd81b7f8b2b4e27f2a0fd998ed6351379558.message:
rsx: vertex array addresses wrap at 28 bits

VERTEX_DATA_BASE_OFFSET was added to an array's offset as a plain 32-bit
(or 64-bit) sum. A sum at or past 0x10000000 then pointed past the end
of the location's 256 MB address space, and the fetch read nothing.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) puts its per-frame world lighting
stream (attribute 4, UB256 x4) at base + offset = 0x1Fxxxxxx. Read
unwrapped it decodes as zeros, and buildings, snow and terrain render
saturated blue. Taken modulo 2^28 it is local 0x0Fxxxxxx, where the
stream is, and the world is lit.

rsx_dsp_resolve_vertex_offset (rsx_dispatch.h) masks base + array
offset to 28 bits before the location translation; the element offset
is added after. The fetch plan's stable span and per-element fetch
(rsx_vertex_compact.c) and the live-draw fetches (rsx_live_draw.c) use
it. Sums below 2^28 are unchanged.

test_vertex_fetch_plan: a stream at base + offset = 0x10000100 reads
local 0x100 through both the stable span and the per-element fetch, and
the random plans also draw bases with high bits set.

21c14a650a346b18a4f79c82689ad5c060c34693.message:
rsx_d3d12: guest depth/stencil state and samplers in the guest-FP pipelines

Every guest-FP pipeline had a fixed LESS_EQUAL depth test with writes,
no stencil, and four static samplers (s0 point/clamp for the dbgfont
atlas, s1-s3 linear/wrap), whatever the title set. In God of War HD:

- Its stencil shadow volumes marked nothing, and the shadow pass, a
  full-screen reverse-subtract quad meant only for the marked pixels,
  darkened the whole frame (0.16 -> 0.012 on a lit pixel).
- Depth state ignored: rain and blood particles were rejected.
- Unit 0 was point-sampled and clamped. The soldiers wrap their texture
  atlas (v up to ~2), sampled the transparent bottom row and drew
  nothing over an untextured base; Kratos' tattoo and skirt came out
  white; textures shimmered.

Depth test/write/func and front/back stencil (func, ops, masks) are
packed per draw into a PSO key (rsx_zs_key); the stencil reference is
set per draw. The cull key now always carries the front face, which
two-sided stencil needs with culling off. Samplers are four descriptor
tables built from each unit's TEXTURE_ADDRESS/FILTER/CONTROL0/BORDER
(one cached descriptor per distinct state); units without guest state
keep the old two defaults.

23540a1007e37f28c404c3adfa8ea2d22e188194.message:
rsx_d3d12: cache converted vertices within a draw

Indexed lists (shared vertices), strips and fans (each vertex in up to
three triangles) and indexed quads expand one guest vertex into several
output vertices, and each one was fetched again: 16 attributes, each with
its own address resolve and conversion, for every reference. God of War
HD's gameplay frames expand ~370k vertices through these paths and the
fetch was a third of the frame.

A direct-mapped cache on the low index bits (8192 entries, 2 MB) keeps
the converted 256-byte vertex; a hit is a memcpy. It is dropped at every
draw, since attribute state and the guest arrays may change between
draws. Measured in GoW HD gameplay: vertex time per 20 frames 0.80 s ->
0.29 s, ~9.0 -> ~12.1 fps. VTX_CACHE_CHECK=1 refetches on every lookup
and counts differences: 0 in 312M lookups. VTX_NOCACHE=1 disables it.

cellPad: restore the closing brace of pad_host_release()

My own mistake resolving the #496 / #472 conflict, and the cause of wave 3
coming back red on all ten jobs.

#496's pad_host_release() and #472's poll-lock/assign-tracking block were
both added at the same point in the file, so the merge presented them as
one conflict whose single trailing brace belonged to whichever side was
taken. I took both sides and put #496's first -- so that brace ended up
closing pad_status_take() at the end of #472's block, and
pad_host_release() ran on into the next 20 lines of file-scope code. Every
platform fails to compile libs/input/cellPad.c, which every target builds.

Found by bisecting wave 3: through #494 the branch is green, through #495
it is not, and #496 is the first merge in that span.

Checked for the same class of error across all 108 C, C++ and Objective-C
files this branch touches: brace-balanced after this commit, and
pad_host_release() was the only one out. The #505 resolution has the same
shape (two sides, one trailing brace) and was already correct.

The generated header now has vm_write*_inl beside vm_read*_inl. A store
is done in place when vm_inl_ok accepts the address, no store diagnostic
is armed (vm_inline_st_ok: PPU_WVAL, PPU_WWATCH, PT), the barrier watch
and the null-page sweep are idle, and no SPU holds a reservation on the
line (g_spu_coh_bits). Anything else goes to the out-of-line store as
before. PPU_NO_INLINE_STORES keeps the calls, and the runtime's own files
keep them through PPU_NO_INLINE_LOADS.

Re-lift to pick it up. God of War HD: the main thread runs about 14.8 ms
a frame instead of 16.2 with the HLE lookup cache, vm_write32 is gone
from its profile and vm_write64 is 1.2%. The executable grows from 57 to
87 MB.

division); rsx_vertex_element_index, the compact fetch's shared span and the

Every guest store called spu_coh_is_reserved, and in God of War HD
gameplay that call was 9.5% of the main PPU thread's samples. Most of it
was not the call: spu_coh_reserve stored s_coh_armed = 1 and or-ed the

cache lines kept moving to the SPU threads' cores, and each PPU store
missed on them.

  they change.
- spu_coh_bitmap.h publishes the bitmap as g_spu_coh_bits, NULL until
  the first reservation, and spu_coh_line_reserved tests it inline.
  VM_WRITE_COH in ppu_loader.cpp and ppu_memory.h, and
  vm_block_reserved, use it. s_coh_armed goes away.
- g_spu_coh_bits is one merged definition per program (selectany /
  weak), so the loader fixtures, which link ppu_loader.cpp without
  spu_coherency.c, still link and see no reserved lines.

3099075391d4105873242cd4c3f3555ed43fe397.message:
ppu_lifter: --insn-patches lifts patched instructions as run-time switches

A patch that changes an instruction word in .text does nothing to a
lifted title, which never executes the guest's code words. Making it a
second lift means a second build of the whole title for one changed
word, and a port that wants it optional ships two.

--insn-patches FILE takes {"patches": [{addr, orig, new, guard}, ...]}.
Each patched instruction is lifted in both forms and emitted as

    if (guard) { <new> } else { <orig> }  /* insn patch 0x...: orig -> new */

guard being an int the port defines and sets before the guest runs; each
function that uses a guard declares it extern "C". The original's branch
label and the code around it are unchanged. The lift stops when the
input does not hold orig at addr (a patch set for one build of a title
never lands on another), when a patch is at an address no lifted
function covers, or when new is a branch, sc or CR op (it would need
labels and call targets the function was not lifted with). The patches
reach the parallel workers too; a mismatch there raises instead of
exiting, so the pool does not hang on a dead worker.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) caps its campaign's frame rate in
code. The port lifts the cap's instructions this way and turns 60 fps on
or off from its settings, with one build.

New tools/test_ppu_lifter_insn_patches.py: a patched branch and a
patched li lift in both forms behind their guards, with the guard
declarations and the branch label in place; a wrong orig stops the lift
serially and with two workers; a patch at an address no function covers
stops it. docs/TOOLS.md describes the file with a generic example.

3bbd31bf98ab6e5f5ff8ef3a950891515376942d.message:
fix(ppu_lifter): resolve a jump-table base that was spilled to the stack

A switch dispatcher inside a loop, in a function with high register
pressure, TOC-loads its table base once, spills it, and reloads it at the
dispatch, then reuses the base register for the case address:

    lwz r10,d(r2) ; std r10,s(r1) ; ...
    ld r11,s(r1) ; lwzx r0,r9,r11 ; add r11,r0,r11 ; mtctr r11 ; bctr

discover_jump_tables took the `add` after the table load as r11's nearest
definition, and the stack reload before it was not a TOC load either, so the
dispatcher was dropped and its bctr lifted to an unresolved indirect call. A
retail title's 32-case dispatcher did exactly this; the main thread's case-1
call never ran and it went on with an uninitialised object, then stalled.

The base search now considers only definitions before the table load, and a
stack reload is followed to the nearest preceding store of that slot and the
stored register's TOC load. Over the whole retail executable (217
dispatchers) this adds exactly that dispatcher and changes no other table.
Two vectors in test_ppu_jumptables: the spilled, reused base; a reload of a
slot nothing stored stays unresolved. The first fails without the fix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

3bf0233d06ff7d1d181a80754a0fbf7a16cfc253.message:
cellAudio: WASAPI keeps 60 ms queued, and the mixing thread runs ahead of the guest

On Windows the shared-mode stream asked for a 20 ms device buffer, and the
mixing thread ran at normal priority. A title that keeps every core busy
with PPU and SPU threads takes the CPU from the mixing thread often enough
for those 20 ms to run dry, and each time is an audible click or stutter.
Movie playback (Bink) was the worst case.

- The buffer is 60 ms by default; PS3_AUDIO_BUF_MS=<10..500> sets it.
- The mixing thread asks for THREAD_PRIORITY_TIME_CRITICAL and joins the
  MMCSS "Pro Audio" task when the service is there. avrt.dll is loaded at
  run time, so nothing new is linked.
- AUDIO_RATE=1 also reports underruns: passes that found the device queue
  under half a block (it is about to play silence). The first 64 blocks are
  not counted, while the stream fills.

The guest still sees 256-sample blocks at 48 kHz paced by the device clock;
only how far ahead of the device the mixer may run changes (up to the buffer
size, so up to ~40 ms more output latency by default).

Seen with inFAMOUS 2 on a Ryzen 5 5600 (6 cores, all of them busy): with
the 20 ms buffer its Bink cutscenes stuttered audibly; with this change
they play cleanly. Only the Windows (WASAPI) path is touched.

3e9311c6287b1220d57e99b3a2a7d3e45a1cf7db.message:
cellGcmSys: forget a park once the walker has left it

The walker gives a self-JUMP park GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS with the same put to
be patched, then resyncs to put. Its record of the park (address, put,
start time) was only cleared by that resync. A park the walker left any
other way -- the title patched it into a JUMP elsewhere, or wrote
commands over it -- kept its start time, so when the walker next stopped
at the same address with the same put, the new park was taken for the
old one. Its grace had run out long before, the resync fired at once,
and the commands the title was about to link in were dropped with the
fences and labels in them. A title that reuses its command blocks
meets its parks again at the same address, frame after frame.

Clear the record as soon as the walker reads anything other than that
park's own self-JUMP: a new park always starts a fresh grace. The three
variables move from the JUMP branch to file scope for that, under the
same names.

rsx_d3d12: stage guest textures in a shared upload ring; LRU slots

texture whenever the slot took a new size or format. In God of War HD's
texture bursts, when new effects first appear, creating resources was
most of the cost: one report interval had 50 new textures, 67 ms of

44ec7ee2574b1f94820756e1f08ab22e876e845e.message:
test(ppu_lifter): a spilled-base switch spans its cases past the first blr

A function inventory that ends functions at their first blr leaves a
switch's case blocks, which sit after an early-return blr and share a later
epilogue, outside the declared range. main() already extends the enclosing
function over the cases of every resolved dispatcher; it could not when the
dispatcher itself was dropped, which is what the spilled table base caused.

End-to-end guard: a tiny big-endian ELF64 with such a function (base
TOC-loaded, spilled, reloaded and the register reused for the target; three
offset-table cases past the first blr), lifted by the real main() from a
--functions list cut at the first blr. The bctr must become a computed goto
to internal case labels, the shared epilogue must be inside the function and
the following function must stay separate. Without the spilled-base fix the
dispatcher is not found and four of the six checks fail; no separate extent
change is needed.

45c634575e648b55b2da417f0a17fff1d65aaf92.message:
Merge PR #421: opt-in per-thread MFC engine lookup cache (@tekulvw)

Conflict with #243 (@Kurtisone, wave 2) at the top of mfc_for(). Both PRs
make the same function cheaper, from different ends, and both are kept.

#243's fix is the SPU_PCSAMPLE hoist: the old guard only latched `started`
when the variable was actually set, so with SPU_PCSAMPLE unset every MFC
channel access paid a getenv -- a tenth of the samples in a Twisted Metal
profile. It sets `checked` either way. #421 adds the generation-checked
per-thread cache in front, which returns before the claim lock on a hit.

#421 was written against master, so its hunk carries the pre-#243 `started`
form. Taking it as written would have reverted #243 while keeping its test
-- and #243 ships test_spu_mfc_env_once.c precisely to catch that, so this
one would have failed loudly rather than silently. Resolved anyway as
#421's cache check first, then #243's once-only latch, then the lock.

Composition is fine in that order: the first call misses the cache, falls
through and starts the sampler thread, and later calls that hit the cache
return before a getenv they no longer need to reach.

There is only one mfc_for() in the file -- the Win32 primitives it uses are
shimmed on POSIX by win32_compat.h -- so there is no second copy needing
the same resolution.

4609b3f0bf7db6fdf3a9c36a5037b0be230b8d7c.message:
spu: halt and iret longjmps without unwinding on 64-bit Windows

On 64-bit Windows longjmp unwinds every host frame between it and its
setjmp: RtlUnwindEx, with a function-table lookup and a virtual unwind per
frame. The SPU runtime longjmps on every halt back to spu_run_with_halt (a
SPURS policy module's run ends that way) and on every iret back to the
drain loop that took the interrupt.

spu_jmp_no_unwind() zeroes the jmp_buf's Frame right after setjmp returns
0, which makes longjmp restore the registers directly. These jumps only
cross C frames of the runtime and of lifted code, which have no destructors
or __finally blocks. SPU_LONGJMP_UNWIND=1 keeps the unwinding jump. No
change on other platforms.

48958fefdf401b95dc3c8ad1d1d15461db2eb89a.message:
ppu: a host thread gives its callback stack slot back when it exits

Slots were handed out by a counter and never returned, so once 64 host
threads had ever made a guest callback, every later thread shared the
last slot and the original bug came back. A movie player starts several
threads per movie, so a normal session gets there. Keep a 64-bit in-use
mask instead: a thread takes the lowest free slot on its first callback
and a thread_local owner releases it when the thread exits. Only more
than 64 live threads making callbacks at once share a slot now.

The test first runs 100 short-lived threads one after another, each
making a callback: they all get the first slot back, and the two
concurrent threads after them still get different stacks. Both checks
fail without the release.

4b8de9100d4cc959a5ccf37c51067d416691dc7a.message:
spu: lifted known-target branches tail-call their target (SPU_DIRECT)

A lifted cross-function branch with a known target (br, the conditional
branches, a fall-through into the next function) set the trampoline and
returned, and the drain loop then called the target: a host return, a
loop pass and an indirect call for every transfer. Most of those steps
have nothing for the drain to do. SPU_DIRECT tail-calls the target with
clang's musttail when that is so: the target is not LS 0, this is not
the run's first transfer, the target is not a registered stack-reset
entry (a 1024-byte hint table, set at registration), and no interrupt
is pending with interrupts enabled. Everything else takes the trampoline
as before, and so does every compiler without musttail.

The drain-step diagnostics (SPU_LOCKSTEP, SPU_TAILRET, SPU_PCHIST,
SPU_NO_LS0_END, SPU_EXITTRACE, SPU_STEPTRACE, SPU_JOBDRAIN,
SPURS_PM_FLOW) turn it off, and PS3_SPU_DIRECT=0 does too.

spu_drain_call now restores the enclosing drain's drain_ret_pc on the
way out instead of 0. The enclosing loop used to re-set it on its next
step; with direct tail calls the code after a nested call can run on for
a long time before it takes one.

In the inFAMOUS 2 port (about 18.8k such sites) the open-world walk went
from 34.5 to 36.3 fps (+5.4%), with SPU time per frame from 128 to 121 ms.

5461d040a9f1788492c9746b087ac5c6d0a79a25.message:
rsx_metal_backend: drain the staging arena's autoreleased reference on the walker

The arena is dropped on Metal's completion thread when the pool is full,
but it was autoreleased on the FIFO walker: the driver's -[MTLBuffer
contents] autoreleases the buffer, and the walker is a PPU host thread
with no autorelease pool, so that reference lived until the thread
exited and no dropped arena was ever freed. In a retail title the
device's allocated size grew from ~0.9 GB to 28.6 GB over a long session
while the engine's object table stayed flat (~1,080 live slots, ~286 MB
of textures), until allocations failed and the renderer's checked guard
tripped. With the fix a long hold that created ~145,000 engine objects
stayed at ~315 MB.

The growth block in eng_stage_reserve gets a pool of its own; the other
-contents queries in the file already sit inside one.

test_metal_stage_pool now records 64 arenas on a pool-less pthread with
the pool full of buffers too small for one, and requires every dropped
arena freed (weak references) while that thread is alive. Without the
fix all 64 stay live and the device grows 256 MB; with it, none and 0.

604bc92130d086c1c483ff97baf35614367ac26c.message:
rsx_shader_msl: cache HLSL -> MSL translations, in memory and optionally on disk

A guest pipeline's first use on Metal decompiles both programs,
translates each HLSL to MSL (glslang + spirv-cross), compiles the MSL
and builds the pipeline state, all on the RSX thread in the middle of a
frame. In inFAMOUS 2 the translation was 83% of that: 218 first uses
over two minutes of play cost 2.1 s, with single frames of up to
366 ms, against ~16% for newLibraryWithSource and under 1% for the
pipeline state, which Metal caches itself.

Keep the MSL the way rsx_shader_spirv.cpp keeps SPIR-V: in memory, and
with PS3RECOMP_MSL_CACHE=<dir> in one file per stage + HLSL text +
PS3RECOMP_MSL_FAST setting. The file header names the glslang and
spirv-cross versions and the translator's build, so a file any other
combination wrote is a miss, as is a damaged one; files are written
under a temporary name and renamed. Unset, nothing touches the disk.

cellSysutilNpEula: answer the PSN terms check through its callback

sceNpEulaCheckEulaStatus asks whether the player has accepted the
title's PSN terms of service, and the answer comes later, through the
callback the title passed, on one of its cellSysutilCheckCallback polls.
None of the three real exports was implemented (the module had only a
made-up cellSysutilNpEulaCheck), so the imports answered CELL_OK and the
callback never came. A title that waits for the answer behind a "Please
wait..." box waits there for the rest of the run; inFAMOUS 2 does it the
first time it tries to go online.

Implement CheckEulaStatus, Abort and ShowCurrentEula as RPCS3 does: one
request at a time (ALREADY_INITIALIZED otherwise), the callback queued
from the next sysutil poll, Abort turning a pending answer into ABORTED.
The answer depends on the connection. Offline, the default, the terms
cannot be fetched and the callback gets SCE_NP_EULA_ERROR, which is what
a console without a connection gets and what makes a title leave its
online features alone; RPCS3's ALREADY_ACCEPTED would send it on to ask
an offline NP manager for a ticket. With PS3_NET_ONLINE=1 or a psnr
server the answer is RPCS3's, ALREADY_ACCEPTED, version 1.
ShowCurrentEula has nothing to show and closes on the next poll.

cellNetCtl exports its PS3_NET_ONLINE check as ps3_netctl_online for
this.
