1443080862.readme_excerpt:
# PS3revamp

**Decrypted PS3 `EBOOT.elf` → native C++ project.**

PS3revamp drives the whole static-recompilation chain from one command: it reads
the ELF, discovers every PPU function from the OPD table (plus IDA/Ghidra if you
have them), lifts PowerPC64 code to C++, binds the firmware imports to HLE
handlers, scaffolds a CMake project and can build the native executable.

It is a **driver**, not a new recompiler. The lifting engine is
[ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) (the toolkit behind the
Project Pyrrhus / Project Helghast ports). PS3revamp adds the parts that toolkit
leaves to you: discovery, coverage accounting, scaffolding, one-command runs and
a per-title report.

---

## Quick start (Windows)

```bat
python ps3revamp.py setup    :: downloads ps3recomp + clang + cmake + ninja
python ps3revamp.py doctor
```

Then either double-click **`PS3revamp.cmd`** (or drag an `EBOOT.elf` onto it), or:

1. Pick the decrypted `EBOOT.elf`. The game folder is detected from the path.
2. Press **Convert to PC**. The log shows loader → lift → HLE → build → boot test.
3. Press **Play** when it finishes.

Command line equivalents:

```bat
python ps3revamp.py doctor
python ps3revamp.py analyze "C:\path\to\EBOOT.elf"
python ps3revamp.py auto    "C:\path\to\EBOOT.elf" --game "C:\...\NPUA80068"
python ps3revamp.py port    "C:\path\to\EBOOT.elf" --game "C:\...\NPUA80068" --build
python ps3revamp.py play    "ports\Title"
```

`auto` is the one-click path: it decrypts/loads the EBOOT, lifts every PPU
function and embedded SPU image, generates the HLE table, builds at `-O2`
(release), boot-tests the result, packages a double-clickable game folder and
records the run in the knowledge base.

Result:

```
ports\<Title>\
  analysis\        EBOOT.functions.json / .imports.json / .image.json
  recompiled\      ppu_recomp.h, func_XXXX.cpp (one per chunk), ppu_hle_nids.cpp
  project\         CMake project (preset "ps3revamp"), main.cpp, stubs.cpp
  spu\             lifted SPE images (only with --spu)
  build.log
  port.json        machine-readable result
  PORT.md          coverage table + honest status + next steps
```

Run the built binary with the ELF path:

```bat
"ports\<Title>\project\build\<Title>.exe" "C:\path\to\EBOOT.elf"
```

---

## Fully offline, self-contained

The folder is the product. Everything it needs is inside it and nothing calls
the network at run time:

```
python\            CPython 3.12 embeddable (python.exe / pythonw.exe)
pylibs\            capstone, construct, pycryptodome, tqdm
toolkit\ps3recomp\ loader, lifter, HLE table generator, runtime sources
toolchain\         clang 23 (llvm-mingw), cmake, ninja, sccache
```

- `PS3revamp.cmd` / `ps3revamp.cmd` use `python\python.exe` when present, so a
  machine needs neither Python nor pip.
- `python ps3revamp.py setup --offline` verifies the bundle without touching the
  network.
- Copy the whole folder to an air-gapped PC and it works the same.
- If Visual Studio is present its `clang-cl` is preferred (better Windows ABI
  fit); otherwise the bundled llvm-mingw clang is used. Both paths are tested;
  the two MinGW gaps in the toolkit (`__try` and a linkage mismatch) are patched
  in the vendored copy, with the changes documented in `docs/PATCHES.md`.
- `setup` (without `--offline`) exists only to re-fetch components if the folder
  was stripped down; normal use never reaches it.

## Works on any EBOOT, not one title

Nothing in the pipeline is keyed to a specific game:

- `EBOOT.BIN` (SELF) is decrypted in place through the toolkit; a decrypted
  `EBOOT.elf` is used as-is.
- Function discovery prefers the title's own OPD table and falls back to a
  CFG/prologue scan when a build has none — with the module TOC applied to the
  recovered functions.
- SPU images are extracted and lifted automatically when the title has any
  (`--no-spu` to skip).
- Titles, IDs and versions come from that title's `PARAM.SFO`; names are
  sanitised for NTFS, so trademark/unicode titles are fine.
- HLE coverage, subsystem risk and missing-NID lists are computed per ELF.
- Compile chunks scale with the function count, so a 13k-function title does not
  become one giant translation unit.

---

## How a PS3 game becomes a native PC game

There is no emulator loop. A PS3 title is converted in five layers, and every
one of them is mechanical until the title does something the runtime has never
seen:

1. **PPU code → C++.** PowerPC64 is translated ahead of time, function by
   function, into C that operates on the guest's 256 MB memory arena and a
   `ppu_context` register file. Calls and returns become host calls; indirect
   calls go through a generated function table keyed by guest address. The CPU
   therefore executes *native* code — this is static recompilation, not
   interpretation.
2. **Firmware → HLE.** The game never talks to a PS3 kernel; it calls import
   stubs by NID. The runtime implements those (`sys_fs`, `sys_memory`,
   `sys_ppu_thread`, `cellSysutil`, `cellPad`, `cellAudio`, `cellGcmSys`,
   `cellSpurs`, `cellSaveData`, …) as ordinary C. Unknown NIDs fall back to
   "log once, return `CELL_OK`" — deliberately load-bearing, because titles
   often only need a call to *succeed*, not to do anything.
3. **RSX → D3D12.** `cellGcmSys` calls and the RSX command buffer are translated
   into D3D12 pipeline state, shaders, textures and render targets by the
   runtime's video backend. This is where most visual gaps live.
4. **SPU → C++ (or a shim).** SPU programs embedded in the title are lifted the
   same way as PPU code and dispatched by the `cellSpurs` HLE; jobs that are
   only side effects can instead get a PPU-side fallback.
5. **Assets → host files.** `cellFs` paths are mapped through a VFS rooted at
   your game folder, so the port reads the original data files in place.

Boot is then: map the ELF segments at their real addresses, register the lifted
function table, initialise the HLE, create a PPU thread at the entry OPD and
run. That is exactly how the Killzone 2 port (Project Pyrrhus) runs native on
Windows.

Where per-title work remains: behaviour the runtime has not implemented yet
(an NID that must do something real, an RSX quirk, a timing patch). PS3revamp's
job is to make that set as small and as *visible* as possible — which is why
`port --test` boots the build and classifies exactly where it stopped.

---

## Commands

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `doctor` | checks toolkit, C++ toolchain, Python deps, IDA/idalib; writes `config.json` |
| `analyze <elf>` | ELF metadata + function count + import list + HLE coverage, no lifting |
| `port <elf> [-o DIR] [--game DIR] [--build] [--spu]` | full pipeline |
| `build <portdir>` | re-configure + rebuild an existing port |
| `play <portdir>` | run the built executable with the right asset root |

The GUI (`ps3revamp_gui.pyw`) only calls `port`, so everything below applies to
both. `EBOOT.BIN` SELF files are decrypted automatically through the toolkit's
`unfself.py`; if that fails you need a decrypted `EBOOT.elf`.

Useful flags:

- `--analyzer auto|native|ida|ghidra` — `auto` uses IDA when idalib is
  reachable, otherwise the OPD/CFG scanner.
- `--jobs N` — lifter and build parallelism.
- `--opt 0..3` — optimisation for the lifted translation units (default 2).
  Runtime and scaffold always build at `/O2` (or `-O1` with MinGW clang).
- `--fast` — build lifted code unoptimised: the quickest way to iterate.
- `--test SECONDS` — boot the result and classify where it stopped.
- `--deep` — after the boot test, also run `probe` and `linkage` automatically
  (blocked thread/wait, SPU spin site, queue state, dead call paths).
- `--chunks N` — number of generated TUs (default: ~2 per compile job, so a
  big title compiles in parallel instead of on one core).
- `--chunk-lines N` — lower for small-RAM hosts (more, smaller C++ files).
- `--names FILE` — `ghidra_names.py` output for readable comments.
- `--lifter-arg "--flag=value"` — passthrough to `ppu_lifter.py`.
- `--spu` — extract and lift embedded SPE images.

## Toolchain choice

`doctor` reports exactly which compiler is used and its version. Selection is by
**highest clang version**, then availability:

1. **clang-cl** from `toolchain\llvm\bin` (the bundled LLVM release, currently
   **23.1.4**), `LLVM_HOME`, `PS3REVAMP_CLANG_CL`, PATH, or Visual Studio.
   clang-cl is clang — it speaks the MSVC command line/ABI because the runtime
   needs `__try/__except`, `#pragma comment(lib)` and the Windows SDK.
   `lld-link` links it.
2. **clang + Ninja from the bundled llvm-mingw** (also 23.x) when clang-cl is not
   available. Configure-time patches in the generated project cover the MinGW
   gaps (`_WIN32_WINNT`, explicit `d3d12/dxgi/d3dcompiler` imports).

Microsoft `cl.exe` is never used: it cannot compile the lifted code (its own
toolkit docs require clang), and `PS3REVAMP_FORCE_MINGW=1` forces the pure
MinGW path when needed.

---

## Performance: where the cores go

Every stage that can run in parallel does:

| Stage | Parallelism |
|---|---|
| ELF load / OPD scan | 1 process (seconds) |
| Analyzer (IDA/Ghidra) | alongside coverage, NID resolution and SPU extraction (4 worker threads, independent subprocesses) |
| PPU lift + mid-function pass | `--jobs` worker **processes**; the mid-function pass lifts its batch in parallel (vendored patch, `PS3RECOMP_MID_JOBS`) |
| SPU lift | one process **per image**, up to `--jobs` |
| C++ compile | Ninja at `--jobs`, auto-capped for very large lifts, with sccache |
| Boot/runtime | PPU threads are host threads |

Tuning knobs:

- `--jobs N` — lift/compile/SPU concurrency (default: all logical cores).
- `--chunks N` — more, smaller TUs means better compile parallelism and less
  memory per TU (auto: ~2 per job once a title passes 1,500 functions).
- `--opt 1` (default) / `2` / `3` / `0` — optimisation of lifted code.
  `--fast` is `0`: quickest rebuild while iterating.
- sccache is used automatically, so a relift or a second title reuses the
  runtime objects.

### Measured on the test title (NPUA80068, 8.1 MB EBOOT)

| Stage | Result |
|---|---|
| load + OPD scan | 13,180 functions, 200 imports in seconds |
| coverage | 164/200 NIDs (82%) |
| lift (16 workers) | 13,987 → 25,378 functions (11,391 mid-function tails) in **2.4 min** |
| output | 1.1 GB of C++ across 49 TUs |
| build (clang-cl, `--fast`) | **162 s** cold, **44 s** with sccache warm; 845 MB executable |
| SPU | 27/27 images extracted and lifted in parallel |
| boot test | ran: PPU threads started, `stream.dat` opened and read, `cellGcm` reached, `cellSpurs` waiting on a workload |

The serial upstream mid-function pass alone took ~15+ minutes on the same
input; that phase is now parallel.

---

---

## Learning without AI

Every finished port is distilled into `knowledge/kb.sqlite` (SQLite, no model,
no telemetry):

| Learned | Used for |
|---|---|
| title identity + ELF SHA | recognising the same title on the next run |
| every import (library, NID, name, covered?) | coverage statistics across titles |
| boot verdict, milestones, unresolved calls | "this title stopped here last time" |
| unimplemented NIDs + whether the title progressed anyway | `safe_to_stub(nid)` |
| settings that produced a build (chunks/opt/jobs per size bucket) | starting point for the next title |

```bat
ps3revamp.py kb                :: totals
ps3revamp.py kb --titles       :: what has been converted
ps3revamp.py kb --nid 0xFF0A21B7   :: has any title survived this NID being stubbed?
ps3revamp.py kb --library cellGcmSys
ps3revamp.py learn <portdir>   :: (re)record a finished port
```

`port` consults the store before lifting (known blockers, proven settings) and
records the result afterwards; `--no-learn` disables writing. Nothing is shared
between machines unless you copy `knowledge/kb.sqlite`.

## Reference cache (`docs`)

PS3/PPC reference material is cached on disk and consulted offline. The toolkit's
MIT docs seed the cache on first run (PPU/ELF, NIDs, syscalls, RSX, SPU, SPURS).

```bat
ps3revamp.py docs                    :: topics + cached state
ps3revamp.py docs --topic gcm        :: read the cached copy
ps3revamp.py docs --topic gcm --fetch :: download it (allowlisted hosts only)
ps3revamp.py port ... --test 10 --fetch-docs
```

`--fetch-docs` maps the boot failure to the references that title actually
needs (unresolved calls → PPU, unimplemented NIDs → NID/lv2, cellSpurs waiting →
SPURS, graphics → GCM) and stores them under `knowledge/docs/`. Network access is
opt-in; the default path is fully offline.

## Optional tools

```bat
ps3revamp.py tools
```

Shows what is available and how it would be used: ps3recomp, clang, Ghidra
(`--analyzer ghidra`), IDA/idalib (`--analyzer ida`), RPCS3 (behaviour oracle),
sccache. A tool is only ever invoked when a run asks for it; nothing is installed
or downloaded implicitly.

## Publishing

`LICENSE` covers this tool's code (MIT). `NOTICE.md` lists every bundled
component and its licence, `vendor.lock.json` pins versions/URLs/SHA-256, and
`.gitignore` keeps generated ports, the knowledge store and third-party trees
out of git (they are user- or licence-specific, not source). See
`docs/GITHUB.md` for the exact publish steps.

---

## Requirements

- Windows x64 (the bundled toolchain path assumes this; Linux/macOS work with a
  system clang once `config.json` points at it).
- Python 3.10+ with `capstone`, `construct`, `pycryptodome`, `tqdm`.
- A **ps3recomp toolkit** checkout. Auto-detected from:
  1. `--toolkit <path>` / `PS3RECOMP_DIR`
  2. `config.json`
  3. `./toolkit/ps3recomp`
  4. a Project Pyrrhus / Helghast portable install on the Desktop
- A C++20 clang + CMake + Ninja. Portable installs ship these under
  `toolchain/`; they are picked up automatically.

`python ps3revamp.py doctor` tells you exactly what is missing.

---

## What it cannot do (read this)

A PS3 title is not a single binary. What PS3revamp produces is **faithful
translated code, not a rewrite**: every PPU function becomes native C++ that
runs on a flat 256 MB guest VM and calls HLE handlers for `cellGcmSys`,
`cellSpurs`, `cellSysutil`, `sys_fs`, etc. That is how the existing
Pyrrhus/Helghast ports work and why they are playable at all.

Automatic:

- OPD/CFG function discovery, jump tables, VMX/Altivec lowering
- import-stub → `ps3_hle_call(nid)` binding
- NID → handler table generation
- SPU image extraction and lifting
- project, toolchain, build

Not automatic — **per title**:

1. **Imports without an HLE handler.** `PORT.md` lists them; each needs a
   handler in `project/stubs.cpp` (or a real lifted firmware module — see
   `docs/FIRMWARE_LLE.md` in the toolkit).
2. **RSX behaviour** the renderer does not translate yet.
3. **Asset/VFS paths**, save data, PSN services.
4. **Game-specific patches** — timing, memory layout, known engine bugs.

A title with high HLE coverage and mostly PPU code (small PSN games, puzzle/
arcade titles) can boot quickly. A title with heavy SPU job systems and custom
RSX use needs the per-game work described in the toolkit's
`docs/GAME_PORTING_GUIDE.md`.

**No tool can turn an arbitrary PS3 game into a working PC game with zero
per-title work.** PS3revamp removes the mechanical 80% and tells you precisely
what is left.

---

## IDA Pro / REA

The original ask was to drive IDA through REA. Three blockers, each verified
against this machine:

- IDA Pro is not installed here.
- REA's `open_binary` rejects the file: *unsupported ELF architecture* — its
  ELF gate does not accept 64-bit big-endian PowerPC.
- REA's `inspect_binary_layout` is limited to a Linux x64 artifact profile.

So the REA bridge cannot analyse PS3 binaries. PS3revamp therefore talks to
**idalib directly** (`tools/ida_analyze.py`), the supported headless path:
install IDA Pro 9.x, activate idalib in its Python, then set `ida_python` in
`config.json`. `--analyzer ida` merges IDA's function map with the OPD scan
(union by address, larger extent wins). Without it, the OPD scanner is used,
which for PS3 is already the authoritative source: the game's own function
descriptors.

---

## Layout

```
ps3revamp.py          CLI + pipeline + report
config.json           generated by `doctor` (toolkit / toolchain / ida_python)
toolkit/ps3recomp/    optional local toolkit copy
ports/                generated ports
work/

1443300913.readme_excerpt:
# Killzone: Liberation importer for Blender

A Blender 5.2 add-on (extension) that imports **models, materials, textures and maps**
from *Killzone: Liberation* (PSP, UCUS-98646 v1.20) directly from the game's UMD image or
from extracted `.core` lumps.

- Whole levels (all 16 missions, challenge courses, multiplayer maps) with every placed
  static mesh and entity at its level transform.
- Static and skinned models, armatures built from the bind pose, vertex weights.
- PSP textures (CLUT4/CLUT8 with palettes, RGBA8888, PSP-order DXT1/3/5, all other GE
  formats), unswizzled with numpy and packed into the .blend or saved as PNG.
- Node materials rebuilt from the GE layer state: alpha test/blend, additive effects,
  vertex-colour lighting, multi-pass lightmaps and detail layers, texture matrices and
  keyframed UV animation.
- Deduplication by resource GUID: importing several lumps reuses textures, materials and
  meshes that are shared between them.
- A 3D View sidebar browser that lists every lump in the configured archive, previews
  its importable placements/models and imports only the checked objects.
- A complete, documented description of the file formats: [docs/FORMATS.md](docs/FORMATS.md),
  plus a generated reference of all 1,170 game classes: [docs/RTTI_CLASSES.md](docs/RTTI_CLASSES.md).

You need your own copy of the game. This project contains no game data.

## Screenshots

| Campaign level | Environment detail |
|---|---|
| ![Chapter 1 Mission 1 imported into Blender](docs/images/out_c1m1.png) | ![Close view of Chapter 1 Mission 1](docs/images/out_c1m1_close.png) |
| **Multiplayer docks** | **Character model** |
| ![Multiplayer docks map imported into Blender](docs/images/out_docks.png) | ![Enemy character model imported into Blender](docs/images/out_enemy2.png) |

### Weapons and props

![Weapon and prop models imported into Blender](docs/images/out_weapons.png)

## Installation

Requires Blender 4.2 or newer; developed and tested with Blender 5.2.2.

1. Zip the `io_import_killzone_liberation` folder (or build it:
   `blender --command extension build --source-dir io_import_killzone_liberation --output-dir dist`).
2. In Blender: *Edit > Preferences > Get Extensions > ⌄ > Install from Disk...* and pick the zip.
3. In the add-on preferences set **Game ISO / PSP.DAT** to your
   `Killzone_Liberation_v1.20_US.ISO`. Preferences also contain the defaults used by the
   archive browser and regular import dialog.

For development you can instead link the folder into your extensions directory, e.g.
`%APPDATA%\Blender Foundation\Blender\5.2\extensions\user_default\io_import_killzone_liberation`.

## Usage

*File > Import > Killzone: Liberation (.core/.iso)*, or drag a `.core`/`.iso` file into the
3D viewport.

- **Browse and import selected objects**: open the 3D View sidebar (`N`) and choose the
  **KZL** tab. Click **Scan Archive**, select a lump, then **Show Importable Objects**.
  Check the placements or models you want and click **Import Selected Objects**.
- **From the ISO**: select the ISO (or an extracted `PSP.DAT`) and type or search a lump in
  the **Lump** field, e.g. `chapter1_mission1`. Several lumps can be given comma-separated,
  and wildcards work (`chapter2_*`, `multiplayer*_art`).
- **From extracted lumps**: select one or more `.core` files (see `tools/kzl_tool.py extract`).

Useful lumps (all under `/localcachepsp/lumps/`):

| lump | content |
|---|---|
| `chapter1_mission1` ... `chapter4_mission4` | campaign levels |
| `multiplayer<map>_art` | multiplayer map geometry (`airfield`, `docks`, `factory`, `islands`, `swampbase`, `trench`) |
| `objectcourse*`, `targetpractice*`, `c4course*`, `spiderminecatch*`, `basedefend*` | challenge maps |
| `characters`, `enemies`, `charactersvips`, `charactersbodyguard`, `charactersdog`, `metrac` | characters (skinned) |
| `weapons`, `multiplayerweapons`, `jetpack`, `flamethrower`, `doors` | weapons, props, entities |
| `menu_background`, `mission_startup`, `imagehint*` | front-end scenes and hint screens |

### Options

| option | effect |
|---|---|
| Map Placements | place `StaticMeshInstance`s, collision mesh instances and entities at their level transforms |
| Entities / Collision Mesh Instances | include those placement types |
| Unplaced Models | *Auto*: import every model when the lump has no placements (laid out on a grid); *Always*: also for maps (into an excluded "Library" collection); *Never* |
| Import Only Highest Detail | on by default; imports primary model geometry (LOD0) and only texture MIP 0. Disable it to retain supplemental texture MIPs as separate Blender images |
| Weld Vertices | merge vertices duplicated between triangle strips |
| Armatures | create armatures and vertex groups for skinned meshes |
| Textures | pack into the .blend, save as PNG to a folder, or skip |
| UV Animation | keyframe `AnimatedMaterial` texture-matrix animations (linear, cyclic) |
| Unlit Shading | emission shaders (textures shown without scene lighting; lightmaps keep the original look) |
| Custom Properties | store the original fields (`kzl_*`) on objects, materials, images and meshes |

These options are available both in the import dialog and as persistent defaults under
*Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Killzone: Liberation Importer*. Changing an option that
affects which objects are eligible requires reloading the browser's object list. The
shipped US game data uses one renderable mesh per model resource and single-mip textures,
but the highest-detail option also handles multi-mip texture payloads.

Each lump becomes a collection `KZL <lump>` with sub-collections for static meshes,
collision meshes, entities and models. Materials keep the original layer state as JSON in
the `kzl_layers` custom property.

## Command-line tool

`tools/kzl_tool.py` uses the same readers without Blender (Python 3.10+ and numpy):

```
python tools/kzl_tool.py list     GAME.ISO [substring]
python tools/kzl_tool.py extract  GAME.ISO OUTDIR [substring] [--decompress]
python tools/kzl_tool.py info     GAME.ISO:chapter1_mission1
python tools/kzl_tool.py dump     GAME.ISO:weapons --type Material --depth 3
python tools/kzl_tool.py textures GAME.ISO:weapons OUTDIR      # PNG
python tools/kzl_tool.py obj      GAME.ISO:weapons OUTDIR      # Wavefront OBJ
python tools/kzl_tool.py classes  docs/RTTI_CLASSES.md
```

`tools/build_schema.py` regenerates the RTTI schema from a guest RAM snapshot (see
[docs/FORMATS.md §13](docs/FORMATS.md#13-reproducing-the-schema)).

## Layout

```
io_import_killzone_liberation/
  blender_manifest.toml   extension manifest
  operators.py            import operator, sidebar browser, drag-and-drop handler, preferences
  formats/                bpy-independent readers (numpy)
    archive.py            ISO 9660 + PSP.DAT
    rttibin.py            .core decompression and RTTIBin<1.12> object reader
    rtti_schema.json      RTTI type database (1,457 types) extracted from the game
    texture.py            texture payloads, palettes, unswizzle, DXT
    geometry.py           vertex/index buffers, dequantization, triangulation, skeletons
    scene.py              meshes, multi-pass folding, models, placements
  blender/                bpy layer: images, materials, meshes/armatures, importer
docs/FORMATS.md           file format documentation
docs/RTTI_CLASSES.md      generated class reference
tools/                    kzl_tool.py, build_schema.py
tests/test_formats.py     reader validation (set KZL_ISO to run against the game image)
```

Run the tests with `KZL_ISO=path/to/game.iso python tests/test_formats.py`; they parse every
lump and decode every texture, primitive and skeleton on the disc.

## Limitations

- Skeletal animations, particle systems, Havok collision/physics, sounds, scripts and
  fonts are parsed as objects but not converted (see [docs/FORMATS.md §12](docs/FORMATS.md#12-what-is-not-decoded-yet)).
- `CoronaInstance` light flares are not imported.
- Chapter 5 was downloadable content and is not on the disc.

## Credits

Format research builds on the archive and runtime work of the
[KillzoneLiberation-Recomp](https://github.com/Tzeentchnet/KillzoneLiberation-Recomp)
project. Killzone is a trademark of Sony Interactive Entertainment; this project is not
affiliated with or endorsed by Guerrilla or Sony.

006af3dfdd24e7044c661f269d2eb7849bdbacfe.message:
ppu_vmx: x86-64-v3 forms of the float ops and word shifts, bit for bit

The merge routes every opcode-4 instruction through ppu_vmx.h's exact
helpers. They compute lane by lane from big-endian bytes, with the NaN,
VSCR[NJ] and saturation rules in branches, where the lift had one SSE
instruction or two. In Drakengard 3's lift vmaddfp alone is at 33,884
sites, vslw (the sign-mask idiom) at 10,378, vnmsubfp at 5,646.

On x86-64 with AVX2 and FMA, the x86-64-v3 the lifted code is built for,
vaddfp, vsubfp, vmaxfp, vminfp, vmaddfp, vnmsubfp, vrefp, vrsqrtefp,
vcfsx, vcmpeqfp/gefp/gtfp and vslw/vsrw/vsraw now have vector forms: the
same IEEE operations in the same order (vmaddfp one fused multiply-add,
as fmaf), the same NaN choice and default NaN, the same NJ flushes, the
same CR6 answer. The scalar forms stay as name_ref; PPU_VMX_SCALAR builds
them alone.

runtime/ppu/tests/test_ppu_vmx_x86.c (tools/test_ppu_vmx_x86.py) holds
the vector forms to the scalar ones over 13,250,000 checks -- random
words, zeros, denormals, infinities, quiet and signalling NaNs, extremes,
equal and sign-flipped operands, NJ off and on: 0 differ. Breaking the

088befac6de09dad63a3fec66e8014d59b1f1e97.message:
ppu_loader: size per-thread TLS blocks by the TLS image, not image + 0x7000

Symptom: a title that creates more than 31 PPU threads (with a small TLS
image) gives the 32nd and every later thread the main thread's TLS, with no
message. Thread-locals that matter then collide: in Killzone 3 two threads
ended up reading one per-thread wait object, one waited forever on the other's
event queue and the level never started.

Cause: ppu_tls_new_block sized each block as memsz + 0x7000, rounded to a
page (0x8000 for a small image). The 0x7000 is the ABI's r13 bias: the guest
addresses TLS as r13 - 0x7000 + off with off < memsz, so nothing lives in it.
The 1 MB window at PPU_TLS_IMG then holds 31 blocks, and the fallback (return
0, the caller uses the main block) is silent.

Change: blocks are memsz rounded up to 4 KB (about 250 fit for a small
image); the first block still starts after the main block's image. When the
window is full, one line is logged before falling back to the shared block.

Verification: tools/test_ppu_tls_blocks.py builds the real
ppu_tls_new_block into a host program and requests 100 blocks with a
0x240-byte image. On v0.14.0 (a2c2010): granted 31/100, FAIL. With this
change: granted 100/100, no overlap with each other or the main image, image
copied into each, PASS. Also run in the Killzone 3 port (v0.13.0 base) since
2026-10-11: the thread that hung now waits on its own event queue.

0aead166fd65ab34bee01df19a341665800a727f.message:
cellGcm: a FIFO user command reaches the handler set with cellGcmSetUserHandler

Symptom: a title's cellGcmSetUserHandler callback never runs for the user
commands it puts in its command buffer. In Killzone 3 that callback submits
the per-frame job that lets the frame continue, so the level stalled.

Cause: the walker decodes GCM_SET_USER_COMMAND (method 0xEB00) as
subchannel 7 / method 0x0B00 and hands it to rsx_raise_user_cmd, the lv2
route: it posts an event to the RSX interrupt queue for a guest interrupt
thread. A title that registered its handler through the HLE
cellGcmSetUserHandler has no such thread; its handler runs from
ppu_gcm_pump. The branch then `continue`s, so the walker's later 0xEB00 case,
which calls cellGcmQueueUserCommand for the pump, is never reached.

queues the command for the pump (cellGcmQueueUserCommand). The lv2 event is
still raised as before.

includes cellGcmSys.c like test_gcm_user_command.c; graphics backends
stubbed) registers an HLE user handler, then five times puts one user
command in the ring, drains it with cellGcm_rsx_process_fifo and calls
ppu_gcm_pump. With this change the handler runs five times, each with its
command's argument, and the lv2 route is still taken five times (gcc and
clang). Against v0.14.0's cellGcmSys.c (a2c2010) the handler never runs
(5/5 fail). test_gcm_user_command.c still passes.

spu_helpers: the exact single-precision fast path on SSE4.1

The merge brings the SPU's own single-precision arithmetic (truncation,
no denormals, extended range), computed exactly, with a NEON fast path
for ordinary operands; elsewhere every lane of every fa/fm/fma took the
scalar route: a dozen tests and a double round trip each.

f64x2 halves, widened, operated on, the 29 low significand bits cleared,
narrowed; a lane qualifies when its operands are ordinary singles or
true zeros and its result a normal single or an exact zero (and, for
fma, the sum's TwoSum error says the double was not rounded onto a
24-bit boundary); the others are redone one by one, out of line.

test_spu_float_neon now covers this path as well: 4,000,000 random
cases, 2,000,000 aimed at the fma boundary and 2,000,000 at zero lanes
match the exact path. An fma and an fm take 7.7 ns there against 21.2 ns
on the scalar route (clang -O2, i9-13900K).

ppu_sysprx: sys_lwcond_t is +0x00 lwmutex EA, +0x04 queue id

Symptom: a title that reads lwcond+0x00 itself sees 0 there and treats the
lwcond as invalid (Killzone 3's file system layer checks it before every
wait and loops). The queue id is also written past the 8-byte structure,
over whatever the title keeps next to it.

Cause: the context-style sys_lwcond_create in ppu_sysprx.cpp writes the
lwmutex EA as a 64-bit value at +0x00 (so the EA lands at +0x04 and +0x00
reads 0) and the id at +0x08. sys_lwcond_t is 8 bytes: +0x00 u32 lwmutex
EA, +0x04 u32 queue id, which is also what libs/system/sysPrxForUser.h
declares as sys_lwcond_t_hle.

Change: 32-bit stores at +0x00 and +0x04 in sys_lwcond_create, and a 32-bit
read of +0x00 in sys_lwcond_wait. Wait/signal behaviour is unchanged.

Verification: tools/test_lwcond_layout.py builds the real
sys_lwcond_create and sys_lwcond_wait into a host program over stubbed
guest memory. With this change +0x00 holds the lwmutex EA, +0x04 a nonzero
id, nothing past +0x08 is written, and the wait finds the lwmutex. On
v0.14.0 (a2c2010) +0x00 reads 0, the EA is at +0x04 and the id is written
at +0x08 (2 of 3 checks fail; the wait found the lwmutex there only because
create and wait agreed on the wrong layout).

16db6bca787b02f598a18b5b5efbbd7b2f882002.message:
cellGcm: GET_REPORT honours the report DMA context and writes main-memory reports to guest memory

Symptom: titles that keep their GPU reports in main memory read stale memory
for every report. Killzone 3 selects the main-memory report context and
issues about 160 reports per frame in a level (timestamps and occlusion
queries); none of them ever reached the memory it reads.

Cause: the FIFO walker ignored NV4097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_REPORT (0x1A8) and
wrote every NV4097_GET_REPORT (0x1800) into the host s_report_data slots,
indexed by offset / 16, whatever context the title had selected.

Change: the walker records the context set by 0x1A8 (reset to local by
cellGcmInit and cellGcmTerminate). With the local context (0xFEED0000, the
default) a report goes to s_report_data as before. With the main-memory
context (0xFEED0001, or CELL_GCM_CONTEXT_DMA_REPORT_LOCATION_MAIN 0xBAD68000)
the report's offset is an IO offset and the 16-byte report is written
big-endian to gcm_io2ea(offset): u64 timestamp, u32 value, u32 0. An offset
with no IO mapping is skipped with a rate-limited log line. Report
timestamps now rise strictly, so two reports in one walker pass never share
or reverse a time stamp.

Verification: tests/gcm_reports (CTest, built with PS3RECOMP_BUILD_TESTS on
POSIX hosts like the host harness) builds a ring with local reports, a
switch to 0xFEED0001, main-memory reports of type 1 and 2, one unmapped
offset and a switch back, drains it once with cellGcm_rsx_process_fifo and
reads every slot back. Run as a MinGW-w64 build under Proton (this machine
has no Linux SDL2 for the POSIX runtime build): with this change 9/9 checks
pass; the same test linked against v0.14.0's cellGcmSys.c (a2c2010) fails
6/9 (main-memory slots keep their sentinel, the reports land in the host
area instead, timestamps not written). Carried as a local patch in the
Killzone 3 port (v0.13.0 base).

1cbca03e2f88454bb4a474816562ef1eae147bc3.message:
ppu: the inline accessors take the base, a page's byte says "store here", one test for a stretch

What the lifted code's loads and stores cost in ppu_vm_fast.h, and three
things about it:

The accessors take the base of guest memory as an argument (vm_fastb_*);
vm_fast_* are macros on whatever `vm_base` names where they are used.
vm_base is a global and the lifted code stores through pointers that may
alias anything, so the compiler loaded it again after every guest store.
The lifter can now give a function a local of that name (the next
commit); code lifted before this still compiles and uses the global.

A store's test was a load, a mask and a compare of two bits ("may be
written inline" and not "an SPU has reserved a line here"). The page's
byte now carries that conjunction as a bit of its own, PPU_VM_PAGE_ST,
and a store tests one bit as a load does. Both parties that change the
byte -- ppu_vm_slow_any_update and spu_coh_reserve -- do it through
ppu_vm_page_update (the new ppu_vm_page.h), which recomputes the bit in
the same compare-and-swap.

One test for a stretch of memory: ppu_vm_frame_ok / PPU_FRAME_INIT for
the saves of a function's entry, ppu_vm_run_ok / PPU_RUN for a run of
accesses off one register, with accessors (PPU_FR*/PPU_FW*, PPU_RR*/
PPU_RW*) that go straight to memory when the test of the stretch's two
ends passed and take their ordinary path, test and all, when it did not.
PPU_RUN_VERIFY makes every access of a run compare the address it was

24286f4b3871aff53cf988448e1fc756956372dc.message:
cellGcm: in-FIFO flip wraps only the runtime's own command ring

Symptom: intermittently a title waits forever on a fence. Killzone 3
stopped about 16 s in, depending on where the walker's get offset was.

Cause: _cellGcmSetFlipCommand's HLE (gcm_flip_into_fifo) writes the flip
marker at ctx->current and then, when less than GCM_FLIP_WRAP_BYTES are
left before ctx->end and the walker is well past begin, wraps the context
it was given: a JUMP to begin after the marker and ctx->current = begin.
That is what the SDK's buffer-full callback does for the runtime's ring.
A title with its own buffer-full callback manages its own buffers, and its
context need not be a ring: Killzone 3 flips on a 0x30000-byte draw
context whose end moves down as it allocates from the top, so it always
looks nearly full. Rewinding it mid-frame cut the frame short, the fence
release in its tail never ran, and the title waited for it.

Change: wrap only when the context's buffer-full callback descriptor
(ctx + 0xC) still points at the runtime's callback
(GCM_FIFO_CALLBACK_SENTINEL_EA, installed by cellGcmSetupContext). Other
contexts get the marker and current advances past it, as when there is
room.

Verification: libs/video/tests/test_gcm_flip_wrap.c (standalone, includes
cellGcmSys.c like test_gcm_user_command.c) flips on two nearly full
contexts with the walker 0x28000 bytes past their begin: the ring made by
cellGcmSetupContext, and a title context with its own callback. With this
change the runtime ring wraps (marker, JUMP to begin, current = begin) and
the title context does not (marker, current past it), with gcc and clang.
Against v0.14.0's cellGcmSys.c (a2c2010) the title context is wrapped too
(1 of 2 fails). test_gcm_user_command.c still passes.

286d3ed9e33988664a79553b347bcf5af96d2673.message:
cellGcm: IO mapping table 16 -> 512 slots, no IO leak on refusal, iomap fills a free slot

Symptom: a title that maps many separate main-memory chunks loses the later
ones. Killzone 3 maps up to 38 one-megabyte chunks at level load and keeps
vertex buffers in them; after the 16th, cellGcmMapMainMemory failed, those
buffers had no IO offset and every geometry draw in a level was degenerate
(only effects over black).

Cause:
- CELL_GCM_MAX_IO_MAPPINGS is 16. libgcm has no such small fixed count; a
  mapping fails when the IO address space runs out.
- cellGcmMapMainMemory allocates the IO region before it looks for a free
  slot, so each refused call still consumes IO address space.
- cellGcm_syscall_iomap writes s_io_mappings[s_io_mapping_count]. After an
  unmap the count no longer points past the last used slot, so a new mapping
  overwrites a live one.

Change:
- 512 slots (16 bytes each; an assumed bound well above what titles use),
  overridable with -DCELL_GCM_MAX_IO_MAPPINGS=N.
- cellGcmMapMainMemory looks for a free slot before allocating the region.
- cellGcm_syscall_iomap takes a slot from find_free_mapping like the other
  mapping paths.
The return codes and every other mapping function are unchanged.

Verification: tools/test_gcm_io_mappings.py builds the real
find_free_mapping, gcm_io_alloc, cellGcmMapMainMemory and
cellGcm_syscall_iomap against stubs. On v0.14.0 (a2c2010): FAIL (15 chunks
before the first refusal, the refusal leaks IO space, iomap after an unmap
overwrites a live mapping). With this change: PASS (510 chunks with distinct
offsets, no leak, live mapping kept). Negative controls on a copy of this
branch: 16 slots fails the chunk check (14), a count-indexed iomap fails the
live-slot check. cellGcmSys.c passes cc -fsyntax-only. Used in the Killzone 3
port (v0.13.0 base): its level geometry draws with this change.

2c800405b6144c016c5c608fefa890809e7e726e.message:
sys_ppu_thread: a thread that has ended gives its slot and its stack back

A port stopped dead a quarter of an hour into play, on Windows, at the
end of a level: black screen, the game thread waiting for a physics
step that no thread would ever finish. The thread table has 64 slots
and the run had used the sixty-fourth. sys_ppu_thread_create returned
EAGAIN without a word, the title did not look, and waited for a thread
that was never started. Three things kept slots from coming back:

- Windows, every joined thread. A thread that ends in
  sys_ppu_thread_exit signals its joiner from inside that call and then
  unwinds to the thread procedure, whose epilogue stamped the slot
  FINISHED again. The joiner did not wait for it: it freed the slot, and
  the epilogue then wrote FINISHED over FREE for good. (POSIX joins the
  host thread first and never saw it.) The epilogue now only stamps a
  thread that returned from its entry, and the joiner waits for the
  host thread to be out before the slot is anyone else's.

- Every thread made without SYS_PPU_THREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE. The flags
  were ignored and every thread made joinable, so one that nobody joins
  kept its slot when it ended. Such a thread now cannot be joined and
  frees itself, as on the console. Drakengard 3 makes its SaveData,
  LoadData, DLCCheck and PreLoadMovie threads that way.

- A detached thread that called sys_ppu_thread_exit was freed there and
  stamped FINISHED by the epilogue afterwards. It is now freed by the
  epilogue, once it is out of its guest code.

Guest stacks went the same way, more slowly: vm_stack_allocate only
moves forward through its 256 MB, and that title makes seven megabytes
of thread stacks in a quarter of an hour. A thread that has ended hands
its stack to the next one of the same size, zeroed.

sys_ppu_thread_create now says so when no slot is free, and logs the
flags. PPU_THREAD_SLOTS=<n> uses the first n slots only, to try a
title's thread turnover against a small table.

Measured in Drakengard 3, hands-off from boot int

32d817d62a6d0a6dbf3387cf2864dad8b169c381.message:
ppu_lifter: lvx and stvx as one 16-byte copy again

The merge brought upstream's vm_raw_ld16/vm_raw_st16 for lvx and stvx:
two 8-byte accesses, each behind an alignment test, so that each half is
single-copy atomic. The quadword is aligned (the address is masked to 16),
and an aligned 16-byte access is a single one on x86 with AVX and on
ARMv8.4 and later, so one memcpy of 16 bytes gives the same guarantee in
one instruction, as before the merge.

It matters more to ppu_nv_dirty.py than to the copy. The pass knows the
memcpy forms: a vector register written whole by lvx, read by stvx, and
a prologue's stvx of v20-v31 is how a function is known to preserve them.
It did not know the helpers, so every function that saved a callee-save
vector register looked as if it clobbered it, and its callers reloaded
their vector locals after every call.

Drakengard 3's lift: 3,731,836 register write-backs (3,737,208 with the
helpers, 3,731,204 before the merge), 1,489,321 of the scratch ones live
(1,502,283; 1,474,964). test_ppu_lift's 1,533 conformance checks, the
NV-pass and VMX tests pass.

40789072e4e6c70539b3e18cddb51a99d25c417e.message:
live-draw: depth buffers read as textures return the real depth

Symptom: a DEPTH24_D8 texture that reads a zeta comes back 0 or partly 0
in three common shapes: a full-screen read of a depth buffer whose first
pass used a smaller clip, a read of an address that is both a colour target
and a zeta, and a draw that reads the zeta it is depth-testing against
(deferred lighting, soft particles). Effects that depend on scene depth
(depth of field, fog, soft particles, deferred lighting) then see a flat 0.

Causes and changes (rsx_live_draw.c):
1. The R32F snapshot of a zeta keeps the clip size of the first pass that
   bound it (512x512 of a 1280x720 depth buffer, say), so later reads get 0
   outside that corner. zdepth_get now grows the snapshot to the largest
   clip bound since, within the depth resource (zdepth_grow_snapshot: a new
   resource, descriptors rewritten, the old one retired, re-resolved at the
   next read).
2. A depth-format read of an address that is also a colour target matched
   the colour surface first. When a written host zeta exists at that
   address the read now takes the zeta.
3. A draw that samples its own bound zeta with depth writes off read guest
   memory, which the host depth never reaches. It now reads the zeta's
   snapshot; the zeta cannot change during such a draw. A draw that writes
   the zeta it reads keeps the old fallback.

fp decompiler: the NV40 pack and unpack opcodes

PK4UB, UP4UB, PKG, UPG, PK4B, UP4B, PK2US, UP2US, PK2H and UP2H had no case:
each was skipped with a TODO comment and its destination kept whatever it
held. inFAMOUS 2's character materials convert sRGB<->linear with PK4UB->UPG

into the preamble only for a program that uses one of the opcodes, so every

host: --depthbounds skips where there is no depth bounds test

The depth bounds test is an optional Vulkan feature, and the lavapipe the
Vulkan workflow runs on (Mesa 25, LLVM 20.1.2) does not report depthBounds.
There the backend falls back as designed, the green triangle wins and the
scene failed with exit 3, which proved nothing about the change.

rsx_vulkan_backend_depth_bounds() says whether draws honour the test (the
draw engine drives the backend and the device enabled depthBounds). Where
they do not -- that device, the fixed-function path, Metal, the null
backend -- the scene prints "skipped, no depth bounds test" and exits 0.
The Vulkan workflow turns that line into a notice for this scene only; its
other checks (exit code, validation messages, engine path) still apply, and
"nothing to check" still fails. On a device with the feature (lavapipe in
Mesa 26.2, RADV) the scene still runs and expects blue.

  either way.

  when it ran since the last sample; self and inclusive shares named
  through the PDB, and RSX_REPLAY_PROF_CALLERS=<name> for one function's

65806f3f3614fca3f40061a3ba0ff2cadfaa36b0.message:
ppu_lifter: big-endian lane order for ten VMX integer ops

Symptom: lifted code computes wrong results for vmulouh, vmsumshm, vadduws,
vadduhs and vpkuwum, and does nothing at all for vmsumuhm, vsubuws,
vpkswss, vsrb and vsrab, which were emitted as "/* TODO */" no-ops.

Cause: ctx->vr holds raw big-endian guest bytes. The first five handlers
read halfword and word lanes through int16_t*/uint32_t* casts, which gives
byte-reversed lanes (and the wrong lane pairing) on a little-endian host.
The other five had no lowering.

Change: one handler for the ten ops that assembles each halfword or word
lane from its bytes in big-endian order, computes the result as the AltiVec
PEM defines it (modulo, saturating or shift) and stores it back in the same
order. The five old handlers are removed.

Verification: tools/test_ppu_vmx_lanes.py lifts each op, compiles the
emitted C with the lifter's own preamble and compares vD with an independent
Python model of the instruction on 300 inputs per op (216 edge combinations
plus random vectors). With this change 10/10 ops agree on every input. On
v0.14.0 (a2c2010) all ten fail: five emit TODO, the other five differ on
244 to 292 of 300 inputs. tools/test_ppu_vcmp_record_cr6.py and
tools/test_ppu_lift.py pass before and after.

662270bdf366da3e360385f421ce5192f82b3443.message:
ppu_loader: indirect-call depth guard can be kept per coroutine

Symptom: a title whose guest jobs run on host coroutines (host fibers that
stand in for a guest fiber scheduler) works for a while, then every
indirect call on that thread is skipped by the recursion guard, even calls
to leaf functions ("[ppu] recursion cap ... skipping"); null calls and an
exit follow. Killzone 3 quit a few minutes into a level.

Cause: the guard in ps3_indirect_call_impl keeps one depth count per host
thread in a function-local thread_local. A coroutine that ends by switching
away from inside an indirect call never unwinds its frames, so each one
leaks its depth into the thread's count until the count passes the 4000
cap. The vcall stack pointer (g_vcall_sp) leaks the same way. Neither can be
reached from outside the function, so a coroutine layer has no way to keep
them per coroutine.

Change: the depth count moves to a file-scope thread-local, and two
accessors, ps3_ppu_dispatch_depth_slot() and ps3_ppu_vcall_sp_slot(), return
the current thread's counters. A coroutine layer saves *slot when it
switches away and restores it when it switches back. Threads that never
switch behave exactly as before.

Verification: tools/test_ppu_dispatch_depth.py builds the real
ppu_loader.cpp with runtime/ppu/tests/test_ppu_dispatch_depth.cpp. 5000
ucontext coroutines each go five ps3_indirect_call levels deep and switch
back to the home context without returning; the home side saves and
restores both counters around each switch. With this change all 5000
chains run to the bottom, the home thread's depth and vcall sp are 0
before and after, and a later indirect call runs. Against v0.14.0's
ppu_loader.cpp (a2c2010; the accessors do not exist, the test declares
them weak) only 800 of 5000 chains run: the guard trips at depth 4001 and
skips every call after that.

into CR, exactly as the hardware does. SO is sticky and only an OE-form
XO instruction (addo, mullwo, ...) or mtxer sets it; XER starts at 0.

a constant 0 and are left out: one XER read in every compare, which kept
XER live across every call of the function. PPU_SO_EXACT=1 keeps them.

spu: SPU_RdDec wrapped 231 s after the base stamp

The decrementer scaled elapsed nanoseconds by 79.8 MHz before dividing, and
ns * 79800000 passes 2^64 at 231 s. A context that writes its decrementer
restamps the base and never gets there; the SPURS kernel context never writes
it, keeps the stamp from boot, and every timed loop on that SPU saw the
counter jump forward by ~16 s of ticks at 231 s, 462 s, 693 s... Scale the
whole seconds and the remainder separately.

83937a9bec73f4d16ed725122cfa65e955629946.message:
runtime: thread-locals stay thread-local under MinGW (__declspec(thread) only for MSVC)

Symptom (MinGW-w64 builds only): two PPU threads that exit close together
crash; one thread's sys_ppu_thread_exit longjmps toward a frame on the other
thread's stack. In Killzone 3 this is the two Bink threads exiting at the
end of the intro movie. The SPURS job mailboxes and the sysutil completion
drain guard are shared between threads the same way.

Cause: sys_ppu_thread.c, spurs_job.c, cellSpurs.c and cellSysutil.c pick
__declspec(thread) when _WIN32 is defined. MinGW GCC defines _WIN32 and
ignores that attribute ("'thread' attribute directive ignored"), so the
exit jmp_buf and its armed flag, g_spurs_job_mbox* and the completion
`draining` flag are plain process-wide globals there. The runtime's other
thread-local macros (PPU_THREAD_LOCAL, SPU_THREAD_LOCAL, SPU_TLS) already
test _MSC_VER.

Change: those four macros use __declspec(thread) only under _MSC_VER and
__thread / _Thread_local otherwise, like the others. MSVC and POSIX builds
are unchanged.

Verification: tools/test_mingw_tls.py finds every macro in runtime/ and
libs/ defined to __declspec(thread), keeps its surrounding preprocessor
conditionals and compiles a static variable with it as MinGW sees it
(x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc when present, else the host compiler with _WIN32
defined and __declspec(x) as __attribute__((x))), then checks the variable
is thread-local in the assembly. Without MinGW gcc the emulation runs only on
ELF hosts and only after two controls (__thread reads as thread-local, a
plain static does not) pass; otherwise, as on macOS, the test prints SKIP. With this change 9/9 qualifiers are
thread-local under both compilers; on v0.14.0 (a2c2010) 4 of 9 are
process-wide globals (spurs_job.c, sys_ppu_thread.c, cellSpurs.c,
cellSysutil.c). The four changed files pass -fsyntax-only with MinGW GCC and
host GCC.

8acdefdae7ede7ccecd4db4285985661ea2faf0b.message:
cellSysCacheMount clears the cache it says it cleared

Mount answers CELL_SYSCACHE_RET_OK_CLEARED, which tells the title the
system wiped its cache and it has to start it anew, and left the files
where they were. A title then trusts whatever the previous run left, and
in this port a run ends with the process going away, not through the
title's shutdown.

Drakengard 3 shows it since the merge registered cellFsGetFreeSize: with
free space reported, its FIOS formats a disc-data cache in
/dev_hdd1/cache/BLES00000/fios, writes the index's header last, and the
run is gone before it does. Every later start found an index without a
header and re-read it 512 bytes at a time, reopening both cache files for
each read -- 312,000 opens, 30 frames a second, never reaching the hub --
and so did an older build sharing the folder.

Mount now deletes the files under the cache directory (the directories
stay), through ppu_fs's own guest-to-host path translation, which
ppu_fs_register hands the runtime (g_ps3_fs_host_path; without it nothing
is touched). cellSysCacheClear clears the contents too, where it used to
unmount the cache and leave the files.

8eb45f8647cde8750f675f5725ea0bd325ec9618.message:
cellFs: 64-bit sizes and offsets in ppu_fs on Windows

Symptom: on Windows a file larger than 2 GiB is mis-sized and mis-seeked.
With a MinGW-w64 (msvcrt) build cellFsStat fails with CELL_ENOENT (the CRT's
stat wrapper reports EOVERFLOW); with UCRT (llvm-mingw) it succeeds with a
truncated size. cellFsLseek and cellFsFstat truncate to 32 bits, so a read
after a seek past 4 GiB lands at the wrong offset.

Cause: ppu_fs.cpp uses stat() with a 32-bit st_size and fseek()/ftell()
with `long`, which is 32 bits on LLP64 Windows. LP64 hosts are unaffected.

Change: _stat64, _fseeki64 and _ftelli64 on Windows; stat, fseeko and ftello
elsewhere, for cellFsStat, cellFsLseek and cellFsFstat. A trailing slash is
stripped before _stat64, which rejects it (MinGW's stat wrapper used to
strip it). The FS_FSTAT_CAP diagnostic now parses and prints 64-bit values.

Verification: tools/test_ppu_fs_large_file.py builds a fixture that
includes ppu_fs.cpp, creates a sparse 5 GiB file with a marker near its end
and checks cellFsStat, cellFsLseek (SET and END), cellFsRead after the seek
and cellFsFstat. Built with x86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ (--build-only) and run
under Wine: master fails 6 of 7 checks (Stat 0x80010006, Lseek 0x40000008,
Fstat 0x40000010); with this change all 7 pass. On Linux it passes on both.

9769173bec32b8faa2a93601a944eb72d1103efe.message:
sys_ppu_thread, POSIX: three things 2c80040 left on this side, and a test that sees them

2c80040 gave ended threads their slots back. On POSIX three things were
still as they had been:

1. A thread made without the joinable flag starts DETACHED and frees its
   own slot, but its host pthread was still made joinable, and nobody
   joins or detaches it: a dead pthread keeps its stack mapped until
   someone does (the whole 256 MB reservation with glibc, the top of it on
   Darwin). One for every save, load and movie pre-load. It is detached
   when it is made.

2. The thread procedure's last lines locked info->finish_mutex and set
   info->finished after the table lock was released -- on a slot that, for
   a self-freeing thread, was FREE by then and could already be another
   thread's. The joiner's signal is given under the table lock now (the
   order sys_ppu_thread_exit takes the two), and nothing of the slot is
   touched after it.

3. sys_ppu_thread_detach of a thread that had FINISHED freed the slot at
   once. A thread that ended in sys_ppu_thread_exit is FINISHED while it
   is still unwinding to the thread procedure; a thread made in that
   moment was given its slot, and the epilogue then took the new thread
   for itself: marked it finished, with whatever its r3 held as the exit
   status. The epilogue now sets proc_out as its last act under the lock,
   and a detach that does not find it leaves the slot DETACHED for the
   epilogue to free, as the Windows branch does on a zero wait. (proc_out
   is set on Windows too, should that branch want it instead of the wait.)
   That detach also gives the guest stack back, which it never did.

ps3recomp_host --threads gains a turnover check: 200 threads not
joinable, 300 joinable and detached while or after they ran, and 100
witnesses, each made the moment a thread that ended by the syscall has
been detached, joined, and required to come back with a status only its
own end can produce. The race in 3 is a few microseconds wide and a test
does not hit it by waiti

9d17419e1eadcf043e8601a1c76167c70625aee6.message:
RSX: presents at even intervals while the host caps the frame rate

A title that caps its own frame rate starts its frames at even intervals,
but they do not reach the present at even intervals: the game's work, the
render thread's and the walker's lie between, and each varies by a
millisecond or two a frame. On the console the flip waited for the
vertical blank. Here a frame is shown when it is made, and Drakengard 3
at a 60 fps cap, with every frame simulated for exactly 16.67 ms, showed
them 13 to 20 ms apart: 40 to 65% of the presents more than 15% off the
one before, and a camera turning at a steady rate juddered.

rsx_present_pace (new, libs/video): called on the presenting thread just
before the present. It takes the frames' spacing from the host
(rsx_present_pace_period: a host that caps the frame rate knows it) or
from the median of the last arrivals, keeps a running measure of how
much they vary, and holds each frame until its turn on an even schedule
set behind them by three times that variation (at most 0.4 of the
spacing, and 8 ms). A late frame is shown at once and the schedule
starts again from it. When the frames come more than 1.2 times slower
than the cap the host named, it gets out of the way and they are shown
as they come. Off unless the host turns it on (rsx_present_pace_enable)
or RSX_PRESENT_PACE=1; RSX_PRESENT_PACE=0 keeps it off whatever the host
says; RSX_PRESENT_PACE_LOG=1 prints the spacing, its variation before
and after, the wait and the late frames every 2 s (=2: a line a frame).

Direct3D 12: while pacing is on (and not in exclusive full screen) the
present is given to a thread of its own, so the walker does not wait out
the delay: a title that waits for its flip before it starts the next
frame would lose every one of those milliseconds. The walker joins it
before it next needs the back buffer, and then asks for the held frame
at once (rsx_present_pace_hurry); so do the swap chain's release, the
return to full screen and the shutdown.

Vulkan: paced on the presenting thread itself

a49553df95b81c628c96c96d2ed0e53a4dd3967e.message:
ppu_vmx: vnmsubfp's scalar form flips the sign as bits

vnmsubfp is -(vA*vC - vB): the difference rounded once, then negated, so
an exact zero comes out -0. GCC folds -fmaf(x, z, -y) into a negated
multiply-add, (-(x*z)) + y, which gives +0 there; clang keeps the
negation. The scalar form now flips the sign bit of fmaf(x, z, -y), which
no compiler folds, and both agree with the x86-64-v3 form: the check of
the two forms had found twelve -0/+0 lanes under GCC 14.

ae3f39164bd2894b0c29dff7c3cebb9481c302f7.message:
D3D12, Vulkan: a level's first frame without the driver's allocator or a copy out of upload memory

A level's first frame brings several hundred textures and tens of MB of
vertices at once. Three things made that frame slow, none of them work:

Staging (both engines). What a submit's records read -- constants,
vertices without a buffer of their own, texture rows -- went into one
arena, grown by copying it into a larger one. That copy reads upload
memory, which is write-combined: the 110 MB such a frame stages took
0.4 to 0.9 s to copy in D3D12 and 0.15 to 0.3 s and more in Vulkan. And
every arena of the pool was then remade at the size the frame had grown
one to. Staging is now a chain of 16 MB chunks; a record's offsets are
offsets into the chain and nothing staged is read back. Chunks beyond
eight that go unused for 600 submits are released.

Textures (D3D12). A committed resource per texture is an allocation in
the driver per texture: 0.3 to 3 ms apiece. Textures are placed in 64 MB
heaps, sub-allocated first fit with a sorted free list (the Vulkan
engine's memory blocks, in D3D12). One over half a heap, or that the
device will not place, is committed as before. RSX_TEX_HEAPS=0 commits
them all.

Vertex-cache buffers (D3D12). The same per buffer, where the pool had
none to give. A buffer is now a range of a 32 MB mapped upload page: the
copy and no call into the driver. RSX_VB_PAGES=0: a buffer each.

Measured on an RTX 4090 at 4K. Replays of three captures from a cold
engine, the machine busy with other work (old -> new):
  creating 352 / 210 / 190 textures   1070-2030 / 120-860 / 90-830 ms -> 15-45 ms
  staging them                        410-920 ms of growth copies     -> 1-33 ms
  360-730 vertex buffers              70-370 ms                       -> 7-10 ms
  Vulkan, the frame outside shaders   280-860 ms                      -> 54-58 ms
In Drakengard 3, chapter 1's first frame (503 textures, 20 MB; 669
vertex conversions, 26 MB): 836 -> 206 ms, the walker's draws 676 -> 66.

The replay regression is unch

b3082644982c43d81c8bf47959317dc4cb3cfbf1.message:
cellGcm: give a parked FIFO time to be patched before following put

A self-JUMP at the write head parks the RSX, and when `put` had meanwhile
moved elsewhere the walker took that as the title having abandoned the park
and resynced to `put` at once. inFAMOUS 2 links its main-memory command
blocks the other way round: it ends a block in a park, writes the next
commands at the ring start, moves `put`, and only then rewrites the park as a
JUMP to them. A drain that landed between the two stores went straight to
`put` and dropped everything from the ring start up to it, the frame's fence
included, so the title waited on that label for the rest of the run and the
main menu froze.

Resync only once the same park has stood with the same `put` for longer than
a title takes between the two stores (50 ms). A park patched in time is
followed as before; the pass reports itself as "parked" in the meantime.

b6dc1e428b4b89c8385595551904bfb21c33d71a.message:
ppu_lifter: jump tables behind a tail-call epilogue

discover_jump_tables drops the blocks that end in `blr` from the backward
scan for the table base register: they return, so they cannot flow into the
dispatcher. An epilogue that leaves by a tail call ends the same way and
restores the same registers, and was not dropped. inFAMOUS 2's func_000B9BD0
loads the base's base into r30 in its prologue, has an early exit
`ld r30,0xE0(r1); ...; b 0xB8570`, and dispatches nineteen instructions later
through `lwz r11,-0x7F80(r30)`: the restore read as r30's nearest definition,
no base resolved, and the switch lifted to an unresolved indirect call.

A `b` leaves the function when it goes back past the function's entry or
forward to another function's entry. Both need func_starts; without them the
scan is bounded by the nearest `blr`, which an early return puts in the
middle of a function, so only `blr` is trusted there.

tools/test_ppu_jumptables.py: the backward shape (the inFAMOUS 2 one), the
forward one, and the no-func_starts control.

b883922940d53efafac47dcc0b63dac7535294c5.message:
rsx_draw_engine, vulkan: honour the depth bounds test

NV4097 SET_DEPTH_BOUNDS_TEST_ENABLE (0x0380) with SET_DEPTH_BOUNDS_MIN and
_MAX (0x0384, 0x0388, floats) rejects a fragment whose stored depth lies
outside the bounds, whatever the depth test says. The draw engine never
read those registers, so a bounded draw covered the whole target.

Twisted Metal's deferred renderer relies on it: its sun pass is bounded to
[0, 0.999984] (the geometry) and the sky drawn right after it to
[0.999984, 1] (the far plane), both with the depth test off. Unbounded, the
sky overwrote the sun light everywhere and the HDR buffer came out almost
black.

The enable is pipeline state (rsx_be_render_state.depth_bounds_test, part
of the pipeline key); the bounds reach the backend before every draw through
a new optional hook, set_depth_bounds, like the stencil reference, so moving
them does not build pipelines. Vulkan enables the depthBounds feature when
the device has it and sets the bounds dynamically, clamped to [0, 1];
without the feature the test stays off, as before, with one log line.
Metal and the fixed-function path leave the hook unset and draw as before.

Tests: test_rsx_draw_engine checks the key, the bounds and that moving them
builds no pipeline (4 new checks, failing without the engine change).
ps3recomp_host --depthbounds draws red at z = 0.25, then blue bounded to
[0, 0.5] and green bounded to [0.5, 1] with the depth test off, and expects
blue; it runs in the Vulkan workflow's engine pass under the validation
layer.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

faster), of 60 per-lane integer ops, and of shufb (tbl); test_spu_float_neon
and test_spu_int_neon compare them against the scalar forms.

  preferred word, mfspr and fscrrd read zero, bisl reads ra before writing
  the link (rt may alias ra), links and the next pc wrap at the end of local
  store, stopd reports code 0x3FFF;
- additions: bgx, mpyui, mpyhhau, rothmi, rotmah(i), bisled, dftsv and the
  double-precision ops (dfa/dfs/dfm/dfma/dfms/dfnms/dfnma, dfceq/dfcgt/

  right register; links wrap at the end of local store; stopd reports 0x3FFF.

  (0x100/0x110/0x111) no longer end a function: the lift resumes there when

bbcf9a53c7efef9fe7ca84c058f0292ed998d0cb.message:
D3D12 engine: texture uploads start on 512 bytes, as Direct3D 12 requires

Texture uploads are written into the stage and copied out of it with
CopyTextureRegion from a placed footprint. Direct3D 12 wants a placed
footprint to start on D3D12_TEXTURE_DATA_PLACEMENT_ALIGNMENT, 512 bytes;
the stage handed out reservations on 256. A device that reports
UnrestrictedBufferTextureCopyPitchSupported (D3D12_OPTIONS13, from the
Agility SDK 1.602 on: Windows 11's own runtime with a current driver)
takes any offset, so nothing showed on such a machine. Windows 10's
runtime does not have it: there the first upload that landed on an odd
multiple of 256 made the whole command list fail to close
(E_INVALIDARG), the engine switched itself off, and the picture froze on
the title's first loading screen while the game and its sound went on --
dod3-recomp issue #1, on an RX 7800 XT under Windows 10 22H2 and on an
RTX 3080 Ti.

The stage now aligns every reservation to 512 (constant buffers need
256, which 512 also is).

At start the engine says whether the device relaxes the rule
("[rsx engine/d3d12] relaxed copy alignment: yes|no"), and where it does
not, each copy is checked against it and the first offenders named.
RSX_D3D12_STRICT_COPY=1 holds a device that relaxes the rule to it all
the same, failing a list with such a copy as that runtime does, and
RSX_D3D12_STAGE_ALIGN=<n> sets the stage alignment: with both, a machine
that has the relaxation shows what one without it does. On an RTX 4090
under Windows 11: with the strict rule held and the old 256, eight
misaligned uploads at boot and the reporters' line, "command list Close
failed: 0x80070057 (removed 0x00000000)", then no picture while the
title music played; with 512, no misaligned copy and no failure through
boot, a save loaded into the hub and the chapter 1 battle.

bcfc012023d710563e62d545062289eaeb93351e.message:
fp decompiler: predicated writes are a select, not a lerp

Upstream's e99cbbf (by undecuple), for the fragment decompiler this fork
keeps: an instruction executed under a condition code wrote its
destination as lerp(dst, v, mask). lerp is arithmetic, dst + mask *
(v - dst), so an Inf or a NaN in the operand the condition leaves alone
gives NaN (0 * Inf), and a register holding raw bits (a packed word) loses
its denormal and NaN patterns on the way through the ALU. The write is now
a per-component select, (mask != 0.0) ? v : dst, which FXC compiles to
movc. Unconditional writes are as they were.

test_fp_decompiler gains upstream's case: MOV r0, COL0 predicated on

Symptom: in the D3D12 live-draw backend a Z16 zeta cleared with 0xFFFF
(its far plane) ends up at depth 0.0000152, so every LESS or LEQUAL draw

#235: Z16 = (value & 0xFFFF) / 65535 with stencil 0, Z24S8 unchanged. The
existing "value 0 clears to 1.0" behaviour is kept for both formats.

bits) leaves the primitive's interpolated depth in the zeta, so a

rsx engine: bind only the texture units a fragment program samples

A unit can stay switched on with a stale binding from an earlier pass (a
shadow pass keeps its map bound). Binding it anyway cost a cache check
and a hash or an upload, the resolve of a depth target on an MSAA run, and
a pipeline variant for its type. Units the draw's fragment program does
not sample are left unbound and out of the cube, shadow, unnormalised and
texel-op masks. The built-in program, RSX_BIND_UNREAD=1 and
RSX_ENGINE_SLOW=1 bind every unit that is on, as before;
g_rsx_bind_unread (DOD3_AB=texreads) switches it in a run.

rsx_fp_scan also returns the sampled units, so the fragment program is
still read once a draw: the scan moved to the draw's first program
lookup, its constants and key kept for the pipeline. A program with a
branch takes rsx_fp_texture_mask's own walk, which treats a branch's
constant bits differently.

The replay regression is byte-identical to the old paths; rsx_replay
--bench CPU within 1% of before.

c55ddaa4379c2897d55f337096cb23e0dd2a6c3d.message:
edat: take the klicensee the title passes to sceNpDrmIsAvailable[2]

Symptom: a free (license type 3) or disc-bound EDAT under a title-specific
klicensee fails to open with -6 ("needs a RIF key"), even though the title
supplies its key the way it does on hardware.

Cause: on hardware a title passes its own klicensee to sceNpDrmIsAvailable
or sceNpDrmIsAvailable2 before it opens such a file, and the kernel keeps it
for later opens. The runtime has neither call, so the key is lost, and the
EDAT reader only tries the built-in platform klicensees.

Change: sceNp.c implements sceNpDrmIsAvailable and sceNpDrmIsAvailable2;
both hand a non-NULL klicensee to edat_add_klicensee() (new, edat.h) and
return CELL_OK. edat.c keeps up to 16 such keys, ignores duplicates, and
tries them before the built-in ones. Each key is still checked against the
file's dev_hash (AES-CMAC under klic ^ NP_OMAC_KEY_2 over header bytes
0x00-0x5F, the same check for NPD versions 2-4) before it is used, and each
block hash is checked as before. A license type 3 file that no key verifies
now fails with a message that names sceNpDrmIsAvailable. Projects that read
the key some other way can call edat_add_klicensee() themselves.

Verification: tools/test_edat_guest_klicensee.py builds
libs/filesystem/tests/test_edat_guest_klicensee.c with sceNp.c. The test
writes a synthetic NPD v3 license-3 EDAT (made-up key, content id and data;
three blocks, the last partial) and checks: -6 before any key, -6 after
sceNpDrmIsAvailable2 with a key that does not verify dev_hash, then 0 with
every block hash verified and the plaintext matching after
sceNpDrmIsAvailable with the right key. The runner passes a scratch
directory as argv[1]. On master the fixture does not link (neither call
exists; without them the file stays at -6). With this change all checks
pass; the fixture also builds with x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc and passes under

PPU runtime: indirect calls through a flat table, HLE calls without lookups, no audio spin

- ps3_indirect_call: targets below 32 MB (a title's own code) are found in
  a flat table filled at registration, one load and no collisions, where
  the 4096-entry cache sent a busy frame's misses down the full path. The
  PRX code above keeps the cache. g_ppu_icall_flat (DOD3_AB=icallflat).
  Drakengard 3's hub: +0.8 +/- 0.8 fps, no change in thread CPU.
- ps3_hle_call and lv2_syscall stamped the profiler's call site by a
  binary search over every lifted function on every call. They keep the
  host return address now, and the profilers and the lock diagnostics name
  it when they read it (ppu_prof_stamp_ra; g_ppu_prof_resolve, set by
  ppu_loader.cpp, so the runtime links without it). The table it searches
  is built once under a lock.
- prx_resolve_export, asked on every HLE call, looks the NID up in a hash
  index instead of scanning the registry.
- Windows: guest sleeps of 0.5-1 ms wait on the thread's high-resolution
  timer and spin only their last 250 us. Drakengard 3's audio system
  thread polls with usleep(800) and spun 2.9-6.7 ms of CPU a frame, two
  thirds of a core; now 0.03 ms. g_usleep_spin_below

d079b5042a4fdb8137f5a45785fc4ac990f7428d.message:
D3D12 and Vulkan engines: an object released with records queued outlives them

eng_obj_release and eng_buffer_release retired an object at the fence of
the last submit made. Records still queued may name it -- a texture
uploaded again in mid-frame is released after the draws that sampled it
were recorded -- and they go out with the next submit; the object was
then destroyed as soon as the earlier fence had passed, while that next
command buffer could still be running. eng_retire_fence(): with records
waiting, the next submit's fence.

Found by the Vulkan validation layer in Drakengard 3 (vkDestroyImage on
an image in use by a command buffer, once in a 200 s battle at 4K); gone
in the same run after the change. Replays: D3D12 102 of 102 frames
identical, Vulkan 102 of 102 within tolerance of the D3D12 reference.

d0d67442f549faf07f8547adcb4fdc6e6dc74c08.message:
spu_channels: MFC engine table 8 -> 64 slots, and a full table is reported as an error

Symptom: intermittent stops where an SPU context waits forever on a DMA
tag that already completed. Killzone 3 holds eleven SPU contexts with an
MFC engine at once (policy-module contexts that keep their engine for as
long as their workload exists, plus SPU thread groups); the runtime prints
"more than 8 contexts hold an MFC engine at once; the rest share one".

Cause: the per-context engine table has SPU_MAX_CONTEXTS = 8 slots. Every
context past the eighth gets one shared fallback engine, where one
context's completion clears the tag bits another context is waiting on.
Eight is a thread group's worth, but a title can hold more contexts at
once than the machine has SPUs. The overflow was reported once, as a note.

Change: 64 slots (overridable with -DSPU_MAX_CONTEXTS). When the table is
still full, the shared engine stays as the last resort, but the runtime now
reports it as an error naming the table size, the context and the
consequence, at the first overflow lookup and again at 1000 and 1000000 so
it stays visible in a long log; s_mfc_overflow_lookups counts them. A
growable table can replace this later.

Verification: runtime/spu/tests/test_spu_mfc_slots.c (built as in the CI
workflows) keeps its 8-thread claim race over 32 rounds and adds: eleven
contexts held at once get eleven distinct engines and keep the state each
wrote; the table holds SPU_MAX_CONTEXTS contexts with no overflow; the next
context gets the overflow engine and the overflow is counted. With this
change 889 checks pass with gcc and clang, and the error line is printed
once. Against v0.14.0's spu_channels.c (a2c2010; the counter compiled as a
constant 0) 3 checks fail: the eleven contexts share engines, their state
is overwritten, and the overflow is not counted.

d168a5412110cf959786a00f50c91f133683ae30.message:
rsx engine: decode an index run per width, reuse a repeated pipeline key

After NoahBPeterson's fork of ps3recomp (2b0def4dba), adapted:
- A draw's index run is decoded by a loop of its own per index width and
  restart mode into room reserved once, where each index was assembled a
  byte at a time with the width tested per index, and pushed one by one.
  Restart indices still become cuts at the reference position they fall
  on. (On a vertex cache miss; RSX_ENGINE_SLOW=1 decodes as before.)
- The pipeline key is reused while every input of it repeats the last
  draw's -- the programs' keys, the masks and their per-unit arrays, the
  layout, the target format and count, and the render state byte for byte
  (it is zeroed before it is decoded) -- instead of hashed again a byte at
  a time.
The replay regression is byte-identical; rsx_replay --bench -0.4 to -1.8%
of the engine's CPU per present on the captures.

d2c054aa7d5b8eaf0b56eb8c90d1cb911b3d733b.message:
ppu_lifter: registers written back where they changed and are read, runs under one page test, SSE AltiVec

--nonvolatile-locals kept a function's registers in C locals and wrote
all of them back to the context before every call and return: 10.1
million stores at the 450,000 transfers of Drakengard 3's executable,
most of them of a value the context already held or nobody would read.
tools/ppu_nv_dirty.py (new; its module comment has the reasoning)
rewrites each lifted body instead:

- a forward dataflow knows which locals have been assigned since the
  context last agreed with them, and only those are stored;
- of the scratch registers (r0, r3-r12, f0-f13, v0-v19, CTR, the
  volatile CR fields, the carry) only those something reads before
  writing: each function is summarised, the summaries are solved over
  the call graph, and code outside the lift is held to the ABI. 3.7
  million stores are left;
- every CR field a function uses, and XER's carry, is a local of its
  own, with mfcr/mtcrf and the CR save slot followed;
- the saves of a prologue share one page test (30,161 functions), and
  so does any run of four or more loads and stores at constant offsets
  from one unchanged register with no label or call between them
  (686,658 accesses in 87,593 runs);
- the base of guest memory is a local, and the trampoline drain after a
  call is left out where the callee cannot have set the trampoline.

The AltiVec operations a compiler made scalar loops of are one helper
each in the source preamble, SSE on x86-64 and a portable form
elsewhere: lvlx/lvrx (a loop over sixteen bytes with a test in it came
to 190 instructions and a dozen branches a site, and the title has
11,800), lvsl/lvsr, vmaxfp/vminfp (four signbit calls a site with
MSVC's library), vctsxs/vctuxs, and the bitwise ones, whose destination
no longer reads as an operand. The dot compares take CR6 from the mask.
The float helpers' NaN rules stay a function instead of being inlined
at every operation (a float-heavy function's object: 318 KB -> 244 KB).
lmw/

ppu_lifter: VSCR[NJ] a constant in a binary with no mtvscr

The VMX float helpers read VSCR for its NJ bit (flush denormals) on
every operation: a load of ctx->vscr, which any store through a pointer

d9870123ea646d8a9a4ad4cd56342d5bd7c57546.message:
spu_channels: SMC micro-interpreter addresses lqa/stqa at I16 << 2

Symptom: a self-modifying SPU stub that saves and restores registers with
stqa/lqa (a job manager's interrupt save/restore stub, written into the
local store at runtime) stores every register at the wrong address and
overwrites unrelated local-store bytes, including the job's stack.

lqa/stqa as I16 << 4. For the RI16 form the address is I16 << 2 (SPU ISA),

4x too high and wrapped around the local store.

local store, and runs both halves through the micro-interpreter. With this
change all 76 registers land in their own slot, all 76 are restored, and no
local-store byte outside the save area changes. On v0.14.0 (a2c2010) no
register lands in its slot and 1198 bytes outside the save area change.

df3a7cbae234fb6701b6e1d1df2d3417b9e03a2a.message:
ppu_lifter: --chunks N cuts the source by guest address and rewrites only changed files

Symptom: any change to the lifter's input or to the lifter (a fix for one
opcode, one function's bounds) makes the build recompile nearly all of the
lifted source. For Killzone 3 (eight 600k-line chunks, 6.5-8 minutes and
2.5-4.4 GB of compiler memory each) that is 15-25 minutes per rebuild.

Cause: (1) chunks are cut every --chunk-lines emitted lines, so a change in
one function's line count moves every later cut point and changes the text of
every later chunk; (2) main() deletes the previous chunk set before writing,
so every file gets a new mtime even when its content is the same, and make or
ninja rebuild it.

Change:
- --chunks N (default 0 = off) cuts the source into N files by guest code
  bytes: chunk k holds the functions, in address order, of the range that
  carries the k-th N-th of the lifted bytes. That is a function of the
  function list alone, so the same functions always land in the same file. The
  function table goes to its own <source>_table.cpp, so a new function does
  not change the last chunk. A chunk over --chunk-lines lines prints a warning
  (MSVC's 16M-line limit).
- Every output file (header, chunks, table, the --single-file source) is
  written through write_if_changed: a temporary file and a rename, and only
  when the content differs, so unchanged files keep their mtime.
- Stale files of an earlier run (other cut points, the single-file source)
  are removed after writing instead of all files before.

How this relates to --chunk-lines (#216): --chunk-lines sets how large a
line-cut chunk may be (fewer lines per translation unit for hosts short on
memory) and stays the default mode; it now also profits from
write_if_changed. --chunks makes the cut points stable across relifts; with
it, --chunk-lines is only the warning threshold. Both can be used.
