e99cbbf0a9c93d99b9ba43fbd142365f4403ba13.message:
fp decompiler: predicated writes are a select, not a lerp

Symptom: a fragment-program instruction executed under a condition code
(exec_if lt/eq/gt) changes components of its destination that the condition
leaves alone when either operand holds Inf, NaN or raw bits. Programs that
keep packed words in a register (the PK*/UP* pack/unpack pattern) read 0 or
NaN after a predicated MOV.

Cause: the predicated destination write was emitted as
lerp(dst, v, mask). lerp is arithmetic (dst + mask * (v - dst)): an Inf or NaN
in the unselected operand gives NaN (0 * Inf), and denormal and NaN bit
patterns are not preserved through the ALU.

Change: emit a per-component select, (mask != 0.0) ? v : dst, which FXC
compiles to movc. The unconditional path is unchanged.

Verification: libs/video/tests/test_fp_decompiler.c gains a case with a MOV
predicated on CC0 > 0 that checks the select form and that no lerp is
emitted. It fails on master (39 passed, 2 failed) and passes with this change
(41 passed, 0 failed). The same select has been in use in a D3D12 title port
under Proton; there a test with predicated writes over raw-bit and Inf/NaN
operands read 8 of 8 values back correctly, 4 of 8 with lerp.

sys_time: the wall clock on Windows is the wall clock; sys_time_get_timezone

A title's C library makes the date it shows, and stamps its saves with,
from two system calls. Both were wrong:

sys_time_get_current_time (145), Windows: answered the performance
counter divided into seconds, which is the time since the PC was
started, as the time since 1970. A machine up for four days told the
title it was the 5th of January 1970. It is now the host's wall clock,
read once and carried on by the guest's ticks, so it stands still while
the title is paused like the guest's other clocks. POSIX already used
the host's.

sys_time_get_timezone (144), every platform: was not there. The
dispatcher answered CELL_OK and wrote nothing, and the library went on
with whatever its two variables held. It now gives the host's zone:
minutes east of UTC without summer time, and the summer time in force
(0 or 60).

Drakengard 3 stamped a save of October 2026 as December 1933 with both
wrong, and as the 5th of January 1970 once the zone was right and the
clock still was not. With both, PS3_TIME_LOG=1 (new: the first answer of
each call) shows the title told 2026-10-11 23:34:52 UTC, zone 0, summer
time 60, on a machine set to British time.

The comments about these numbers colliding with the event flag calls
are gone: they do not (event flags are 82 to 87 and 118, 132, 139).

efef265f81209865b56cd7d9eee577577a2cd2b2.message:
cellHttp: response getters under their SDK names; RecvResponse into guest memory

Symptom: a title that reads an HTTP answer through
cellHttpResponseGetStatusCode, cellHttpResponseGetContentLength and
cellHttpResponseGetAllHeaders gets CELL_OK with the status unset and a NULL
header array, and drops every response. A body that outgrows the header read
is recv()'d into the host address equal to the guest buffer's EA (recv fails
with EFAULT, or writes into host memory).

Cause: the runtime has cellHttpGetStatusCode and
cellHttpGetResponseContentLength, whose computed NIDs match no firmware
import, and no cellHttpResponseGetAllHeaders, so the three imports take the
unresolved-NID path. In cellHttpRecvResponse the overflow copy translates
the guest buffer but the socket read does not.

Change: add cellHttpResponseGetStatusCode, cellHttpResponseGetContentLength
(0x80710017 when the response has no Content-Length) and
cellHttpResponseGetAllHeaders ({name, value} guest pointers followed by the
strings in the caller's pool; a size query with no pool writes only
*required; a pool too small returns NO_BUFFER). Titles call them before the
first cellHttpRecvResponse, so they read the headers first. The older
functions keep their names. cellHttpRecvResponse recv()s into the
translated guest buffer.

Verification: tools/test_http_response_getters.py builds
libs/network/tests/test_http_response_getters.c against a loopback
listener: a 200 answer with three headers and a 3000-byte body of which
only 100 bytes arrive with the headers, then a response without
Content-Length. On master: 4 failed (the three getters missing; the body
stops at 100 bytes, recv() error); with this change all 13 checks pass.

f110c349c230521f60cb5f27f7449fd90144e779.message:
cellSaveData: UserAutoSave keeps its ninth argument; handlers registered at init

Symptom: a title that saves with cellSaveDataUserAutoSave gets
cbResult->userdata == 0 in its stat and file callbacks. A title that keeps
its save state behind userdata writes through a null pointer and saves an
empty profile.

Cause: cellSaveDataUserAutoSave takes nine arguments; the ninth (userdata)
is in the caller's parameter save area at SP+112. UserAutoLoad already has
a context handler that reads it, UserAutoSave has none, and nothing in the
runtime calls cellSaveData_register_ctx_handlers(), so both calls go through
the generic eight-argument binding unless a project registers the handlers
itself.

Change: a context handler for cellSaveDataUserAutoSave (NID 0x52AAC4FA),
the same as UserAutoLoad's, registered in
cellSaveData_register_ctx_handlers(). It calls cellSaveDataAutoSave rather
than AutoSave2: AutoSave2 maps dirName to a host pointer and hands it to
AutoSave, which maps it again, so a host address below 4 GiB (seen on
Windows) would be read as a guest address. ppu_sysprx_register() now calls
cellSaveData_register_ctx_handlers() next to np_score_register_ctx(), so
every project gets both handlers. A project that already calls it keeps
working: the first registration of a NID wins and both point at the same
handler.

Verification: tools/test_savedata_user_autosave.py checks that
ppu_sysprx_register() calls cellSaveData_register_ctx_handlers(), then
builds libs/system/tests/test_savedata_user_autosave.c, which registers the
handlers into a local table and calls UserAutoLoad and UserAutoSave with a
userdata value at SP+112; the runner passes a scratch save root as argv[1].
On master: 2 failed (no call from
ppu_sysprx_register, no handler for 0x52AAC4FA; UserAutoLoad passes). With
this change all checks pass. test_savedata_fixed.c and test_savedata_io.c
still pass. The fixture also builds with x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc and passes
under Wine.

f58d67dee6877a65e432de979917034be93dbb89.message:
cellPad, cellAudio: SDL leaves SIGINT and SIGTERM alone

SDL's events subsystem, which the pad and the audio device each bring up,
installs handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that only queue an SDL_QUIT
event. Outside the Linux Vulkan backend nothing reads SDL's events -- the
window is the Metal or the Win32 one -- so the process ignored Ctrl-C in a
terminal and `kill` alike. A benchmark harness's kill at 180 s was
ignored that way and the game ran for 18 hours.

SDL_HINT_NO_SIGNAL_HANDLERS is set before either subsystem starts (either
may be first), except where PS3RECOMP_RSX_VULKAN is defined: that
backend's window is SDL's and its pump acts on the event.

Drakengard 3 on macOS, signalled 25 s after launch with the pad and the
audio device up: before, still running 10 s after SIGTERM; now gone
0.17 s after SIGTERM and 0.10 s after SIGINT, ended by the signal. The
cursor a port holds is back afterwards (the window server's doing).

f788adc836653bf2717af4eef5566eeaf12f20a4.message:
spu_channels: the engine lookup answers from a per-thread copy

The merge brought upstream's registry of private MFC engines, which takes
its read lock on every lookup -- and every DMA looks its engine up. Two
interlocked operations on one cache line that every SPU thread shares,
per transfer; the fork's 64-slot table had answered from a per-thread
copy of the last answer.

mfc_for now keeps that copy again (context, engine, and a generation),
good while no node has been freed since it was taken: s_mfc_gen counts
frees, bumped under the writer lock before the node goes. A node lives
until its owner releases it, which only happens once the owner has
stopped using the context, so a thread holding a copy for a live context
always holds a live node; a new context at a freed one's address -- the
next job's stack context -- finds the count moved and asks the registry.
SPU_MFC_TLS=0 asks the registry every time.

Drakengard 3, hub, uncapped 720p, the build without and with it run back
to back with 0.2.5 in between: SPU image 1 0.84 -> 0.72 ms of CPU a
frame (0.2.5: 0.74), the frame rate 168.5 -> 181.5 (0.2.5: 176.6 and
177.9). The registry tests (test_spu_context_registries, both the
concurrent-lookup and the slot cases) pass.

# ps3recomp

### *Because the Cell processor deserves a second life*

> Static recompilation runtime libraries for PlayStation 3 titles.
> Turn PS3 binaries into native executables. No emulator required.

**[Join the sp00nznet recomp Discord](https://discord.gg/CRpzGWZFcu)** — the
community hub for sp00nznet's recomp projects, where ps3recomp development
happens in the open. Good place to ask questions, show a port you are working
on, or find out what people are stuck on before you duplicate the effort.

---

## What Is This?

**ps3recomp** is an open-source toolkit that provides the runtime libraries, system stubs, and analysis tools needed to **statically recompile PlayStation 3 games into native PC executables**.

Instead of interpreting or dynamically recompiling PowerPC/SPU instructions at runtime (what emulators like RPCS3 do brilliantly), we take the opposite approach: **translate everything ahead of time** into C/C++ that compiles with your favorite compiler on any modern platform.

This is the same philosophy behind:
- [N64Recomp](https://github.com/N64Recomp/N64Recomp) (N64 -> native)
- [UnleashedRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp) (PS2 -> native)
- [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) (Original Xbox -> native)
- [ReXGlue](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk) (Xbox 360 -> native)
- [AnyPS5](https://github.com/boykopovar/AnyPS5) (PS5 -> native)

...but for the PS3's glorious, terrifying **Cell Broadband Engine**.

## Why PS3?

The PlayStation 3 has over **3,000 titles** and some of the most beloved games ever made. RPCS3 has done heroic work making ~70% of the library playable through emulation, but static recompilation offers something different:

- **Native performance** — no runtime translation overhead
- **Lower hardware requirements** — runs on mid-range PCs
- **Moddability** — recompiled C/C++ is infinitely more hackable than PPC binaries
- **Preservation** — native ports survive long after emulators stop being maintained
- **Portability** — the output is C/C++, so it can target any platform a compiler does (see [platform support](#platform-support) for where the runtime actually stands today)

## Platform support

CI builds and tests every row on every pull request: Windows (clang-cl), macOS
arm64, Linux (GCC and Clang), and Linux with the Vulkan backend on lavapipe
under the validation layer. A green check means the runtime built and the tests
passed. It does not mean a game ran; the last row is the only one that claims
that.

| | Windows | macOS (arm64) | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime library builds | yes | yes | yes |
| Lifter test suites + C unit tests | yes | yes | yes |
| Render backend | D3D12 | Metal | Vulkan (opt-in); null (headless, CI) |
| Runs a recompiled game, in this tree | **yes** | **no** | **no** |

**What stops macOS and Linux running a title is the PPU boot scaffold.**
`ppu_loader.cpp`, `boot_main.cpp` and the HLE dispatch are compiled per game,
not into the library. They compile on POSIX with zero errors (a CI ratchet
keeps it that way) and the frame clock runs there, but no title has yet been
booted to gameplay from this tree on either OS.

**The renderers are further along than that.** `ps3recomp_host` drives cellGcm
→ RSX → backend end to end with no game. With guest programs on, Metal and
Vulkan both run the title's own shaders on the shared register-file draw
engine. Every `ps3recomp_host` scene passes on both, including render-to-texture,
MRT, depth textures, cube maps and stencil. Linux's default stays the headless
null backend, a CPU triangle filler that CI draws with.

**Downstream, people are already past this.** Twisted Metal's menus run on
Linux/Vulkan, inFamous on macOS, and Killzone 3 under Proton (see
[In the community](#in-the-community)). Those ports carry patches that are
still on their way upstream, which is why the table still says "no".

## The Challenge

The PS3's Cell processor is a beast unlike anything else:

| Component | What It Is | Why It's Hard |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|
| **PPU** | PowerPC 64-bit main CPU | Custom ISA extensions, VMX/AltiVec SIMD |
| **6x SPU** | 128-bit SIMD vector processors | Proprietary ISA, 256KB local store, explicit DMA |
| **Memory** | 256MB XDR RAM | 128-byte alignment requirements, split bus |
| **LV2 Kernel** | Proprietary OS layer | ~300+ system calls, complex threading model |
| **PRX Modules** | Dynamic libraries | 100+ system libraries with intricate interdependencies |

We don't shy away from hard problems. We just break them into smaller ones.

## Architecture

```

├── tools/                    # Binary analysis & recompilation pipeline
│   ├── elf_parser.py         # Parse PS3 ELF/SELF/PRX binaries
│   ├── ppu_disasm.py         # PowerPC disassembler with PS3 extensions
│   ├── ppu_lifter.py         # PPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── spu_disasm.py         # SPU instruction set disassembler
│   ├── spu_lifter.py         # SPU assembly -> C code lifter
│   ├── extract_spu_images.py # Extract embedded SPU images from PRX/ELF
│   ├── find_spu_functions.py # SPU function boundary detection
│   ├── wrap_spu_elf.py       # Wrap a raw SPU blob as a loadable ELF

## How It Works

The pipeline follows the same proven approach as our [burnout3](https://github.com/sp00nznet/burnout3) project, adapted for the Cell architecture:

```
   PS3 Game Disc / PKG
         │
         ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  SELF/EBOOT  │  Encrypted PS3 executable
   │  Decryption  │  (requires keys / fSELF)
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  ELF Parser  │  Extract sections, segments, relocations
   │  + PRX Scan  │  Identify imported NIDs & library deps
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Disasm  │  Disassemble PowerPC 64-bit + VMX
   │  + Analysis  │  Function boundaries, jump tables, ABI
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  PPU Lifter  │  PowerPC → C code generation
   │  + SPU Lift  │  SPU programs → C code generation
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Link with   │  ps3recomp runtime + HLE libs
   │  Runtime     │  Provides all PS3 OS services
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │  Compile &   │  MSVC / GCC / Clang
   │  Ship!       │  Native x86-64 executable
   └─────────────┘
```

## SPU Strategy

The SPU is the elephant in the room. Each SPU has its own instruction set, its own 256KB memory, and communicates with the PPU via DMA and mailbox channels. Our approach:

1. **SPU programs are self-contained** — they live in ELF segments loaded to local store (`extract_spu_images.py` pulls them out of PRX/ELF)
2. **Recompile each SPU program separately** — dedicated `spu_disasm.py` + `spu_lifter.py` handle the SPU ISA
3. **SPU local store becomes an array** — 256KB per "virtual SPU"
4. **DMA operations become memcpy** — via the MFC engine (`spu_dma.h`)
5. **Channels become cross-thread message queues** — preserving ordering guarantees
6. **Per-image function-table dispatch** — `image_id` lets multiple SPU programs (e.g. a SPURS kernel, a policy module, and a job) coexist at overlapping local-store addresses

This mirrors how RPCS3 handles SPU but at compile time rather than runtime. The
disassembler, lifter, and runtime are functional and covered by self-contained
tests (`runtime/spu/tests/`: sum, shufb, DMA, brsl-return).

# Demon's Souls — native PC port (ps3recomp)

A native Windows build of **Demon's Souls** (PS3, USA, **BLUS-30443**), made by statically
recompiling the game's PowerPC (PPU) and SPU code to C/C++ with
[ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp), plus a PS3 runtime and a Direct3D 12 renderer.
It is not an emulator: the game's code runs as a normal x64 program.

> **No game files are included.** This repo holds only the tools, patches and build scripts. You
> need your own copy of the game, dumped from your own disc. The setup reads your disc image and
> builds everything on your PC.

## Status

**The entire game seems playable.** It runs with sound and music at 60 fps (or 50 on a 100 Hz
screen, 30, uncapped, or any frame rate you pick), with keyboard + mouse or an Xbox controller. The game's movies play (title screen, intro,
story and endings; `set DES_MOVIES=0` skips them). There is no online play.

I'm currently playing through the whole game to find and fix any spots that still run slower
than they should (stutters, frame drops in heavy scenes). Boletarian Palace, the heaviest area
tested so far, is already smooth. Expect more performance fixes as the playthrough goes on; see
[docs/NOTES.md](docs/NOTES.md) for the full development log (50 fixes and counting).

If you hit a stutter or a crash, please report it: see
[Reporting stutters and crashes](#reporting-stutters-and-crashes). Every run is recorded, so all it
takes is pressing **F8** when it happens and running `REPORT.bat` afterwards.

## What you need

- **Windows 10/11 x64** and a **Direct3D 12** GPU. AVX2 (Intel Haswell / AMD Ryzen or newer) is used
  when your CPU has it; on older CPUs BUILD.bat builds without it (a couple of fps slower in the
  heaviest areas).
- About **12 GB** free disk space (8 GB game files + build).
- **Your disc image** of Demon's Souls USA (BLUS-30443): a `.iso` (a Redump `.zip` works as is), or a
  dumped disc folder with `PS3_GAME` in it. A Redump-style encrypted image also needs its
  **disc key** (the `.dkey` file that comes with the dump, or the "Disc Key" on its Redump page).
- **[RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net/download)**, used once to decrypt the game's `EBOOT.BIN`. Unzip it anywhere.
- **Python 3.10+** and **Git**. If they are missing, SETUP.bat offers to install them with winget.
- **Visual Studio 2022** (Community or the free **Build Tools**) with *Desktop development with C++*,
  and **LLVM** (clang-cl) 17 or newer. If they are missing, setup offers to install them with winget.

## Build it (one time)

1. Download this repo (green **Code** button → *Download ZIP*, or `git clone`) and unpack it
   somewhere with enough space, ideally a path without unusual characters.
2. **Drag your disc image onto `SETUP.bat`**, or double-click `SETUP.bat` and it asks for it.
3. Answer its questions: the disc key if the image is encrypted, and where `rpcs3.exe` is.

That's it. SETUP.bat then:

| step | what happens | time* |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | extracts all game files from the image (and decrypts them) into `game/` | 2–5 min |
| 2 | decrypts `EBOOT.BIN` → `EBOOT.elf` with RPCS3 and checks it is the tested version | < 1 min |
| 3 | downloads ps3recomp at the tested commit and applies this port's runtime patch | < 1 min |
| 4 | recompiles the game: ~94,000 PPU functions + 12 SPU programs → C/C++ in `port/` | 2–4 min |
| 5 | applies this port's edits to the recompiled code (`patches/lifted-code.patch`) | seconds |
| 6 | compiles everything with clang-cl into `port/build_opt/DemonsSoulsRecomp.exe` | 10–30 min |

\* on a fast 16-core PC; the first compile is the long part. If anything fails, fix what it says
and run SETUP.bat again: finished steps are skipped.

## Play

Double-click **`PLAY.bat`**. The logos and first load take about a minute.

| launcher | what it does |
|---|---|
| `PLAY.bat` | 60 fps (50 fps automatically on a ~100 Hz monitor, every frame shown exactly 2 refreshes) |
| `PLAY_30FPS.bat` | the original 30 fps |
| `PLAY_50FPS.bat` | 50 fps locked to a 100 Hz screen |
| `PLAY_UNLIMITED.bat` | uncapped (up to 240 fps), no vsync, game speed stays correct |
| `PLAY_CHOOSE_FPS.bat` | a menu of the above, plus **any frame rate you type in** (31–240) |
| `PLAY_REMASTER.bat` | runs with the *PC Remaster* mod installed (see below) |
| `PLAY_DUMP_TEXTURES.bat` | saves every texture the game draws, for texture packs (see below) |
| `PLAY_MODDED.bat` | runs your imported models (see *model import/export* below) |

**Custom frame rate.** `PLAY_CHOOSE_FPS.bat` → *6* → type a number, e.g. 45, 72, 120 or 144. The game
runs at real speed at any of them. If your monitor's refresh rate is a whole multiple of the number
(72 or 144 on a 144 Hz screen, 40 or 120 on 120 Hz), every frame is shown for the same number of
refreshes and motion is perfectly even. Otherwise vsync is turned off, which looks fine on a
G-Sync / FreeSync screen but can tear on others. The launcher says which one you got. You can also
`set DES_FPS=<number>` before running `PLAY.bat`.

**Controls.** An Xbox (XInput) controller works when plugged in (A = Cross, B = Circle, X = Square,
Y = Triangle, LB/RB = L1/R1, LT/RT = L2/R2, Back = Select). A DualShock/DualSense needs Steam Input or
DS4Windows. Keyboard + mouse:

| | |
|---|---|
| WASD | move |
| mouse (or IJKL) | camera |
| left mouse | attack (R1) |
| Shift | strong attack (R2) |
| right mouse | block (L1) |
| Ctrl | parry (L2) |
| Space | roll / dash / back (Circle) |
| E | interact / confirm (Cross) |
| F | two-hand (Triangle) |
| R | use item (Square) |
| Tab / middle mouse | lock on (R3) |
| arrows | d-pad (switch items) |
| Enter / Backspace | Start / Select |
| F1 | capture / release the mouse |
| Alt+Enter / F11 | borderless fullscreen on/off (`set DES_FULLSCREEN=1` starts in it) |
| F9 | god mode on/off (no death, HP/MP/stamina stay full) |

Keys go by position, not by letter: on an AZERTY or QWERTZ keyboard you move with the keys where
WASD would be (ZQSD on AZERTY), and the others follow the same way. `set PAD_KEYS_BY_LETTER=1` = by letter.

At *Create Profile* a text box opens for the character name. Saves go to `gamedata/`. Each run
writes logs to `logs/` (they grow by ~600 MB an hour; the previous run is kept as `*_prev.txt`).

## Reporting stutters and crashes

Every launcher records frame timing while you play (about 25 MB an hour, no visible cost; the newest
10 sessions are kept in `perf\`). The window title shows `[RECORDING - F8 = stutter, N marked]`.

1. **Press F8** in the game right after you see a stutter, hitch or slowdown. Each press puts a mark
   in the recording at that moment, so the exact frames can be found later. Press it as often as you
   like.
2. **After you quit** (or right after a crash), double-click **`REPORT.bat`**. It packs the last
   session into one zip, shows it in Explorer and opens the GitHub *New issue* page.
3. **Open an issue** with the *Stutter / slowdown* or *Crash / bug* template, **drag the zip into
   it**, and say where you were in the game and what you saw at each F8 press.

What the zip contains (nothing else, and your Windows user name is removed from all of it):

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `report.txt` | the summary from `tools/perf_report.py`: frame pacing, every hitch with its likely cause (a slow game step, shader compile, slow file read, the renderer, the GPU), and what happened just before each F8 mark |
| `perf.txt` | the recording itself, so we can dig into the exact frames (trimmed to the minutes around your F8 marks if the session is too long for GitHub's 25 MB limit) |
| `system.txt` | Windows version, CPU, RAM, GPU + driver, monitor resolution / refresh, the frame-rate setting and which version of this port you built |
| `log_tail.txt` | the last 400 lines of the game's log, from the same session (shows what it was doing if it crashed) |

Curious yourself? `.venv\Scripts\python tools\perf_report.py` prints the same summary for your newest
recording. To play without recording, `set DES_RECORD=0` before running a launcher.

## Optional: PC Remaster mod

The *Demon's Souls PC Remaster* mod by fromsoftserve (Nexus Mods, Demon's Souls mod 106)
(made for RPCS3) works with this port. Download the mod's zip yourself, then:

```bat
.venv\Scripts\python tools\install_remaster.py "path\to\the mod.zip" --apply
```

That builds `game_remaster/` as a hard-linked copy of `game/` (no extra disk space) with the mod's
files swapped in. Your normal `game/` is not changed. Play with `PLAY_REMASTER.bat`.

## Optional: texture packs

Textures can be replaced without unpacking any game files, at any resolution:

1. Run `PLAY_DUMP_TEXTURES.bat` and play through the part you want to change. Every texture the game
   draws is saved once to `textures\dump\` as `<KEY>_<width>x<height>_<format>.png`, exactly as it
   looks in game. The 16-character KEY comes from the texture's contents, so it is the same on every PC.
2. Edit a PNG (or make a bigger one) and put it in `textures\replace\` with a name that starts with
   the same KEY, e.g. `0123456789ABCDEF_armour_4k.png`. Sub folders are fine.
3. Start any launcher. Replacements load in the background; `.dds` files (DXT1/3/5, BC7, BC4 or 32-bit
   RGBA, with or without mipmaps) load faster and use less video memory than PNG.

Details and settings: `textures\README.txt`. Cubemaps (reflections) are not covered; for models see
the next section. Packs are made from the game's art -- share them only where that is allowed.

## Optional: model import/export

Armour, weapons, characters, objects and map pieces can be exported to glTF, edited in Blender (or
anything that reads and writes glTF 2.0) and imported back:

```
.venv\Scripts\python tools\flver_tool.py export game\PS3_GAME\USRDIR\PARTS\bd_f_5010.partsbnd.dcx
  -> models\BD_F_5010\BD_F_5010.gltf (+ .bin and the textures as PNG)
  ... Blender: File > Import > glTF 2.0, edit, File > Export > glTF 2.0 (.glb is fine) ...
.venv\Scripts\python tools\flver_tool.py import models\BD_F_5010\edited.glb game\PS3_GAME\USRDIR\PARTS\bd_f_5010.partsbnd.dcx
```

Import writes `game_mod\`, a copy of `game\` made of hard links (no extra disk space); `game\` is
never changed. Play it with `PLAY_MODDED.bat`; delete `game_mod\` to undo everything. Shape, UVs,
vertex colours and bone weights come from your file; materials, textures, skeleton, collision and
animations stay the game's (change textures with texture packs). Edit the `_l` low-detail copy too,
or the old shape shows from far away. Which file holds what and the rules: `models\README.txt`.
`flver_tool.py selftest` checks every model in your game reads and writes back byte for byte.
Exported models are the game's art -- share them only where that is allowed.

## Repo layout

```
SETUP.bat / BUILD.bat        one-time setup / rebuild after code changes
PLAY*.bat                    launchers (environment switches documented inside PLAY.bat)
REPORT.bat                   packs the last session into a zip for a GitHub issue
setup/setup.py, build.py     the setup pipeline and the toolchain finder + build
project/                     CMake project: CMakeLists.txt, main.cpp, stubs.cpp
patches/ps3recomp-local.patch   this port's changes to the ps3recomp runtime/renderer (applied to
                                ps3recomp @ 4e8f3ca, v0.18.0)
patches/lifted-code.patch    this port's edits to the recompiled game code (frame pacing, 60 fps
                             step, god mode, test hooks)
tools/                       disc extraction, UDF names, SPURS job lifting, perf report + issue zip, mod installer,
                             model export/import (flver_tool.py, souls_formats.py)
docs/NOTES.md                development log: every fix, why, and how it was measured
```

Everything SETUP.bat produces (`game/`, `port/`, `deps/`, `.venv/`, saves, logs) is in `.gitignore`.
**Never commit or share those**: they are the game.

## Troubleshooting

- **"RPCS3 did not write EBOOT.elf"**: close any open RPCS3 window and run SETUP.bat again, or decrypt
  by hand: RPCS3 → *Utilities* → *Decrypt PS3 Binaries* → `game\PS3_GAME\USRDIR\EBOOT.BIN`.
  If RPCS3 itself complains, install the PS3 firmware in RPCS3 first (*File → Install Firmware*).
- **"EBOOT.BIN is not the tested one"**: only the USA disc (BLUS-30443, version as on the disc) is
  supported. Other regions or updated EBOOTs need different patches.
- **Build tools not found**: install Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools with *Desktop development with C++*
  and LLVM (`winget install LLVM.LLVM`), or set `LLVM_DIR` to an LLVM folder, then run BUILD.bat.
- **The game window stays black / closes**: look at the end of `logs\last_run_err.txt`.
- **Uneven frames at 100+ fps in busy areas** (e.g. the Valley of Defilement swamp): the game's own
  frame work can need more than 10 ms there; the 50 fps mode is even everywhere. On CPUs with two
  core complexes the game pins itself to the one with the biggest L3 (docs/NOTES.md fix 65);
  `set DES_AFFINITY=0` turns that off.
- **A character or object is black, or missing, for a moment the first time you see it**: its shaders
  are being compiled in the background (instead of freezing the game; docs/NOTES.md fix 62). It only
  happens the first time a shader is ever seen. `set LD_PSO_ASYNC=0` before PLAY.bat = wait instead.
- **"needs AVX2"** message box: this build was made on a PC with AVX2 and yours has none. Run
  BUILD.bat on this PC (it picks the right setting), or `set DS_AVX2=0` before BUILD.bat on the other one.

1d8a73450385526becace94a5f8ce49d3103d53f.message:
Havok: lift the switch in func_010CB728 (HavokRunnerThread exit)

The "indirect call to 0x010CC17C" was case 4 of a 26-case switch whose
jump-table base is loaded two-level (lwz r30,d(r2); lwz r3,d2(r30)) and
spilled to the stack before the dispatch. The lifter handled each form
alone but not both, so the bctr became an unresolved indirect call and
HavokRunnerThread exited with status 1.

Patch 0010 follows a spilled base through a two-level load. After a
relift and full build, two runs of the test recipe played the cutscene
to the end of 110 s with no exit.

22db438f7cc62d1fb34ec5a8d0b9eaba8a816b2f.message:
Sound after the menu: mixer stall, voices and 5.1 movies

The silence after the menu was five things, not one. Two were not bugs of the
port: the test recipe's START opens the pause menu when a save exists, and
e0031.at3 is silent for its first 52 seconds on the disc.

The other three:
- libmixer locks for 100 us and ignores the result. When the holder lost its
  core the signal was lost and the mixer waited forever: 3 stalls in 24 runs,
  0 in 30 after raising short lock timeouts to one second (patch 0015).
- cellAtracGetStreamDataInfo returned an error for a file on memory, which the
  game takes as a failure, so every voice clip ended after one frame (0016).
- cellAdec decoded stereo only, and e0000 is 5.1 (0017).

Measured from the output with AUDIO_WAV, not by listening.

2552a557b7643b0497a00ffca40c5a05ca70189d.message:
Fix the credits movie stripes: read linear textures at their pitch

The small movie beside the credits (CAST) came out as slanted,
near-horizontal stripes. The game copies each 480x272 picture into an
A8R8G8B8 texture in local memory with a 2048-byte pitch, and the D3D12
backend read every linear texture w * bpp bytes a row (1920), so each
row started 32 texels early. Consecutive rows of the striped frame line
up after exactly that shift; the 1280-wide movies were unaffected
because their pitch equals their row.

Patch 0041 carries SET_TEXTURE_CONTROL3's pitch from the bind to the
upload and adds TEX_PITCHDBG. Verified before/after on the same frame of
a deterministic route to the credits (SONIC06_BOOT=dev, Ending); the
opening movies still play, and no texture in the town, Wave Ocean,
Crisis City or Egg Cerberus has a pitch other than its row.

PHASE1 section 55 has the details; HANDOFF drops the item, adds the
credits recipe, and records a freeze in the town after 11-12 restarts
found on the way.

327ce940d941d261efd3c117cf51b265fe648eff.message:
Frame pacing: flip handler on completion, flip time in microseconds, exact 60 Hz vblank

The frame loop waits on a semaphore its flip handler posts and runs one
fixed 1/60 s step per frame. The flip handler fired when a flip was
requested, so the game ran at the host's frame rate (thousands of steps a
second). The title screen's 30 s idle timer ran out in half a second and
the game fell into the attract movie, which was earlier taken for the main
menu's background.

- src/sonic06_config.c defaults GCM_FLIPCB_ONTICK=1.
- patch 0003: cellGcmGetLastFlipTime in microseconds, stamped at completion.
- patch 0004: cellResc hands its flip and vblank handlers to cellGcm.
- patch 0005: the boot harness ticks the vblank at 60 Hz on the us clock.

Now 60.0 steps a second; one START reaches the main menu with its intro
animation, and CROSS opens the single player submenu. docs/PHASE1.md
corrects the earlier menu findings and maps the menu state machine.

36b003e6d4a60693e1ba110451eb014a51ac8bb7.message:
Ring wraps no longer wait for the walker (patch 0033), and frame-time tools

The story scene's long frames came once every 0.9 s: the game's command
ring filled, and the buffer-full callback waited for the walker to read
the whole tail, most of a frame, 1.4-35 ms each time. Patch 0033 holds the
context's end at the walker instead and returns at once. Over 45 s of the
scene the waits went from 323-344 ms to 0; the rate moved from 29.08-29.49
to 29.58-29.64 (two alternating pairs, a small difference). The rest of
the gap to 30 is mostly one half-second stall at a scene cut, compiling
vertex shaders inside the frame.

tools/re/ft_frames.py reads a PS3_FTRACE timeline: frame times in vblanks,
the long frames with what the main thread and the RSX did, and the wraps.
tools/re/samp_window.py says what a thread ran inside a time window, from
PS3_SAMPLE_RVAS_TIME samples.

RSX: vertex fetch in SIMD, streaming stores into the vertex buffer (patch 0027)

In the first scene the indexed path converts about 11M vertices a second,
40% of the RSX thread. Converting four components at a time (bit-exact
with the scalar decode; 532M vertices of the scene compared, 0
mismatches) alone barely moved the cost: the time was in writing each
256-byte vertex into write-back memory, which reads every line from DRAM
first. Streaming stores fix that, and then the SIMD decode saves another
20%: 43-45 ns per conversion down to 27.9-30.9.

Wave Ocean 59.7-59.8 either way, frames of both checked. VTX_NT=0 and
VTX_SCALAR=1 turn each part off.

GCM: counted vblanks, and the vblank on its own thread (patches 0028-0029)

The main thread's 1 ms usleep loop at 0x23254 is AppMarathon's frame
limiter (slot 5, 0xF00C34): it sets a flag and waits until the vblank
handler (0xEFF3FC) has run m_13c times, two in a scene. Two things in the
runtime cost it frames:

- Vblank delivery was a pending bit, so ticks that came in a burst ran the
  handler once: 24 of 1365 lost in the first scene. Patch 0028 owes one
  call per tick. 28.9 -> 29.4 flips/s, faster in all 4 alternating pairs.
- The tick shared the walker thread with the FIFO drain, so half the
  ticks fired more than 4 ms late (up to 98 ms). Patch 0029 moves it to a
  thread of its own: mean 0.3 ms late. Scene rate within the noise (+0.2
  over 3 pairs); Wave Ocean 59.4-59.8, where one run without it fell to
  55.9 with late ticks.

Found with a temporary hook (tools/re/hook.py) on func_00022FB0 naming
DocMarathonState and AppMarathon; REA could not open the PPC64 EBOOT.

1444578063.readme_excerpt:
Soleanna (sonic06-recomp) is an unofficial PC port of the PlayStation 3 version of Sonic the Hedgehog (2006), made by static recompilation.
No emulator at runtime, and no game files in this repository: the launcher builds the game on your PC from your own disc.

Download 0.2.0 · Screenshots · Getting started · Status · How it works · FAQ · Report a problem

> [!IMPORTANT] > **Version 0.2.0 is an early work in progress.** Every stage and boss starts, but nobody has played a stage to the end yet, and it has been tested on one PC. You need your own copy of the game (BLES00028). This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by SEGA. ## Screenshots
Wave Ocean, running on the water Crisis City, on a rail
Wave Ocean, a jump over the sea Soleanna, the town
Captured with F12 in this port, on Windows, from the author's own copy, at an internal resolution of 3840×2160 and shown here at 1920×1080. The game and its images belong to SEGA. The pictures are attached to the release, not kept in git. ## Status | Area | Where it stands | |---|---| | ✅ Menus and story | The title screen, menus and movies, and the story up to Soleanna's town, with music and voices | | ✅ Stages and bosses | All 83 stage entries and 18 bosses start without a crash, in tests of about a minute each | | ⚠️ Playthrough | No stage has been played to the end by a person yet | | ✅ Speed | The story scenes hold the game's own 30 fps cap; Wave Ocean runs at 57–59 fps | | ⚠️ Controllers | Supported through SDL2, but not yet tried with a real controller | | ⚠️ Hardware | Tested on one Windows PC | What is in each version is in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md). ## The launcher The project and its launcher are named **Soleanna**, after the game's city; `sonic06-recomp` is the repository's name. The launcher copies your disc, decrypts it with your RPCS3, installs the build tools, downloads FFmpeg, SDL2 and ps3recomp, builds the game, and starts it. It ships no artwork of the game: once your disc is copied, it shows the pictures from the disc itself.
Play: one button once setup is done Setup: everything the build needs, in order
Graphics: presets, resolution, filters and colour Keyboard and mouse: two keys for every control
It speaks English, Hebrew, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese (Brazil), Japanese, Russian and Arabic, and starts in your Windows language. The translations have not been checked by native speakers yet: corrections to `launcher/Strings/*.json` are welcome. ## Getting started **You need** - Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, with 8 GB of RAM or more, and about 10 GB of free disk space - [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net), to decrypt the game's `EBOOT.BIN` on your machine - Your own BLES00028 disc, as an ISO or a folder **Then** 1. Download `Soleanna-0.2.0.exe` from the [release](https://github.com/DrummingBird1/sonic06-recomp/releases/tag/v0.2.0) and run it. It asks where to install (a `Soleanna` folder next to it, or one you pick), unpacks the build scripts there, adds a desktop shortcut and opens the launcher. The file is not signed, so Windows may warn about it first: **More info**, then **Run anyway**. Running it again opens your install, and a newer version offers to update it. In a git checkout, run `Sonic06.cmd` instead, which builds the launcher first (it needs the .NET SDK). 2. Open **Setup** and press **Set up everything**. It lists what it will do and asks before it installs or downloads anything. Then it: - installs the missing build tools: LLVM, CMake, Ninja, Git, uv and PowerShell 7 with winget, and Microsoft's C runtime and Windows SDK (about 630 MB, with [xwin](https://github.com/Jake-Shadle/xwin)) once you accept Microsoft's license. Visual Studio is not needed; if you have it with the C++ tools, the build uses it. - copies your disc into `game/` and decrypts it with your RPCS3, - downloads FFmpeg 8 (LGPL) for the movies, SDL2 2.32.10 (zlib) for controllers, and ps3recomp, - translates the game code and builds it. This is the long part: about 17 minutes on a fast PC with 32 GB, longer on a slower one or with less memory. 3. Press **Play**. From a console, `tools/launcher.ps1` has the same steps without the window.
How long the build takes, and how much memory it uses The launcher builds as many files at a time as the memory allows: one with 8 GB, four with 16 GB, ten with 32 GB. On the 20-thread PC it was made on, ten at a time took 14 minutes, and two at a time took 23 minutes with a peak of 5 GB. A PC with less memory has not been tried yet.
## Controls Controllers work through SDL2: Xbox, DualShock 4, DualSense and Switch Pro. Without SDL2 the game falls back to XInput, which sees Xbox-style controllers only. Without a controller, the keyboard and mouse are the pad: | Action | Keys | |---|---| | Move | W A S D or the arrows | | Jump, confirm (✕) | Space, Enter | | Back (○) | Left Ctrl, right mouse button | | □ / △ | E or left mouse button / F | | L1 / R1 · L2 / R2 · R3 | Q / R · 1 / 2 · middle mouse button | | Pause (START) · SELECT | Esc · Tab | | Camera | the mouse | Every control takes up to two keys or mouse buttons on the **Settings** page, which also has the mouse sensitivity, a switch to invert either camera axis, and the stick dead zone. ## Graphics - Window or borderless fullscreen, window size, aspect ratio (keep 16:9 or stretch) and VSync - **Internal resolution**: the size the game draws at, from 1280×720 as on the PS3 up to 3840×2160, or automatic, which matches your window. Set above your window, it is supersampling: every pixel is the average of everything drawn under it, which smooths the edges. - Upscaling filter (smooth, sharp pixels, bicubic, nearest), sharpening, FXAA and texture filtering - Brightness, saturation and contrast - Performance, balanced and quality presets, and one of your own - Shaders are kept on disk after their first use. The first time a scene appears there can be a short pause while its shaders compile; "Compile shaders in the background" removes it, and some objects can then appear a few frames late. - F12 saves a screenshot in `Pictures\Sonic06`. **Measured** | | RTX 4070 SUPER | Intel UHD 770 | |---|---|---| | First story scene | 30 fps, the game's cap | 30 fps | | Wave Ocean, one player | 57–59 fps | not measured | | Wave Ocean, split-screen | 59.5–59.8 fps | about 47 fps | | 3840×2160 internal resolution | as fast as 1280×720 | not measured | Weaker graphics cards and AMD cards have not been tried. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR disc["Your disc
(BLES00028)"] --> copy["The launcher
copies it"] copy --> dec["RPCS3 decrypts
EBOOT.BIN"] dec --> lift["ps3recomp translates
the PowerPC code to C"] lift --> build["clang-cl builds
sonic06.exe"] build --> play["Native x86-64
with Direct3D 12"] ``` The game's PowerPC code is translated ahead of time into C and compiled for x86-64. The PS3's system libraries are reimplemented at a high level, its SPU programs run on host threads, and the RSX graphics commands go through a Direct3D 12 renderer. The port builds on [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp), with 47 changes of its own kept as patches in [`patches/ps3recomp`](patches/ps3recomp). Everything made from the game stays in `game/`, `work/` and `build/` on your PC, and git ignores them. ## FAQ
Is this legal? The repository holds only the project's own code and patches: no SEGA code and no game assets. You need your own copy of the game, and the launcher builds it on your PC. This isn't legal advice, and the project isn't affiliated with or endorsed by SEGA.
Where do I get the game files? From your own PS3 disc (BLES00028), as an ISO or a folder. Please don't ask for game files, or share them, in issues or discussions.
Why not just use RPCS3? RPCS3 is excellent, and this project uses it to decrypt your disc. A native port runs without an emulator, so it can be changed at the source level: so far PC options like supersampling, a mouse camera and remappable keys, and later fixes and mods.
Does it work with the US disc, or the Xbox 360 version? Only the PS3 BLES00028 release has been tried. Other PS3 releases may need changes; the Xbox 360 version is a different program altogether.
Linux, Steam Deck, Mac? Windows 10 and 11 only for now: the renderer is Direct3D 12, and the build uses the Windows toolchain. Nobody has tried it under Proton yet.
Does it fix the original's bugs or loading times? Not yet. It runs the original game logic, so the game's own bugs are still there, and loading times haven't been compared with the PS3.
Will it run on my PC? It has been tested on one PC: an RTX 4070 SUPER, plus a short run on Intel UHD 770 graphics. You need 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, 8 GB of RAM or more and about 10 GB of disk. If you try it, a [hardware report](https://github.com/DrummingBird1/sonic06-recomp/issues/new?template=hardware.md) helps a lot, whether it worked or not.
Was this made with AI? Yes, with a lot of help from Claude, and the commits say so. Every claim in this README and in the docs comes from a run, a log or a measurement.
## Reporting a problem On the **Support** page, **Create a bug report** saves a zip on your desktop: your PC's specs, the setup status and the last game logs. It has no game files, and your Windows user folder is replaced by `%USERPROFILE%`. The launcher then opens a [new issue](https://github.com/DrummingBird1/sonic06-recomp/issues/new?template=bug.md): attach the zip, with what you did and what you saw. ## Contributing The most useful help right now needs no code: a [hardware report](https://github.com/DrummingBird1/sonic06-recomp/issues/new?template=hardware.md) from your PC, or a stage played to the end. For code and translations, start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md): building from source, where things are, the toolkit patches and the tests. [docs/HANDOFF.md](docs/HANDOFF.md) (in Hebrew) has the state of the project and the test recipes, and [docs/PHASE1.md](docs/PHASE1.md) the history of every fix, with its measurements. Keep game files, and anything derived from them, out of git: the ISO, `game/`, `work/` and the built executable. A check on every pull request looks for them. ## Credits - [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) by sp00nznet, the toolkit this port is built on (MIT) - [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net), which decrypts your disc - [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org) for the movies, [SDL2](https://libsdl.org) for controllers, [xwin](https://github.com/Jake-Shadle/xwin) for Microsoft's C runtime and SDK, and [LLVM](https://llvm.org) for the compiler ## License The code in this repository is under the [MIT license](LICENSE). It does not cover the game, which belongs to SEGA, or the tools the launcher downloads, which have their own licenses. Sonic the Hedgehog is a trademark of SEGA, and this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by SEGA.

spu_interp: SPU_INTERP_STATS also lists where the interpreter is entered

Entries are credited to the image that owns the resident code region, so
the list names the lift that is missing them. Entries spread over a code
body mean its lift isn't dispatched at all; a few hot ones inside an
otherwise lifted body are resume points (return addresses after an SPU
interrupt) or function starts the lifter didn't find. In God of War HD the
remaining interpreted SPU time comes from four of them (0xA68 in the
Wws_Job policy module, 0x5318 and 0x87E8 in the mixer job).

06aa9375568380b75c2a35b9bd91959aa321310b.message:
sceNp: tickets, account region and network time answer OFFLINE

sceNpManagerRequestTicket2, GetTicket, GetTicketParam,
GetAccountRegion and GetNetworkTime were not implemented, so their
imports answered CELL_OK with nothing written. A title that asked for a
ticket waited for a GOT_TICKET manager event that never came, and one
that read the region or the time used whatever was in its buffer.

Implement them with RPCS3's argument checks and offline answers: without
a psnr server the NP manager is OFFLINE and so are these
(SCE_NP_ERROR_OFFLINE), and there is never a ticket, so GetTicket
reports a size of 0 and GetTicketParam INVALID_STATE. Signed in to a
psnr server, which issues no tickets, a request is answered at once with
a GOT_TICKET event carrying an error instead of a ticket size; the
region is the fake account's (US, English) and the network time is the
host clock as a CellRtcTick.

06b2292def31186d507aa8cfd38ed487ec220a9c.message:
.github/workflows: pin the five third-party actions to commit SHAs

release.yml fires on `push: tags: ['v*']` with `permissions: contents:
write`, so every action it invokes runs holding a token that can write to
this repo and attach release assets. Referenced by floating major tag, any
of those five actions could be retargeted upstream -- a tag is mutable, and
whoever controls it controls what executes inside that job. Pinning to a
commit SHA makes the referenced code immutable.

Each SHA is the commit the action's current major tag points at, so this
changes no behaviour: the same code runs, it just can no longer be swapped
out from under us. The readable version stays in a trailing comment because
a bare SHA tells a later reader nothing about how stale the pin is.

Only `uses:` lines and their comments change -- 13 references across all
five workflows, no other workflow edits.

(cherry picked from commit 903d023f4a88ace083b0d9843fd3cf71a40f6572)

0e8b9ef2ca28fae79e8e24d2dede074581350fb7.message:
rsx engine: a depth snapshot is the region the texture names

The engine's host depth target is at least canvas-sized
(eng_zdepth_get), but a depth texture covers only the top-left
width x height of it. eng_zdepth_snapshot resolved the whole target and
the Metal resolve sampled it with normalized coordinates, so a 128x160
shadow map in the corner of a 1280x720 target was stretched over the
whole canvas and the lookups landed outside the map.

eng_zdepth_snapshot takes the texture's size and asks the backend for
that region (clamped to the target); a cached snapshot is reused only at
the same size. The Metal resolve reads the depth 1:1 (src.read at the
fragment's pixel) instead of sampling it, so a smaller snapshot is the
top-left region. The Vulkan backend's copy already works this way.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) samples small shadow maps from
canvas-sized zetas. In the port, this together with #424 and the port's
other depth-texture changes removes the dark rectangles on the ground
under shadows; the effect was not isolated per change.

Tests: test_color_feedback_engine (a 128x160 texture over a 256x256 zeta
asks for a 128x160 snapshot), test_metal_depth_readback (a 2x2 snapshot
holds the top-left texels 1:1).

11690a51b493e28537e6b0601ce9bf3cc5016233.message:
spu: fi on 32-bit lanes, frest/frsqest tables without a gather

fi's fixed-point magnitude is 2^32 + d with d = base * 2^19 - step * y,
so one unsigned compare gives the normalisation and 32-bit lanes hold
the rest: no widening to 64-bit lanes and back.

The fraction tables are read with one cross-lane permute per eight
entries and a select on the row, not a gather: on Zen 2 the gather made
frest slower than the scalar loop. Throughput of frest + fi (the
reciprocal pair): GCC 8.5 ns scalar, 9.5 before, 6.4 now; clang 12.1
scalar, 6.1 before, 5.4 now. test_spu_float_est still finds no
mismatch under either compiler.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

118b6281a756697391f178e523a409e0b1f60ce1.message:
cellGcmSys: GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS sets how long a FIFO park may stand

When the drain stops on a self-jump park and `put` has moved, it waits
GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS (50 ms) for the title to patch the park and then follows
`put`. That suits a title that leaves a park standing when it switches
segments. It does not suit one that appends commands right after the
park, moves `put` there and patches the park last: if the patch comes
after the grace, the drain skips the commands in between.

God of War HD does the latter, and while it loads its menu the two stores
have been more than 50 ms apart: the drain jumped from 0x57C40 to put
0x5AA2C, dropped ~11 KB of commands with a fence among them, and the boot
stopped (once in about 45 runs). The RSX itself would wait.

GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS=<ms> now sets the grace; the default is unchanged.

13a7676ba2139314035649dd94cc7bc075de2868.message:
perf(spu): copy only the reserved lines of a PUT under the lock-line lock

A PUT whose span touches a reserved line held the global lock-line lock for
the whole copy, keeping every other SPU's GETLLAR/PUTLLC waiting behind a
multi-line memcpy. Only the reserved lines can be inside a peer's
compare-and-commit window. In a multi-line span the other lines are now
copied first, without the lock, as the unreserved path already copies a
whole span; the locked pass then copies the lines it skipped and notifies
every reserved line, including one reserved after its unlocked copy.

That late line is notified but not copied again: between the two passes a
peer can reserve it, read our bytes and commit, and a second copy would
write that commit back over. Single-line spans keep the single locked copy.

test_spu_lockline_peer: an unaligned PUT over a reserved middle line raises
once, lands exactly, and leaves the bytes either side alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

147e59a79e63cefcf0c2f53fc7314d83f54167e2.message:
rsx_d3d12: pass the FP depth-export bits of SHADER_CONTROL

Draws recorded only the 32-bit-exports bit of SET_SHADER_CONTROL, so a
fragment program that replaces the fragment depth (bits 1-3) was
translated without SV_Depth. God of War HD's resolve pass writes the
scene depth it reads from the 2x-AA depth surface into the resolved
one this way; without it the pass wrote the quad's own depth (0), and
every depth-tested pass after it failed everywhere: the stencil
shadows, the fog, rain, the waterfall mist and the glows.

The draw now records the export bits (32-bit exports and depth export)
as fp_ctrl, part of the pipeline key, and hands them to the
decompiler, which already emits SV_Depth from r1.z.

15265cf84c72fa3def867b7732f498108cd8f863.message:
feat(tools): --handled and --image-ids for SPU program discovery

build_spu_workloads --input discovers every embedded SPU ELF in a carrier,
lifts it and registers it by fingerprint, and reports coverage as complete
only when every program is registered. A title that already registers some
programs another way (a hand-reviewed lift, an interpreter route) could not
use it without registering those twice, and its content-derived image ids
(0x10000000 | sha prefix) cannot be reviewed or kept stable against ids the
title already uses.

--handled JSON {sha256: reason}: such programs are not lifted, count as
covered and carry the reason in inventory.json. --image-ids JSON
{sha256: id}: every registered program takes its pinned id; a discovered
program missing from the map is reported unsupported, so coverage fails
instead of silently assigning one. Entries naming programs that were not
discovered are errors. With both, inventory.json's `complete` is a usable
build gate: a newly discovered SPU program cannot go unregistered silently.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

1530be7cfd1295f9db57e380a3dc2314770a82c1.message:
ppu_lifter: per-function copy of the memory model; PPU_FAST_FP

A guest store goes through vm_base + ea, a byte pointer the compiler
cannot tell apart from the memory-model globals, so the inline load and
store paths reloaded vm_base, ppu_vm_size, ppu_hle_inject_base and the
two enable flags after every store. Each lifted function now copies them
into a local at entry (PPU_MM_SNAP) and its accesses use the copy. They
are all set before guest code runs. The SPU reservation bitmap and the
store watches can change while a function runs, so those are still read
from the globals. Code outside lifted functions keeps vm_read*_inl and
vm_write*_inl, which now take a fresh copy per access.

PPU_FAST_FP, off unless the build defines it, drops the NaN checks in
ppu_fp_bin and ppu_fmadd_core. The host's NaN differs from the PPC one
only in its sign and in which of two NaN operands propagates.

God of War HD, func_001BEFA4, built with FMA3: 6,195 instructions before,
5,855 with the copy, 4,553 with PPU_FAST_FP as well (branches 1,342,
1,063, 583).

test_ppu_lift.py: the conformance driver defines PPU_NO_INLINE_LOADS. Its
vm_read*/vm_write* are its own functions, and its statements do not run
inside a lifted function.

170be32ac21c17795a97d244d8fa559ed47e21f0.message:
ftrace: a span for each HLE import call

PS3_FTRACE recorded syscalls and timer sleeps but not HLE imports, so a
guest thread blocked or busy inside an import (a file read, a SPURS
wait, a lock taken hundreds of thousands of times) showed up nowhere.
ps3_hle_call's exit guard now closes a PS3_FT_HLE span (who = thread,
a = NID, b = guest lr) for calls at least PS3_FTRACE_MIN_US long. With
the trace off it costs one load per call.

This is what found God of War HD's 360 ms frame: 320,355 lwmutex
lock/unlock pairs in it (PS3_FTRACE_MIN_US=0), against 71 in a normal
frame.

1891b8fe718534bef9d143c7b665beb762adbc07.message:
gcm: count the drain's own ring recycle as the JUMP to begin

Once a title has been seen to overrun its ring, the drain recycles the
ring itself when current nears end. A title whose callback also
recycles (cellGcm_fifo_recycle) can be in that callback at the same
moment: it writes its JUMP and put, and only then marks itself waiting,
so a pass that read the mark clear still teleports get to begin. The
callback then waits for a backward JUMP that never comes, because get
is already at begin == put, and gives up after 2 s of no progress.

God of War HD stopped for 2-4 s this way at random points in about
half of the gameplay runs. Counting the teleport as the backward JUMP
ends the callback's wait at once.

1be9e80d533ae0ff253fa169f5d2f5f783a1364d.message:
rsx_shader_msl: compile a vertex program's position invariant

Titles draw the same geometry twice with two different vertex programs,
the second pass testing EQUAL against the depth the first one wrote. The
RSX runs the position arithmetic instruction by instruction, so both
programs land on the same depth. The Metal compiler optimises each
program on its own (it may fuse a multiply and an add into one FMA in one
of them and not in the other), the two depths can then differ in the last
bit, and the EQUAL pass leaves holes.

Resistance: Fall of Man's foliage writes depth through an alpha-tested
program, then colour through one that also lights it, with
SET_DEPTH_FUNC EQUAL.

The translator now marks a vertex program's position [[position,
invariant]], and the Metal backend compiles guest programs with
MTLCompileOptions.preserveInvariance (macOS 11 and later), so programs
that compute the position the same way get the same bits.
PS3RECOMP_MSL_INVARIANT=0 leaves the position as it was.

test_shader_msl checks the vertex program's MSL for
"[[position, invariant]]" (and for "[[position" under
PS3RECOMP_MSL_INVARIANT=0).

1c7c1d914374d59451f5b73421119af501606cfb.message:
rsx engine: a scissored CLEAR_SURFACE clears only the scissor

RSX clears what the surface clip and the scissor let through. The engine
cleared every colour and depth target whole, whatever the scissor said.

Resistance: Fall of Man's co-op split screen renders both views into one
2x1 antialiased 1280x720 scene target: the scissor on the left half, a
colour and depth clear and player 1's view, then the scissor on the right
half, a clear and player 2's view. The second clear wiped player 1's view,
and the left half of the screen was black under the HUD.

sink_clear now asks eng_clear_rect what the clear may write: the clip
from the origin, then the scissor (eng_scissor_rect, the draw path's
scissor code moved into a function). Only a scissor narrower than the
clip makes a clear partial; a clip smaller than the target alone stays a
whole clear, as before. A partial clear goes to two new optional backend
hooks, clear_color_rect and clear_depth_stencil_rect. A backend without
them, or PS3RECOMP_ENG_RECT_CLEAR=0, clears whole as before. A depth clear
that covers everything the zeta was ever bound with (ext_w/ext_h) stays
whole, and a partial depth clear keeps had_write.

The Metal backend records a rectangle clear as a clear record with the
rectangle in its scissor and encodes it as a pass of its own: the
attachment is loaded and a full-target triangle under that scissor writes
the colour, or the depth and stencil with the test always passing. Such a
record is never folded into a pass's load action.

New test_clear_rect in test_rsx_draw_engine (the co-op frame, whole and
empty scissors, a zeta only bound at a small clip, a backend without the
hooks), and test_metal_rect_clears.m (tools/test_metal_rect_clears.py) on
the GPU: a rectangle clear of the right half keeps the left half, for
colour, depth and stencil, and a whole clear after one covers the target.

211cdd81b7f8b2b4e27f2a0fd998ed6351379558.message:
rsx: vertex array addresses wrap at 28 bits

VERTEX_DATA_BASE_OFFSET was added to an array's offset as a plain 32-bit
(or 64-bit) sum. A sum at or past 0x10000000 then pointed past the end
of the location's 256 MB address space, and the fetch read nothing.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) puts its per-frame world lighting
stream (attribute 4, UB256 x4) at base + offset = 0x1Fxxxxxx. Read
unwrapped it decodes as zeros, and buildings, snow and terrain render
saturated blue. Taken modulo 2^28 it is local 0x0Fxxxxxx, where the
stream is, and the world is lit.

rsx_dsp_resolve_vertex_offset (rsx_dispatch.h) masks base + array
offset to 28 bits before the location translation; the element offset
is added after. The fetch plan's stable span and per-element fetch
(rsx_vertex_compact.c) and the live-draw fetches (rsx_live_draw.c) use
it. Sums below 2^28 are unchanged.

test_vertex_fetch_plan: a stream at base + offset = 0x10000100 reads
local 0x100 through both the stable span and the per-element fetch, and
the random plans also draw bases with high bits set.

21c14a650a346b18a4f79c82689ad5c060c34693.message:
rsx_d3d12: guest depth/stencil state and samplers in the guest-FP pipelines

Every guest-FP pipeline had a fixed LESS_EQUAL depth test with writes,
no stencil, and four static samplers (s0 point/clamp for the dbgfont
atlas, s1-s3 linear/wrap), whatever the title set. In God of War HD:

- Its stencil shadow volumes marked nothing, and the shadow pass, a
  full-screen reverse-subtract quad meant only for the marked pixels,
  darkened the whole frame (0.16 -> 0.012 on a lit pixel).
- Depth state ignored: rain and blood particles were rejected.
- Unit 0 was point-sampled and clamped. The soldiers wrap their texture
  atlas (v up to ~2), sampled the transparent bottom row and drew
  nothing over an untextured base; Kratos' tattoo and skirt came out
  white; textures shimmered.

Depth test/write/func and front/back stencil (func, ops, masks) are
packed per draw into a PSO key (rsx_zs_key); the stencil reference is
set per draw. The cull key now always carries the front face, which
two-sided stencil needs with culling off. Samplers are four descriptor
tables built from each unit's TEXTURE_ADDRESS/FILTER/CONTROL0/BORDER
(one cached descriptor per distinct state); units without guest state
keep the old two defaults.

23540a1007e37f28c404c3adfa8ea2d22e188194.message:
rsx_d3d12: cache converted vertices within a draw

Indexed lists (shared vertices), strips and fans (each vertex in up to
three triangles) and indexed quads expand one guest vertex into several
output vertices, and each one was fetched again: 16 attributes, each with
its own address resolve and conversion, for every reference. God of War
HD's gameplay frames expand ~370k vertices through these paths and the
fetch was a third of the frame.

A direct-mapped cache on the low index bits (8192 entries, 2 MB) keeps
the converted 256-byte vertex; a hit is a memcpy. It is dropped at every
draw, since attribute state and the guest arrays may change between
draws. Measured in GoW HD gameplay: vertex time per 20 frames 0.80 s ->
0.29 s, ~9.0 -> ~12.1 fps. VTX_CACHE_CHECK=1 refetches on every lookup
and counts differences: 0 in 312M lookups. VTX_NOCACHE=1 disables it.

SET_STENCIL_MASK (the write mask), SET_TWO_SIDED_STENCIL_TEST_ENABLE and

27745b54d1b60e5232e48a1234a182fc6f52e113.message:
ppu_lifter: inline guest stores, the store side of the inline loads

Every lifted store called vm_write8/16/32/64 out of line. In God of War
HD gameplay those calls were about a fifth of the main thread.

The generated header now has vm_write*_inl beside vm_read*_inl. A store
is done in place when vm_inl_ok accepts the address, no store diagnostic
is armed (vm_inline_st_ok: PPU_WVAL, PPU_WWATCH, PT), the barrier watch
and the null-page sweep are idle, and no SPU holds a reservation on the
line (g_spu_coh_bits). Anything else goes to the out-of-line store as
before. PPU_NO_INLINE_STORES keeps the calls, and the runtime's own files
keep them through PPU_NO_INLINE_LOADS.

Re-lift to pick it up. God of War HD: the main thread runs about 14.8 ms
a frame instead of 16.2 with the HLE lookup cache, vm_write32 is gone
from its profile and vm_write64 is 1.2%. The executable grows from 57 to
87 MB.

fetch read frequency 0 and 1 as an ordinary per-vertex array whatever the
bit. rsx_vertex_freq_plain() names the ordinary case (frequency 0, or 1 with
division); rsx_vertex_element_index, the compact fetch's shared span and the
legacy rsx_fetch_attrib use it.

gameplay that call was 9.5% of the main PPU thread's samples. Most of it

cache lines kept moving to the SPU threads' cores, and each PPU store
missed on them.

  they change.

  the first reservation, and spu_coh_line_reserved tests it inline.
  VM_WRITE_COH in ppu_loader.cpp and ppu_memory.h, and
  vm_block_reserved, use it. s_coh_armed goes away.
- g_spu_coh_bits is one merged definition per program (selectany /
  weak), so the loader fixtures, which link ppu_loader.cpp without
  spu_coherency.c, still link and see no reserved lines.

3099075391d4105873242cd4c3f3555ed43fe397.message:
ppu_lifter: --insn-patches lifts patched instructions as run-time switches

A patch that changes an instruction word in .text does nothing to a
lifted title, which never executes the guest's code words. Making it a
second lift means a second build of the whole title for one changed
word, and a port that wants it optional ships two.

--insn-patches FILE takes {"patches": [{addr, orig, new, guard}, ...]}.
Each patched instruction is lifted in both forms and emitted as

    if (guard) { <new> } else { <orig> }  /* insn patch 0x...: orig -> new */

guard being an int the port defines and sets before the guest runs; each
function that uses a guard declares it extern "C". The original's branch
label and the code around it are unchanged. The lift stops when the
input does not hold orig at addr (a patch set for one build of a title
never lands on another), when a patch is at an address no lifted
function covers, or when new is a branch, sc or CR op (it would need
labels and call targets the function was not lifted with). The patches
reach the parallel workers too; a mismatch there raises instead of
exiting, so the pool does not hang on a dead worker.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) caps its campaign's frame rate in
code. The port lifts the cap's instructions this way and turns 60 fps on
or off from its settings, with one build.

New tools/test_ppu_lifter_insn_patches.py: a patched branch and a
patched li lift in both forms behind their guards, with the guard
declarations and the branch label in place; a wrong orig stops the lift
serially and with two workers; a patch at an address no function covers
stops it. docs/TOOLS.md describes the file with a generic example.

3bbd31bf98ab6e5f5ff8ef3a950891515376942d.message:
fix(ppu_lifter): resolve a jump-table base that was spilled to the stack

A switch dispatcher inside a loop, in a function with high register
pressure, TOC-loads its table base once, spills it, and reloads it at the
dispatch, then reuses the base register for the case address:

    lwz r10,d(r2) ; std r10,s(r1) ; ...
    ld r11,s(r1) ; lwzx r0,r9,r11 ; add r11,r0,r11 ; mtctr r11 ; bctr

discover_jump_tables took the `add` after the table load as r11's nearest
definition, and the stack reload before it was not a TOC load either, so the
dispatcher was dropped and its bctr lifted to an unresolved indirect call. A
retail title's 32-case dispatcher did exactly this; the main thread's case-1
call never ran and it went on with an uninitialised object, then stalled.

The base search now considers only definitions before the table load, and a
stack reload is followed to the nearest preceding store of that slot and the
stored register's TOC load. Over the whole retail executable (217
dispatchers) this adds exactly that dispatcher and changes no other table.
Two vectors in test_ppu_jumptables: the spilled, reused base; a reload of a
slot nothing stored stays unresolved. The first fails without the fix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

3bf0233d06ff7d1d181a80754a0fbf7a16cfc253.message:
cellAudio: WASAPI keeps 60 ms queued, and the mixing thread runs ahead of the guest

On Windows the shared-mode stream asked for a 20 ms device buffer, and the
mixing thread ran at normal priority. A title that keeps every core busy
with PPU and SPU threads takes the CPU from the mixing thread often enough
for those 20 ms to run dry, and each time is an audible click or stutter.
Movie playback (Bink) was the worst case.

- The buffer is 60 ms by default; PS3_AUDIO_BUF_MS=<10..500> sets it.
- The mixing thread asks for THREAD_PRIORITY_TIME_CRITICAL and joins the
  MMCSS "Pro Audio" task when the service is there. avrt.dll is loaded at
  run time, so nothing new is linked.
- AUDIO_RATE=1 also reports underruns: passes that found the device queue
  under half a block (it is about to play silence). The first 64 blocks are
  not counted, while the stream fills.

The guest still sees 256-sample blocks at 48 kHz paced by the device clock;
only how far ahead of the device the mixer may run changes (up to the buffer
size, so up to ~40 ms more output latency by default).

Seen with inFAMOUS 2 on a Ryzen 5 5600 (6 cores, all of them busy): with
the 20 ms buffer its Bink cutscenes stuttered audibly; with this change
they play cleanly. Only the Windows (WASAPI) path is touched.

3caa2509782dc42ecbde0d224cf7937b2ccd2320.message:
rsx_draw_engine: evict the least recently used entry from a full surface or zeta table

g.surfaces and g.zdepths hold 64 entries each and nothing ever took one out.
Once a title has filled them, a new zeta gets no slot: a shadow map rendered
after that has no depth target and reads back as zeros. A full table now
gives up the entry used longest ago (bound, sampled or presented), never one
used this frame or the last nor the last presented surface; with nothing
older the caller gets no slot, as before. The zeta's depth snapshot is now
released when its entry is reused.

3e9311c6287b1220d57e99b3a2a7d3e45a1cf7db.message:
cellGcmSys: forget a park once the walker has left it

The walker gives a self-JUMP park GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS with the same put to
be patched, then resyncs to put. Its record of the park (address, put,
start time) was only cleared by that resync. A park the walker left any
other way -- the title patched it into a JUMP elsewhere, or wrote
commands over it -- kept its start time, so when the walker next stopped
at the same address with the same put, the new park was taken for the
old one. Its grace had run out long before, the resync fired at once,
and the commands the title was about to link in were dropped with the
fences and labels in them. A title that reuses its command blocks
meets its parks again at the same address, frame after frame.

Clear the record as soon as the walker reads anything other than that
park's own self-JUMP: a new park always starts a fresh grace. The three
variables move from the JUMP branch to file scope for that, under the
same names.

41bae9560bd0def7d49aa3675e89fa388e27f74e.message:
rsx_d3d12: stage guest textures in a shared upload ring; LRU slots

Each texture slot had its own committed upload buffer, created with the
texture whenever the slot took a new size or format. In God of War HD's
texture bursts, when new effects first appear, creating resources was
most of the cost: one report interval had 50 new textures, 67 ms of
CreateCommittedResource (41 ms of it for the upload buffers) against
18 ms of decoding.

- Uploads are staged in one persistently mapped upload buffer, 32 MB per
  frame in flight, reset where that frame index's command allocator is
  reset (its copies have finished by then). A texture that does not fit
  in what is left uses the slot's own upload buffer, created on demand.
- A new texture takes an empty slot, else the least recently used one.
  Taking the first slot not used this frame evicted textures the next
  frame needed again: up to 22 a report interval in those bursts.
- 192 slots instead of 96; the game used up to 66.
- A frame with no free slot returned slot -1 and indexed vp_tex with it;
  it now returns -1 to the caller (untextured), as the lookup failure
  path does.

God of War HD: the drain stalls of 67-75 ms in the bursts at 131 and
135-136 s are now under 40 ms. The rendering check passes.

44ec7ee2574b1f94820756e1f08ab22e876e845e.message:
test(ppu_lifter): a spilled-base switch spans its cases past the first blr

A function inventory that ends functions at their first blr leaves a
switch's case blocks, which sit after an early-return blr and share a later
epilogue, outside the declared range. main() already extends the enclosing
function over the cases of every resolved dispatcher; it could not when the
dispatcher itself was dropped, which is what the spilled table base caused.

End-to-end guard: a tiny big-endian ELF64 with such a function (base
TOC-loaded, spilled, reloaded and the register reused for the target; three
offset-table cases past the first blr), lifted by the real main() from a
--functions list cut at the first blr. The bctr must become a computed goto
to internal case labels, the shared epilogue must be inside the function and
the following function must stay separate. Without the spilled-base fix the
dispatcher is not found and four of the six checks fail; no separate extent
change is needed.

45c634575e648b55b2da417f0a17fff1d65aaf92.message:
Merge PR #421: opt-in per-thread MFC engine lookup cache (@tekulvw)

Conflict with #243 (@Kurtisone, wave 2) at the top of mfc_for(). Both PRs
make the same function cheaper, from different ends, and both are kept.

#243's fix is the SPU_PCSAMPLE hoist: the old guard only latched `started`
when the variable was actually set, so with SPU_PCSAMPLE unset every MFC
channel access paid a getenv -- a tenth of the samples in a Twisted Metal
profile. It sets `checked` either way. #421 adds the generation-checked
per-thread cache in front, which returns before the claim lock on a hit.

#421 was written against master, so its hunk carries the pre-#243 `started`
form. Taking it as written would have reverted #243 while keeping its test
-- and #243 ships test_spu_mfc_env_once.c precisely to catch that, so this
one would have failed loudly rather than silently. Resolved anyway as
#421's cache check first, then #243's once-only latch, then the lock.

Composition is fine in that order: the first call misses the cache, falls
through and starts the sampler thread, and later calls that hit the cache
return before a getenv they no longer need to reach.

There is only one mfc_for() in the file -- the Win32 primitives it uses are
shimmed on POSIX by win32_compat.h -- so there is no second copy needing
the same resolution.

4609b3f0bf7db6fdf3a9c36a5037b0be230b8d7c.message:
spu: halt and iret longjmps without unwinding on 64-bit Windows

On 64-bit Windows longjmp unwinds every host frame between it and its
setjmp: RtlUnwindEx, with a function-table lookup and a virtual unwind per
frame. The SPU runtime longjmps on every halt back to spu_run_with_halt (a
SPURS policy module's run ends that way) and on every iret back to the
drain loop that took the interrupt.

spu_jmp_no_unwind() zeroes the jmp_buf's Frame right after setjmp returns
0, which makes longjmp restore the registers directly. These jumps only
cross C frames of the runtime and of lifted code, which have no destructors
or __finally blocks. SPU_LONGJMP_UNWIND=1 keeps the unwinding jump. No
change on other platforms.

48958fefdf401b95dc3c8ad1d1d15461db2eb89a.message:
ppu: a host thread gives its callback stack slot back when it exits

Slots were handed out by a counter and never returned, so once 64 host
threads had ever made a guest callback, every later thread shared the
last slot and the original bug came back. A movie player starts several
threads per movie, so a normal session gets there. Keep a 64-bit in-use
mask instead: a thread takes the lowest free slot on its first callback
and a thread_local owner releases it when the thread exits. Only more
than 64 live threads making callbacks at once share a slot now.

The test first runs 100 short-lived threads one after another, each
making a callback: they all get the first slot back, and the two
concurrent threads after them still get different stacks. Both checks
fail without the release.

4b8de9100d4cc959a5ccf37c51067d416691dc7a.message:
spu: lifted known-target branches tail-call their target (SPU_DIRECT)

A lifted cross-function branch with a known target (br, the conditional
branches, a fall-through into the next function) set the trampoline and
returned, and the drain loop then called the target: a host return, a
loop pass and an indirect call for every transfer. Most of those steps
have nothing for the drain to do. SPU_DIRECT tail-calls the target with
clang's musttail when that is so: the target is not LS 0, this is not
the run's first transfer, the target is not a registered stack-reset
entry (a 1024-byte hint table, set at registration), and no interrupt
is pending with interrupts enabled. Everything else takes the trampoline
as before, and so does every compiler without musttail.

The drain-step diagnostics (SPU_LOCKSTEP, SPU_TAILRET, SPU_PCHIST,
SPU_NO_LS0_END, SPU_EXITTRACE, SPU_STEPTRACE, SPU_JOBDRAIN,
SPURS_PM_FLOW) turn it off, and PS3_SPU_DIRECT=0 does too.

spu_drain_call now restores the enclosing drain's drain_ret_pc on the
way out instead of 0. The enclosing loop used to re-set it on its next
step; with direct tail calls the code after a nested call can run on for
a long time before it takes one.

In the inFAMOUS 2 port (about 18.8k such sites) the open-world walk went
from 34.5 to 36.3 fps (+5.4%), with SPU time per frame from 128 to 121 ms.
