1450314287.readme_excerpt:
# Make Soccer Club Game Project

This is a native PC port of **サカつく プロサッカークラブをつくろう！** (PlayStation 3, SEGA, BLJM61064, 1.03 update).
- The game's PPU code is statically recompiled to C++ with [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp).
- RSX graphics are drawn with Direct3D 12.

> **The game is not included.** You need files from your own disc (BLJM61064) and its 1.03 update.
> All rights to the game and to the data and code in it belong to **SEGA**. This repository is a non-profit fan project unrelated to SEGA, and it contains no game data.
> - The recompiled game code (`recompiled/`, `prx_src/`) and the SPU programs (`spu_jobs/*.elf`) are built locally from each user's own game files.
> - The `patches/recompiled-*.patch` files contain a few lines of recompiled code at the places where hooks are inserted.

## Features

- **60 fps at the original game speed:**
  - The match calculation stays at 30 Hz.
  - Player and ball motion are smoothed between match ticks, including the ball's jumps.
- **Launcher (`Sakatsuku Launcher.exe`):**
  - Settings, saves and backups, and cheats.
  - Player and list editors. They read the running game or a save slot you choose.
  - Korean patch.
- **In game (F2, or L3+R3 on a pad):** the cheat menu, with cheats, players and lists. F7 is double speed and F8 is turbo.
- **Korean patch:** the original files stay untouched; the game reads the Korean files from `game\mods\korean` instead. To turn it on, go to launcher settings → Korean patch, and install it from the patch exe.

## Folders

| Folder | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `game/` (not in the repository) | `EBOOT.ELF` (1.03), `dev_bdvd/` (disc), `dev_hdd0/` (1.03 update), `firmware/` |
| `gamedata/` (not in the repository) | Saves and backups |
| `patches/` | Patches to the `ps3recomp` submodule (`git -C ps3recomp apply ../patches/00NN-*.patch`, in number order, on the pinned v0.18.0 commit) and patches to the recompiled code (`recompiled-*`) |
| `tools/launcher/` | The launcher (C#/WPF, .NET Framework 4) |
| `NOTES.md` | The full record of how the port was made and what was analyzed |

## Download

Ready-to-run builds are on the [Releases](https://github.com/PrimeTimerer/Make-Soccer-Club-Game-Project/releases) page: `Sakatsuku Launcher.exe` and `build-release\SakatsukuRecomp.exe` in one zip. Unzip it, put the files from your own disc in `game\` (see `읽어주세요.txt` in the zip), and run `Sakatsuku Launcher.exe`. The zip contains no game data.

## Build (Windows)

1. Run `git clone --recursive`, then apply the `patches/0001`, `0002`, … patches to `ps3recomp` in order. There is no 0020: the cheat engine is `saka_hooks.c` in this repository.
2. Build `recompiled/`, `prx_src/` and `spu_jobs/` from your own game files, then configure and build `build-release/` with CMake (Release, Ninja, clang-cl). `PORT_SPU_INPUTS` lists `game/EBOOT.ELF`, `game/firmware/libsre.prx`, `game/firmware/libspurs_jq.prx` and the `spu_jobs/cri_*.elf` files.
   - Requires Visual Studio 2022 with clang-cl, Ninja, and Python in `.venv`.
   - The conversion process is recorded in `NOTES.md`.
3. Build `Sakatsuku Launcher.exe` from `tools/launcher/*.cs` with the C# compiler of the .NET Framework 4 that comes with Windows (`csc.exe /target:winexe`, WPF, `Theme.xaml` as a resource, `icon.ico` as the icon).
4. `tools/make_release.ps1` makes the release zip.

## License

- The port's own code and files are under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Anyone may use, change and share them, in mods too, as long as the copyright notice stays.
- `third_party/imgui` (Dear ImGui) and the `ps3recomp` submodule keep their own MIT licenses.
- `cheats/BLJM61064.txt` is converted from a VitaCheat list for the PS Vita version (`PCSG00198.psv`). The original codes are the work of their authors.
- The license does not cover the game or anything taken from it; those belong to SEGA. This includes the recompiled lines in `patches/recompiled-*.patch` and the recompiled game code inside the release exe.

Linux: the port on Linux and the Steam Deck

dod3 builds and runs on Linux (x86-64), tested on a Steam Deck (SteamOS,
RADV): the game boots, plays the attract sequence's in-engine scenes and
the chapter 1 battle on the Vulkan draw engine, with the Deck's pad.

  - The renderer is ps3recomp's Vulkan draw engine in an SDL2 window
    (rsx_vulkan_engine_init); the frame clock runs on the main thread and
    the guest's main thread on one with a 256 MB stack, as on the Mac.
  - The setup and the launcher: an SDL2 window drawn with SDL_Renderer
    (src/ui/ui_linux.cpp, ImGui 1.92.9b's SDL2 and SDL_Renderer2 backends

  - Timer slack 1 ns for every thread (DOD3_TIMERSLACK_NS; DOD3_AB=slack):

    code at x86-64-v3 as with clang-cl, DOD3_PGO in clang's spelling, no

The mouse moves the dragon's shooting cursor (#22)

In the sky the dragon aims with a cursor on the screen, the lock-on's red
ring: holding Square sweeps it over enemies to lock them, and the release
fires a shot at each. The title moves it with the left stick
(ASqex03GamePawnPlayerDragon::UpdateShootingCursor, func_009D26F8, reached
by vtable) and springs it back to the top of the screen once the stick is
let go. The mouse look turns the view through the right stick's values, so
on the keyboard and mouse the cursor only ever answered to WASD and stayed
at the top however the mouse moved: nothing was locked, and the release
fired one shot -- the report in #22 (at 120 fps, but the frame rate was not
the cause: with a pad the lock-on locks and fires at 30 and 120 alike).

src/patches/dragon_cursor.cpp wraps the update: while the cursor is on
screen (IsEnableShootingCursor, func_0096B9A8) the mouse moves it, it stays
where the mouse leaves it (the spring back undone after the update), and a
move past the edge of its rectangle turns the view as before
(src/input/camera.cpp hands the mouse to the cursor meanwhile). A stick --
a pad's, or WASD -- takes it back as soon as it moves it. DOD3_MOUSE=0
leaves the mouse out; DOD3_CURSOR_LOG=1 says when the mouse takes the
cursor or gives it back. DOD3_MOUSE_TEST_FILE="dx dy" adds counts to the
mouse every frame, for tests without the window's focus.

m_xShooting: mouse counts move the cursor, it stays put, and the lock-on
locks a wyvern and fires; a pad with the mouse look on and the mouse still

123bf526d26913cdae31ec5b6bc54dbac29646eb.message:
The launcher updates the port from its GitHub releases (Windows)

When the launcher opens it reads the repository's release list -- not
GitHub's "latest release", which leaves pre-releases out, and every
release so far is one -- on a thread nothing waits for, and offers the
newest release above its own version that has a Windows zip with a
SHA-256 digest: "Update to ..." in the footer opens an Update panel with
the release's notes, Install Update and Release Page.

Install Update (src/install/update.cpp): the zip is downloaded into
.update/ beside the program (WinHTTP), checked against the size and digest
GitHub lists, unpacked (install/zip.h, CRC-checked; the '\' names of
PowerShell's Compress-Archive taken), and each file swapped in: the old one
renamed to <name>.old, which Windows allows for the running program and its
DLLs, the new one moved into its place. A failed swap puts back every file
swapped so far; a failed try leaves nothing. game/, gamedata/ and an
existing dod3.ini are never written. The launcher then starts the new
dod3.exe and closes; the new one's first start removes the .old files and
says what it was updated from. The approach follows King Kong
Recompiled's updater (MIT).

Settings > System > Check for Updates (DOD3_UPDATE_CHECK = 0 turns it
off). The Mac's app is replaced another way: compiled out there for now.

Checked: a build acting as 0.4.0 (DOD3_UPDATE_AS) found 0.4.1 on GitHub,
downloaded it, matched its digest and installed it -- the folder then
equal to the 0.4.1 zip file for file but for dod3.ini, which kept the
player's line -- and started 0.4.1. From a local release
(DOD3_UPDATE_API, DOD3_UPDATE_ZIP): the new build cleaned up after itself
and said "Updated from"; a wrong digest installed nothing; a file held
open mid-swap put every file back (1,736 files unchanged).

1acc3d9bfdc9d8cdbfb2c1bc1725bd9c869ef236.message:
Loading screens: the async loader in the frame limiter's sleep

A chapter's packages come in through Unreal's async loader, which
UObject::StaticTick runs once a frame for 5 ms at most -- and for less:
it gives the frame up whenever the read it needs next has not come
back, though here that takes a fraction of a millisecond. The rest of
the frame the game thread sleeps in the limiter. So a loading screen
lasted a number of frames, not an amount of work: about 265 for the
first chapter's whatever the machine, which is 4.5 s at 60 fps, 2.9 s at
a 120 cap and 9 s at the console's 30.

While no scene is drawn (fewer than 300 draws a frame for three frames:
a loading screen, a menu, a movie) and packages are pending
(GObjAsyncPackages, 0x01A0C2A0), the limiter's sleep goes to the loader:
ProcessAsyncLoading (func_0005E59C) again, for what is left of the
sleep, as often as it gives up. It runs on the game thread at the top
of FEngineLoop::Tick with the guest registers saved around it, from the
hook the deferred purge already has there, and the sleep is shortened by
what it took, so the frame rate is what it was. Without a frame cap, or
in a frame over its budget, there is no sleep and nothing changes.

Chapter 1's loading screen at a 60 cap, hands-off runs: 4.3-4.7 s
(254-269 frames) before, 2.7 s (146 frames) after; with the machine busy
with other work, 5.5 s (283 frames) against 4.0 s (201). What is left is
the title's own sequence: each package is asked for a tick after the
last one is done.

Tried and measured as nothing: a larger time limit in StaticTick (the
float at 0x000C3C24; it is the giving up that paces it, and this
build's loader takes no "use the full time" argument), a spin before an
event-queue wait blocks, and a higher cap while loading on top of this.

DOD3_LOAD_IDLE=0 turns it off; =2 does it with a scene on screen as
well (not the default: untried beyond the first chapter).
DOD3_LOAD_IDLE_LOG=1 says what each second of it did. No re-lift: it
calls a lifted function, it hooks none.

1e6df732b934e2d9c5080d893b9603821d2d7d93.message:
A launcher at each start: Play, the mods, the DLC and the settings

Once the game is installed, dod3.exe (the app on a Mac) opens a launcher
(src/ui/launcher.cpp) before the game: the game's own key art from the
player's install (PS3_GAME/PIC1.PNG; the Dolby and DTS logos and their
trademark lines painted out of the disc's copy) behind the title and a menu
-- Play, Mods, DLC, Settings, Quit -- each section a panel over the art. Set
in Inter 4.1 (SIL Open Font License, third_party/fonts/inter), built into
the executable; everything sized by the window's height. Mouse, keyboard
and controller all work; Enter or the pad's confirm button plays.

- Mods: the Spanish translation and the DLC Undub as cards (what of each is
  installed, Remove), any other mod, and Add Files / Add Folder; a review of
  what was added, the voice pack's requirement and the space, then the
  install on its own thread, as the setup does it.
- DLC: the 20 packs by group, which are in, Add DLC Packages.
- Settings: the in-game pages' rows (one list for both now:
  dod3_setting_rows, settings_menu.cpp), the window size, mouse camera,
  camera speed and the launcher itself, and the keyboard's keys (press one
  to set it). Each change is written to dod3.ini at once, its comments kept
  (src/ui/ini.cpp, which the in-game pages write through too).
- Game Files: the setup, then back.

DOD3_LAUNCHER = 0 in dod3.ini starts the game straight away; Shift held at
start (Option on a Mac, which used to open the setup) opens the launcher
anyway; --setup still opens the setup.

A mod can now be removed by itself, without the update package: installing
one lists its files (game/modfiles/<id>.txt) and keeps aside the update's
own files it replaces, which Remove puts back. Mods installed before keep
the old way. The setup's and launcher's windows are made smaller where the
screen has no room for them.

Tested on Windows on a separate install: the Spanish translation's five
files added, reviewed and installed from the launcher, then removed -- the
update's folder

2673be812a5fcf66fd9fb9019b892b418f9f5b9e.message:
macOS: an update's shader cache reaches a data folder that has one

ps3recomp at 31f490b (Metal: the MSL cache keyed msl-v2; pipeline archives
turned off after a launch that loaded them and built nothing).

The first-run setup copied the package's pipelines.list only when the data
folder had none. The ps3recomp v0.17 merge added two render-state words to
a list line, and the warm-up skips a line of another length, so a player
updating from 0.4.0 kept a list the warm-up read nothing from and compiled
every pipeline in play. The package's lines the player's list lacks are now
appended to it (a final newline added first when it has none).

The packaged app, run over a copy of a 0.4.0 data folder (61
lines in the old form, 541 v1 translations): 251 lines after, the 190 new
ones read by the warm-up ("190 of 190 listed pipelines ready in 0.1 s"),
736 translations; launched again, 251 lines, none twice. Over an empty
data folder: 190 of 190 in 5.1 s, no draw waiting on a compile at the title
or the menus.

27d7a2b3c65a2cc440ad3b10207990916a1ae06d.message:
ps3recomp: ended threads on macOS and Linux, the rest of it

5f7b215 -> d294e93. The thread-slot fix of 0.2.2 gave slots back on every
system; three things on the POSIX side were left as they were and are
done now: a thread nobody can join has its host thread released when it
ends (it kept part of its stack mapped: one for every save, load and
movie pre-load), the thread procedure no longer touches a slot it has
given up, and detaching a thread that ended by the syscall cannot hand
its slot to a new thread while it is still on its way out, which would
have ended the new one in its place. Nothing in the game is known to do
the last.

macOS, PPU_THREAD_SLOTS=24, boot into the chapter 1 battle: 30 threads,
highest id 23, none refused; the runtime's thread check (600 threads of
every kind) passes on macOS and Linux and fails on the old code.

2d002a83ecff26238f51402a9e21091ceff2b120.message:
Aspect Ratio: the pause screen clipped to the HUD's sides

The pause screen's pages park a ring and an arrow just outside the HUD's
16:9 -- off the screen at 16:9 -- and a box wider than 16:9 showed them in
its room at the sides: on the Combo List page a radar ring with an "E" at
the top-left and an arrow at the right edge (found on the Mac). DrawPause
is now bracketed (bridge 17, 7 and 8) and its HUD clipped to the HUD's 1280
across, through the depth as the narrower views' room above and below is.
In play the sides are not clipped: the markers on the view reach there.

2e87a0061f01bcc59898b233381bd923b15c3441.message:
Loads: the package loader's reads natively; DOD3_LOAD_LOG; DOD3_PROF on macOS

What a load waits on, measured on the Mac (start-up, New Game -> prologue):
the game thread, running Unreal's package loader. Reads take ~85 us and the
I/O and inflate threads are idle over 80% of a load; the loader is millions
of tiny reads, each a virtual call to FArchiveAsync::Serialize and the
guest's memcpy, both lifted with a page-table test on every load and store.

src/patches/archive_native.cpp, through the function registry (no re-lift):
- FArchiveAsync::Serialize (func_00141420): bytes already in the precache
  buffer, with the read done, are one memcpy; anything else (outside the
  buffer, a read in flight, pages a diagnostic watches, overlap) runs the
  lifted body. Over 99.9% of reads take the native path.

6099f694dc668396f14ddab9c7f86619f137a65c.message:
Movies: their frames 33.4 ms apart, not 25, 25 and 50

With no render commands to run -- a movie playing -- Unreal's rendering
thread ticks the Bink player itself, at most
GRenderingThreadMaxIdleTickFrequency times a second: 40 in this title
(the float at 0x01991234). A 29.97 fps movie's frames, each shown at the
first tick after it is due, therefore came out on a 25 ms grid: 25, 25,
50 ms, over and over. The console's flip waited for a 60 Hz vblank on
top of that; here a frame is shown as it is made, so the grid was the
pacing.

While a movie plays (the renderer counts its planes' uploads:
g_rsx_video_plane_uploads) the tick is set to 1000 Hz. The player only
decodes and shows a frame when one is due, so nothing more is drawn.
Otherwise the tick is the frame-rate cap (120 uncapped; the title's 40
with its own 30 fps scheme). DOD3_RENDER_TICK_HZ=<hz> holds it at one
value; 40 is the title's.

Measured on the chapter 1 opening movie at a 60 cap with vsync, the
time between movie frames: 1% of them within 3 ms of 33.4 before, 96%
after (standard deviation 1.7 ms). The rendering thread's load is the
same 35% of a core: its idle loop spins either way.

79546d2ab6bf9a518ebc3fd47cc31651afc70896.message:
ps3recomp: even presents, the system clock

Fork 8b9a035 and 480da8d.

The clock: the slot list showed a save of October 2026 as made in
December 1933. On Windows the game was told the time since the PC was
started in place of the time since 1970, and on every platform the call
for the time zone did not exist, so the game's C library shifted that by
whatever its variables held. Both are the host's now. The date is kept
inside the save (a 64-bit count of seconds at +0x48 of PAYLOAD; the save
at hand holds 348,789, four days), so a save made before this shows the
5th of January 1970 until the game writes it again. PS3_TIME_LOG=1, in
the debugging guide, prints what the game was told.

The pacer (rsx_present_pace) does nothing until a host turns it on; the
next commit does. It is a new source file in the fork, so CMake has to
run again on an existing build folder. No re-lift is needed.

90099b4ee903aa7df67a905a94c59a28cbeeb789.message:
ps3recomp: a thread that has ended gives its slot back

Fork 5f7b215. A session stopped with a black screen a quarter of an hour
into the story, on Windows, as a level ended: the game's thread waited
for a physics step and there was no physics thread. The thread table
has 64 slots; the game makes two physics threads for every level, two
more for every movie and one for each save, load and movie pre-load,
and no slot was ever used twice. The sixty-fifth thread was refused,
the game did not check, and waited for it.

Hands-off from boot into chapter 1: 31 threads made in each case, the
highest thread id 31 before and 23 now (the physics pair in the same two
slots at every level change, save, load, DLC check and movie pre-load
sharing one), and the same run completes on a table of 24 with
PPU_THREAD_SLOTS=24, which the debugging guide now lists.

macOS and Linux freed the threads that are joined (physics, movies) and

The setup's moves wait out a scanner holding a new file

Installing the disc over an install, the move of the fresh 15 GB copy into

right after thousands of files are written, a scanner (Windows Defender,

aa4936901a6a916cb952f6101283175d71d4e700.message:
Pipeline states built ahead at start-up; a tool for the shipped shader cache

ps3recomp at 26ca8af: the D3D12 engine records each pipeline state it
builds in cache/dxbc/pipelines.bin and builds the listed ones on
low-priority threads at start-up, so the draw that first needs one no longer
waits a frame or more for the driver's compile (one level, played twice:
1,416 ms of pipeline builds in play without the list, 62 ms with it; 26
draws skipped in play, then 5). And the PPU store-conditional fails, as on
the Cell, when an SPU rewrote its line while it waited for the lock-line
lock: the game's PhysX task queues let about 2,000 such stores through in
four minutes of a battle on four host threads.

tools/shader_cache.py: `build` compiles shader dumps into the bytecode cache
exactly as the engine does (byte for byte the same files), `list` counts,
checks against a cache and merges pipeline lists. The upstream merge changed
the shader text, so the 0.4.0 cache holds only 584 of the 1,494 programs a
sweep of every chapter met; the next release's cache is to be rebuilt this
way, with the list its play-throughs record.

c01e96c6a88df4941f1129ff6ca950777081be17.message:
Frame rate: a cap is shown at even intervals, and Adaptive

The camera juddered at any frame rate, with a controller as with the
mouse. The camera's own law holds frame by frame (the turn is what the
stick and the frame's time say it should be); what was uneven was the
time each frame stayed on screen.

Capped: the game's frames are exactly 16.67 ms of simulation at 60, but
they were presented 13 to 20 ms apart. The renderer's pacer (fork
8b9a035) is turned on whenever a cap is in force, and told the cap's
period: at 60, 1 to 7% of the presents are now more than 15% off the one
before, against 40 to 65%.

Uncapped: the frames take 5 to 20 ms each, half of them more than 15%
off the one before, and each is simulated for the time the last one
took, so a steady turn comes out at 60 to 210 degrees a second from
frame to frame. There is no slack to pace that in. DOD3_FPS=adaptive
(Frame Rate: Adaptive on the Graphics Settings page) is a cap that
follows the scene: the highest of 120, 110, 100, 90, 80, 72, 66, 60, 55,
50, 45, 40, 36, 33, 30 at which 95 in 100 of the last second and a
half's frames were made in time with 4% to spare. It steps down at once
and up after two seconds within reach, so it stays put for long
stretches and the pacer can do its work. In a played session it sat at
120 with 0 to 2% of the presents more than 15% off the one before (the
arrivals: 44 to 53%); on a loaded machine, about 3% at 60 to 70 where
uncapped averaged 115 to 120 on paper.

DOD3_FPS_ADAPT=<quantile>,<margin>,<seconds> and DOD3_FPS_ADAPT_LOG=1
are in the debugging guide with RSX_PRESENT_PACE_LOG.

Not measured: v-sync on with a cap that does not divide the display's
refresh rate.

Draw Distance (DOD3_DRAW_DISTANCE = 2, 3, 5, 10): the engine's
MaxDrawDistanceScale, which the scene renderer multiplies every
primitive's own cull distance by each frame. Live. It moves the props,
bushes and small trees that have such a distance.

Tree Detail (DOD3_TREE_LOD = 2, 3, 5, 10): the SpeedTrees have four
distances of their own (the model's detail from 500 to 6,000 units, the
flat billboard from 8,000, nothing past 12,000 to 16,000 for most trees
of the first chapter's coast), which the draw distance does not reach.
They are copied into the tree's scene proxy when it is made, and read
from there once, as the tree's meshes are put in the draw lists. So the
proxy's are multiplied as it is made: USpeedTreeComponent::
CreateSceneProxy (func_00817FD4, a virtual and the constructor's only
caller) is replaced in the function registry. Trees already in the
scene keep what they were added with -- writing a live proxy changes
nothing on screen, which is why earlier attempts at this from outside
showed nothing -- so the row says "from the next area".

Checked in three runs to the same spot on the coast's landing stage:
at 0.2 the woods on either side are gone, at 1 the pines on the cliff
are their soft billboards, at 3 they are their models and a tree past
the far bank is drawn that was not. And set from the page itself to 3
before the level was loaded: all 64 trees' proxies hold three times
their components' distances.

What still appears late is what the game has not loaded yet: the further
parts of a level are streamed in as the player nears them.

1.01 only (the addresses are not mapped for 1.00, where the tree row is
left out). No re-lift is needed.

da6a1a510cf4d30c0393f7f16a17add079c3a177.message:
Aspect Ratio: the HUD fitted into the view; 16:10; movies and the title as on that screen

In a view boxed to another shape the HUD's canvas is the view's: moved to
its corner and as big as it is. The HUD lays itself out on 1280x720 whatever
the canvas, so at 21:9 it ran off the bottom of the view. Now
Sqex03GameHUD.DrawHUD hands its canvas to the port (bridge 17) and
src/patches/hud_aspect.cpp makes the canvas's top transform a scale and a
move that put the 16:9 HUD in the middle of the view, as big as fits; the
canvas reports 1280x720 meanwhile, as the HUD's native code places some
things by its size. The markers placed on the view (enemy gauges, lock-on,
talk icons) are mapped back through it in hooks on UCanvas::execProject and
ASqex03GameHUD::CalcTransformPosition, so they stay on their targets. The
30 full-screen layers of the HUD's scripts -- fades, dimming, filters, the
dying overlay, the screen-split effect -- are marked by the script patch and
cover the whole view. A narrower view's room above and below the HUD is
clipped (through the depth, the 2D canvas having no depth test): the HUD
keeps a bar parked above itself there.

The HUD's begin also tells the present the view's shape each frame, and the
setting the screen's (ps3recomp: rsx_present_set_screen_aspect), so that
the title, menus and movies are 16:9 in the middle of that screen: a 16:9
window set to 21:9 shows what a 21:9 screen would.

16:10 is a choice of the setting (and auto takes a window narrower than
16:9): the view keeps its FOV and is taller. The fit only runs when the
setting has boxed the view, so 16:9 is as it was.

1.00 keeps the HUD as it was (the hooks' addresses are 1.01's) and gets the
present's half. Replay regression: 110 of 110 frames identical.

df1c0b49f15cc73df2c64de6f90f3c5a69969912.message:
The setup takes the US PSN release's game package in place of the disc

Drakengard 3 was also sold on PSN in the US (NPUB31251). Its game package,
UP0082-NPUB31251_00-DOD3MAINGAME0000 (1.00), holds the disc's files but for
four: an executable of its own build, COALESCED_INT.BIN as an .EDAT, both
under the buyer's licence, a PARAM.SFO of its own, and a PS3TOC.TXT whose
one line names that .EDAT. The port runs the disc release's 1.01 executable
and reads the config from its update, so neither locked file is wanted.

The setup now takes the package in the disc's slot, checked by the SHA-1 its
footer carries, and unpacks it as the disc is laid out (PS3_GAME/...),
leaving out its EBOOT.BIN and the .EDAT; the file list's line goes back to
the disc's, which makes the list the disc's own (checked by its hash). The
update is the disc release's for either: the PSN release's own 1.01 update
and the European release (NPEB01407, a build of its own) are refused with
what to add instead. An installed game is now told by its PARAM.SFO and
PS3TOC.TXT, not by EBOOT.BIN, which a 1.01 build never reads there.

pkg_extract takes an optional layout naming where each entry goes (or that
it is left out). The setup's pages, README.md, docs/PLAYING.md and
docs/BUILDING.md name the PSN package beside the disc.

Tested: an install from the package with the update and a DLC pack has
8,791 files identical to a disc install's, the others as above; a new game
from it reaches the chapter 1 battle at 60 fps, the settings pages in place
and the config read from the update. The disc installed over it, and the
package over that, each swap the game and keep the update and the DLC.

e88a969901b8e5a7116191c79acfbd6f9e301e97.message:
The frame to the GPU while it is recorded: the heaviest parts ~15% faster

ps3recomp at a27ad6e: the D3D12 engine submits every 256 records instead of
at fences and the present only. The level sweep found every part under the
120 cap held up in one place, the walker waiting 2-5 ms a frame at the fence
after the occlusion queries for a frame of GPU work it had only just handed
over. Paired runs: one part 95 -> 109 fps (91 -> 107 at 4K), the heaviest
77 -> 89, a part at the cap unchanged.

DOD3_AB=earlysubmit switches it in a run (RSX_SUBMIT_EVERY sets the size,
0 turns it off). TECHNICAL.md drops "submitting partial batches early" from
what measured as no gain: the present's pacing counted submits, and a split
in the draw call read the next chain's constants.

f9d4b21d29657725dca40f68bced2c5740d51ab1.message:
Motion Blur and Post-Processing set Off stay off (#12)

The title writes both switches of FSystemSettings itself, through four
small setters it reaches by pointer (func_00A54554/func_00A54578 set one to
r4, func_00A54720/func_00A5474C flip it). In chapter 1's play and cutscenes
it set DepthOfField back to 1 every frame (func_00A54B58, the setter's
vtable slot 0x38C), so Post-Processing Off -- depth of field, bloom and the
colour grade, which DepthOfField gates -- lasted until the next frame.
MotionBlur it set to 0 once, at the title.

src/patches/sysset.cpp wraps the four: each runs as the title's, and a
switch the player has turned off is put back to off after it.
DOD3_SYSSET_LOG=1 says when the title writes one. The same moments with
Post-Processing Off now show the scene without the bloom and grade.

1450364731.readme_excerpt:
# Drakengard 3 Recompiled **A native port of the PlayStation 3 game Drakengard 3.** [![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/soyjxck/dod3-recomp?include_prereleases&label=release)](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/releases) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/total?label=downloads)](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/releases) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/soyjxck/dod3-recomp?style=flat)](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/stargazers) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)](LICENSE) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/soyjxck/dod3-recomp?label=last%20commit)](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/commits/main) [![Open issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/soyjxck/dod3-recomp?label=issues)](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/issues) [![Support on Ko-fi](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ko--fi-support-FF5E5B?logo=kofi&logoColor=white)](https://ko-fi.com/soyjack) ![Windows x64](https://img.shields.io/badge/Windows-x64-0078D6) ![Linux x64](https://img.shields.io/badge/Linux-x64-FCC624?logo=linux&logoColor=black) ![macOS arm64](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-arm64-000000?logo=apple&logoColor=white) ![Direct3D 12](https://img.shields.io/badge/Direct3D-12-5E5E5E) ![Vulkan](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vulkan-AC162C?logo=vulkan&logoColor=white) ![Metal](https://img.shields.io/badge/Metal-147EFB) ### [Download](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/releases) · [Installing](#installing) · [Playing guide](docs/PLAYING.md) [Report an issue](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/issues) · [Build from source](#building) · [Technical notes](docs/TECHNICAL.md) · [Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/soyjack)
## Contents - [About](#about) - [Installing](#installing) - [Building](#building) - [Status](#status) - [How it fits together](#how-it-fits-together) - [Legal](#legal) - [Credits](#credits) ## About A native PC port of **Drakengard 3** (Drag-On Dragoon 3, PlayStation 3, BLUS31197) for Windows, macOS and Linux, made by static recompilation of the game's code on the [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) toolkit. The game's PowerPC and SPU code is translated to C++ ahead of time and built into a normal executable, with the PS3's system libraries replaced by native implementations and the RSX graphics by Direct3D 12, Metal or Vulkan. There is no emulation at run time. ![The start of the game, running natively on Windows](docs/images/opening.jpg) **Nothing of the game is in this repository.** You need your own copy of Drakengard 3: the US disc and the game's 1.01 update, plus whatever DLC you own. The installer takes them from there. If this helped you, consider [buying me a coffee](https://ko-fi.com/soyjack) ## Installing What you need: - A PC with Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), a GPU with Direct3D 12 and a CPU with AVX2 (Intel Haswell / AMD Zen or newer), or a Mac with Apple silicon on macOS 13 or newer. About 16 GB of free disk space, 10 GB more for the Japanese voice pack and about 3 GB for the Spanish translation. - Your copy of the game, US release, as either: - the disc (BLUS31197), dumped to a folder or a **decrypted** `.iso` ([PS3 Disc Dumper](https://github.com/13xforever/ps3-disc-dumper) writes one; an image from an ordinary disc tool is still encrypted and is refused), or - the PSN release (NPUB31251): the game's package as a PlayStation 3 downloads it (`UP0082-NPUB31251_00-DOD3MAINGAME0000`, 15.6 GB). No licence files are needed. Other regions, the European PSN release among them, are refused. - The 1.01 update, as the package a PlayStation 3 downloads: `UP0082-BLUS31197_00-DOD3PATCH0000000-A0101-V0101-PE.pkg`. This is the disc release's update; the PSN release takes it too. - Optionally, the DLC packages you own (`UP0082-NPUB31251_00-...`). No licence files are needed. - Optionally, mods: the Spanish fan translation and the DLC Undub (Japanese voices for the DLC chapters), which the launcher installs on its Mods page; see [docs/PLAYING.md](docs/PLAYING.md#mods). Windows: 1. Download `dod3-recomp--win64.zip` from the [releases](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/releases) and unzip it anywhere (not inside Program Files). 2. Run `dod3.exe`. SmartScreen may warn the first time, as the program is not signed: "More info", then "Run anyway". 3. In the setup that opens, add your files (the disc image or folder, or the PSN game package; the update package; any DLC packages) with Add Files / Add Folder, in any order, then Install. The game's files are copied into the `game` folder next to `dod3.exe` (a few minutes). 4. Play. From then on `dod3.exe` opens the launcher: Play, and the game's mods, DLC and settings. macOS: 1. Download `dod3-recomp--macos-arm64.zip` from the [releases](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/releases), unzip it and move "Drakengard 3 Recompiled.app" to Applications. 2. The app is not notarised, so macOS refuses it the first time. On macOS 15 and later: open it once, then allow it in System Settings > Privacy & Security ("Open Anyway"). On macOS 13 and 14: Control-click the app, choose Open, then Open again. 3. The setup opens as on Windows. The game's files go into `~/Library/Application Support/Drakengard 3 Recompiled`. Linux (x86-64; the Steam Deck included), experimental: 1. Download `dod3-recomp--linux-x86_64.tar.gz` from the [releases](https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp/releases) and unpack it anywhere you can write to. It needs a Vulkan 1.3 driver (Mesa's RADV, ANV, or NVIDIA's), SDL2 (`sdl2` or `sdl2-compat`; SteamOS has it) and glibc 2.38 or newer. 2. Run `dod3` in the folder. The setup opens as on Windows, and the game's files are copied into the `game` folder beside it. Add Files uses the desktop's picker (kdialog or zenity); without either, `./dod3 --install ` in a terminal does the same. 3. On a Steam Deck: install from Desktop Mode, then add `dod3` to Steam as a non-Steam game to play it in Game Mode. `dod3.log` beside it says what happened if it does not start. Settings (resolution, display mode, frame-rate cap, anti-aliasing, field of view, draw distance, skipping the intro, the keyboard's keys) are in the launcher's Settings, in the game's own Settings menu (Graphics Settings, System Settings, Advanced Graphics and Picture Settings), or in `dod3.ini`. [docs/PLAYING.md](docs/PLAYING.md) has the controls, the saves, the Japanese voices, and what to do if something goes wrong. ## Building The port is built in three steps: the game's PPU code is lifted to C++, its SPU programs are lifted, and the whole is compiled with CMake. Lifting needs the game's executable, so you need your own copy of the game first. 1. **Toolchain.** Windows: Visual Studio 2022 or newer (the Build Tools are enough, with "Desktop development with C++" and the Windows SDK), LLVM with clang-cl, CMake 3.20 or later, Ninja, Python 3.11 or later, Git for Windows, and vcpkg with `zlib:x64-windows` and `sdl2:x64-windows` (`VCPKG_ROOT`, or `C:\vcpkg`). macOS: Xcode's command-line tools and, from Homebrew, `cmake ninja python zlib sdl2 glslang spirv-cross`. Linux: Clang, CMake, Ninja, Python and the SDL2, zlib, Vulkan and glslang development files (Ubuntu 24.04 package names, and the Steam Deck's distrobox, in [docs/BUILDING.md](docs/BUILDING.md#prerequisites)). All three also need a decrypted `libsre.prx` from the PS3 firmware ([docs/BUILDING.md](docs/BUILDING.md#the-games-files)). 2. **The sources.** ```sh git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/soyjxck/dod3-recomp cd dod3-recomp python3 -m venv .venv # py -3 -m venv .venv on Windows .venv/bin/pip install -r ps3recomp/tools/requirements.txt -r tools/requirements.txt ``` 3. **The game's files.** Any built `dod3` (a release's, or one from another machine) installs the game into the repository root, which decrypts the update's executable to `elf/EBOOT_101.ELF` and lays out `game/disc`: ```sh DOD3_INSTALL_BASE=. path/to/dod3 --install [DLC .pkg ...] ``` 4. **Lift the PPU code** (a few minutes; about 550 MB of C++ in `recompiled_101/`): ```sh .venv/bin/python ps3recomp/tools/ppu_loader.py elf/EBOOT_101.ELF -o out/v101/ .venv/bin/python ps3recomp/tools/ppu_lifter.py elf/EBOOT_101.ELF \ --functions out/v101/EBOOT_101.functions.json \ --hle-stubs out/v101/EBOOT_101.imports.json \ --code-end 0x157fc00 \ --nonvolatile-locals \ --hook 0x000C1E50 --hook 0x00EE7728 --hook 0x00272E58 \ -o recompiled_101/ ``` 5. **Lift the SPU programs** into `spu/`, with the native fast paths hooked in: ```sh tools/lift_spu.sh ``` 6. **Compile.** Windows, from a plain command prompt (the script finds Visual Studio, LLVM, CMake and vcpkg): ```bat tools\build_win.bat ``` macOS: ```sh cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build ``` A clean build takes about 15 minutes, nearly all of it the lifted code. 7. **Run** the game installed in the repository root: ```sh DOD3_INSTALL_BASE=. build/dod3 ``` [docs/BUILDING.md](docs/BUILDING.md) has the CMake options, the developer run form, packaging a release and regenerating the committed tables; [docs/TECHNICAL.md](docs/TECHNICAL.md) how the port works; [docs/DEBUGGING.md](docs/DEBUGGING.md) the switches, profiling and the regression tests; [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) the layout of the tree and the conventions. ## Status | | | |---|---| | Windows 10/11, Direct3D 12 | Playable. 60 fps at 4K on an RTX 4090 / i9-13900K (chapter 1 through the heavy destruction scene, open areas, the village); 120 fps holds at lower resolutions | | Windows, Vulkan | Experimental (`RSX_BACKEND = vulkan`) | | Linux, Vulkan | Experimental. Tested on a Steam Deck (SteamOS, Desktop Mode): the chapter 1 battle at 55-65 fps uncapped, the heaviest moments in the 40s; Gaming Mode not yet tried | | macOS 13+, Apple silicon, Metal | Playable. 60 fps at 1080p in battle on an M1 Pro | | Game version | The 1.01 update (required) | | DLC | All 20 packs, including the Japanese voice pack | What the port adds over the original: any internal resolution (supersampling included), windowed, borderless or full-screen display, wider screens (16:10, 21:9, 32:9), a frame-rate cap of your choice (60 and 120 tested) or one that follows the scene, with the frames shown at even intervals, FXAA or MSAA, anisotropic filtering, a wider field of view, sharper shadows, a longer draw distance for scenery and for trees, HDR (Windows and macOS: the light the game clips at white goes up to your display's peak), a depth of field and bloom drawn smoothly at high resolutions, depth of field and the blood on the screen each on or off, skipping the intro logos and movie, pausing or muting when the window is in the background, keyboard and mouse, trophies (a pop-up as you earn one, and their list in the launcher), cheats, and the button prompts of the pad you hold -- set in the launcher, or in a Graphics Settings, a System Settings, an Advanced Graphics and a Picture Settings page added to the game's own Settings menu. The launcher also installs your DLC and two fan-made mods (the Spanish translation, with the added pages in Spanish, and the DLC Undub), and on Windows updates the port from its releases. Known issues: the game has been tested on few machines, and at 16:10, 21:9 and 32:9 some of the HUD is still out of place. ## How it fits together ``` elf/EBOOT_101.ELF --ppu_loader/ppu_lifter--> recompiled_101/*.cpp (the game's PPU code as C++) SPU programs --tools/lift_spu.sh------> spu/ (SPURS tasks, jobs, the audio DSP) src/ ---------------------------> the port: the runner, native fast paths, the settings menu, the installer ps3recomp/ ---------------------------> runtime, HLE libraries, the RSX draw engine and its backends ``` The executable `dod3` installs the game from your files (a Dear ImGui setup, `src/install/` and `src/ui/`), then opens a launcher for its mods, DLC and settings, and runs it. ## Legal This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Square Enix, Access Games or Sony Interactive Entertainment. Drakengard 3 and all of its assets belong to their owners; none are included, and the port only runs from a copy of the game you own. The code in this repository is under the [MIT License](LICENSE). It builds on ps3recomp (MIT) and includes Dear ImGui (MIT) and the Inter typeface (SIL Open Font License 1.1); see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). ## Credits - [ps3recomp](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp) by sp00nznet: the recompiler, the runtime and the PS3 library implementations. This port's changes to it are in the [soyjxck/ps3recomp](https://github.com/soyjxck/ps3recomp) fork, the `ps3recomp/` submodule. - [RPCS3](https://rpcs3.net): the reference for much of the PS3's behaviour, and the source of two techniques used here (write-watched texture memory, a guest clock that stops while the game is paused). - [XenonRecomp](https://github.com/hedge-dev/XenonRecomp) and [Unleashed Recompiled](https://github.com/hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp): the model for a recompiled port, and for its installer. - [Dear ImGui](https://github.com/ocornut/imgui) by Omar Cornut: the setup's and the launcher's user interface. - [Inter](https://github.com/rsms/inter) by Rasmus Andersson: their typeface. - The mods the launcher installs are their authors' work: the Spanish translation by Traducciones Vacuno ([TraduSquare](https://tradusquare.es)), the DLC Undub by Canzah and Slow.

spu_interp: SPU_INTERP_STATS also lists where the interpreter is entered

Entries are credited to the image that owns the resident code region, so
the list names the lift that is missing them. Entries spread over a code
body mean its lift isn't dispatched at all; a few hot ones inside an
otherwise lifted body are resume points (return addresses after an SPU
interrupt) or function starts the lifter didn't find. In God of War HD the
remaining interpreted SPU time comes from four of them (0xA68 in the
Wws_Job policy module, 0x5318 and 0x87E8 in the mixer job).

06aa9375568380b75c2a35b9bd91959aa321310b.message:
sceNp: tickets, account region and network time answer OFFLINE

GetAccountRegion and GetNetworkTime were not implemented, so their
imports answered CELL_OK with nothing written. A title that asked for a

that read the region or the time used whatever was in its buffer.

Implement them with RPCS3's argument checks and offline answers: without
a psnr server the NP manager is OFFLINE and so are these
(SCE_NP_ERROR_OFFLINE), and there is never a ticket, so GetTicket
reports a size of 0 and GetTicketParam INVALID_STATE. Signed in to a
psnr server, which issues no tickets, a request is answered at once with
a GOT_TICKET event carrying an error instead of a ticket size; the
region is the fake account's (US, English) and the network time is the
host clock as a CellRtcTick.

06b2292def31186d507aa8cfd38ed487ec220a9c.message:
.github/workflows: pin the five third-party actions to commit SHAs

release.yml fires on `push: tags: ['v*']` with `permissions: contents:
write`, so every action it invokes runs holding a token that can write to
this repo and attach release assets. Referenced by floating major tag, any
of those five actions could be retargeted upstream -- a tag is mutable, and
whoever controls it controls what executes inside that job. Pinning to a
commit SHA makes the referenced code immutable.

Each SHA is the commit the action's current major tag points at, so this
changes no behaviour: the same code runs, it just can no longer be swapped
out from under us. The readable version stays in a trailing comment because
a bare SHA tells a later reader nothing about how stale the pin is.

Only `uses:` lines and their comments change -- 13 references across all
five workflows, no other workflow edits.

(cherry picked from commit 903d023f4a88ace083b0d9843fd3cf71a40f6572)

0e8b9ef2ca28fae79e8e24d2dede074581350fb7.message:
rsx engine: a depth snapshot is the region the texture names

The engine's host depth target is at least canvas-sized
(eng_zdepth_get), but a depth texture covers only the top-left
width x height of it. eng_zdepth_snapshot resolved the whole target and
the Metal resolve sampled it with normalized coordinates, so a 128x160
shadow map in the corner of a 1280x720 target was stretched over the
whole canvas and the lookups landed outside the map.

eng_zdepth_snapshot takes the texture's size and asks the backend for
that region (clamped to the target); a cached snapshot is reused only at
the same size. The Metal resolve reads the depth 1:1 (src.read at the
fragment's pixel) instead of sampling it, so a smaller snapshot is the
top-left region. The Vulkan backend's copy already works this way.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) samples small shadow maps from
canvas-sized zetas. In the port, this together with #424 and the port's
other depth-texture changes removes the dark rectangles on the ground
under shadows; the effect was not isolated per change.

Tests: test_color_feedback_engine (a 128x160 texture over a 256x256 zeta
asks for a 128x160 snapshot), test_metal_depth_readback (a 2x2 snapshot
holds the top-left texels 1:1).

118b6281a756697391f178e523a409e0b1f60ce1.message:
cellGcmSys: GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS sets how long a FIFO park may stand

When the drain stops on a self-jump park and `put` has moved, it waits
GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS (50 ms) for the title to patch the park and then follows
`put`. That suits a title that leaves a park standing when it switches
segments. It does not suit one that appends commands right after the
park, moves `put` there and patches the park last: if the patch comes
after the grace, the drain skips the commands in between.

God of War HD does the latter, and while it loads its menu the two stores
have been more than 50 ms apart: the drain jumped from 0x57C40 to put
0x5AA2C, dropped ~11 KB of commands with a fence among them, and the boot
stopped (once in about 45 runs). The RSX itself would wait.

GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS=<ms> now sets the grace; the default is unchanged.

147e59a79e63cefcf0c2f53fc7314d83f54167e2.message:
rsx_d3d12: pass the FP depth-export bits of SHADER_CONTROL

Draws recorded only the 32-bit-exports bit of SET_SHADER_CONTROL, so a
fragment program that replaces the fragment depth (bits 1-3) was
translated without SV_Depth. God of War HD's resolve pass writes the
scene depth it reads from the 2x-AA depth surface into the resolved
one this way; without it the pass wrote the quad's own depth (0), and
every depth-tested pass after it failed everywhere: the stencil
shadows, the fog, rain, the waterfall mist and the glows.

The draw now records the export bits (32-bit exports and depth export)
as fp_ctrl, part of the pipeline key, and hands them to the
decompiler, which already emits SV_Depth from r1.z.

1530be7cfd1295f9db57e380a3dc2314770a82c1.message:
ppu_lifter: per-function copy of the memory model; PPU_FAST_FP

A guest store goes through vm_base + ea, a byte pointer the compiler
cannot tell apart from the memory-model globals, so the inline load and
store paths reloaded vm_base, ppu_vm_size, ppu_hle_inject_base and the
two enable flags after every store. Each lifted function now copies them
into a local at entry (PPU_MM_SNAP) and its accesses use the copy. They
are all set before guest code runs. The SPU reservation bitmap and the
store watches can change while a function runs, so those are still read
from the globals. Code outside lifted functions keeps vm_read*_inl and
vm_write*_inl, which now take a fresh copy per access.

PPU_FAST_FP, off unless the build defines it, drops the NaN checks in
ppu_fp_bin and ppu_fmadd_core. The host's NaN differs from the PPC one
only in its sign and in which of two NaN operands propagates.

God of War HD, func_001BEFA4, built with FMA3: 6,195 instructions before,
5,855 with the copy, 4,553 with PPU_FAST_FP as well (branches 1,342,
1,063, 583).

test_ppu_lift.py: the conformance driver defines PPU_NO_INLINE_LOADS. Its
vm_read*/vm_write* are its own functions, and its statements do not run
inside a lifted function.

159a47de817b1ef3206f4df7ddab80ceb0312801.message:
ps3_indirect_call: one thread-local lookup a call, not two

On macOS every access to a __thread variable is a call to tlv_get_addr, and
the fast path made two a call: the recursion depth before it and the
trampoline after it. Unreal's package loader is virtual calls through and
through, and in a load tlv_get_addr was up to a fifth of the game thread's
samples (5-20%, in-process sampler). Both variables are this file's
thread-locals, so they are one per-thread block at a fixed distance; the
fast path looks up the trampoline's address once and reaches the depth by
that distance (worked out at the first call). Same behaviour; the depth
test (tools/test_ppu_dispatch_depth.py) passes.

Measured on the Mac, Drakengard 3 start-up to the title, interleaved runs:
3.23 -> 3.14 s median (5 runs each). Where a thread-local is a load off a
register (Windows, Linux) it saves an instruction or two.

170be32ac21c17795a97d244d8fa559ed47e21f0.message:
ftrace: a span for each HLE import call

PS3_FTRACE recorded syscalls and timer sleeps but not HLE imports, so a
guest thread blocked or busy inside an import (a file read, a SPURS
wait, a lock taken hundreds of thousands of times) showed up nowhere.
ps3_hle_call's exit guard now closes a PS3_FT_HLE span (who = thread,
a = NID, b = guest lr) for calls at least PS3_FTRACE_MIN_US long. With
the trace off it costs one load per call.

This is what found God of War HD's 360 ms frame: 320,355 lwmutex
lock/unlock pairs in it (PS3_FTRACE_MIN_US=0), against 71 in a normal
frame.

180e324be8066b0566143dcfb403bdbbb1403a0b.message:
Draw engine: the guest pipeline list, and the caches rebuilt from it

A backend's caches hold what the decompilers made of a title's programs --
the D3D12 bytecode cache and its pipeline-state list -- so a change to a
decompiler leaves them stale, and only playing everything again refilled
them (the v0.17 merge left a release's cache matching 584 of 1,494
programs). The engine now also keeps what the title gave.

Every pipeline the engine translates is written once, by its key, as a line
of <dir>/guest_pipelines.txt: the two programs by hash (their bytes once each
in <dir>/guest_programs.bin), every input the decompilers take (shader
control, cube, volume, vertex-texture, shadow-compare, texel-addressed and
texel-op units), the vertex layout, the target format and count, the render
state field by field by name, and the hashes of the HLSL made of it then.
<dir> is PS3RECOMP_GUEST_DIR, else PS3RECOMP_DXBC_CACHE; PS3RECOMP_GUEST_LIST=0
records nothing.

RSX_GUEST_REBUILD=1 runs the list through the decompilers and the backend's
pipeline_create as they are now, on the build workers, when the engine
starts, and exits: the bytecode and the pipeline states are made again
without playing, and <dir>/guest_remap.txt lists each pipeline whose HLSL
changed (old and new hashes). RPCS3 keeps its shader cache the same way.

Drakengard 3, one level: 328 pipelines recorded (260 KB of lines, 575 KB of
programs); rebuilt into an empty cache in 11 s including the game's start,
328 built, the same 344 bytecode files byte for byte as play made, every
rebuilt pipeline state one that play had built.

1891b8fe718534bef9d143c7b665beb762adbc07.message:
gcm: count the drain's own ring recycle as the JUMP to begin

Once a title has been seen to overrun its ring, the drain recycles the
ring itself when current nears end. A title whose callback also
recycles (cellGcm_fifo_recycle) can be in that callback at the same
moment: it writes its JUMP and put, and only then marks itself waiting,
so a pass that read the mark clear still teleports get to begin. The
callback then waits for a backward JUMP that never comes, because get
is already at begin == put, and gives up after 2 s of no progress.

God of War HD stopped for 2-4 s this way at random points in about
half of the gameplay runs. Counting the teleport as the backward JUMP
ends the callback's wait at once.

1be9e80d533ae0ff253fa169f5d2f5f783a1364d.message:
rsx_shader_msl: compile a vertex program's position invariant

Titles draw the same geometry twice with two different vertex programs,
the second pass testing EQUAL against the depth the first one wrote. The
RSX runs the position arithmetic instruction by instruction, so both
programs land on the same depth. The Metal compiler optimises each
program on its own (it may fuse a multiply and an add into one FMA in one
of them and not in the other), the two depths can then differ in the last
bit, and the EQUAL pass leaves holes.

Resistance: Fall of Man's foliage writes depth through an alpha-tested
program, then colour through one that also lights it, with
SET_DEPTH_FUNC EQUAL.

The translator now marks a vertex program's position [[position,
invariant]], and the Metal backend compiles guest programs with
MTLCompileOptions.preserveInvariance (macOS 11 and later), so programs
that compute the position the same way get the same bits.
PS3RECOMP_MSL_INVARIANT=0 leaves the position as it was.

test_shader_msl checks the vertex program's MSL for
"[[position, invariant]]" (and for "[[position" under
PS3RECOMP_MSL_INVARIANT=0).

1c7c1d914374d59451f5b73421119af501606cfb.message:
rsx engine: a scissored CLEAR_SURFACE clears only the scissor

RSX clears what the surface clip and the scissor let through. The engine
cleared every colour and depth target whole, whatever the scissor said.

Resistance: Fall of Man's co-op split screen renders both views into one
2x1 antialiased 1280x720 scene target: the scissor on the left half, a
colour and depth clear and player 1's view, then the scissor on the right
half, a clear and player 2's view. The second clear wiped player 1's view,
and the left half of the screen was black under the HUD.

sink_clear now asks eng_clear_rect what the clear may write: the clip
from the origin, then the scissor (eng_scissor_rect, the draw path's
scissor code moved into a function). Only a scissor narrower than the
clip makes a clear partial; a clip smaller than the target alone stays a
whole clear, as before. A partial clear goes to two new optional backend
hooks, clear_color_rect and clear_depth_stencil_rect. A backend without
them, or PS3RECOMP_ENG_RECT_CLEAR=0, clears whole as before. A depth clear
that covers everything the zeta was ever bound with (ext_w/ext_h) stays
whole, and a partial depth clear keeps had_write.

The Metal backend records a rectangle clear as a clear record with the
rectangle in its scissor and encodes it as a pass of its own: the
attachment is loaded and a full-target triangle under that scissor writes
the colour, or the depth and stencil with the test always passing. Such a
record is never folded into a pass's load action.

New test_clear_rect in test_rsx_draw_engine (the co-op frame, whole and
empty scissors, a zeta only bound at a small clip, a backend without the
hooks), and test_metal_rect_clears.m (tools/test_metal_rect_clears.py) on
the GPU: a rectangle clear of the right half keeps the left half, for
colour, depth and stencil, and a whole clear after one covers the target.

1f23584802ab365a38eb51e5f103e786dda68cdf.message:
Metal: HDR (EDR) present and the highlight plane, as the D3D12 engine's

RSX_HDR=1 on a screen with EDR headroom puts the window's layer in EDR:
RGBA16Float, extended linear sRGB, wantsExtendedDynamicRangeContent. 1.0 is
the system's SDR white; the headroom (maximumExtendedDynamicRangeColorComponent
Value, which follows the brightness) is read on the main thread every half
second and after a settings change, and the layer is switched on the render
thread before it takes a drawable. Off -- or on a screen without headroom --
nothing changes.

The present into an EDR drawable is eng_present_hdr_fs, the MSL of
rsx_present_passes.h's ps_blit_area_hdr: each tap decoded to linear light (2.2
power, or the sRGB curve with RSX_HDR_GAMMA=srgb), the area average when
scaling down, scaled to the paper white, rolled off from max(white, peak/2) to
the peak. The video out's gamma and the sharpening (CAS, now a helper the SDR
present shares) go on each tap after the highlight test, which they would
fail. RSX_HDR_WHITE/RSX_HDR_PEAK are nits with 100 nits as 1.0 (what EDR 1.0
is in the display's reference modes); unset, the white is the system's and the
peak the headroom, which also caps a peak that is set.

The highlight plane: a pipeline whose HLSL names rsx_hdr_plane (the composite
override) gets a build with an RGBA16Float colour attachment 1. Metal binds
attachments per pass, and a pipeline without attachment 1 fails validation in
a pass that has it, so those draws get a pass of their own, the first since
the last present clearing the plane. The present reads it for the frame it
was drawn beside (the same surface and size): RSX_HDR_HIGHLIGHTS=0 turns it
off, RSX_HDR_DEBUG=1 shows it. A fragment function that writes color(1) with
no attachment 1 is accepted (API and GPU validation) and the output dropped, so
the override needs one build. PS3RECOMP_METAL_WINDOW_GRAB of an EDR window
writes the values to <prefix>.pfm and the share above white to the log.

Measured on an M1 Pro's XDR panel (headroom

21c14a650a346b18a4f79c82689ad5c060c34693.message:
rsx_d3d12: guest depth/stencil state and samplers in the guest-FP pipelines

Every guest-FP pipeline had a fixed LESS_EQUAL depth test with writes,
no stencil, and four static samplers (s0 point/clamp for the dbgfont
atlas, s1-s3 linear/wrap), whatever the title set. In God of War HD:

- Its stencil shadow volumes marked nothing, and the shadow pass, a
  full-screen reverse-subtract quad meant only for the marked pixels,
  darkened the whole frame (0.16 -> 0.012 on a lit pixel).
- Depth state ignored: rain and blood particles were rejected.
- Unit 0 was point-sampled and clamped. The soldiers wrap their texture
  atlas (v up to ~2), sampled the transparent bottom row and drew
  nothing over an untextured base; Kratos' tattoo and skirt came out
  white; textures shimmered.

Depth test/write/func and front/back stencil (func, ops, masks) are
packed per draw into a PSO key (rsx_zs_key); the stencil reference is
set per draw. The cull key now always carries the front face, which
two-sided stencil needs with culling off. Samplers are four descriptor
tables built from each unit's TEXTURE_ADDRESS/FILTER/CONTROL0/BORDER
(one cached descriptor per distinct state); units without guest state
keep the old two defaults.

23540a1007e37f28c404c3adfa8ea2d22e188194.message:
rsx_d3d12: cache converted vertices within a draw

Indexed lists (shared vertices), strips and fans (each vertex in up to
three triangles) and indexed quads expand one guest vertex into several
output vertices, and each one was fetched again: 16 attributes, each with
its own address resolve and conversion, for every reference. God of War
HD's gameplay frames expand ~370k vertices through these paths and the
fetch was a third of the frame.

A direct-mapped cache on the low index bits (8192 entries, 2 MB) keeps
the converted 256-byte vertex; a hit is a memcpy. It is dropped at every
draw, since attribute state and the guest arrays may change between
draws. Measured in GoW HD gameplay: vertex time per 20 frames 0.80 s ->
0.29 s, ~9.0 -> ~12.1 fps. VTX_CACHE_CHECK=1 refetches on every lookup
and counts differences: 0 in 312M lookups. VTX_NOCACHE=1 disables it.

26ca8af13554a947fac135b3303d58447a3c140e.message:
D3D12 engine: a pipeline-state list, built ahead at start-up

The bytecode cache saves the HLSL compile, but a pipeline state is the
driver's compile of that bytecode for one GPU -- milliseconds to tens of
them the first time a machine meets it -- and while the build runs the draw
that wanted it is skipped. The states themselves cannot be shipped; the list
of them can.

Every guest pipeline state the engine builds (the triangle, point and line
classes, the WPOS-undivided build, the snapshot-copy build, the multisampled
build) goes through eng_create_pso, which writes it once to
<PS3RECOMP_DXBC_CACHE>/pipelines.bin as a canonical record: the two programs
by their DXBC checksum and every value of the description, a sample count
above one recorded as one with a flag. At start-up, workers at the lowest
priority (two thirds of the cores, at most eight) build every state the list
names, in the order it was met, the multisampled form too when the player
has MSAA on, and a draw that first needs one gets it built. The programs come
from the bytecode cache's files, found by their checksum. A title ships the
list its own play-throughs recorded; a player's sessions add to it.

This is the approach of UnleashedRecomp's precompiled pipelines (recorded in
development, built behind the boot logos, the player's options masked out of
the record), DXVK's state cache and RPCS3's pipeline cache.

Drakengard 3, one level played twice from a complete bytecode cache: without
the list 319 states were built in play, 1,416 ms of driver compile, and 26
draws skipped in play; with it 337 states were built ahead in 0.1 s before
the title screen, the 313 asked for in play took 62 ms, and 5 draws were
skipped. With MSAA x4 the second session built 646 states ahead.

PS3RECOMP_PSO_LIST=0: no list. PS3RECOMP_PSO_PREWARM=0: recorded, not built
ahead. Neither runs with RSX_ASYNC_SHADERS=0 (the replays). A list from
another record layout is set aside as pipelines.bin.old.

27745b54d1b60e5232e48a1234a182fc6f52e113.message:
ppu_lifter: inline guest stores, the store side of the inline loads

Every lifted store called vm_write8/16/32/64 out of line. In God of War
HD gameplay those calls were about a fifth of the main thread.

The generated header now has vm_write*_inl beside vm_read*_inl. A store
is done in place when vm_inl_ok accepts the address, no store diagnostic
is armed (vm_inline_st_ok: PPU_WVAL, PPU_WWATCH, PT), the barrier watch
and the null-page sweep are idle, and no SPU holds a reservation on the
line (g_spu_coh_bits). Anything else goes to the out-of-line store as
before. PPU_NO_INLINE_STORES keeps the calls, and the runtime's own files
keep them through PPU_NO_INLINE_LOADS.

Re-lift to pick it up. God of War HD: the main thread runs about 14.8 ms
a frame instead of 16.2 with the HLE lookup cache, vm_write32 is gone
from its profile and vm_write64 is 1.2%. The executable grows from 57 to
87 MB.

279bd0049a1cf1abb66b1cb69e65fd4d8dd8006f.message:
rsx vertex fetch: frequency 1 under a modulo divider bit is one element per draw

NV4097_SET_FREQUENCY_DIVIDER_OPERATION's bit makes an attribute's element
vertex % frequency. At frequency 1 that is element 0 for every vertex; the
fetch read frequency 0 and 1 as an ordinary per-vertex array whatever the
bit. rsx_vertex_freq_plain() names the ordinary case (frequency 0, or 1 with
division); rsx_vertex_element_index, the compact fetch's shared span and the
legacy rsx_fetch_attrib use it.

29154bc66a6956228da34bcac3de4ea7fa4c2080.message:
ppu: test the SPU reserved-line bitmap inline on guest stores

Every guest store called spu_coh_is_reserved, and in God of War HD
gameplay that call was 9.5% of the main PPU thread's samples. Most of it
was not the call: spu_coh_reserve stored s_coh_armed = 1 and or-ed the
line's bit into the bitmap on every GETLLAR, the same values each time.
The SPURS kernel reserves the same few lines over and over, so those
cache lines kept moving to the SPU threads' cores, and each PPU store
missed on them.

- spu_coh_reserve writes the bit, and the published pointer, only when
  they change.
- spu_coh_bitmap.h publishes the bitmap as g_spu_coh_bits, NULL until
  the first reservation, and spu_coh_line_reserved tests it inline.
  VM_WRITE_COH in ppu_loader.cpp and ppu_memory.h, and
  vm_block_reserved, use it. s_coh_armed goes away.
- g_spu_coh_bits is one merged definition per program (selectany /
  weak), so the loader fixtures, which link ppu_loader.cpp without
  spu_coherency.c, still link and see no reserved lines.

2fa6555a304eb2f9323a3dc45eca0e57abd74b58.message:
HDR: the plane carries each pixel's HDR colour; 203-nit white, highlight hue, PQ roll-off

The highlight plane only said how many times brighter a pixel was, so bright
colours could only get brighter as the SDR picture had them (fire whitened)
and everything below the clip was the SDR picture at Windows' SDR white
(often 400-500 nits, leaving little room above it). On D3D12 and Vulkan the
plane is now R32G32 uint: the pixel's HDR colour as RGB9E5 beside the 8-bit
colour it wrote to the frame (rsx_draw_backend.hdr_plane_packed; the engine
puts RSX_HDR_PLANE_PACKED above the override's text). The HDR present
resolves each frame pixel against it before any scaling, mixes the plane's
hue with the frame pixel's colour at the HDR luminance (RSX_HDR_HUE, 0.5
unless set), and rolls the brightest channel off toward the peak on the PQ
curve above a third of the peak. The paper white is 203 nits unless set
(RSX_HDR_WHITE=windows: the system's SDR white). Metal keeps the RGBA16F
plane. RSX_HDR_DEBUG shows bands of brightness, purple where the HUD or
anything else was drawn over the plane's picture.

3099075391d4105873242cd4c3f3555ed43fe397.message:
ppu_lifter: --insn-patches lifts patched instructions as run-time switches

A patch that changes an instruction word in .text does nothing to a
lifted title, which never executes the guest's code words. Making it a
second lift means a second build of the whole title for one changed
word, and a port that wants it optional ships two.

--insn-patches FILE takes {"patches": [{addr, orig, new, guard}, ...]}.
Each patched instruction is lifted in both forms and emitted as

    if (guard) { <new> } else { <orig> }  /* insn patch 0x...: orig -> new */

guard being an int the port defines and sets before the guest runs; each
function that uses a guard declares it extern "C". The original's branch
label and the code around it are unchanged. The lift stops when the
input does not hold orig at addr (a patch set for one build of a title
never lands on another), when a patch is at an address no lifted
function covers, or when new is a branch, sc or CR op (it would need
labels and call targets the function was not lifted with). The patches
reach the parallel workers too; a mismatch there raises instead of
exiting, so the pool does not hang on a dead worker.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) caps its campaign's frame rate in
code. The port lifts the cap's instructions this way and turns 60 fps on
or off from its settings, with one build.

New tools/test_ppu_lifter_insn_patches.py: a patched branch and a
patched li lift in both forms behind their guards, with the guard
declarations and the branch label in place; a wrong orig stops the lift
serially and with two workers; a patch at an address no function covers
stops it. docs/TOOLS.md describes the file with a generic example.

31f490b531f5ad846c9ca7e7b6f952af67cef697.message:
Metal: a launch that loaded the pipeline archives and built nothing turns them off

A Drakengard 3 player on an M1 Pro with macOS 26.0 got a black screen with
the sound playing on every launch after the first. Their logs: every
pipeline the engine asked for stayed "compiling (draw skipped until it is)",
no build finished (no [pipe-slow] line either), and the warm-up never
reported. The first launch, with no archive yet, played; deleting the data
folder gave one more good launch. The builds hung in the archive's load or
lookup.

<archive dir>/launch is now written before the archives are loaded and
removed when the first pipeline is built (eng_pipeline_state, from the
archive or compiled). Found at the next launch, the archives are deleted
and <archive dir>/off records the macOS version: with it, pipelines are
compiled from the MSL cache as on a first launch, and the log says so. An
OS update removes off and tries the archives again. A player who meets the
hang sees one black launch, not every launch.

Checked on macOS 27.0.1 (no hang here): a normal launch leaves no marker
(190 of 190 pipelines from the archives); a marker left by hand gives
"archives dropped, and off on Version 27.0.1 (Build 26A434)" and the title
and menu render; the next launch keeps them off; an off file naming
another macOS is removed and the archives are used again.

3527ea5aba9ab659464a77669988ce67697de197.message:
Merge PR #456: cellFs repositions the stream on a read/write switch (@feanor-noldorin)

Four conflicts with #430 (@tekulvw), earlier in this wave, all the same
shape: #456 was written against master, where the fd handlers re-read
g_files[fd] directly, and #430 replaced that with one snapshot per handler
(fd_file()) behind g_fd_lock. Each resolution keeps #430's snapshot and
adds #456's direction tracking: g_fd_dir[i] = 0 on allocate and on close,
fs_set_dir() before the fread and the fwrite.

One fix beyond either PR, and it is the reason this one needed reading
rather than resolving mechanically. #456's fs_set_dir(int fd, uint8_t dir)
re-reads g_files[fd] to issue its FS_SEEK64 -- which is exactly the race
#430 exists to remove. A concurrent cellFsClose can null that slot between
the caller's fd_file() and the seek, and FS_SEEK64(nullptr, 0, SEEK_CUR)
is a crash, not an error return. Merged as written, #456 would have put
back the one window #430 closed, on the FIOS media threads that are the
reason #430 was written.

So fs_set_dir() takes the caller's FILE* snapshot: fs_set_dir(fd, f, dir).
The only remaining direct g_files[fd] accesses are the two inside
g_fd_lock in cellFsClose. #456's own fixture does not touch fs_set_dir, so
the signature change is contained to this file.

36b1ea43a0c35189b2d0a6445964f7c20846588b.message:
rsx_vertex_fetch: decode CMP (11-11-10) vertex attributes

rsx_fetch_attrib had no case for type 6, CELL_GCM_VERTEX_CMP, so a
compressed attribute fell to the float default and its packed word was
read as a float. The D3D12, Metal and null backends all fetch through it.

God of War HD stores its skinned meshes' normals this way (about 43% of
gameplay draws), and they were lit from garbage: Kratos and the enemies
rendered close to black. Decode it like rsx_vertex_compact.c and
rsx_live_draw.c already do: x and y signed 11 bits, z signed 10, divided
by 1023, 1023 and 511, w = 1.

3702040d6cbc4afd16f8bed77a619fb6d8875045.message:
Merge PR #441: GETLLAR without the lock-line lock for registered holders (@tekulvw)

spu_coh_wake_watches(line) to both notify paths; #441 adds

3b3fdfaa7b6ecaaee70d18b5948da69de5eefe59.message:
sys_timer: one host clock for mftb, system time and timers (mach_absolute_time on macOS)

On POSIX hosts the PPU timebase (every lifted mftb), the
sys_time_get_system_time HLE and the lv2 timers' expiration times each
called clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and scaled it themselves. On macOS
that call is not a plain counter read: it goes through
_mach_boottime_usec and gettimeofday every time, and the mftb site is
hot in game loops that poll the time.

Resistance: Fall of Man (BCUS98107) reads the timebase in a loop on its
main thread; in a profile of the campaign that mftb site was about 14%
of the main thread's time.

host_monotonic_ns() is now the one source: mach_absolute_time scaled by
mach_timebase_info on macOS (split so the multiply cannot overflow),
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) elsewhere. ppu_timebase_now,
sys_time_get_system_time and timer_now_us derive from it, so guest code
that mixes mftb, the system time and timer events reads one clock.
Windows is unchanged (QueryPerformanceCounter).

New tests/test_host_monotonic_clock.c (tools/test_host_monotonic_clock.py,
skipped on Windows): the clock is monotonic over a million reads, runs at
CLOCK_MONOTONIC's rate over a 200 ms sleep (to within 1 ms), and a
timebase or timer-clock reading falls between two host_monotonic_ns
readings. It prints the cost of a read: 11.6 ns against 18.7 ns for
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) on an M-series Mac.

3bf0233d06ff7d1d181a80754a0fbf7a16cfc253.message:
cellAudio: WASAPI keeps 60 ms queued, and the mixing thread runs ahead of the guest

On Windows the shared-mode stream asked for a 20 ms device buffer, and the
mixing thread ran at normal priority. A title that keeps every core busy
with PPU and SPU threads takes the CPU from the mixing thread often enough
for those 20 ms to run dry, and each time is an audible click or stutter.
Movie playback (Bink) was the worst case.

- The buffer is 60 ms by default; PS3_AUDIO_BUF_MS=<10..500> sets it.
- The mixing thread asks for THREAD_PRIORITY_TIME_CRITICAL and joins the
  MMCSS "Pro Audio" task when the service is there. avrt.dll is loaded at
  run time, so nothing new is linked.
- AUDIO_RATE=1 also reports underruns: passes that found the device queue
  under half a block (it is about to play silence). The first 64 blocks are
  not counted, while the stream fills.

The guest still sees 256-sample blocks at 48 kHz paced by the device clock;
only how far ahead of the device the mixer may run changes (up to the buffer
size, so up to ~40 ms more output latency by default).

Seen with inFAMOUS 2 on a Ryzen 5 5600 (6 cores, all of them busy): with
the 20 ms buffer its Bink cutscenes stuttered audibly; with this change
they play cleanly. Only the Windows (WASAPI) path is touched.

3d7b7cf783b9cc0d6fd1695da34ac060d9d7498f.message:
Vulkan: HDR output and highlights (RSX_HDR), as the D3D12 engine

RSX_HDR=1 on the Vulkan engine: where the display under the window has HDR
on, the swap chain is scRGB (R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT, EXTENDED_SRGB_LINEAR) or,
where the driver offers no scRGB, HDR10 (10-bit, HDR10_ST2084; the present
pass then writes the BT.2020 primaries through the PQ curve, hdr2.x). The
instance enables VK_EXT_swapchain_colorspace where the loader has it. The
present runs kPresentHdrHLSL at the window's size into a target in the swap
chain's format -- decoded, area-averaged, the paper white, the highlights
rolled off toward the peak -- in place of the area pass, then the same blit.
Its constants are 8 floats at b1 (256 bytes a frame slot); t1 is the plane.

The highlight plane: a pipeline whose text names rsx_hdr_plane gets a build
with an FP16 second attachment (eng_pso_plane), used for a pass into one
target without MSAA while HDR is on, in a rendering instance of its own;
the present reads the plane for the frame it was drawn beside.
RSX_HDR_WHITE, RSX_HDR_PEAK, RSX_HDR_GAMMA, RSX_HDR_HIGHLIGHTS and
RSX_HDR_DEBUG as on D3D12; the settings page's reload and a poll every 60th
pump make a new swap chain when HDR is switched or the display's changes.

rsx_hdr_display.c: the display query (DXGI's colour space and peak,
DisplayConfig's SDR white level) and its staleness check, moved out of the
D3D12 engine so both Windows engines ask the same; a stub elsewhere, where a
backend decides from what its surface offers. kPresentHdrHLSL's constants
gain hdr2 (D3D12 passes zeros there).

Live, RTX 4090 on an HDR display: Vulkan picks scRGB FP16 at Windows' 480
nits white and the display's 1499 nit peak, makes the plane, and the debug
view marks the sword trails brightened and the HUD drawn over, as on D3D12;
D3D12 HDR unchanged. Replays (headless, never HDR) byte-identical to 0.4.1's
on both engines: 111 of 111 frames each.

3e9311c6287b1220d57e99b3a2a7d3e45a1cf7db.message:
cellGcmSys: forget a park once the walker has left it

The walker gives a self-JUMP park GCM_PARK_GRACE_MS with the same put to
be patched, then resyncs to put. Its record of the park (address, put,
start time) was only cleared by that resync. A park the walker left any
other way -- the title patched it into a JUMP elsewhere, or wrote
commands over it -- kept its start time, so when the walker next stopped
at the same address with the same put, the new park was taken for the
old one. Its grace had run out long before, the resync fired at once,
and the commands the title was about to link in were dropped with the
fences and labels in them. A title that reuses its command blocks
meets its parks again at the same address, frame after frame.

Clear the record as soon as the walker reads anything other than that
park's own self-JUMP: a new park always starts a fresh grace. The three
variables move from the JUMP branch to file scope for that, under the
same names.

41bae9560bd0def7d49aa3675e89fa388e27f74e.message:
rsx_d3d12: stage guest textures in a shared upload ring; LRU slots

Each texture slot had its own committed upload buffer, created with the
texture whenever the slot took a new size or format. In God of War HD's
texture bursts, when new effects first appear, creating resources was
most of the cost: one report interval had 50 new textures, 67 ms of
CreateCommittedResource (41 ms of it for the upload buffers) against
18 ms of decoding.

- Uploads are staged in one persistently mapped upload buffer, 32 MB per
  frame in flight, reset where that frame index's command allocator is
  reset (its copies have finished by then). A texture that does not fit
  in what is left uses the slot's own upload buffer, created on demand.
- A new texture takes an empty slot, else the least recently used one.
  Taking the first slot not used this frame evicted textures the next
  frame needed again: up to 22 a report interval in those bursts.
- 192 slots instead of 96; the game used up to 66.
- A frame with no free slot returned slot -1 and indexed vp_tex with it;
  it now returns -1 to the caller (untextured), as the lookup failure
  path does.

God of War HD: the drain stalls of 67-75 ms in the bursts at 131 and
135-136 s are now under 40 ms. The rendering check passes.

Merge PR #421: opt-in per-thread MFC engine lookup cache (@tekulvw)

#243's fix is the SPU_PCSAMPLE hoist: the old guard only latched `started`
when the variable was actually set, so with SPU_PCSAMPLE unset every MFC
channel access paid a getenv -- a tenth of the samples in a Twisted Metal
profile. It sets `checked` either way. #421 adds the generation-checked
per-thread cache in front, which returns before the claim lock on a hit.

form. Taking it as written would have reverted #243 while keeping its test
-- and #243 ships test_spu_mfc_env_once.c precisely to catch that, so this
one would have failed loudly rather than silently. Resolved anyway as
#421's cache check first, then #243's once-only latch, then the lock.

Composition is fine in that order: the first call misses the cache, falls
through and starts the sampler thread, and later calls that hit the cache
return before a getenv they no longer need to reach.
